Our framework adopts an explicit mesh as an intermediate representation for cross-model verification and fusion, reconciling noisy outputs from vision-language and segmentation models into spatially consistent part structures. To estimate joint parameters without observed motion, we use a video diffusion model to synthesize articulation hypotheses and validate them through geometric consistency. Our approach achieves accurate part decomposition and physically plausible articulation, performing competitively with motion-observing reconstruction-based, generation-based, and modular pretrained-model baselines.

</details>


### [27] [EgoGVAE: Ego-body Mesh Reconstruction via Guided Variational Autoencoder](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27755)
*Jaehun Jung,Wonjun Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A one-shot head-to-full-body pose reconstruction method that aligns latent spaces between a VAE-based guidance network (full-body poses) and a head-to-motion network, enabling fast ego-body mesh reconstruction from head pose.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recovering a complete body mesh from head pose is important for AR/VR devices, but existing head-conditioned methods (e.g., diffusion) are costly/time-consuming; a fast, data-efficient alternative is needed.

Method: Train a guidance network as a variational autoencoder on full-body poses and enforce similarity between its latent distribution and that of the head-to-motion network. During inference, sample from the guided latent distribution and decode to a plausible full-body pose in a single step, bypassing diffusion. This leverages latent-space alignment to translate head pose into full-body motion.

Result: Experiments on benchmark datasets show that the proposed method improves ego-body mesh reconstruction accuracy while delivering substantial speedups—more than 50x faster than diffusion-based approaches due to one-step sampling.

Conclusion: Latent-space alignment between a VAE-guided full-body pose model and a head-to-motion network enables fast, natural, and accurate ego-body mesh reconstruction from head pose, suitable for real-time use in head-mounted devices.

Abstract: We address the problem of recovering the full-body mesh from only the head pose. This task has become essential for various applications based on head-mounted devices or smart glasses. The challenge of this task lies in estimating the pose information of unobserved body parts based solely on a single joint (i.e., head) trajectory. Several studies have begun to adopt head-conditioned generative models, however, such previous methods are costly and time-consuming due to the diffusion-based iterative process. As an alternative, we propose a simple yet novel method that leverages the latent space of the guidance network, which is designed as a variational autoencoder taking full-body poses as inputs. By enforcing latent distributions of this guidance network and our head-to-motion network to be similar, latent features sampled from the 'guided' distribution, i.e., distribution learned in our head-to-motion network, can be reliably decoded for natural representations of full-body poses even only with the head pose. One important advantage of the proposed method is that one-step sampling scheme achieves remarkably fast inference (more than 50 times faster) compared to diffusion-based approaches. Experimental results on benchmark datasets show that the proposed method efficiently improves the performance of ego-body mesh reconstruction.

</details>


### [28] [DS@GT ARC at ImageCLEFmedical 2026: Architectural Diversity for Concept Detection and Foundation-Model Scaling for Caption Prediction in Medical Image Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27763)
*Bowen Wang,Youwen Zhang,Ritesh Mehta*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Competitive two-task submission to ImageCLEFmedical Caption 2026: a top-tier concept-detection ensemble with Honest Threshold Tuning and a cost-efficient KNN baseline, plus diverse captioning approaches from fine-tuned large models to zero-shot prompts across varying costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Advance radiology image understanding by evaluating robust concept detection and caption generation on ROCOv2, while exploring regularization to prevent overfitting on rare CUIs and cost-effective baselines.

Method: Task 1: three-way late-fusion ensemble of ConvNeXt-V2, BiomedCLIP ViT-B/16, DenseNet-169 with Honest Threshold Tuning; training-free KNN over frozen BiomedCLIP embeddings. Task 2: fine-tuned Gemma-3 27B, fully fine-tuned BLIP with Vizwins merging, and zero-shot MedGemma-4B with PubMed-style prompt.

Result: Task 1 primary F1 0.5790; secondary F1 0.9657 (ensemble). KNN baseline primary F1 0.5780; secondary F1 0.9599. Task 2: Gemma-3 27B 0.3571 (rank 3 official), BLIP with Vizwins 0.3564, MedGemma-4B zero-shot 0.3186.

Conclusion: Ensembles with regularization can outperform or closely match strong baselines, while cost-efficient, training-free methods can nearly match fine-tuned ensembles for Task 1. Task 2 results show a broad cost-performance spectrum across model scales, underscoring trade-offs between performance and training costs; code is available for replication.

Abstract: We describe the DS@GT submissions to the ImageCLEFmedical Caption 2026 challenge, which continues a long-running benchmark on the ROCOv2 dataset with two tracks: Concept Detection (Task 1), assigning UMLS Concept Unique Identifiers (CUIs) to radiology images, and Caption Prediction (Task 2), generating natural-language captions. For Task 1, our primary submission was a three-way late-fusion ensemble of ConvNeXt-V2, BiomedCLIP ViT-B/16, and DenseNet-169 with a regularized ''Honest Threshold Tuning'' procedure designed to avoid validation overfitting on rare concepts; this submission ranked first on the official submission with a primary $F_1$ of $0.5790$ and a secondary $F_1$ of $0.9657$. In parallel, we submitted a training-free KNN retrieval pipeline over frozen BiomedCLIP embeddings, which reached a primary $F_1$ of $0.5780$ and a secondary $F_1$ of $0.9599$-essentially matching the fine-tuned ensemble on the primary track at a fraction of the cost. For Task 2, our submissions included a fine-tuned Gemma-3 27B model (overall $0.3571$, ranking third in the official submission), a fully fine-tuned BLIP pipeline with custom Vizwins merging ($0.3564$), and a zero-shot MedGemma-4B run with a PubMed-style prompt ($0.3186$), spanning a wide range of model scales and training costs. Code: https://github.com/dsgt-arc/imageclef-caption-2026.

</details>


### [29] [Private Face Recognition Training Dataset Publication via Identity-Decoupled and Geometry-Preserving Face Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27764)
*Shuhuan Chen,Xiangyu Zhu,Weisong Zhao,Siran Peng,Tianshuo Zhang,Haoyuan Zhang,Haichao Shi,Xiao-Yu Zhang,Zhen Lei*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Private Face Distillation decouples source identity from proxy identities while preserving geometry to enable private FR training data publication without compromising recognition performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Privacy risk in publishing private FR training data due to identity leakage; need to maintain recognition utility while reducing linkability to real individuals.

Method: Orthogonal Geometry Preservation to construct decoupled proxy identities preserving hyperspherical geometry; Relational Topology Alignment to maintain identity relations for FR learning.

Result: Outperforms publication baselines in multiple domain-shifted FR settings; On IJB-C surveillance, TAR@FAR=1e-3 improves by 3.94% while reducing source-identity linkability.

Conclusion: Decoupling source-identity semantics from recognition-useful proxy geometry improves privacy-utility trade-offs; supports publishing private FR training data with decoupled source IDs but preserved proxy identity structure.

Abstract: Publishing private face recognition~(FR) training datasets is privacy-sensitive because faces expose identity information. Private FR training dataset publication mitigates this risk by releasing protected proxies as substitutes for private training faces. However, training FR models with such data introduces an identity paradox: \emph{the identity cues that make released faces useful for recognition supervision are also the cues that make them linkable to real individuals.} A protected face should be decoupled from the original identity, yet still behave as a reliable identity sample for training. Removing these cues too aggressively may destroy the class structure needed for recognition learning, whereas preserving them too faithfully may increase source-identity linkability. We argue that this paradox stems from conflating source-aligned identity semantics with recognition-useful proxy identity geometry. The former should be suppressed to reduce linkage to private individuals, while the latter should be preserved for FR learning. Based on this insight, we propose \textbf{Private Face Distillation}, an identity-decoupling and geometry-preserving framework. It uses Orthogonal Geometry Preservation to construct decoupled proxy identities from private identity representations while maintaining hyperspherical geometry, and Relational Topology Alignment to preserve identity relations for recognition learning. Experiments across multiple domain-shifted FR scenarios show that Private Face Distillation achieves stronger utility than the evaluated publication baselines. On IJB-C surveillance, it improves $\mathrm{TAR}@\mathrm{FAR}{=}1\text{e-}{3}$ by 3.94\% over the baseline while reducing source-identity linkability. These results suggest that private FR training dataset publication should decouple source-identity correspondence while preserving proxy identity geometry.

</details>


### [30] [CXR-Retrieve: Compositional Text-to-Image Retrieval in Chest Radiography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27779)
*Tomer Erez,Moshe Kimhi,Chaim Baskin,Ehud Rivlin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes CXR-Retrieve benchmark for compositional chest X-ray text-to-image retrieval and a label-aware contrastive fine-tuning objective to handle conjunctions and negations, improving retrieval accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-language models often optimize for report-to-image matching, not clinical query satisfaction, especially for conjunctions and negations; a structured benchmark is needed to evaluate and guide retrieval under these constraints.

Method: Introduce CXR-Retrieve with 5,159 test images from MIMIC-CXR-JPG test split and 145 textual queries; develop a label-aware contrastive fine-tuning objective starting from CXR-CLIP to align image-text pairs with compatible pathology constraints and repel contradictions.

Result: Starting from CXR-CLIP, Precision@5 improved by 8.5 percentage points on two-pathology conjunctions and by 22.0 points on negation queries.

Conclusion: Retrieval performance for chest radiographs hinges on training objectives that capture not only mentioned findings but also their clinical assertion (present/absent) to meet complex query constraints.

Abstract: Large chest radiography archives are difficult to search because most studies are paired only with free-text reports rather than structured clinical annotations. Vision-language models offer a natural interface for text-to-image retrieval, but current biomedical models are primarily optimized for report-to-image matching rather than for satisfying short clinical search queries. This creates an objective mismatch: a model may retrieve images related to words in the query while failing to satisfy the full clinical constraint, especially for conjunctions and negations such as ``atelectasis and no pneumonia.''
  We introduce CXR-Retrieve, a structured benchmark for compositional chest X-ray text-to-image retrieval. The benchmark contains 5,159 test images from the official test-split of MIMIC-CXR-JPG and 145 textual queries spanning single and conjunction findings, both positive and negative. Relevance is defined by whether a retrieved image satisfies all asserted pathology constraints, rather than by whether it matches a paired report.
  We further propose a label-aware contrastive fine-tuning objective for clinical retrieval. Our method attracts image-text pairs with compatible asserted pathology constraints, including shared confirmed absences, while explicitly repelling contradictory pairs. Starting from the in-domain CXR-CLIP checkpoint, our method improves Precision@5 over CXR-CLIP by 8.5 percentage points on two-pathology conjunctions and by 22.0 percentage points on negation queries. These results show that reliable chest X-ray retrieval requires training objectives that model not only which findings are mentioned, but also how they are clinically asserted.

</details>


### [31] [Filling the Pareto-Optimal Front for Affordance Segmentation on Embedded Devices Using RGB-D Cameras](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28293)
*Edoardo Ragusa,Giovanni Paolo Canuti,Simone Lugani,Rodolfo Zunino,Paolo Gastaldo*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Two hardware-aware methods fuse depth with RGB for affordable, real-time RGB-D affordance segmentation on wearable robots: (1) a depth-aware NAS with a new search space for compact models; (2) a depth-RGB fine-tuning pipeline with a preprocessing layer. Demonstrated Pareto-optimal trade-offs between accuracy and hardware metrics on real devices (Jetson Nano + RealSense) with real-time performance under smartphone-like energy budgets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Extend RGB-based affordance segmentation to exploit depth sensing on resource-constrained wearables, addressing underexplored use of depth data and the need for hardware-efficient, real-time solutions.

Method: 1) Reformulated hardware-aware neural architecture search (HA-NAS) with a search space designed to integrate depth information into small networks. 2) A dedicated fine-tuning approach including a preprocessing layer to merge depth with RGB data, enabling compatibility with conventional architectures.

Result: On two real-world datasets, the methods frequently identify Pareto-optimal fronts, balancing generalization performance and hardware requirements. A prototype using Jetson Nano and RealSense demonstrates real-time capability within energy budgets compatible with standard smartphone batteries.

Conclusion: Depth integration with hardware-aware optimization yields practical, energy-efficient RGB-D affordance segmentation for wearables, with demonstrated real-time performance and hardware-friendly solutions.

Abstract: While depth sensors have the potential to complement RGB data for affordance segmentation in wearable robots, their usage seems to remain underexplored. The paper proposes two approaches: a reformulated version of hardware-aware neural architecture search, endowed with a newly designed search space to integrate depth (D) information into small-sized deep networks, and a dedicated fine-tuning approach, including a preprocessing layer to merge depth information with RGB data and make it compatible with conventional architectures. In both cases, those methods aim to generate solutions that benefit from modern (portable) hardware accelerators and overcome existing tiny-like approaches, which often fail to tackle critical scenarios due to the severe constraints set by the supporting hardware. Extensive experiments on a pair of real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method as compared with existing solutions. The approach presented in the paper generates, in most cases, solutions that identify the Pareto optimal front to balance generalization performance and hardware requirements. The paper also describes the supporting prototype, including a Jetson Nano board and a RealSense RGB-D camera. When considering the energy profile of the device, the overall system can attain real-time performances within an energy budget that is compatible with standard batteries, such as those used in smartphones.

</details>


### [32] [FDDWAN: A Frequency-Decoupled Diffusion Network for Watermarking Attack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27800)
*Chunpeng Wang,Yuxin Li,Xiaoyu Wang,Jidong Yang,Suo Gao,Qi Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A two-stage, wavelet-domain diffusion-based watermark removal framework (FDDWAN) that decouples frequency subbands and refines residuals, achieving a better trade-off between watermark removal and perceptual fidelity than prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing invisible watermark removal techniques struggle to suppress watermarks without degrading perceptual image quality, due to poor capture of watermark-bearing features; a frequency-aware, residual-diffusion approach could improve effectiveness while preserving content. 

Method: Proposes a coarse-to-fine pipeline: (1) WFPAM performs wavelet-based decomposition of watermarked images into low/high-frequency subbands and applies frequency-specific attacks; (2) FRDAM models residual distributions between preliminarily attacked outputs and watermark-free references and diffuses only the frequency-domain residuals to reduce watermark-related discrepancies without over-editing content.

Result: Empirical evaluation on CelebA and ImageNet across four watermarking schemes shows FDDWAN achieves a more favorable trade-off between watermark removal and perceptual quality than both conventional and learning-based attacks.

Conclusion: Frequency-decoupled diffusion in the wavelet domain enables selective, residual-focused refinement that targets watermark artifacts while preserving image content, offering improved robustness across schemes and datasets.

Abstract: Existing invisible watermark removal methods often struggle to accurately capture the watermark-bearing features, leading to an unfavorable trade-off between watermark suppression and perceptual fidelity. In this paper, we propose the Frequency-Decoupled Diffusion Watermark Attack Network (FDDWAN), a coarse-to-fine framework that performs watermark removal through wavelet-domain decomposition and residual diffusion refinement. In the initial stage, the Wavelet-based Frequency-domain Preliminary Attack Module (WFPAM) decomposes the watermarked image into low- and high-frequency subbands and applies frequency-specific attack strategies tailored to their respective contributions to watermark robustness and perceptual quality. In the next stage, the Frequency-domain Residual Diffusion Attack Module (FRDAM) separately models the residual distributions between the preliminarily attacked outputs and the corresponding watermark-free references during training. Rather than reconstructing the entire image, FRDAM selectively refines frequency-domain residuals, directing the diffusion process toward the remaining watermark related discrepancies while minimizing modifications to image content. Extensive experiments on CelebA and ImageNet across four representative watermarking schemes demonstrate that FDDWAN achieves a more favorable trade-off between watermark removal effectiveness and visual fidelity than conventional and learning-based attack methods.

</details>


### [33] [LoMeVQA: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Longitudinal Medical VQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27806)
*Zhilin Wu,Zhangkai Ni,Chengmei Yang,Longzhen Yang,Yihang Liu,Ying Wen,Lianghua He*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces LoMeVQA, a large longitudinal medical VQA benchmark (206K QA pairs) across five tasks; shows current MLLMs underperform on temporal reasoning; presents MedLong-8B as SOTA; dataset and analysis provided.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the underexplored area of longitudinal medical visual reasoning; enable reliable temporal analysis of disease progression and treatment response using MLLMs.

Method: Build automated pipeline: chronologically organize patient records; extract entities via a medical knowledge graph; model temporal evolution to guide LLMs; construct dataset; evaluate MLLMs; develop MedLong-8B.

Result: LoMeVQA reveals substantial limitations in temporal reasoning for both general-purpose and medical MLLMs; MedLong-8B achieves state-of-the-art across all tasks; detailed analyses of failure modes and improvement directions.

Conclusion: The benchmark exposes gaps in current models, enables future research, and provides data/resources at GitHub for advancing longitudinal medical visual reasoning.

Abstract: In clinical practice, patients often undergo multiple imaging examinations over successive visits, yielding longitudinal data. Modeling such temporal information is crucial for reliable assessment of disease progression and treatment response. However, despite the rapid advancement of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), longitudinal medical visual reasoning remains largely underexplored. To fill this gap, we propose LoMeVQA, a comprehensive benchmark consisting of 206K longitudinal visual question answering (VQA) pairs for temporal medical image analysis. LoMeVQA covers five tasks: progress classification, progress description, progress report generation, differential region grounding, and differential region description. To construct the dataset, we develop an automated pipeline that (1) organizes patient records chronologically, (2) extracts clinically meaningful entities via a medical knowledge graph, and (3) models their temporal evolution to guide large language models in generating high-quality longitudinal VQA pairs. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that both general-purpose and medical-domain MLLMs perform poorly on LoMeVQA, revealing substantial limitations in temporal reasoning. To address these limitations, we introduce MedLong-8B, which achieves state-of-the-art performance across all tasks. Beyond benchmarking, we conduct detailed analyses that uncover key failure modes and shed light on how to improve longitudinal medical visual reasoning. Our data is available at: https://github.com/pepperbubble/LoMeVQA

</details>


### [34] [SPFM-Net: Semantic-Prior-Guided Frequency-Constrained Mamba for Invisible Watermark Attack](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27811)
*Chunpeng Wang,Yanan Shi,Zhiqiu Xia,Jidong Yang,Suo Gao,Qi Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SPFM-Net crafts a semantic-prior-guided, frequency-constrained attack to suppress invisible watermarks by disrupting spatial coherence, reconstructing semantically consistent images, and aggregating watermark-related features across scales and long-range dependencies, optimized with spatial-, frequency-, and edge-domain objectives to preserve perceptual quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current watermark attacks rely on predefined signal-processing steps or localized restoration, failing to model global, long-range watermark signals and forcing a trade-off between removal effectiveness and visual fidelity.

Method: 1) High-ratio masking to disrupt spatial coherence of watermark signals. 2) Partially fine-tuned pretrained Masked Autoencoder (MAE) to reconstruct semantically consistent images while suppressing watermark information. 3) Multi-scale Residual Frequency Feature Interaction module to aggregate watermark-related residuals across receptive fields with adaptive suppression of watermark-irrelevant regions. 4) Lightweight Mamba-based Global State-space Feature Modeling (GSFM) unit to capture long-range dependencies and separate watermark features from content. 5) Multi-level objective combining spatial-, frequency-, and edge-domain constraints to balance watermark suppression with perceptual quality.

Result: Extensive experiments across spatial-domain, transform-domain, orthogonal moment-based, and deep learning-based watermarking schemes show SPFM-Net achieves a favorable trade-off between watermark attack effectiveness and perceptual fidelity.

Conclusion: SPFM-Net demonstrates that integrating semantic priors with frequency constraints and long-range dependency modeling enables effective invisible watermark attacks while preserving perceptual quality, outperforming baseline approaches across diverse watermarking schemes.

Abstract: Existing watermark attacks typically rely on predefined signal-processing operations or locally constrained restoration networks, making it difficult to capture the long-range dependencies of globally distributed watermark signals and resulting in an unfavorable trade-off between removal effectiveness and visual fidelity. In this paper, we propose SPFM-Net, a semantic-prior-guided and frequency-constrained Mamba framework for invisible watermark attack. SPFM-Net first employs high-ratio masking to disrupt the spatial coherence of invisible watermark signals, and then utilizes a partially fine-tuned pretrained Masked Autoencoder to reconstruct semantically consistent image from sparse observations while suppressing watermark-related information. A Multi-scale Residual Frequency Feature Interaction module subsequently aggregates watermark-related residual features across multiple receptive fields, while adaptively suppressing responses from watermark-irrelevant regions. To further capture the long-range dependencies of globally distributed watermark signals, a lightweight Mamba-based Global State-space Feature Modeling (GSFM) unit is introduced to separate watermark-related features from natural image content and suppress the remaining watermark traces. In addition, SPFM-Net is optimized using a multi-level objective that jointly imposes spatial-, frequency-, and edge-domain constraints, enabling effective watermark suppression while preserving perceptual quality. Extensive experiments on representative spatial-domain, transform-domain, orthogonal moment-based, and deep learning-based watermarking schemes demonstrate that SPFM-Net achieves a favorable trade-off between watermark attack effectiveness and perceptual fidelity.

</details>


### [35] [Hallucinations Leave a Grounding Signature:Verifier-Guided Decoding for Selective Object Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27823)
*Lei Yang,Xinze Liu,Dayan Wu,Ding Wang,Hengjie Zhu,Zihao Zhang,Tianzhu Hu,Hanqi Wu,Peng Fu,Zheng Lin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VGD uses an Intrinsic Grounding Signature to detect high-risk object mentions during generation, rolling back the KV cache to suppress hallucinated objects and regenerating, achieving strong object-hallucination reduction with minimal loss of grounded coverage.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Object hallucination in large vision-language models remains a challenge due to weak object-level grounding diagnostics and overreliance on language priors; a reliable, low-overhead diagnostic signal is needed to selectively intervene during generation.

Method: Introduce Intrinsic Grounding Signature (IGS) as a distributed signed attention pattern; propose Verifier-Guided Decoding (VGD) where a lightweight verifier flags high-risk object mentions, rolls back KV cache, suppresses the object and synonyms, and regenerates the continuation, intervening only on high-risk mentions.

Result: VGD achieves state-of-the-art reductions in object hallucination on CHAIR and AMBER-G datasets (e.g., AMBER-G CHAIR reduced by 43.6% at rec90) while preserving ~99.6% of grounded-object coverage and without shortening captions; also reduces CHAIR-MSCOCO CHAIRS by 37.0%/30.4%.

Conclusion: Selective, verifier-guided intervention based on the intrinsic grounding signal can substantially mitigate object hallucination in LVLMs while preserving grounding capabilities and caption length.

Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) often hallucinate objects that are absent from an image. Despite recent progress, existing mitigation methods still lack reliable object-level grounding diagnostics and therefore tend to apply coarse-grained interventions, which can impair visual understanding, shorten responses, and reduce coverage of genuinely grounded objects. The key challenge is thus to detect, during generation, whether each emerging object mention is supported by reliable visual evidence, so that hallucination can be mitigated selectively. Yet output confidence reflects next-token plausibility rather than visual support, allowing language priors to make absent objects appear certain. We show that the missing diagnostic evidence is encoded in an Intrinsic Grounding Signature (IGS), a distributed signed attention pattern that remains informative for such confident hallucinations. Based on IGS, we propose Verifier-Guided Decoding (VGD), a decoding framework in which a lightweight verifier examines each emerging object mention, rolls back the KV cache when the mention is identified as high risk, suppresses the object and its synonyms, and regenerates the affected continuation. Because VGD intervenes only on object mentions identified as high risk, it reduces object hallucination while preserving the model's original visual understanding and grounded object coverage. Experiments on CHAIR and AMBER-G show that VGD achieves state-of-the-art object hallucination reduction: at @rec90, it cuts AMBER-G CHAIR by 43.6\% while retaining 99.6\% of grounded-object coverage, and reduces CHAIR-MSCOCO CHAIR$_i$/CHAIR$_s$ by 37.0\%/30.4\% without shortening captions.

</details>


### [36] [Thinking Once Is Enough: Intermediate-Layer Evidence Routing for High-Resolution VQA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27830)
*Zhongkuan Mao,Xianjie Liu,Tianyu Meng,Yidong Wang,Wenzhuo Zhao,Ronghao Xian,Yao Jiang,Fei Shen,Junfeng Fang,Yong Dai,Yi Zhang,Keren Fu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Thinking-Once is a training-free, single-pass evidence-routing method for high-resolution VQA that reuses already-encoded evidence from intermediate layers by reconstructing question-conditioned attention at a routing window and routing it to later layers, avoiding extra visual encoding while improving accuracy and reducing memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In HR-VQA, crucial fine-grained evidence can survive initial visual encoding but be diluted before answer generation. The common fix—re-encoding or cropping—adds computation. The paper argues that evidence already present in intermediate representations can be effectively exploited by routing it to later layers.

Method: Train-free approach that performs a single visual pass. It reconstructs a question-conditioned attention map at an intermediate routing window to preserve core entity tokens and compact background context, and routes this evidence forward to later layers without additional visual encoding. The method is evaluated across five base models, on multiple HR-VQA benchmarks, with ablations and comparisons to open-source baselines. Code is provided in the appendix.

Result: Across five base models, Thinking-Once improves or matches the base settings, with gains of +3.1, +3.0, and +2.7 on V*-Bench, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K respectively, and reduces average peak memory by ~4 GB. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, gains of +9.9, +4.6, and +5.5 points raise cross-benchmark mean from 72.5 to 79.1. With ZwZ-8B, mean reaches 82.7. Among 11 open-source HR-VQA baselines, it achieves best or tied-best on all three benchmarks and the best overall mean; notably, it reduces V*-Bench inference time by 97.2% versus DeepScan. Code is available in the appendix.

Conclusion: HR-VQA can be substantially improved by routing already encoded evidence rather than repeatedly acquiring fresh visual inputs, enabling higher accuracy and lower memory usage across diverse models and benchmarks.

Abstract: High-resolution visual question answering (HR-VQA) is often treated as a problem of insufficient evidence acquisition, where failing multimodal large language models must inspect images again through cropping, re-encoding, or multi-round search. We show that this view is incomplete: in many cases, fine-grained evidence has already survived visual encoding and become identifiable and influential within an intermediate-layer routing window, but is later diluted before answer generation. We propose Thinking-Once, a \textbf{training-free, single-visual-pass} evidence-routing method that reconstructs question-conditioned attention at this window, preserves core entity tokens and compact background context, and routes this evidence to later layers without extra visual encoding. Across five base models, Thinking-Once consistently improves or matches the corresponding base setting, increasing the average scores on V$^*$Bench, HRBench-4K, and HRBench-8K by \textit{+3.1}, \textit{+3.0}, and \textit{+2.7} points while reducing the average peak memory by about 4,GB. On Qwen2.5-VL-7B, it improves the three benchmarks by \textit{+9.9}, \textit{+4.6}, and \textit{+5.5} points, raising the cross-benchmark mean from 72.5 to 79.1. With the ZwZ-8B base model, Thinking-Once reaches a mean score of 82.7. Against 11 open-source HR-VQA baselines, it obtains the best or tied-best score on all three benchmark averages and the best overall mean; for example, compared with DeepScan, it reduces V$^*$Bench inference time by \textbf{97.2\%} while improving the cross-benchmark mean from 77.8 to 79.1. These results show that HR-VQA can be improved by routing already encoded evidence rather than repeatedly acquiring new visual inputs. Code is available in the appendix.

</details>


### [37] [SAFViT: Spatial Attention Fusion Gating for Vision Transformer-Based Nucleus Segmentation and Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27835)
*Harshit Mittal,Arash Rabbani*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Spatial Attention Fusion (SAF) gating replaces standard skip connections in a CellViT-based encoder-decoder for histopathology segmentation, creating per-pixel trust maps to fuse encoder and decoder features, improving minority class (Dead) detection and overall mPQ on PanNuke/MoNuSeg.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard skip connections treat all spatial locations equally, leading to redundant/conflicting information and underutilization of global context. Gating often filters encoder features but ignores decoder context; SAF aims to leverage both to boost minority-class segmentation and panoptic quality.

Method: CONCAT encoder skip with upsampled decoder features, pass through two pointwise convolutions with ReLU, apply channel-wise softmax to produce a per-pixel distribution (heatmap of trust) summing to 1 at each spatial location, then fuse features using these weights. Compared against six gating schemes (no gating, attention gates, squeeze-and-excitation, CBAM, cross-attention, attentional feature fusion) on PanNuke and MoNuSeg datasets.

Result: SAF gating yields the highest multi-class panoptic quality (mPQ) of 0.471 on the evaluated dataset(s). It achieves a substantial 14.5-point increase in Dead-class F1 score versus the ungated CellViT baseline, driven by better minority-class detection.

Conclusion: SAF gating effectively leverages both encoder and decoder context through a learnable per-pixel trust distribution, improving minority-class segmentation and overall panoptic performance, outperforming other gating schemes across studied datasets.

Abstract: Accurate cell segmentation and classification are foundational to digital pathology, enabling quantitative tissue analysis for diagnosis and treatment planning. Encoder-decoder architectures that fuse multi-scale features through skip connections have become the dominant paradigm for this task, yet standard direct skip connections treat every spatial location equally, which leads to redundant and potentially conflicting information reaching the decoder. To overcome this problem, various gating mechanisms have been introduced, but most of them operate solely on filtering encoder information, neglecting the benefit of global contextual information from the decoder. This study proposes replacing conventional skip connections in a CellViT-based model with a novel Spatial Attention Fusion (SAF) Gating module. Each SAF gate concatenates the encoder skip and upsampled decoder features, compresses them through two pointwise convolutions with an intermediate ReLU, and applies a channel-wise softmax to produce a per-pixel "heatmap of trust" that sums to unity at every spatial location, allowing the network to learn where each source is most trustworthy. The resulting fused features improve the model's ability to detect the minority "Dead" class, which in turn enhances the multi-class panoptic quality (mPQ) on the PanNuke dataset. SAF Gating is compared against six gating alternatives including no gating, attention gates, squeeze-and-excitation, CBAM, cross-attention, and attentional feature fusion on PanNuke and MoNuSeg datasets. SAF Gating achieves the highest mPQ (0.471), a gain driven primarily by a 14.5-point improvement in Dead-class F1 score compared to ungated CellViT baseline.

</details>


### [38] [FeatFix: Reuse What You Verify through Local Exact-Feature Correction for Faster Cached Diffusion Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27842)
*Hanshuai Cui,Zhiqing Tang,Zhi Yao,Qianli Ma,Fanshuai Meng,Weijia Jia*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FeatFix proposes local exact-feature correction at a fixed sparse set of layer-timestep sites to reuse exact features for correcting cached diffusion inference, reducing drift and achieving up to 6.70x speedup with competitive quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the high computational cost of diffusion model inference by reusing cached intermediate features or forecasting future ones, while preventing draft drift. Existing verification features are discarded after checking; this work repurposes them for correction to improve accuracy and speed.

Method: Select a fixed sparse set of layer--timestep sites. At each site, compute the exact block output from the current incoming state and replace the draft block output with this exact value, avoiding token- or channel-level partial replacement and full-timestep recomputation. This corrects the draft residual and reduces downstream feature error without recomputing entire timesteps.

Result: Empirical evaluation across four image and video backbones shows consistent acceleration, achieving up to 6.70× speedup over Vanilla diffusion inference while maintaining competitive output quality.

Conclusion: Local exact-feature correction via FeatFix effectively mitigates draft drift and residual errors at selected sites, enabling faster diffusion inference with preserved output quality.

Abstract: Diffusion models are widely used to generate high-quality images and videos, but their iterative denoising process remains computationally intensive. A growing class of training-free accelerators reduces this cost by reusing cached intermediate features or forecasting future ones. To control draft drift, these methods sometimes compute an exact block feature for verification. Yet the resulting exact feature is typically used only to measure discrepancy or guide a later decision and is then discarded. We find that this previously computed feature can instead be reused for correction. Forwarding it at the verification site resets the local draft residual and reduces downstream feature error. Based on this observation, we introduce FeatFix, a local exact-feature correction method for cached diffusion inference. FeatFix operates at a fixed sparse set of layer--timestep sites. At each selected site, it replaces the complete draft block output with the exact output computed from the same incoming state, avoiding token- or channel-level partial replacement and full-timestep recomputation. Experiments across four image and video backbones show that FeatFix consistently accelerates generation, achieving a speedup of up to $6.70\times$ over Vanilla while maintaining competitive output quality.

</details>


### [39] [VCP-DCN: Beyond Visual Concealed Property via Depth Collaborative Network for Camouflaged Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27843)
*Songsong Duan,Xi Yang,Nannan Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes VCP-DCN, a depth-collaborative network for camouflaged object detection that uses multi-modality alignment, interaction, and fusion to exploit depth-specific information via SPE, MDA, and DAI, achieving strong results on three datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RGB-D COD methods often treat depth as a generic auxiliary cue, ignoring depth-specific characteristics of concealed objects; there is a need to mine distinguishable multi-modality features beyond a visual prototype in the depth domain.

Method: A three-stage framework: (1) alignment with Separable Prototype Embedding (SPE) to learn modality-consistency and modality-specific RGB/depth prototype tokens via prototype contrastive learning; (2) interaction with Multi-modality Dual Attention (MDA) to refine cross-modal representations using local response maps between prototype tokens and visual tokens; (3) fusion with Depth Adaptive Injection (DAI) to adaptively weigh RGB/depth contributions by measuring similarity between modality-specific prototypes and modality-consistent prototypes.

Result: Extensive experiments on three authoritative COD datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of VCP-DCN.

Conclusion: The proposed depth-collaborative framework effectively leverages depth information to enhance camouflaged object detection through prototype-based alignment, cross-modal attention, and adaptive fusion, with strong empirical validation.

Abstract: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to identify and segment camouflaged objects in complex environments, which are often concealed because their color and texture are similar to the background. Several existing COD methods introduce depth maps to boost detection performance via learning complementary RGB-D features, ignoring modality-specific characteristics of concealed objects in the depth domain. To address this issue, we propose a depth collaborative network, called VCP-DCN, to mine distinguishable multi-modality features beyond visual concealed prototype in depth domain. Specifically, VCP-DCN progressively performs multi-modality alignment, interaction, and fusion for the COD task. In the \textbf{alignment} stage, we propose a Separable Prototype Embedding (SPE) module to learn modality-consistency and modality-specific RGB/depth prototype tokens through prototype contrastive learning. Furthermore, we develop a Multi-modality Dual Attention (MDA) module to enhance the cross-modal feature representation through local response maps between modality-consistency RGB/depth prototype tokens and visual tokens on the \textbf{interaction} stage. Finally, we design a Depth Adaptive Injection (DAI) module to adaptively measure contribution of RGB/depth features with a decision-making mechanism, which calculates similarity distance between RGB/depth modality-specific prototype tokens and modality-consistency ones on the \textbf{fusion} stage. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our VCP-DCN on three authoritative datasets.

</details>


### [40] [Benchmarking Foundation and Large Language Models for Few-Shot Medical Image Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27856)
*Jinghong Liu,Yuchuan Deng,Fanping Liu,Meng Huang,Xirong Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Introduces FAME, a unified benchmark for few-shot medical image segmentation (FS-MIS) spanning specialists, SAM-based, CLIP-based, and MLLM-based methods; evaluates zero-shot and ten-shot with target-absence recognition and covariate/semantic shifts across 14,958 samples, 7 anatomical sites, 9 modalities, and 14 ROI categories; yields insights on support usage, scaling, and semantic transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fragmented evaluation of FS-MIS methods makes it hard to compare approaches and gauge generalization. A standardized, comprehensive benchmark is needed to assess effectiveness across modalities, sites, and ROI categories under realistic settings.

Method: Define FAME benchmark with standardized protocols and datasets: 14,958 test samples across 7 anatomical sites, 9 imaging modalities, and 14 ROI categories. Evaluate zero-shot and ten-shot performance, include target-absence recognition and generalization tests under covariate and semantic shifts. Compare candidates from diverse paradigms (specialists, SAM-based, CLIP-based, MLLM-based) and analyze how support examples are utilized.

Result: Empirical findings show that direct visual adaptation generally outperforms prompt-based strategies in leveraging support, increasing support helps only when models can effectively use it, semantic transfer remains far more challenging than imaging-domain adaptation, and strong localization does not guarantee reliable target-absence recognition.

Conclusion: FAME provides a comprehensive, standardized framework to evaluate FS-MIS solutions, promoting development of more effective and reliable few-shot medical segmentation methods and highlighting areas—especially semantic transfer and target-absence recognition—that require further attention.

Abstract: Few-shot medical image segmentation (FS-MIS) aims to segment novel regions of interest (ROIs) from a few annotated support examples. Despite rapid progress, existing FS-MIS solutions span diverse paradigms but are evaluated under inconsistent settings, leaving their relative effectiveness unclear. We introduce FAME, a unified benchmark for evaluating FS-MIS solutions, covering specialists, SAM-based methods, CLIP-based methods, and MLLM-based methods. FAME contains 14,958 test samples across 7 anatomical sites, 9 imaging modalities, and 14 ROI categories, and evaluates models under zero-shot and ten-shot settings with additional assessment of target-absence recognition and generalization under covariate and semantic shifts. Our evaluation reveals several findings. First, effective few-shot segmentation depends on how models exploit support examples: direct visual adaptation generally outperforms prompt-based strategies. Second, increasing support examples improves performance only when models can effectively utilize them. Third, semantic transfer remains substantially more challenging than imaging-domain adaptation, and strong localization ability does not necessarily imply reliable target-absence recognition. We hope FAME provides a comprehensive understanding of current FS-MIS solutions and facilitates the development of more effective and reliable few-shot medical segmentation methods.

</details>


### [41] [EEG-EditBench: Probing Visual Information in EEG-Image Retrieval Models with Controlled Image Edits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27857)
*Kaifan Zhang,Lihuo He,Yuqi Ji,Junjie Ke,Lukun Wu,Tianhao You,Xinbo Gao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EEG-EditBench reveals that high EEG-to-image retrieval accuracy masks sensitivity to fine-grained visual edits, showing attribute-level changes are especially challenging.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To diagnose what visual information EEG-based image decoders preserve beyond aggregate retrieval, by introducing a controlled diagnostic benchmark.

Method: Construct EEG-EditBench from 200 Things EEG2 images, generating 2,137 controlled edits across object identity, attributes, background, and presence; evaluate eight EEG-based decoding models.

Result: Standard retrieval performance fails to predict edit-based robustness; fine-grained attribute edits pose the greatest challenge; reveals hidden model behavior; dataset/code are publicly available.

Conclusion: EEG-EditBench provides a controlled framework to study preserved visual information in EEG-to-image models and can guide evaluation and model design.

Abstract: Recent EEG-to-image retrieval models have achieved strong performance in identifying viewed images from semantically diverse candidates. Yet such success does not reveal what visual information supports the match. A model may readily identify a cheetah among tools, plants, and vehicles, but can it still distinguish the viewed cheetah from the same scene with the cheetah replaced by a dog? Motivated by this question, we introduce EEG-EditBench, a diagnostic benchmark that examines this question through controlled edits of object identity, attributes, background, and object presence. Built from the 200 THINGS-EEG2 test images, EEG-EditBench contains 2,137 quality-controlled edits and evaluates eight representative EEG visual decoding models. Our results show that strong standard retrieval does not consistently transfer to edit-based evaluation, with fine-grained attribute changes presenting the greatest challenge. EEG-EditBench reveals model behavior hidden by aggregate retrieval accuracy and provides a controlled basis for studying what visual information EEG-image models preserve. The code and complete dataset are publicly available.

</details>


### [42] [Learning to Understand Body Language from Flight through Robust 3D Avatar Placing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27865)
*Dragos Costea,Alina Marcu,Cristina Lazar,Marius Leordeanu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Drones2BodyLanguage: a 4K UAV dataset with avatars performing ten intents in real drone scenes, plus a lightweight 3D grounding pipeline using monocular depth anchors and affine weights; yields strong cross-model improvements in long-range intent recognition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address data scarcity for recognizing long-range human motion and intent in aerial robotics; provide realistic, metrically accurate ground-truth 3D placement in unmodified drone footage.

Method: Create Drones2BodyLanguage by embedding avatars into real 4K drone footage with consistent scale/pose; build a geometric world model using anchors lifted to 3D via streaming monocular depth; predict placement via affine anchor combinations with rigid-invariant weights; re-render with SVD-based ground rotation; evaluate twelve architectures on disjoint scene/motion splits.

Result: Training on the placed data improves mean intent accuracy across real, retargeted, and generated motion; gains validated in two in-the-wild scenes.

Conclusion: The proposed data-generation and grounding approach enables effective long-range human intent perception for aerial robots, improving generalization and reducing data demands.

Abstract: Perceiving human motion and intent at long range is a prerequisite for socially intelligent aerial robots, yet the data to learn it barely exists. We introduce Drones2BodyLanguage, a dataset grounding human motion in real UAV footage: avatars manifesting ten communicative intents are placed into unmodified 4K drone scenes with metrically correct position, scale and orientation, maintained over hundreds of frames of camera motion. Enabling it is a lightweight geometric world model of the local scene - semantically selected anchors lifted to 3D through streaming monocular depth - in which a placement point is predicted as an affine anchor combination with provably rigid-invariant weights, and re-rendered under an SVD-fitted ground rotation. Across twelve architectures on scene- and motion-disjoint splits, training on placed data lifts mean intent accuracy by a wide margin for real, retargeted and generated motion alike, with gains confirmed on two in-the-wild scenes.

</details>


### [43] [DECODE: Tackling Representation and Decision Degradation in Continual AI-Generated Image Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27882)
*Zihao Cai,Xinghan Li,Ruiyan Yang,Xue Song,Haijun Shan,Jingjing Chen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DECODE is a decoupled continual detection framework that mitigates both representation- and decision-level forgetting in AI-generated image detectors across evolving domains, using Subspace Diversity Regularization (SDR) and Closed-Form Decision Alignment (CDA).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Continual adaptation of AI-generated image detectors to new generative domains suffers from catastrophic forgetting. Prior work stabilizes feature representations but ignores drift in the decision boundary, leading to a compounded failure (Dual Degradation).

Method: Introduce DECODE, a decoupled continual detection framework that jointly addresses representation- and decision-level forgetting. Subspace Diversity Regularization (SDR) preserves diverse forensic representations. Closed-Form Decision Alignment (CDA) recalibrates the shared classification head after adapter merges without manual hyperparameter tuning.

Result: Extensive experiments across 19 generative domains show average accuracy of 99.36% with only 0.39% forgetting. The approach generalizes to 11 unseen generators with 95.36% accuracy.

Conclusion: DECODE effectively mitigates both representation- and decision-level forgetting, delivering robust continual forensic detection across diverse and unseen generative domains.

Abstract: As generative models continue to evolve, AI-generated image detectors must incrementally adapt to emerging generative domains while preserving knowledge acquired from previous ones. This continual learning setting is particularly challenging because forensic traces are often subtle and generator-specific, making detectors highly vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. Existing methods primarily address this problem by stabilizing feature representations, implicitly treating forgetting as a representation-level issue. In this paper, we show that this perspective is incomplete. We demonstrate that even when feature representations remain discriminative, the decision boundary can progressively drift as the classification head is continually optimized on new domains. These two effects jointly give rise to a compound failure mode, termed Dual Degradation. To overcome this challenge, we propose DECODE, a decoupled continual detection framework that jointly mitigates representation- and decision-level forgetting. Specifically, we introduce Subspace Diversity Regularization (SDR) to preserve diverse forensic representations and Closed-Form Decision Alignment (CDA) to recalibrate the shared classification head after each adapter merge without manual hyperparameter tuning. Extensive experiments on 19 generative domains show that DECODE achieves an average accuracy of 99.36% with only 0.39% forgetting, while further generalizing to 11 unseen generators with 95.36% accuracy.

</details>


### [44] [Unifying Adversarially Robust Model Experts in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27897)
*Nguyen Duc Thai,Junhao Dong,Sua Qi Rong,Hua Yu,Yew-Soon Ong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CARE is a collaborative adversarial robustness framework that maintains multiple fine-tuned expert models during training, aligns their embedding spaces to exchange protective knowledge, and merges them into a single unified robust model that inherits complementary robustness properties.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Individual adversarially fine-tuned models often specialize to specific evaluation settings, limiting overall robustness; collaborative strategies can aggregate complementary strengths to improve defense against attacks.

Method: During training, CARE maintains multiple expert models corresponding to different adversarial fine-tuning strategies, performs embedding-space harmonization to enable knowledge exchange among experts, and consolidates their knowledge into one unified robust model.

Result: Empirical evaluation on classic image classification and downstream vision-language tasks shows CARE outperforms each individual expert, validating that collaborative learning among model experts yields improved adversarial robustness.

Conclusion: Collaborative learning across model experts is a promising direction for robust VLM defense, with CARE effectively transferring complementary robustness properties into a single model and generalizing across strategies and tasks.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, are vulnerable to adversarial attacks, posing a serious problem for real-life applications and deployment. Adversarial fine-tuning emerges as a prominent defense method; however, different fine-tuning strategies often produce specialized models with distinct robustness characteristics. Each fine-tuned model in turn thrives in some evaluation settings but falters on others, limiting their defensive capabilities. We refer to these specialized fine-tuned models as robust model experts and propose a collaborative adversarial fine-tuning framework: CARE - Collaborative Adversarial Robustness fine-tuning using Embedding alignment. CARE maintains multiple experts during training, enables knowledge exchange through embedding-space harmonization, and consolidates the learned knowledge into a single unified robust model. Experts benefit from one another while preserving their individual specializations, enabling the final model to inherit complementary robustness properties. In this paper, we demonstrate CARE on two different adversarial fine-tuning strategies with complementary robustness behaviors. Extensive experiments on classic image classification and downstream vision-language tasks display the effectiveness of our approach, with CARE being able to outperform individually learned model experts. The results suggest that collaborative learning across model experts is a promising direction for improving adversarial robustness.

</details>


### [45] [CoRE-UIR: Prior-guided common and residual experts for efficient all-in-one remote sensing image restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27898)
*Zaiyan Zhang,Qiangqiang Yuan,Jie Li,Ziyang Lihe,Yu Wan,Yuzeng Chen,Xin Su,Liangpei Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CoRE-UIR introduces a universal image restoration framework for UAV/satellite imagery, using common-and-residual experts (CoRE) to separate degradation-invariant from degradation-specific restoration. It uses Degradation Prior Embedding (DPE) with frozen CLIP features and Global Feature Modulation (GFM). A new large-scale MDVD-108K dataset is created. Empirically, it achieves ~1.05 dB PSNR gain, 11.83x speedup, and 85.3% less peak memory over the strong baseline BaryIR, with good generalization and downstream-task transfer; code/dataset to be released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Remote sensing imagery suffers from co-occurring degradations due to weather, lighting, and artifacts, causing global distribution shifts and local corruption. All-in-One restoration methods struggle due to weak degradation cues and redundant parameters from full-rank multi-experts. A principled, efficient architecture is needed to adaptively specialize restoration features while remaining compact.

Method: Decompose restoration into a Common Dense Expert for degradation-invariant restoration and a set of low-rank Residual Experts for degradation-specific compensation (CoRE). Introduce Degradation Prior Embedding (DPE) to inject explicit degradation priors by adapting frozen CLIP features into restoration. Apply Global Feature Modulation (GFM) to align global feature statistics before local residual processing. Build MDVD-108K (Multi-Degradation VisDrone), a UAV restoration dataset with single and compound degradations plus a real-world test set.

Result: Extensive experiments on multiple datasets show CoRE-UIR improves average PSNR by 1.05 dB, runs 11.83× faster, and reduces peak memory by 85.3% compared to BaryIR. The method generalizes to unseen degradations and supports downstream tasks.

Conclusion: CoRE-UIR delivers a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off for universal image restoration in remote sensing, supported by a scalable dataset and strong generalization. The authors will release code and MDVD-108K dataset.

Abstract: Remote sensing images acquired by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and satellites are often degraded by adverse weather, illumination variation, and imaging artifacts, which may co-occur and jointly induce global distribution shifts and local structural corruption. Although All-in-One image restoration offers an appealing unified alternative to task-specific pipelines, existing methods still suffer from weak or implicit degradation cues and parameter redundancy caused by full-rank multi-expert designs with overlapping restoration behaviors. We propose CoRE-UIR (Common and Residual Experts for Universal Image Restoration), a prior-guided global-local framework centered on the Common-and-Residual Expert Block (CoRE). CoRE explicitly decomposes restoration capacity into a common dense expert for degradation-invariant restoration and low-rank residual experts for degradation-specific compensation, enabling adaptive specialization without redundant expert replication. Built on this design, Degradation Prior Embedding (DPE) adapts frozen CLIP features into an explicit restoration-oriented prior, while Global Feature Modulation (GFM) aligns global feature statistics before local residual compensation. We also construct MDVD-108K (Multi-Degradation VisDrone), a large-scale UAV restoration dataset covering both single and compound degradations, together with a real-world test set. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets show that CoRE-UIR improves the overall average PSNR by 1.05 dB while running 11.83$\times$ faster and reducing peak memory by 85.3% relative to the strongest baseline, BaryIR, thereby maintaining a favorable quality-efficiency trade-off. Evaluations on downstream tasks and unseen degradation also validate the generalizability of CoRE-UIR. The code and dataset will be released at https://github.com/zzaiyan/CoRE-UIR.

</details>


### [46] [One Patch Is Enough: Reinforcement-Optimized Visual Token Grounding for MLLM-Based Scene Text Spotting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27902)
*Rui Tang,Wentao Yang,Peirong Zhang,Yongxin Shi,Shun Zhang,Huiguo He,Lianwen Jin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Single-Patch Text Spotting (SPaTS) uses a single anchor visual token to locate text, with SPaSO RL to select anchors and DEA/PED for robust features and decoding, achieving strong gains over MLLMs and OCR MLLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address misalignment and localization ambiguity in scene text spotting with dense/small text; reduce noise from multi-patch grounding in MLLMs.

Method: SPaTS routes each text instance through one anchor token; SPaSO RL selects anchor; DEA decouples magnitude and direction in embeddings; PED fuses anchor with language semantics and cross-attends on full-image to regress geometry.

Result: Extensive experiments show SPaTS significantly outperforms frontier closed-source MLLMs and OCR MLLMs; code to be released.

Conclusion: SPaTS provides a robust, geometry-aware text spotting framework reducing anchor noise and improving alignment in multimodal text understanding; the proposed components contribute to better robustness and precision.

Abstract: Scene text spotting requires high-precision alignment between textual recognition and spatial localization. While visual-token grounding has emerged as a promising formulation for Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), the previous multi-patch paradigm often introduces redundant noise and localization ambiguity, particularly for dense or small text instances. To address this, we propose Single-Patch Text Spotting (SPaTS), a vision-centric framework that routes each text instance through a single anchor visual token and then recovers geometry via full-image refinement. To accurately identify this anchor without oracle labels, we introduce Single-Patch Selective Optimization (SPaSO), a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes discrete visual-token selection using patch-level rewards. To further improve representation robustness and localization precision, we introduce Directional Embedding Alignment (DEA) to suppress unstable norm bias by decoupling feature magnitude and direction, and Patch-Enhanced Decoding (PED) to fuse the routed anchor with language semantics and cross-attend over the full-image feature map for geometry-aware boundary regression beyond coordinate-space surrogates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPaTS consistently and significantly outperforms both frontier closed-source MLLMs and OCR MLLMs. Code will be released soon.

</details>


### [47] [ARD-REFSM: Enhancing Reflection Symmetry Detection with Asymmetric Denoising and Rotation Equivariance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27927)
*Dongfu Yin,Rourou Su,Cong Zhao,Fei Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes ARD for asymmetric region denoising and REFSM for rotation-equivariant feature matching to detect reflection symmetry; introduces GMSYM dataset; achieves state-of-the-art on standard datasets and GMSYM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reflection symmetry detection is confounded by asymmetric background clutter and non-rotation-equivariant CNN features, leading to unreliable symmetry predictions.

Method: ARD module suppresses asymmetric interference to refine symmetry; REFSM module performs feature similarity matching between original and rotated inputs; dual-input REFSM uses rotation loss to align score maps and predict rotation-equivariant symmetry axes. Also introduces GMSYM benchmark with diverse interferences.

Result: Empirical evaluation on DENDI, NYU, LDRS, SDRW and GMSYM shows state-of-the-art accuracy and robustness in symmetry detection.

Conclusion: The approach advances symmetry detection under clutter and arbitrary orientations, with a new benchmark; potential future work includes broader evaluations, efficiency analysis, and extension to other symmetry types.

Abstract: Reflection symmetry detection remains challenging due to interference from asymmetric regions and arbitrary orientations of symmetric patterns. Asymmetric regions introduce background clutter that disrupts symmetric pattern matching, whereas conventional convolutional neural networks lack rotation equivariance, leading to inconsistent feature representations under rotational transformations. To address these issues, we propose an Asymmetric Region Denoising (ARD) module and a Rotation Equivariant Feature Similarity Matching (REFSM) module. The ARD module suppresses asymmetric interference to refine symmetric patterns, while the REFSM module enhances rotation equivariance through feature similarity matching between original and rotated images. Specifically, our dual-input REFSM framework leverages rotation loss to maximize consistency between the score maps of original and rotated images, thereby enabling precise prediction of rotation-equivariant symmetry axes. Furthermore, we introduce GMSYM, a new benchmark dataset that categorizes images into diverse scenarios and incorporates various interferences to address the limitations of existing reflection symmetry detection benchmarks. Extensive experiments on four standard datasets (DENDI, NYU, LDRS, SDRW) and our proposed GMSYM dataset demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and robustness.

</details>


### [48] [LAST: The Last Query Token Guides Visual Token Pruning for Edge-Cloud Collaborative MLLM Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27952)
*Feng Yang,Xinrui Ju,Keyang Zhang,Xiandong Meng,Rongqun Lin,Howard Leung,Shiqi Wang,Haoliang Li,Chris Xing Tian*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LAST is a training-free, query-dependent visual token pruning framework for edge-cloud multimodal LLMs. It uses a compact edge VLM as guidance proxy and the last query token's attention to visual tokens as an importance signal to prune tokens, enabling query-aware selection without cloud-model access or heavy aggregation. It achieves strong accuracy with a small token budget across 11 benchmarks (95.4% full-token accuracy with 12.5% tokens).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce cloud-side inference costs and data transmission in edge-cloud multimodal LLMs by pruning visual token sequences in a query-aware, training-free manner. Existing methods are either query-agnostic (vision-driven) or rely on cloud-model internals and multi-position aggregation, which are costly or infeasible in edge-cloud settings.

Method: A training-free framework (LAST) that uses a compact edge-side VLM as a guidance proxy. It computes a lightweight importance signal from the last query token's attention to the visual token sequence under causal attention, allowing the edge device to identify query-relevant tokens without cloud access, autoregressive generation, or multi-position aggregation. It then preserves a diverse set of query-relevant tokens within a fixed token budget.

Result: Empirical evaluation on 11 multimodal benchmarks shows LAST consistently outperforms pruning methods with various guidance strategies, preserving 95.4% of full-token accuracy while retaining only 12.5% of visual tokens, with low edge-side overhead and reduced cloud-side computation.

Conclusion: LAST provides a practical, training-free, query-aware pruning mechanism for edge-cloud MLLMs that maintains high accuracy under tight token budgets, across diverse benchmarks, and mitigates cloud-side compute and communication costs.

Abstract: Multimodal foundation models are reshaping edge-cloud visual intelligence from task-specific feature pipelines into token-based interfaces, where edge devices encode visual inputs into tokens for a general-purpose cloud MLLM. However, dense visual-token sequences increase cloud-side inference costs. Existing pruning methods mainly target centralized inference: vision-driven methods can operate before cloud execution but are typically query-agnostic, whereas query-guided methods often rely on internal states of the target MLLM and cannot determine token relevance before transmission. Compact guidance models offer an alternative, but existing designs may require costly attention aggregation or auxiliary generation. We propose LAST, a training-free framework for query-dependent visual token pruning in edge-cloud collaborative MLLM inference. LAST uses a compact edge-side VLM as a guidance proxy and derives a lightweight importance signal from the last query token's attention to visual tokens. Under causal attention, the last query token can attend to the full visual sequence and the entire query context, enabling query-aware pruning without cloud-model access, autoregressive generation, or costly aggregation over multiple query positions. LAST then retains a diverse set of query-relevant visual tokens under a fixed token budget. We evaluate LAST on 11 multimodal benchmarks under multiple token budgets against pruning methods with different guidance strategies. Experiments show that LAST consistently achieves the strongest performance, preserving 95.4% of the full-token accuracy while retaining only 12.5% of the visual tokens, with low edge-side selection overhead and reduced cloud-side computation.

</details>


### [49] [FiRE: Enhancing MLLMs with Fine-Grained Context Learning for Complex Image Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27959)
*Bohan Hou,Haoqiang Lin,Xuemeng Song,Haokun Wen,Meng Liu,Yupeng Hu,Xiangyu Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Two-stage fine-grained multimodal fine-tuning combined with an automated fine-grained CIR quintuple dataset pipeline yields strong zero-shot image retrieval across five complex tasks, using a lightweight MLLM backbone.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of prior MLLMs in fine-grained context modeling and entangled fine-tuning objectives, which hinder long-text-to-image, visual dialog, and composed image retrieval.

Method: 1) An automated pipeline generates a fine-grained CIR dataset with image captions and modification text (quintuple format) to enable rich context modeling. 2) A two-stage fine-tuning: (a) context reasoning-oriented fine-tuning and (b) retrieval-oriented fine-tuning, decoupled, using a lightweight MLLM backbone.

Result: Across five diverse retrieval datasets, the method achieves superior zero-shot retrieval performance compared with existing approaches, even with lighter backbones.

Conclusion: Decoupling context reasoning and retrieval objectives, aided by fine-grained data, improves cross-task CIR and related multimodal retrieval tasks; promising for broader multimodal reasoning and retrieval applications, with room for further ablations and scalability studies.

Abstract: Due to their strong generalizable multimodal processing and reasoning capabilities, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have demonstrated significant potential as universal image retrievers, effectively addressing diverse real-world image retrieval tasks. Nevertheless, pioneering studies, while promising, overlook the potential of fine-grained context modeling and disentangled fine-tuning objectives in enhancing MLLMs' retrieval performance, particularly for complex tasks such as long-text-to-image retrieval, visual dialog retrieval, and composed image retrieval (CIR). Therefore, in this work, we propose an automated fine-grained multimodal quintuple dataset construction pipeline and a novel two-stage fine-grained multimodal fine-tuning strategy. The dataset generation pipeline produces a comprehensive CIR dataset with fine-grained image captions and modification text, facilitating fine-grained context modeling. Beyond the previously entangled fine-tuning paradigm, our approach separates the fine-tuning process into two distinct stages: (1) fine-grained context reasoning-oriented fine-tuning and (2) fine-grained retrieval-oriented fine-tuning. These stages aim to sequentially enhance the model's context understanding and query-target alignment capabilities, thereby improving retrieval performance. Extensive experiments across five datasets encompassing diverse and complex image retrieval tasks demonstrate the remarkable superiority of our method over existing approaches in zero-shot retrieval settings, even with a more lightweight MLLM backbone compared to those methods.

</details>


### [50] [FootprintNet: State-Transition-Guided Dynamic Footprint Learning for Multi-temporal Remote Sensing Change Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27969)
*Haotian Zhang,Hao Chen,Han Guo,Zhengxia Zou,Zhenwei Shi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Proposes Urban Building Dynamics Detection (UBDD) and FootprintNet for multi-change MTCD, introducing dynamic footprints and a temporal-change boundary-aware framework, plus Building Change Dynamics Score (BCDS) to measure temporal proximity; shows state-of-the-art results on TSCD, MUDS, WUSU; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional MTCD methods assume a single change category per pixel over the entire observation period, which misrepresents recurrent or multiple changes tied to human activities.

Method: UBDD identifies temporal intervals of changes (footprints); introduces a separate multi-change class for pixels with two or more changes; FootprintNet models change dynamics as latent state-action interactions with transition constraints and uses temporal change-boundary cues; introduces BCDS as a metric. Datasets: TSCD, MUDS, WUSU; code link provided.

Result: FootprintNet outperforms state-of-the-art on multiple datasets; BCDS better reflects temporal proximity and semantics; code released.

Conclusion: Shifts MTCD to footprint-based, temporally aware modeling; enables unified handling of single- and multi-change processes and provides a more meaningful evaluation metric; potential for improved understanding of human-activity-related dynamics.

Abstract: Despite substantial progress in remote sensing multi-temporal change detection (MTCD), most existing MTCD methods still represent the dynamic process at each spatial location over the entire observation period using a single change category associated with the final observation. This implicit single-change assumption limits their ability to characterize regions of recurrent change closely related to human activities. To address this limitation, we introduce Urban Building Dynamics Detection (UBDD), which identifies building-change dynamic footprints, i.e., the temporal intervals in which changes occur, from multi-temporal imagery and produces pixel-wise classification masks. For regions undergoing two or more changes, UBDD introduces an independent multi-change class for unified representation, thereby enabling unified modeling of single- and multi-change processes. Furthermore, we propose FootprintNet, which abstracts building-change processes as interactions between latent states and actions, and imposes state-action transition constraints to guide the learning of causally coherent change trajectories. It further exploits temporal change-boundary cues to enhance feature contrast across boundary sides, thereby improving the discrimination among different dynamic footprints and enabling accurate detection of dynamic footprints. Moreover, we introduce the Building Change Dynamics Score (BCDS) to address the inability of conventional metrics to reflect the temporal proximity between predicted footprints and labels. It evaluates predictions according to their preservation of change semantics and temporal offsets from the corresponding labels. Extensive experiments on TSCD, MUDS, and WUSU demonstrate that FootprintNet outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/zmoka-zht/FootprintNet.

</details>


### [51] [Now You Have My Healthy Attention: A U-DiT for Brain-MRI Inpainting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27974)
*Danilo Danese,Angela Lombardi,Tommaso Di Noia*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A deterministic 3D inpainting model for healthy tissue completion in masked T1 MRI using a downsampled self-attention network with occlusion-attention constraints and contralateral symmetry prior; achieves high distortion metrics on BraTS-2026.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Provide anatomically plausible, tumor-free references within masked regions for downstream analysis by exploiting long-range context while preserving high-frequency details.

Method: U-DiT-style volumetric encoder–decoder with downsampled global self-attention and 3D rotary position embeddings; occluded (void) tokens attend only to known healthy tokens of the same volume with a learned bias toward the contralateral homologue; includes a contralateral-symmetry input as a patient-specific prior.

Result: On BraTS-2026 validation, mean healthy-region SSIM 0.864, PSNR 24.7 dB, MSE 4.6e-3 over 219 cases.

Conclusion: Shows strong distortion-based performance, discusses residual-smoothness implications for anatomical realism and the effect of symmetry priors on bilaterally symmetric organs with unilateral lesions.

Abstract: The ASNR-MICCAI BraTS Local Synthesis (Inpainting) task asks for the anatomically plausible completion of healthy brain tissue within a masked region of a T1-weighted MRI, providing a tumor-free anatomical reference for downstream analysis. As the task is scored by distortion metrics (SSIM, PSNR, MSE), we build a deterministic regression model and focus on giving it inductive biases tailored to inpainting. Our network follows the U-DiT principle of performing self-attention on a downsampled token grid: a volumetric encoder-decoder imports long-range context through a downsampled global self-attention block with three-dimensional rotary position embeddings, while convolutions and skip connections preserve high-frequency detail. Two ideas drive our results.
