Conclusion: Fragility-guided mixed-precision PTQ with KL-divergence-based fragility estimation and MCKP-based bit allocation is effective for Vision Transformers, enabling adaptive precision allocation that improves performance under practical bit-budget constraints and generalizes to both classification and detection/segmentation tasks.

Abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) has emerged as an effective solution for deploying Vision Transformers (ViTs) on resource-constrained devices. However, existing PTQ methods typically employ uniform bit-widths across transformer components, overlooking their heterogeneous sensitivity to quantization and leading to inefficient precision allocation. In this paper, we propose {MixFrag, a fragility-guided mixed-precision PTQ framework for Vision Transformers. MixFrag first estimates component-level quantization fragility by measuring the Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence between full-precision and isolated quantized output distributions using a small calibration set. It then formulates bit allocation as a Multiple-Choice Knapsack Problem (MCKP), enabling adaptive layer-wise precision assignment under a target bit budget. Extensive experiments on ImageNet-1K across multiple Vision Transformer architectures demonstrate that MixFrag achieves competitive classification performance under practical mixed-precision settings. Furthermore, evaluations on COCO object detection and instance segmentation show that MixFrag achieves state-of-the-art performance among existing mixed-precision PTQ methods, improving the previous best method by up to 9.6 AP under the challenging MP3/MP3 setting. Additional analyses validate the proposed fragility metric and demonstrate its strong correlation with the learned bit allocation. These results establish MixFrag as an effective framework for mixed-precision post-training quantization of Vision Transformers.

</details>


### [102] [VAD: Attributing Visual Evidence for Target Reconstruction in Multimodal On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28590)
*Kangning Zhang,Yixing Li,Shuai Shao,Qingyao Li,Zhengxi Lu,Zhiyuan Yao,Jianghao Lin,Wenxiang Jiao,Yuan Lu,Weiwen Liu,Weinan Zhang,Yong Yu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VAD isolates visually grounded teacher corrections via counterfactual target reconstruction, outperforming standard privileged-view distillation on six visual benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In multimodal on-policy distillation, next-token corrections are confounded by linguistic priors and teacher effects. There is a need to identify corrections that are truly supported by visual evidence.

Method: Introduce Visual Attribution Distillation (VAD): at each student prefix, compare a fixed teacher with and without the relevant visual evidence. Compute ut as the change in centered log-probabilities, giving a signed proxy of visual-evidence direction. Project the original correction onto ut to get an intervention-aligned component and a proxy-unexplained residual; reconstruct a student-anchored target from the aligned component. During training, the reconstructed target provides primary supervision, while the teacher acts as a weak regularizer.

Result: VAD outperforms direct privileged-view distillation and visual-advantage weighting across six fine-grained visual benchmarks at 4B and 9B scales. Token-level and controlled-target analyses show the proxy-aligned component is enriched in task-relevant visual corrections and yields stronger target shifts, particularly when evidence refutes a mistaken answer.

Conclusion: Counterfactual target reconstruction is an effective alternative to source-mixed supervision for multimodal on-policy distillation.

Abstract: Multimodal on-policy distillation (OPD) transfers fine-grained visual knowledge by supervising student-generated trajectories with a privileged-view teacher. Yet its next-token corrections are source-mixed, combining visual signals with linguistic priors and teacher-specific effects. The key challenge is to estimate which corrections are supported by visual evidence, not merely where or how strongly to distill. We introduce Visual Attribution Distillation (VAD), a counterfactual target-reconstruction algorithm that estimates the visually attributable part of a teacher correction. At each student-generated prefix, VAD evaluates the same fixed teacher with the relevant evidence present and removed. The corresponding change in centered log-probabilities defines ut, a signed proxy for the visual evidence direction that estimates how revealing the evidence supports or refutes candidate tokens. VAD projects the original correction onto this proxy to obtain an intervention-aligned component and a proxy-unexplained residual, then reconstructs a student-anchored target from the former. During training, this reconstructed target supplies the primary supervision signal, while the privileged teacher contributes a weak regularizer. Across six fine-grained visual benchmarks at 4B and 9B scales, VAD outperforms direct privileged-view distillation and visual-advantage weighting. Token- level and controlled-target analyses show that the proxy-aligned component is enriched in task-relevant visual corrections and yields stronger target shifts, especially when evidence refutes a mistaken answer. These results support counterfactual target reconstruction as an effective alternative to source-mixed supervision.

</details>


### [103] [Beacon: Knowing When and How to Perform Agentic Visual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28595)
*Qixun Wang,Yang Shi,Letian Cheng,Zhuoran Zhang,Yan He,Yuqi Tang,Qi Zhang,Xinlei Yu,Ruizhe Chen,Tianrun Xu,Yuanxing Zhang,Pengfei Wan,Haotian Wang,Xianghua Ying*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper defines Mode Adaptiveness (MA) and Tool Effect (TE) for agentic visual reasoning, shows existing models struggle to deploy tools adaptively and to ensure tool use yields gains without hurting easy tasks, and presents Beacon. Beacon uses Necessity-Aware Adaptive Reward and Hint-Guided Capability Expansion to promote adaptive tool invocation via reinforcement learning, achieving stronger overall performance with improved MA and TE across benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To maximize MLLMs' success on complex tasks by enabling adaptive use of tools while avoiding unnecessary computation, and to quantify MA and TE to guide future model design.

Method: Systematic analysis of current agentic visual reasoning models to quantify MA and TE; design of Beacon architecture; two RL-based mechanisms: Necessity-Aware Adaptive Reward (N-AAR) and Hint-Guided Capability Expansion (HGCE); extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks.

Result: Beacon outperforms baselines with higher mode adaptiveness and genuine tool-induced gains, preserving or improving performance on easy tasks while delivering substantial improvements on hard tasks.

Conclusion: Adaptive tool invocation is crucial for robust agentic visual reasoning. Beacon demonstrates that constraining tool use to task necessity and guiding capability expansion yields superior overall performance and clearer tool benefits.

Abstract: The fundamental goal of agentic visual reasoning is to improve the success rate of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on complex tasks, rather than merely equipping them with a sophisticated yet inefficient reasoning paradigm. In this work, we rethink agentic visual reasoning through two key dimensions of tool use: Mode Adaptiveness (MA) and Tool Effect (TE). Mode Adaptiveness characterizes whether an MLLM can recognize when tools are truly necessary and invoke them accordingly, thereby avoiding unnecessary computational overhead while improving performance on challenging problems that require tool assistance. Tool Effect characterizes the actual impact of tool use: tools should extend the model's capabilities on problems unsolvable through text-only reasoning, while avoiding additional errors on problems that the model can already solve without tools. We conduct a comprehensive analysis to quantify these two properties and empirically reveal that existing agentic visual reasoning models exhibit limited Mode Adaptiveness, while the gains produced by tool use on hard examples are largely offset by the harm introduced on easy examples that the models can already solve. Motivated by these observations, we propose Beacon, a novel agentic visual reasoning model that achieves stronger overall performance, improved Mode Adaptiveness, and genuine tool-induced performance gains. At the core of Beacon are the Necessity-Aware Adaptive Reward and the Hint-Guided Capability Expansion mechanism in the reinforcement learning stage, which respectively encourage adaptive tool invocation based on task necessity and strengthen the model's tool-use capability on the most challenging problems. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks demonstrate the strong overall performance of Beacon and its substantial improvements in both Mode Adaptiveness and Tool Effect.

</details>


### [104] [Chimera: Designing and Chinchilla-Scaling Hybrid Visual Diffusion Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28611)
*Chongjian Ge,Hanwen Jiang,Tianyu Wang,Jiuxiang Gu,Yiran Xu,Ziwen Chen,Shaoteng Liu,Jing Shi,Yicong Hong,Zefan Cai,Hailin Jin,Hao Tan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Chimera is a scalable, long-context diffusion backbone that combines Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), interleaved Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA), and modality-aware short convolutions with Sparse MoE, guided by HeteroP scaling laws. It enables efficient scaling to large, long-context visual generation and achieves strong zero-shot extrapolation for videos.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The quadratic cost of full attention in high-resolution images and long videos hinders scalable, multimodal diffusion models. A hybrid architecture with efficient long-context components and principled scaling is needed to push beyond current limits.

Method: Chimera processes text, image, and video tokens in a raster-ordered stream without positional embeddings. It uses KDA for long-context state tracking with O(N) complexity, interleaved MLA for direct global interaction, modality-aware short convolutions for local spatiotemporal context, and Sparse MoE layers to scale capacity. HeteroP provides module-wise, fan-in/depth-based hyperparameter transfer to fit Chinchilla-style compute-optimal laws relating activated model size, training-token count, and data ratios for images and videos.

Result: An 11B-parameter Chimera with 2B activated parameters achieves 1.7x compute efficiency over a matched Wan-2.1 2B baseline for the dense backbone and 7.3x for the complete system. It can zero-shot extrapolate from 5-second training clips to 30-second videos with only 6.5% FID degradation in the last five seconds without length-specific fine-tuning. The compute-optimal pretraining for images divides compute roughly evenly between activated size and token count; for video, larger model size is favored at higher budgets.

Conclusion: The work establishes scalable principles and a concrete design for efficient long-context diffusion architectures. HeteroP enables consistent, compute-aware scaling across width/depth, enabling Chimera to efficiently handle long-context visual diffusion and multimodal tasks.

Abstract: Visual generation increasingly requires high-resolution images, long videos, and multimodal context, making the quadratic cost of full attention prohibitive. We introduce Chimera, a hybrid visual diffusion backbone with a principled scaling recipe. Chimera processes text, image, and video tokens in one raster-ordered stream without positional embeddings. It combines Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) for long-context state tracking with O(N) complexity, interleaved Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) for direct global interaction, and modality-aware short convolutions for local spatiotemporal context. Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers expand capacity while controlling activated compute. To scale this heterogeneous architecture, we introduce HeteroP, a module-wise scheme that transfers hyperparameters across width and depth according to each tensor's functional fan-in and model depth. HeteroP yields a consistently tuned family used to fit Chinchilla-style compute-optimal laws for activated model size, training-token count, and image-video data ratio. Guided by these laws, we train an 11B-parameter Chimera with 2B activated parameters. Experiments show three results. First, measured by pretraining diffusion loss, the dense backbone is 1.7x as compute-efficient as a matched full-attention Wan-2.1 2B baseline, while the complete system reaches 7.3x. Second, without length-specific fine-tuning, Chimera extrapolates zero-shot from 5-second training clips to 30-second videos, with only 6.5% FID degradation in the last five seconds. Third, the fitted laws show that compute-optimal image pretraining divides compute nearly evenly between activated model size and training-token count, whereas video pretraining modestly favors model size at higher budgets. These results establish a foundation for designing and scaling efficient long-context diffusion architectures.

</details>


### [105] [PhiZero: A World Model Built Around Physical Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28624)
*Shuyao Shang,Yuqi Wang,Ruopeng Gao,Xu Chen,Tieniu Tan,Lue Fan,Zhaoxiang Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PhiZero proposes a self-supervised, language-based world model that reasons about future physics as a physical-language sequence before rendering it into video, enabling explicit reasoning, interactive simulation, and zero-shot transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional pixel-space world models entangle dynamics in high-dimensional predictors; humans reason about physics using language. The work aims to provide an explicit, compositional representation of world dynamics to improve interpretability and controllability.

Method: Learn physical language from in-the-wild videos via self-supervision and employ a reason-then-render pipeline: infer future evolution as a physical-language sequence, then render the inferred transitions into videos.

Result: Experiments show physically coherent world evolution on generation and understanding benchmarks; demonstrates potential for realistic interactive world modeling, fine-grained action-conditioned simulation, and zero-shot motion transfer.

Conclusion: A physical-language world model can offer explicit, interpretable reasoning about physical dynamics, with advantages for controllable video synthesis, planning, and transfer across tasks.

Abstract: We introduce PhiZero, a physical world model built around physical language, a compact discrete representation of world-state transitions. Existing physical world models typically predict future videos directly in pixel space, leaving the underlying world dynamics implicit within high-dimensional visual predictors. Motivated by humans' ability to abstract predictive structure from visual experience and organize it in natural language for explicit reasoning, we learn physical language from in-the-wild videos through self-supervision and use it to explicitly reason about how the physical world evolves. Accordingly, PhiZero adopts a reason-then-render paradigm: it first infers future world evolution as a physical-language sequence and then renders the inferred transitions into videos. Extensive experiments across generation and understanding benchmarks validate the ability of PhiZero to model physically coherent world evolution. We further show its potential for realistic and interactive world modeling, fine-grained action-conditioned simulation, and zero-shot motion transfer.

</details>


### [106] [ACE-Data-0: Human-Centric Ambient Capture as Embodied Data Engine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28625)
*Yukang Cao,Haozhe Xie,Beichen Wen,Runmao Yao,Yinghao Liu,Yue Huang,Zhichao Liao,Yunxiang Wang,Haiheng Liu,Xingshun Tian,Dawei Su,Long Zhuo,Dacheng Tao,Xiaogang Wang,Liang Pan,Ziwei Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ACE introduces Ambient Capture Engine (ACE) to convert real homes into synchronized, multisensory recording studios at table and room scales. It yields ACE-Data-0 (150 hours, 17M frames, 200 tasks, 50 participants, 2 environments, 75k episodes) and a hierarchical benchmark, exposing gaps in SOTA for contact, occlusion, egomotion, and long horizons; enabling scalable embodied AI research.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the data bottleneck in embodied intelligence by capturing a holistic, synchronized perception–action stream across first-person and multi-view modalities, over body-scale and object-scale interactions, within naturalistic home environments.

Method: Deploy the Ambient Capture Engine to create two scales of recording rigs in real homes. Collect synchronized egocentric and exocentric video, full-body and articulated hand motion, 6-DoF object trajectories, 3D geometry, audio, and tactile signals as a unified multisensory stream. Build ACE-Data-0 (150 h, 17M frames, 200 tasks, 50 participants, 2 environments, 75,000 interaction episodes). Introduce a hierarchical benchmark progressing from signals to scene components to interactions.

Result: A rich, synchronized multimodal dataset (ACE-Data-0) with extensive coverage of atomic and long-horizon household activities. Evaluations reveal substantial gaps in current methods under contact, occlusion, egomotion, and long temporal horizons, establishing a challenging testbed and a scalable foundation for multiple embodied AI paradigms.

Conclusion: ACE-Data-0 provides aligned perceptual, kinematic, and contact supervision, enabling imitation learning, world models, vision–language–action systems, and embodied AI in naturalistic home settings, and highlights future directions for modeling long-horizon, contact-rich interactions.

Abstract: Embodied intelligence faces a fundamental data bottleneck. Models must capture how first-person perception, whole-body motion, dexterous manipulation, object state, sound, and touch evolve together as humans pursue goals over time. Existing datasets fragment this experience across viewpoints, modalities, or spatial scales, leaving the full perception-action loop only partially observed. We introduce the Ambient Capture Engine (ACE), a human-centric data engine that transforms real home environments into spatially calibrated, temporally synchronized recording studios. ACE operates at two complementary scales: a table-scale configuration resolves hand-object manipulation, while a room-scale configuration captures whole-body motion, locomotion, and interactions across a furnished home. ACE records egocentric and multi-view exocentric video, full-body and articulated hand motion, object geometry and 6-DoF trajectories, audio, and tactile signals as a unified multisensory stream. Using ACE, we build ACE-Data-0, comprising 150 hours and 17M video frames across 200 task categories, performed by 50 participants in 2 environments, for a total of 75,000 interaction episodes. The dataset spans atomic manipulation, long-horizon chains of household activities, and human-scene interaction, while preserving natural behavioral variation through goal-level rather than step-by-step instructions. We further introduce a hierarchical benchmark that progresses from signals to scene components and then to interactions. Evaluations of state-of-the-art methods expose substantial gaps under contact, occlusion, egomotion, and long temporal horizons. ACE-Data-0 provides synchronized human demonstrations with aligned perceptual, kinematic, and contact supervision, offering a scalable foundation for imitation learning, world models, vision-language-action systems, and embodied AI.

</details>


### [107] [ReToken: One Token to Improve Vision-Language Models for Visual Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28627)
*Yao Xiao,Reuben Tan,Zhen Zhu,Yuqun Wu,Jianfeng Gao,Derek Hoiem*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ReToken introduces a single learnable embedding that retrieves a sparse set of relevant visual tokens from a pre-filled KV cache, enabling efficient long-context vision-language processing with strong gains on image and video benchmarks using minimal training data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long visual context degrades accuracy as distractors increase and processing all tokens is memory-inefficient; there is a need for scalable, memory-efficient retrieval for vision-language models.

Method: A single learnable embedding acts as an explicit retrieval target to select sparse query-relevant visual tokens from a pre-filled visual KV cache. Trained on a small image-QA dataset, it enables sparse token selection for long-context inputs.

Result: On Visual Haystacks, Qwen3VL-8B improves by 13.4 points and InternVL3.5 by 12.4 points (>20% relative). On LVBench, zero-shot transfer to long video yields +8.0 points with Qwen3VL-8B. Training and long-video inference fit on a single H100; code available at the provided GitHub link.

Conclusion: ReToken demonstrates that a compact, trainable retrieval target can substantially boost long-context vision-language performance with minimal data and resource needs, offering a practical path toward scalable long-context models for image and video tasks.

Abstract: Long visual context poses a challenge for vision-language models: performance degrades as the number of distractors grows, and processing all tokens at once is computationally infeasible under GPU memory constraints. We present ReToken, a single learnable embedding trained as an explicit retrieval target that selects a sparse set of query-relevant visual tokens from a pre-filled visual KV cache. Trained on only a small image-QA dataset, ReToken yields consistent gains across image and video benchmarks: on Visual Haystacks it improves Qwen3VL-8B by 13.4 points and InternVL3.5 by 12.4 points (>20% relative), and on LVBench it transfers zero-shot to long video for an 8.0-point gain with Qwen3VL-8B. Thanks to its lightweight design, both training and long-video inference fit on a single H100. Code is available at: https://github.com/avaxiao/ReToken

</details>


<div id='cs.AI'></div>

# cs.AI [[Back]](#toc)

### [108] [Multi-Head Attention Residuals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27230)
*Cheng Luo,Zefan Cai,Junjie Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MHAR introduces per-subspace routing heads in attention residuals to reduce cross-subspace read disagreement, improving validation loss and throughput across 100M–1B scales; an optimal number of heads exists (roughly 4–8), with delta-attention residuals enabling mid-training gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Transformer attention residuals use a single shared query over depth, forcing all feature subspaces to read history through one distribution. As model width grows, subspaces disagree more about which layers to read, hurting efficiency and learning. MHAR aims to decouple reads across subspaces to reduce cross-subspace disagreement.

Method: Reshape the routing query into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over depth history, creating a block-diagonal read. The reshape adds zero parameters and negligible compute; H=1 reproduces attention residuals. Trained from scratch on a deduplicated Nemotron-based anneal corpus with STEM/code emphasis; uses fused Triton kernels for speedups.

Result: Validation loss improves vs standard Transformer at 100M (-0.061), 350M (-0.149), and 1B (-0.140). MHAR is best among four methods across settings, with gains growing with scale. Validation loss vs H is U-shaped with optimum at H=4 or H=8; adopts H=8 for large-scale models; H=16 reduces gains. Probes show learned subspace disagreement drives the gains. Throughput increases from 0.2–0.5x baseline to 0.55–0.88x with fused Triton. Delta attention residuals enable 8B mid-training with +3.2 GSM8K and +3.1 GPQA.

Conclusion: MHAR demonstrates that allowing per-subspace, depth-wise routing reduces cross-subspace disagreement and yields consistent improvements in quality and throughput across scales. The optimal number of heads is modest (4–8), and beyond that gains erode. The work provides practical guidance for deploying per-subspace routing and shows compatibility with delta attention residuals for large-scale mid-training gains.

Abstract: Transformers propagate information across depth through a single additive residual stream: every sublayer reads only the most recent state. Attention residuals relax this by letting each sublayer attend, through a learned softmax. However, that read uses a single query shared across the entire width, so every feature subspace must read the depth history through one distribution. The cost of this forced compromise grows with how much the subspaces disagree about which layers to read, and disagreement grows with model width. We introduce Multi-Head Attention Residuals (MHAR): the routing query is reshaped into H per-subspace heads, each with its own softmax over the depth history. The read becomes block-diagonal, the reshape adds zero parameters and negligible compute, and H = 1 recovers attention residuals exactly. Trained from scratch on a deduplicated Nemotron-based anneal corpus that is quality-filtered and STEM- and code-heavy, MHAR improves validation loss over a standard Transformer at 100M, 350M, and 1B (-0.061, -0.149, and -0.140). It achieves the best result among four methods in every setting, with the gain increasing from 100M to the larger scales. The head count is a real design axis rather than a free knob: validation loss is U-shaped with respect to H, with a flat optimum at H = 4 or H = 8 across scales. We adopt H = 8 for large-scale models; over-splitting beyond this point (H = 16) consistently gives back part of the gain. A direct probe of the trained queries confirms that learned subspace disagreement is the underlying driver. Fused Triton routing kernels increase attention-residual training throughput from 0.2-0.5x to 0.55-0.88x of the baseline while maintaining near-baseline peak memory. An identity-preserving conversion using delta attention residuals supports 8B mid-training, yielding improvements of +3.2 on GSM8K and +3.1 on GPQA.

</details>


### [109] [KernelGenBench: A Multi-Source and Multi-Chip Benchmark for LLM-based Kernel Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27231)
*Peiyu Zang,Jian Tao,Jialing Zhang,Yichen Yuan,Wentao Zhang,Guang Liu,Yonghua Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KernelGenBench is a unified benchmark for evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across multiple sources and hardware; it features two sub-benchmarks, reports that agent-based methods outperform pure sampling, shows cross-platform performance degradation, and highlights high token costs for autonomous kernel generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a growing demand for efficient accelerator kernels to accompany LLMs, but kernel development is specialized and lacks a comprehensive benchmark that covers diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware. A standardized evaluation framework is needed to guide method development and compare approaches.

Method: KernelGenBench comprises two sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source) with 210 operators from three sources beyond standard PyTorch tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip) with a 110-operator subset evaluated across six heterogeneous hardware platforms. A large-scale evaluation consuming over 15 billion tokens compares agent-based methods to pure LLM sampling, assesses cross-platform portability, and quantifies generation cost using metrics like tokens per successful operator (AKO) and AKO4all.

Result: Findings include: (1) agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling, while cuBLAS operators are the most challenging across methods; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms, with notable cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation is highly cost-intensive, averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator, with AKO4all at 5.19 million.

Conclusion: KernelGenBench reveals substantial cross-source and cross-platform variability in LLM-/agent-generated kernels. While agent-based generation yields higher-quality kernels than simple sampling, it incurs very high token costs and suffers from cross-platform degradation, underscoring the need for improved cross-platform generalization, efficiency, and robust benchmarking to guide future kernel-generation research.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly increased the demand for efficient accelerator kernels, but kernel development remains a highly specialized and labor-intensive task. The recent rise of LLMs and agentic frameworks offers a promising pathway toward automatic kernel generation. However, despite rapid progress, there is still no comprehensive benchmark to rigorously evaluate LLM-generated kernels across diverse operator sources or heterogeneous hardware platforms. We present KernelGenBench, a unified benchmark for systematically evaluating LLM- and agent-generated Triton kernels across diverse operator sources and heterogeneous hardware platforms. It comprises two complementary sub-benchmarks: KernelGenBench-MS (Multi-Source), evaluating 210 operators from three sources beyond standard PyTorch-centric tasks, and KernelGenBench-MC (Multi-Chip), measuring performance portability across six heterogeneous hardware platforms using a 110-operator subset. Our large-scale evaluation, consuming over 15 billion tokens, shows: (1) agent-based methods consistently outperform pure LLM sampling methods, while cuBLAS operators are the most challenging across all methods; (2) generation performance varies significantly across hardware platforms, with even recent kernel-specialized agents experiencing severe cross-platform degradation (e.g., AutoKernel drops from 87% on NVIDIA to 25% on Platform E); (3) autonomous kernel generation remains highly cost-intensive, with specialized agent methods averaging 5.11 million tokens per successful operator (AKO4all reaches 5.19 million), orders of magnitude higher than simple LLM sampling approaches.

</details>


### [110] [RadHarmony: Radiological Data Handling in the Era of Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27235)
*Frank Li,Bardia Khosravi,Mohammadreza Chavoshi,Theo Dapamede,YoungSeok Jeon,Janice Newsome,Hari Trivedi,Judy Gichoya*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: RadHarmony provides a unified, open-source API to load, harmonize, and augment heterogeneous radiology datasets, with AI-assisted integration and a ViT baseline trained on chest radiographs across multiple datasets without dataset-specific code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the fragmentation of radiology datasets (varying formats, directories, schemas) that hinders scalable DL model development.

Method: RadHarmony standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format, wraps MONAI map-style datasets with optional on-disk caching, supports classification labels, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, and radiology report text, includes an interactive visualization tool, and introduces an AI-agent skill for end-to-end integration workflow; demonstrates by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT on three chest radiograph datasets with no dataset-specific code.

Result: An open-source library enabling unified data ingestion and preprocessing across heterogeneous radiology datasets; a pretrained RadHarmony-ViT model is demonstrated; code and pretrained weights available at GitHub.

Conclusion: RadHarmony lowers the barrier to integrating new radiology datasets and accelerates dataset-driven model development in radiology.

Abstract: Training deep learning models on radiological images requires integrating heterogeneous datasets across different sources, file formats, directory layouts, label schemas, and annotation types. We present RadHarmony, an open-source Python library that provides a unified API for loading, harmonizing, and augmenting radiological datasets, with a primary focus on chest radiographs and early support for computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). RadHarmony standardizes metadata from 24 public datasets into a single tabular format, wraps MONAI's map-style datasets for deep-learning-ready sample delivery with optional on-disk caching, and supports classification labels, segmentation masks, bounding boxes, and radiology report text through a single interface, with an interactive visualization tool for dataset exploration and verification. To lower the barrier for integrating new datasets, RadHarmony introduces an AI-agent skill that guides the full integration workflow from raw data inspection through code generation and testing. We demonstrate the library's utility by pretraining RadHarmony-ViT, a reference vision transformer baseline that combines three heterogeneous chest radiograph datasets with no dataset-specific code. The code and pretrained model weights are available at https://github.com/f10409/RadHarmony.

</details>


### [111] [Asymmetric Collapse in Model Merging: When Refusal Over- writes Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27240)
*Aarnav Choudhary,Matheus Fonseca Rocha,Jiwon Seo,Vasu Sharma,Maheep Chaudhary*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Merging two safety-focused finetunes preserves attack resistance far better than task accuracy; high-level refusal dominates when task vectors differ in scale.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether standard model merging preserves multiple safety-relevant behaviors when finetuned on complementary safety objectives and merged without further training.

Method: Merge two Gemma-3-1B-IT finetunes for CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal using Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES; evaluate merged models on classification accuracy, attack resistance (jailbreak refusal), and benign compliance; analyze per-layer task-vector magnitudes and cosine similarity to explain observed asymmetries.

Result: All four merging methods show stronger transfer of attack resistance than of classification accuracy. Merged models retain 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates while CARES accuracy drops to at most 12.9%. Task vectors are nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity ~0.011); however, the refusal fine-tune has larger per-layer magnitudes, causing magnitude-sensitive merging methods to favor refusal updates. This leads to safety recognition collapsing into broad refusal when safety vectors differ mainly in scale.

Conclusion: Standard model merging can disproportionately preserve or transfer one safety objective (refusal) at the expense of another when task vectors differ in scale; the direction of task vectors is not the primary factor, but magnitude differences drive the outcome. Mitigation may require scale-aware merging, normalization, or task-balancing techniques to preserve multiple safety behaviors.

Abstract: Model merging is often used to combine capabilities from separately fine-tuned models without additional training, but it is unclear whether standard merging methods preserve multiple safety-relevant behaviors simultaneously. We study this question through a controlled case study using two Gemma-3-1B-IT finetunes on two complementary safety objectives: CARES harm-level classification and WildJailbreak adversarial refusal. We merge the two fine-tunes using Linear, SLERP, TIES, and DARE-TIES, and evaluate the merged models on classification accuracy, attack resistance, and benign compliance. Across all four methods, attack resistance transfers significantly more than classification accuracy: merged models retain 81-85% jailbreak refusal rates while CARES accuracy falls to at most 12.9%. Weight-space measurements suggest that this asymmetry is not caused by strongly opposing task-vector directions: the two task vectors are nearly orthogonal (cosine similarity 0.011). Instead, the refusal fine-tune induces consistently larger per-layer task-vector magnitudes, causing magnitude-sensitive methods to favor refusal updates. These results show that standard model merging can collapse safety recognition into broad refusal when safety-relevant task vectors differ substantially in scale.

</details>


### [112] [Divergence Decoding: Training-Free Capability Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27248)
*Yimi Wang,Hao Li,Shuo Yang,He Cao,Dechen Zhang,Ziang Wu,Zhiyuan Yan,Fanyang Mo,Li Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A training-free framework that fuses generalist and domain-specialist LLMs via per-token Jensen-Shannon divergence-based routing to route to the generalist when divergence is high, enabling inference-time capability fusion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the knowledge gap of generalist LLMs in specialized scientific domains and the reduced robustness/logic of domain-specific models; seeks a training-free method for combining capabilities at inference time.

Method: Divergence Decoding computes token-level Jensen-Shannon divergence between the generalist and specialist distributions. When divergence is large, control is routed to the generalist; otherwise the system preserves domain expertise by continuing with the specialist. This creates an adaptive, inference-time policy that fuses capabilities without additional training.

Result: Evaluated across model families (Qwen and Llama) on scientific benchmarks (GPQA, ChemBench, ChemCoTBench). Divergence Decoding outperforms both domain-specialized and general-purpose models and surpasses most single-model baselines.

Conclusion: Divergence Decoding offers a general, training-free paradigm for combining diverse LLM capabilities via adaptive inference-time collaboration between a generalist and a specialist.

Abstract: While large language models excel in reasoning, these generalists often lack knowledge for specialized scientific domains. Conversely, domain models~(specialists), while knowledgeable, suffer from specialization side-effects including diminished logic and reduced robustness.To address this dilemma, we introduce Divergence Decoding, a training-free framework for capability fusion. It reconstructs the "draft-and-verify" skeleton of speculative decoding into an adaptive routing mechanism. The core is using Jensen-Shannon divergence to monitor the distributional disagreement between the two models at each token. When the specialist exhibits significant divergence, our method identifies it as a potential reasoning risk and instantaneously routes control to the generalist. This allows the dynamic injection of general reasoning while preserving domain expertise, achieving inference-time policy composition of the generalist and the specialist.We evaluate Divergence Decoding across diverse model families (Qwen and Llama series) on challenging scientific benchmarks (GPQA, ChemBench, and ChemCoTBench). Experimental results demonstrate that Divergence Decoding outperforms both the domain-specialized and general-purpose models, effectively surpassing the performance of most single-model baseline. This suggests that Divergence Decoding provides a general, training-free paradigm for fusing diverse LLM capabilities through adaptive inference-time collaboration.

</details>


### [113] [PIE-APT: A Unified Framework for Temporal Planning and Contradiction Hunting via Incremental Direct-Derivation Abduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27287)
*Amir Hossein Sharafi,Alireza Shahbazi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A unified framework of PIE-Abducer and PIE-APT performs abductive planning over temporal DL-based dynamic knowledge graphs, avoiding combinatorial MHS search, achieving better planning quality than classical planners and baseline abductive methods on four OWL benchmarks that stress open-world and DL entailment aspects.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-world dynamic knowledge graphs (DKGs) with incomplete information pose reasoning and planning challenges, including decidability constraints, ramification problems, and the combinatorial cost of handling incomplete knowledge. A unified approach operating directly on expressive DLs aims to maintain decidability while enabling non-monotonic updates and abductive enrichment.

Method: Introduce PIE-Abducer (incremental direct-derivation abduction) and PIE-APT (Abductive Planning for Temporal KGs). Model state transitions along a linear timeline as non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories. Use OWL-native action representation and consider the incremental reasoner as a black box to preserve decidability. PIE-Abducer injects the logical negation of the target goal to obtain missing premises via direct refutation consequences instead of MHS enumeration. PIE-APT uses a recursive Generate-and-Test architecture that interleaves backward-chaining A* search with PIE-Abducer up to a bounded causal depth, followed by forward-chaining Temporal Projection for validation.

Result: Evaluations on four OWL benchmarks reveal qualitative superiority over classical planners and quantitative improvement over an MHS-faithful baseline in abductive enrichment, especially under open-world and DL entailment stress tests.

Conclusion: A unified, DL-native abductive planning framework preserves decidability while delivering practical performance gains in reasoning and planning over dynamic, open-world knowledge graphs; the direct-derivation abduction approach outperforms traditional MHS-based methods in abductive enrichment.

Abstract: Reasoning and planning over Dynamic Knowledge Graphs (DKGs) present significant challenges, especially in open-world environments with incomplete information. Existing action formalisms often face decidability issues and the Ramification Problem, while managing incomplete knowledge via structural abduction requires expansive combinatorial search. This paper introduces a unified framework with two integrated modules---\textbf{PIE-Abducer} (incremental direct-derivation abduction) and \textbf{PIE-APT} (Abductive Planning for Temporal KGs)---operating natively on the highly expressive Description Logic. We model state transitions along a linear timeline as non-monotonic updates to deductively closed DL theories. Treating the incremental reasoner as a black-box and representing actions natively in OWL without external modal operators preserves logical decidability. To address incomplete knowledge, \textbf{PIE-Abducer} circumvents traditional Minimal Hitting Set (MHS) enumeration. Instead of combinatorial syntactic search, it injects the logical negation of a target goal into a consistent branch and extracts missing premises via direct refutation consequences. \textbf{PIE-APT} then employs a recursive \textit{Generate-and-Test} architecture, interleaving backward-chaining A* search with \textbf{PIE-Abducer} up to a bounded causal depth, followed by strict validation via forward-chaining Temporal Projection. We evaluate four OWL benchmarks stressing semantic abilities absent in classical planning: parameterized goals with witness search, mid-search DL entailment, open-world assumption injection, and adversarial contradiction hunting. Results demonstrate qualitative superiority over classical planners and prove our direct-derivation approach quantitatively outperforms an MHS-faithful baseline during abductive enrichment.

</details>


### [114] [PAUSE: A User-Centric Benchmark for Personal AI Assistants in Unified Service Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27354)
*Haoyu Chen,Xirui Shi,Yuyao Wang,Jerry Chen,Di Niu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PAUSE is a user-centric benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in stateful, service-integrated environments, featuring realistic user simulation, multi-regime evaluation, and scalable environment synthesis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks fragment contexts and ignore persistent user state and permissions, hindering evaluation of long-horizon, constraint-aware, multi-service assistant behavior.

Method: Proposes PAUSE benchmark with stateful reasoning, environment-service coordination across heterogeneous resources, explicit user-agent interaction via realistic user simulation, and a multi-regime evaluation framework with semantic/trajectory metrics for open-ended tasks and deterministic state-based verification for constraint-intensive tasks; includes a synthesis pipeline for generating environments, configurations, and tasks.

Result: State-of-the-art models fail to reach 70% task completion on stateful scenarios; results show consistent, interpretable failure patterns; benchmarks reveal gaps in stateful reasoning and configuration awareness.

Conclusion: PAUSE enables scalable, extensible evaluation of personal AI assistants in realistic service settings and facilitates future research into user-centric, stateful agent behavior.

Abstract: Personal AI assistants are increasingly deployed as task-oriented, tool-augmented agents that operate within unified service environments to support everyday user activities. In realistic settings, such assistants must reason over persistent user state, respect user-specific configurations and permissions, and sustain long-horizon, constraint-aware interactions across multiple services. Existing benchmarks, however, often fragment service contexts or abstract away user state, limiting their ability to evaluate user-centric personal assistant behavior in realistic service settings. We introduce PAUSE, a user-centric benchmark for evaluating personal AI assistants in stateful, service-integrated environments. PAUSE captures core challenges of real-world assistant deployment by requiring agents to coordinate actions across heterogeneous user-owned resources while maintaining consistency with environment state, authorization constraints over multi-turn interactions. The benchmark incorporates explicit user-agent interaction via realistic user simulation, enabling evaluation beyond static tool execution. To support principled and reproducible evaluation, PAUSE adopts a multi-regime evaluation framework aligned with task characteristics. Open-ended service management tasks are assessed using semantic and trajectory-level behavioral metrics, while constraint-intensive tasks admit deterministic, state-based verification. Benchmark results show that even state-of-the-art proprietary models fail to reach 70% task completion on scenarios requiring stateful reasoning and configuration awareness, revealing consistent and interpretable failure patterns. Finally, we present a user-centric synthesis pipeline that enables scalable generation of coherent service environments, user configurations, and reliably annotated tasks, supporting benchmark extensibility and future research.

</details>


### [115] [SkillMentor: LLM Agent Self-Evolution via Learning Blind-Spot Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27360)
*Xiaoyi Bao,Yuanzhen Xie,Yunzhi Tan,Jinghang Gu,Zhongqing Wang,Chu-Ren Huang,Bo Hu,Zang Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SkillMentor trains a diagnostic policy to generate diagnostic tasks, identify recurring failure modes, and assemble reusable corrective skills, achieving about 44.2% average improvement in executor performance without changing executors or using annotated data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap of learning to discover what agents do not know by treating blind-spot diagnosis as a separate, learnable capability, independent of executor adaptation or human supervision.

Method: Train a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to (1) generate diagnostic tasks, (2) identify recurrent failure modes, and (3) curate them into reusable corrective skills; evaluate on AppWorld and BFCLv3 by measuring improvements in executor performance without updating executor weights or using labeled data.

Result: Average executor performance improvement of 44.2% across AppWorld and BFCLv3; evidence that blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability.

Conclusion: Blind-spot diagnosis can be learned to enable self-evolution without modifying executor parameters or requiring human-curated data, suggesting a pathway to autonomous improvement via diagnostic capability.

Abstract: Agent self-evolution has primarily focused on learning how to act, while overlooking an equally important capability: learning to discover what an agent does not know. Existing approaches typically assume that failure discovery is given, focusing on how to repair failures once they are identified. We ask whether blind-spot diagnosis itself can be learned. We thus study diagnosis as an agent capability separate from execution, and exclude two alternative sources of progress: executor adaptation and human supervision. Under these constraints, performance cannot improve through executor updates or annotated examples, forcing all improvements to originate from the learned diagnostic capability. We propose SkillMentor, which trains a Mentor policy via reinforcement learning to generate diagnostic tasks, identify recurrent failure modes, and curate them into reusable corrective skills. Across AppWorld and BFCLv3, SkillMentor improves executor performance by an average of 44.2%. These results suggest that blind-spot diagnosis is a learnable capability, enabling self-evolution without updating executor weights or relying on human-curated data.

</details>


### [116] [Beyond the Bidirectional Promise: Re-evaluating the Robustness of Diffusion Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27386)
*Saurabh Yadav,Badri Narayana Patro,Vijay Srinivas Agneeswaran*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Diffusion Language Models exhibit a mixed robustness profile: they resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes due to stochastic loss landscapes but do not inherently handle natural input noise; robustness is weight-dependent rather than architectural. Mechanistic probes show all models encode input corruption, with fragility arising from decoder routing, not encoder representations. Surface prompt patching underperforms; robust behavior cannot be fixed by patching and must be integrated into the iterative decoding loop.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate how diffusion language models fare under natural input noise and adversarial perturbations, compared to autoregressive baselines, to determine whether architectural features confer intrinsic robustness or if robustness is primarily weight- and decoding-dependent.

Method: Use two parameter-matched model pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) and test across 32 natural perturbations, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses; include surface prompt-patching experiments to assess potential mitigation, isolating architecture vs. weight effects through paired design.

Result: DLMs show high resistance to gradient-based adversarial suffixes due to stochastic loss landscapes but lack inherent robustness to natural noise; models exhibit systematic overconfidence; mechanistic probes reveal input corruption is encoded in hidden states, with fragility rooted in decoder routing; surface prompt patching fails to improve performance over noisy baselines; robustness cannot be patched via prompts and must be integrated into the iterative decoding loop.

Conclusion: Robustness in diffusion language models is not architecture-intrinsic; it stems from how decoding routes decisions within the iterative loop. Effective robustness requires design changes that integrate robustness into the decoding process, rather than relying on prompts or weight adjustments alone.

Abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) offer a compelling alternative to autoregressive (AR) generation by enabling bidirectional context and iterative refinement. However, their reliability under natural input noise and adversarial attacks remains under-explored. To address this, we systematically evaluate DLM robustness and calibration against AR baselines, using two parameter-matched pairs (LLaDA-8B vs. LLaMA-3-8B and Dream-7B vs. Qwen2.5-7B) across 32 natural perturbation conditions, adversarial gradient probes, and mechanistic hidden-state analyses. This paired design effectively isolates architecture-intrinsic properties from weight-dependent behaviors. We find a nuanced robustness profile: while highly stochastic DLM loss landscapes naturally resist gradient-based adversarial suffixes, they provide no guaranteed defense against natural noise, proving that everyday robustness is weight-dependent rather than inherently architectural. Furthermore, DLMs exhibit systematic overconfidence, presenting a practical deployment hazard. Most crucially, mechanistic probing reveals that all models perfectly encode input corruption, isolating behavioral fragility entirely to a decoder routing failure. Consistent with this diagnosis, we show that surface-level prompt patching fails to improve over noisy baselines. Ultimately, DLM robustness cannot be patched on; it must be fundamentally integrated into the iterative decoding loop.

</details>


### [117] [Bridging Inference-Time Scaling and Episodic Memory with Action-Centric Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27415)
*Xu Zheng,Chaohao Lin,Zhuomin Chen,Weijieying Ren,Haifeng Chen,Wei Cheng,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GAMER introduces a dynamic Action-Centric Graph for episodic reasoning, decoupling memory from LLMs to improve inference efficiency and performance in agents via a dual-stream Temporal Difference learning mechanism, achieving notable gains on success and progress metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address inefficiencies in inference-time scaling for agent reasoning that rely on stateless LLMs and costly memory mechanisms, by integrating episodic memory in a graph-structured, action-centric framework

Method: Constructs an Action-Centric Graph representing historical reasoning; decouples memory from LLMs to reduce token usage; applies a dual-stream Temporal Difference learning process to estimate positive and negative action-node values from past outcomes; during inference, uses the learned value function to guide action selection with efficient graph search

Result: Experiments on multiple benchmarks show GAMER improves success rate by 20.81% and progress rate by 6.17% over vanilla baselines

Conclusion: GAMER effectively integrates episodic memory with inference scaling, yielding significant efficiency and performance gains through a decoupled, graph-based memory plus TD learning framework for agent decision-making

Abstract: Recent advancements in inference-time scaling have significantly unlocked the complex reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models~(LLMs). However, for agents, these approaches suffer from a critical inefficiency, operating in a stateless manner and engaging in redundant search processes. Existing memory mechanisms largely rely on the reasoning capabilities of LLMs, leading to prohibitive computational costs. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, \textit{GAMER}~(Graph-based Action-centric Memory with Episodic Reasoning), that bridges the gap between inference scaling and episodic memory. Our approach models historical reasoning as a dynamic \textit{Action-Centric Graph}. By decoupling the memory mechanism from LLMs, our method can save token/money usage by providing less memory context than memory mechanism baselines. To extract knowledge from the graph effectively, we use a dual-stream Temporal Difference learning mechanism to estimate the positive~(suggestion) and negative~(avoidance) value of action nodes based on past successes and failures. During the inference phase, this learned value function optimizes decision-making bi-directionally, so that positive values provide action suggestions, while negative values indicate high-risk actions. By performing efficient searches on the graph, our method significantly improves the efficiency of inference scaling. Experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that \textit{GAMER} achieves superior performance by \textbf{20.81\%/6.17\%} for success/progress rate compared to vanilla baselines.

</details>


### [118] [Dimensionality and Measurement Precision in HLE's Multiple-Choice Subset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27420)
*Mayank Sharma,Savira Nadela,Tyler Matteson*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HLE's domain subscores do not reflect separable constructs; the benchmark largely measures a single general reasoning factor; domain labels contribute minimal variance and offer little incremental validity; measurement precision concentrates around moderate ability and poorly discriminates top-end models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To test whether HLE's domain categories correspond to empirically separable latent traits and whether HLE can differentiate among frontier models.

Method: Administered text-only MC subset (J=428) to 29 LLMs; fit a two-parameter logistic (2PL) IRT model; assessed dimensionality via factor structure, domain variance, residual correlations; computed McDonald's omega_h; examined domain-ability vs total score; analyzed test information function.

Result: Support for a single general factor; domain labels explain ~3.5% variance; within- and between-domain residual correlations nearly identical (d=0.016); domain-specific ability estimates nearly redundant with total score (r ≥ 0.81); measurement precision strongest at moderate ability; drops above theta=0; limited discrimination among highest-ability models.

Conclusion: Domain subscores should not be interpreted as distinct capabilities; HLE has limited ability to differentiate among frontier LLMs; revision or reinterpretation of HLE subscores is warranted.

Abstract: Humanity's Last Exam (HLE) is widely used to evaluate frontier language models. HLE organizes its questions into eight subject-domain categories, whose subscores are often interpreted as evidence of distinct capabilities. However, no study has assessed whether these labels correspond to empirically separable latent constructs, nor whether the benchmark effectively differentiates between models of similar ability. We evaluate 29 LLMs on the text-only multiple-choice subset of HLE ($J = 428$ items) and apply psychometric methods to assess both the dimensionality of the benchmark and the distribution of its measurement precision. Fitting a two-parameter logistic IRT model, we find convergent evidence that HLE measures a single general reasoning factor: McDonald's $ω_h = 0.998$, domain labels explain only 3.5\% of item response variance, within- and between-domain residual correlations are nearly identical (Cohen's $d = 0.016$), and domain-specific ability estimates are near-redundant with the total score ($r \geq 0.81$). A separate analysis of the test information function reveals that measurement precision concentrates at moderate ability levels and drops sharply above $θ= 0$, where frontier models sit. These findings suggest that HLE's domain subscores do not warrant distinct capability interpretations and that the benchmark's ability to discriminate among the strongest models is limited.

</details>


### [119] [Leveraging Trajectory Graphs for Pre-Execution Error Diagnosis in Agentic LLM Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27443)
*Xu Zheng,Zhuomin Chen,Chaohao Lin,Hua Wei,Haifeng Chen,Wei Cheng,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Trajectory Graph Copilot introduces a graph-based, pre-action diagnostic system for LLM agents in long-horizon tasks, using a Graph Neural Network to predict and warn about risky action sequences before execution, achieving ~14.69% average improvement in pass ratio across four benchmarks and three LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon interactive tasks exhibit compounding errors due to large action spaces; preemptively diagnosing and preventing suboptimal actions can conserve limited step budgets and improve task success without costly fine-tuning.

Method: Historical trajectories are represented as a probabilistic graph; a Graph Neural Network (Graph Debugger) learns to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure and provides early warnings to prompt self-correction before actions are taken, functioning as a diagnostic sandbox (Trajectory Graph Copilot).

Result: Extensive experiments across four benchmarks with three LLM agents show an average pass ratio improvement of 14.69%. The approach reduces costly mistakes by preemptively flagging potentially flawed actions.

Conclusion: Proactive, graph-based pre-action diagnostics can significantly enhance long-horizon LLM-assisted autonomy by preventing errors before execution, offering a generalizable copilot framework without requiring fine-tuning.

Abstract: Large Language Model~(LLM)-based agents have demonstrated exceptional performance across a wide range of complex interactive tasks. However, they often struggle with long-horizon interactive tasks common in domains, such as embodied AI. The complexity and vast action spaces in these settings lead to compounding errors, where a single suboptimal action can derail an entire trajectory, causing the agent to exhaust its limited step budget on inefficient or unrecoverable paths. To overcome this without costly fine-tuning, we draw inspiration from software debugging, where execution logs are analyzed to preemptively catch errors. We propose \textit{Trajectory Graph Copilot}, a novel framework that acts as a ``copilot'' for LLM agents by diagnosing potential action errors before they are executed. At its core,\textit{Graph Debugger} models historical trajectories as a probabilistic graph and uses a Graph Neural Network to identify sequential action patterns that frequently lead to failure. Functioning as a proactive diagnostic sandbox, our method provides early warnings on potentially flawed actions, prompting the agent to self-correct. This pre-action error diagnosis prevents costly mistakes, significantly enhancing the agent's ability to complete long-horizon tasks successfully. The extensive experiments on four benchmarks with three LLM agents demonstrate a $14.69\%$ pass ratio improvement on average.

</details>


### [120] [VAmoS Bench: Voice Agent Simulation Bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27453)
*Joshua Meyer,Sahar Shayegan,Ritiz Tambi,Ali Khan,Sun Kim,Victor Shih,Mehdi Jamei,Andi Partovi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A new end-to-end benchmark for voice agents in customer support, VAmoS Bench, evaluating containment (call resolution) with simulated callers and a stateful backend across 100 scenarios, including adversarial pressure and tool-enabled SQL access, enabling evolving leaderboards.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks emphasize component quality (WER, latency, naturalness) rather than end-to-end containment in phone calls. There is a need for a realistic, end-to-end evaluation platform that measures whether a voice agent can resolve calls autonomously and safely, including correct data updates and privacy safeguards.

Method: A simulator-based benchmark where an agent Riley (credit-card support) interacts with 100 scenarios. Each scenario provides a private goal, a seeded PostgreSQL backend, and a simulated caller via audio. The agent has five real SQL tools to interact with the backend; binary assertions define expected outcomes. A grader assesses the full dialogue, tool usage, and backend state changes to ensure correctness and privacy. The setup supports a leaderboard and extensibility to additional tasks and scenarios in future versions.

Result: Introduction of VAmoS Bench with an end-to-end evaluation protocol for voice agents in financial-services scenarios, including stateful backends, adversarial callers, and a traceable grader. Demonstrates the feasibility of end-to-end containment measurement and paves the way for multiple versions and expanded tasks.

Conclusion: The paper presents a first version of an end-to-end, stateful voice-agent benchmark focused on containment in financial services, with a scalable evaluation framework and a pathway for future extensions and broader domains.

Abstract: Production voice agents span cascaded, speech-to-speech, and hybrid architectures. Voice-agent benchmarks typically measure component quality and conversational properties such as word error rate, latency, naturalness, and turn-taking. Fewer measure whether the agent handled a phone call correctly on its own. Contact centers refer to this as ``containment'': the share of phone calls the automated system resolves without handing off to a human. On some phone calls the right outcome is refusal or a redirect. To address this gap, we introduce VAmoS Bench, the Voice Agent Simulation Bench. It measures complete voice-agent systems end to end in a stateful customer-support task. The agent is Riley, a credit-card support representative for a fictional bank who can freeze, cancel, replace, or activate a card. Each of 100 scenarios supplies a simulated caller with a private goal and a seeded PostgreSQL backend. The platform uses each scenario to populate and activate an isolated simulation in which the caller reaches Riley over audio; roughly one-third apply adversarial pressure. The agent can use five tools that execute real SQL against the backend. Each scenario also defines binary assertions. A grader evaluates them against the complete trace of what the caller and agent said and what the agent did, including tool invocations, arguments, and returned rows. This catches an agent that claims to have changed a card without updating the database, as well as one that makes the right database change while disclosing protected information. This first benchmark version focuses on financial services. Its evaluation protocol supports an evolving leaderboard: additional voice agents can be evaluated on the same version, while later versions can expand the tasks and scenarios.

</details>


### [121] [Skill Use or Skill Theater? Evaluating the Reasoning Backroom in Skill-Augmented Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27484)
*Jinwei Hu,Yi Qi,Xinmiao Huang,Youcheng Sun,Yi Dong,Xiaowei Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces BACKTRACE to audit skill-conditioned reasoning in language agents by pairing each skill-based answer with a counterfactual no-skill response, intervening on various aspects of skills, and eliciting attribution after commitment, instantiated as BACKROOMBench to reveal a general AI provenance gap (Reasoning Backroom).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the mismatch between claimed skill use and actual influence on decisions, and to establish robust provenance auditing for skill-augmented language agents across domains and model families.

Method: Develop BACKTRACE evaluation framework pairing skill-conditioned answers with matched no-skill counterfactuals, perform interventions on skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment, and elicit attribution only after the answer is committed. Implement as BACKROOMBench—a verified testbed spanning controlled logic and competition mathematics, multiple skill conditions, single- and multi-agent settings, and diverse model families.

Result: Reveals pervasive provenance failure: stated skill use remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary; evidence of silent uptake and performative use; behavioral effects align with procedural content more than skill identity; attributions are sensitive to artifact availability; standard detectors fail to identify true skill dependence; in multi-agent settings, skill influence can persist despite source loss, while teams still name unused skills; demonstrates Reasoning Backroom as a general AI provenance problem requiring intervention.

Conclusion: The Reasoning Backroom is a general AI provenance problem that necessitates active auditing through interventions; conventional, observational indicators of skill use are insufficient to reveal actual causal influence, underscoring the need for frameworks like BACKTRACE/BACKROOMBench to diagnose and validate skill-based reasoning in AI systems.

Abstract: Reusable skills are becoming a standard interface for extending language agents with task procedures. Yet evaluators usually infer skill use from visible reasoning or the agent's own attribution. These signals show what the agent appears to use, not whether the skill changed its decision. We ask whether skill-augmented agents exhibit a \textbf{Reasoning Backroom}, a systematic gap between stated skill use and intervention-measured influence. We introduce BACKTRACE, an evaluation framework that pairs each skill-conditioned answer with a matched no-skill counterfactual, intervenes on skill meaning, wording, identity, content, and assignment, and elicits attribution only after the answer is committed. We instantiate the framework as BACKROOMBench, a verified testbed spanning controlled logic and competition mathematics, multiple skill conditions, single-agent and multi-agent settings, and diverse model families. Our evaluation reveals a pervasive provenance failure. Across models and domains, stated skill use often remains stable while causal reliance and signed utility vary, producing both silent uptake and performative use. Behavioral effects follow procedural content more reliably than displayed skill identity, whereas stated attributions respond strongly to artifact availability. Observational detectors based on direct skill-use claims, text mentions, trace similarity, and an LLM judge do not identify which decisions actually depend on the skill. In multi-agent systems, skill influence can survive communication even after its source is lost, while no-skill teams still name skills and sources that were never supplied. These findings establish the Reasoning Backroom as a general AI provenance problem whose audit requires intervention.

</details>


### [122] [INCLAIR: Inception-Based Longitudinal Clinical Anomaly Detection with Informed Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27487)
*Maxx Richard Rahman,Wolfgang Maass*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: INCLAIR is a framework for anomaly detection in longitudinal clinical profiles that scores observations against historical contexts, uses U-statistic-based aggregation with incomplete-subset approximations to control complexity, and provides grounded natural-language explanations; it outperforms baselines across three datasets and shows actionable results in a case study with steroid profiles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical data is clinically important but challenging due to sparse abnormal evidence, unequal sequence lengths, and the need for interpretable explanations under limited expert supervision.

Method: Score each observation against multiple historical contexts; aggregate at profile level; generate grounded natural-language explanations. Under within-profile exchangeability, the complete mean subsequence score forms an order-l U-statistic; provide variance decomposition and an incomplete-subset approximation to keep combinatorial cost independent of profile length. Show mean aggregation attenuates localized anomalies by a factor dependent on anomaly support and profile length; motivate top-k pooling chosen by validation. Empirically validate on three clinical datasets; include a case study on longitudinal steroid profiles with DNA-supported expert assessments.

Result: INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across three clinical datasets. The case study demonstrates alignment between INCLAIR's predictions/explanations and domain-expert assessments supported by DNA analysis, indicating clinically actionable anomaly detection with limited supervision.

Conclusion: INCLAIR enables actionable anomaly detection in longitudinal clinical profiles under limited expert supervision by providing robust scoring, interpretable explanations, and scalable inference.

Abstract: Detecting anomalies in longitudinal clinical profiles is clinically important but difficult: abnormal evidence is often sparse, patient histories have unequal length, and expert explanations are costly. We propose INCLAIR, a framework that scores each observation against multiple historical contexts, aggregates evidence at the profile level, and generates grounded natural-language explanations under limited expert supervision. Under stated within-profile exchangeability assumptions, the complete mean subsequence score takes an order-$l$ U-statistic form, yielding a variance decomposition and an incomplete-subset approximation that controls combinatorial inference cost independently of profile length. The same analysis shows that mean aggregation attenuates localized anomalies by a factor set by the anomaly support and profile length, motivating validation-selected top-$k$ pooling. Across three clinical datasets, INCLAIR consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. We further validate practical relevance through a case study on longitudinal steroid profiles, comparing INCLAIR's predictions and explanations against domain-expert assessments supported by DNA analysis. The results show that INCLAIR enables clinically actionable anomaly detection under limited expert supervision.

</details>


### [123] [MedLLM: An Open Medical Language Model at the Sub-Billion Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27490)
*Maxx Richard Rahman,Asim Ahmed,Mihan Mohagheghzadeh,Wolfgang Maass*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MedLLM shows that a compact 0.1B medical LLM, trained through a fully open three-phase pipeline, can rival larger 7B models on certain medical tasks and reveal a task-type dependent degradation pattern when compressed. 


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Characterize sub-billion parameter medical LLMs and assess whether small, open models can achieve practical medical competence across key benchmarks, addressing the gap left by large 7B+ models and closed pipelines.

Method: Three-phase open pipeline: (1) general pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, (2) domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb (a reference-guided medical corpus derived from general web data via embedding similarity to medical QA data), and (3) preference-aligned fine-tuning combining supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO).

Result: At sub-billion scale, medical competence dissociates by task: context-grounded QA is within 2.9 percentage points of a medically adapted 7B model and beats 7B baselines; knowledge-recall QA is weak on clinical-vignette MedQA but excels on MedMCQA relative to all 7B/sub-7B baselines. This dissociation is masked at 7B when both capabilities co-occur but becomes evident as capacity shrinks.

Conclusion: Sub-billion medical LLMs can achieve competitive performance in some tasks while lagging in others, highlighting a capacity-driven trade-off between retrieval-based recall and grounded reasoning. Open pipelines and targeted fine-tuning strategies enable practical medical competence at small scales, though limitations emerge under severe compression.

Abstract: Open medical language models have converged on a single scale: every widely used system runs at 7B parameters or more, leaving the sub-billion regime uncharacterized. We present MedLLM, an open 0.1B-parameter medical language model trained through a fully open three-phase pipeline: general pretraining with curriculum sequence-length scheduling, domain fine-tuning on MedFineWeb, a reference-guided medical corpus we release that is selected from general web data by embedding similarity to medical question-answering (QA) data, and preference-aligned fine-tuning combining SFT with direct preference optimization (DPO). Across medical benchmarks, MedLLM shows a pattern visible only at sub-billion scale: medical competence does not degrade uniformly under compression but splits by task type. On context-grounded QA it comes within $2.9$pp of a medically adapted 7B model and surpasses the instruction-tuned and general-purpose 7B baselines; on knowledge-recall QA it stays near the task floor on clinical-vignette MedQA yet significantly exceeds every 7B and sub-7B baseline on MedMCQA, indicating that where recall fails the constraint is model capacity rather than adaptation. This dissociation is masked at 7B, where both capabilities are present, and surfaces only when capacity is scarce.

</details>


### [124] [A dataset of rated conceptual arguments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27499)
*Emery Cooper,Caspar Oesterheld,Linh Chi Nguyen,Alexander Kastner,Ethan Perez*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A dataset and evaluation framework for conceptual questions: 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts across AI safety, ethics, etc.; six expert raters evaluate centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity; two scoring functions proposed; benchmarks across models showing performance tracks general capability rankings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address evaluation of conceptual questions lacking ground-truth or standard resolution methods by leveraging reliably evaluable structured arguments and expert judgments.

Method: Assemble a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts spanning AI safety, decision theory, ethics, and politics. Obtain 1,458 ratings by six expert raters on dimensions such as centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. Propose two scoring functions and benchmark a range of models on the dataset.

Result: Introduces a resource and evaluation approach for conceptual reasoning; performance across models correlates with general capability rankings, suggesting the method captures meaningful differences in argumentative quality.

Conclusion: The dataset and scoring framework offer a way to evaluate model reasoning on ill-defined conceptual questions through structured arguments, with potential applications in AI safety, ethics, and related fields; performance mirrors general capability differences among models.

Abstract: Large language models have improved rapidly on tasks with verifiable answers, such as mathematics and programming. Much less is known about their ability to reason about what we call conceptual questions: questions for which no ground truth is realistically accessible and no widely accepted resolution methodology exists, but on which progress can still be made by debating arguments. Most philosophical questions are of this kind, as are central components of questions in AI safety, decision theory, and social choice. Our approach is based on the view that while bottom-line conclusions on such questions are hard to evaluate, individual contextualized arguments can be evaluated far more reliably. We therefore introduce a dataset of 951 argumentative critiques of 442 position texts, spanning topics from AI safety and decision theory to ethics and politics, with 1,458 ratings by six expert raters along dimensions including centrality, strength, correctness, and clarity. We propose two scoring functions and benchmark a range of models. Performance tracks general capability rankings.

</details>


### [125] [Automated Transcript Analysis for Detecting Flaws in Agentic Benchmarks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27518)
