*Jeff Mohl,Nelson Gardner-Challis,Magda Dubois,Harry Coppock,Benjamin Allan-Rahill,Kaelan Yim,Damian Sójka,James Mann,Justin Olive*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AI scanners can detect four types of validity problems in benchmark transcripts (ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, answer-format ambiguity) and, evaluated on Inspect Evals benchmarks, reveal quality issues in multiple widely used benchmarks; results are promising but uneven across benchmarks and criteria, highlighting challenges and the need for standardization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Manual audits of benchmarks are labor-intensive and prone to missing flaws; automated scanners offer scalable quality assurance to ensure benchmark validity for frontier-model assessments.

Method: Developed four scanners targeting ground-truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer-format ambiguity; created grading rubrics to guide human labeling; evaluated scanners against human labels on a held-out Inspect Evals benchmark set; applied to five widely used benchmarks to surface validity issues.

Result: Scanners identified several verified quality issues in five benchmarks, including issues unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection; however, not all issues were detected, and scanner performance varied across benchmarks, criteria, and models.

Conclusion: Automated transcript analysis is a feasible proof-of-concept for auditing benchmark quality at scale; findings underscore broader standardization gaps and open challenges in scanner design, suggesting areas for methodological improvement to strengthen future QA claims.

Abstract: Capabilities of frontier models are often assessed using agentic benchmarks. To trust these results, benchmarks must accurately measure what they claim to and be free from invalidating flaws. Previous manual audits of benchmarks such as SWE-Bench-Verified have uncovered several validity issues in transcripts. However, manual review is difficult to scale, and it is unclear whether automated methods can reliably surface flaws that compromise benchmark validity. In this paper, we developed AI scanners to detect four types of validity issues: ground truth access, tool failure, guessing vulnerability, and answer format ambiguity. We produced grading rubrics for each to instruct human labeling, and evaluated the scanners against human labels on a held-out test set of Inspect Evals benchmarks. Our scanners identified several verified quality issues in five widely used benchmarks, including cases unlikely to be caught by random manual inspection. Not all cases were identified, and scanner performance varied substantially across benchmarks, criteria and models. We highlight several open challenges to be addressed to improve scanners for stronger quality assurance claims, including broader standardization gaps in the evaluation field that degrade scanner performance. Together, these results serve as a proof of concept for using automated transcript analysis to audit benchmark quality more broadly.

</details>


### [126] [AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27547)
*Brady D. Lund,Zoë Abbie Teel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Reconceptualizes AI literacy as a critical, agentive practice rooted in power-knowledge, not mere technical skill; proposes a three-part framework (contextual use, critical interrogation, participatory governance) to empower individuals as epistemic agents and address inequalities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address limitations of consumer-oriented AI literacy that reproduce epistemic injustices and to advance a framework that enables critical evaluation, resistance to structuring assumptions, and governance participation in AI systems.

Method: Theoretical synthesis drawing on Foucault's power-knowledge, Freire's critical pedagogy, and digital literacy scholarship; constructs a three-part AI literacy framework and discusses its implications for empowerment and governance.

Result: Introduces a three-part AI literacy framework oriented toward empowerment and governance, reframing literacy as epistemic agency rather than consumer competence; highlights structural inequities as a central concern.

Conclusion: AI literacy should cultivate epistemic agents capable of contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance, thereby mitigating epistemic injustice and expanding inclusive governance of AI technologies.

Abstract: As generative artificial intelligence becomes one of the most significant systems of knowledge production in our society today, questions relating to who can access and shape that production grow increasingly important in our discourse. This paper argues that the existing frameworks for AI literacy, which are dominated by technical competency and responsible-use principles, are insufficient because they enforce a "consumer" orientation toward AI rather than fostering genuine epistemic agency. Based upon Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and scholarship of digital literacy, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of AI literacy as a critical practice that equips individuals not just to use AI systems, but to critically evaluate them, resist their structuring assumptions, and participate in their governance. The paper further argues that unequal access to AI tools in society recapitulates longstanding epistemic injustices, and that a literacy framework oriented toward empowerment must account for these structural inequities. A three-part framework of AI literacy based on the notions of contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance frames this literacy as a cultivation of epistemic "agents" rather than the training of competent consumers of AI-generated information.

</details>


### [127] [Using Large Language Models for Idea Generation in Innovation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27553)
*Lennart Meincke,Karan Girotra,Gideon Nave,Christian Terwiesch,Karl T. Ulrich*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs (GPT-4) produce higher-average-purchase-intent product ideas than human brainstorms for a $50 college-targeted market, with few-shot prompting outperforming zero-shot; however, AI ideas are less novel and more similar, especially with few-shot; yet AI dominates top-tier idea ranking (7x more likely to be in top 10%), implying strong quality and potential productivity gains despite reduced diversity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether large language models can generate high-quality, market-ready product ideas targeting college students at a $50 price point, and compare AI-generated ideas to human-generated ideas across quality, novelty, and diversity.

Method: Three pools of ideas (pre-LLM human-generated; GPT-4 zero-shot; GPT-4 few-shot). Assess quality via predicted purchase intent using standard market research techniques; assess similarity via text mining; assess novelty via human ratings. Compare average quality vs. top-decile performance.

Result: AI-generated ideas show higher average predicted purchase intent than human-generated ideas; few-shot prompting yields slightly higher intent than zero-shot; AI ideas are perceived as less novel and more similar, with the few-shot set most similar; however, AI ideas are seven times more likely to rank in the top 10% of ideas, indicating a strong relative advantage for high-quality ideas and a conservative estimate of productivity gains.

Conclusion: AI creativity substantially benefits new product development by delivering higher-quality ideas and superior top-decile performance, albeit with drawbacks in novelty and solution diversity; productivity gains from AI may be substantial but are not fully captured in the study.

Abstract: This research evaluates the efficacy of large language models (LLMs) in generating new product ideas. To do so, we compare three pools of ideas for new products targeted toward college students and priced at 50 dollars or less. The first pool of ideas was created by university students in a product design course before the availability of LLMs. The second and third pools of ideas were generated by GPT-4 from OpenAI using zero-shot and few-shot prompting, respectively. We evaluated idea quality using standard market research techniques to predict average purchase intent probability. We used text mining to assess idea similarity and human raters to evaluate idea novelty. We find that AI-generated ideas outperform human-generated ideas in terms of average purchase intent, with few-shot prompting yielding slightly higher intent than zero-shot prompting. However, AI-generated ideas are perceived as less novel and exhibit higher pairwise similarity, particularly with few-shot prompting, indicating a less diverse solution landscape. When focusing on the quality of the best ideas rather than the average ideas, we find that AI-generated ideas are seven times more likely to rank among the top 10 percent of ideas, demonstrating a significant advantage over human-generated ideas. We propose that this seven-to-one advantage is a conservative estimate because it does not account for the greater productivity of AI. Our findings suggest that despite some drawbacks, AI creativity presents a substantial benefit in generating high-quality ideas for new product development.

</details>


### [128] [Evaluating Agentic Bioinformatics through Function, Evidence, and Validation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27556)
*Phuc Pham,Truong-Son Hy*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces the Function–Evidence–Validation (FEV) framework for evaluating agentic bioinformatics by focusing on the inspectable workflow trajectory, mapping 109 systems and 28 resources across domains, and highlighting gaps in replayability and validation; advocates workflow-correctness as the evaluation criterion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address credibility gaps for large language model (LLM) agents in bioinformatics by moving beyond final outputs and architectures to the auditability and traceability of complete workflows.

Method: Proposes the FEV framework comprising Function (demonstrated workflow operations), Evidence (traceable support for actions/claims), and Validation (use-case-specific checks). Applies FEV to a survey of 109 agentic or agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark resources, spanning genomics, single-cell/spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation, covering 128 publications.

Result: FEV provides a practical basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows. Across domains, planning and tool-mediated execution outpace replayability, provenance, validation, external testing, and prospective evaluation, indicating a gap between capability and accountability.

Conclusion: Agentic bioinformatics should be evaluated through workflow correctness, not only final answers. FEV offers a concrete framework for cross-domain comparison and the development of transparent, auditable workflows that support scientific accountability and potential standardization.

Abstract: Large language model agents increasingly plan, execute, and interpret biological analyses, yet fluent responses, successful tool calls, and benchmark performance alone do not establish scientific credibility. Existing reviews primarily organize biological agents by application, architecture, and agentic capability, but do not jointly operationalize the accountability of agent-generated workflows. We address this gap by treating the inspectable workflow trajectory, rather than architecture or final output alone, as the primary unit of analysis. We introduce the Function--Evidence--Validation (FEV) framework, which separates demonstrated workflow operations, traceable support for actions and claims, and use-case-specific validation. Using FEV, we map 109 agentic or agent-adjacent systems and 28 benchmark or evaluation resources, representing 128 unique publications across genomics, single-cell and spatial omics, protein science, drug discovery, computational pathology, and general bioinformatics automation. Across domains, planning and tool-mediated execution have advanced more rapidly than replayability, provenance, robust scientific assessment, external validation, and prospective empirical testing. We therefore argue that agentic bioinformatics should be assessed through workflow correctness rather than final-answer correctness alone. FEV provides a practical basis for comparing systems and designing transparent, auditable, and scientifically accountable bioinformatics workflows.

</details>


### [129] [DeepResearch Agent System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27562)
*Yong Huang,Yulu Huang,for the team Collaboration*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A sparsely activated, 30B-parameter LLM with 3B active per token achieves faster inference, a 128K context window, and dual-mode reasoning (ReAct + IterResearch) with multi-tool coordination and RL optimization, yielding strong benchmark performance and full open-sourcing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve deep information retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and autonomous research tasks by increasing context length, efficiency, and robustness of tool-use in LLMs, while enabling scalable, open research.

Method: Sparse-activation architecture (30B total, 3B active per token); 128K-context with hierarchical attention; dual-mode reasoning (ReAct for base solving, IterResearch for iterative research up to 20 steps); multi-tool coordination (retrieval, computation, web search, file parsing); GRPO-based reinforcement learning with token-level policy gradients; automated seed-based data synthesis; fully open-source data, training, and inference code.

Result: 3.2× faster inference vs dense models of equal scale; 128K context enables 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall gains over standard long-context baselines; IterResearch yields 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass; 92.1% tool-use accuracy; GRPO improves training stability by 35% and convergence by 42%; seed-based data synthesis achieves 92.5% usability; benchmarks: 87.3% Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% BrowserComp Chinese, 91.2% WebWalkerQA; fully open-sourced.

Conclusion: The system demonstrates strong, scalable performance for agent-based research tasks, combining efficient sparse computation, extended context, robust multi-tool coordination, and RL-based optimization, with broad openness for academic, business, and educational applications.

Abstract: The DeepResearch Agent System is a large language model system engineered for deep information retrieval, multi-step reasoning, and autonomous research tasks. Built upon a sparse activation architecture with 30 billion total parameters of which only 3 billion are activated per token, the system achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple agent search benchmarks while delivering 3.2 times faster inference compared to dense counterparts of equivalent scale. The system supports a 128K-token context window with hierarchical attention mechanisms that yield 18.7% accuracy and 23.4% recall improvements over standard long-context approaches. A dual-mode reasoning engine provides both a ReAct paradigm for basic multi-step problem solving and an IterResearch mode for high-performance iterative research with up to 20 reasoning steps, collectively delivering a 31.2% accuracy improvement over single-pass baselines. Multi-tool coordination integrates retrieval, computation, web search, and file parsing modules to achieve 92.1% tool-use accuracy. A reinforcement learning optimization framework based on the GRPO algorithm provides token-level policy gradients that improve training stability by 35% and accelerate convergence by 42%. An automated data synthesis pipeline with seed-based expansion achieves a 92.5% usability rate. Benchmark results include 87.3% on Humanity's Last Exam, 85.3% on BrowserComp Chinese, and 91.2% on WebWalkerQA. The system is fully open-sourced, including data synthesis, training, and inference code, and supports applications in academic research, business analysis, R&D support, and education.

</details>


### [130] [What makes prompts a graph: necessary and sufficient conditions for prompt graph engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27578)
*Sandeco Macedo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes an operational definition and vocabulary for prompt graph engineering, treating prompts as executable graph nodes, with four conditions and a practical test, validated against six systems; concludes with a research agenda.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a gap between industry practice of graph-based orchestration in LLM pipelines and a stable vocabulary. A reference definition is needed to unify concepts, enable reproducibility, and guide tooling across systems like LangGraph, DSPy, and Prompt Flow.

Method: Conceptual analysis of sources with persistent identifiers augmented by primary grey literature; genealogical reconstruction from dataflow and build systems to prompt chaining and graph topologies; define a constitutive notion of prompt graph engineering; derive four conditions; craft an inclusion/exclusion test; apply to six systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, Claude Code subagents); delineate neighboring concepts; propose a four-axis design tension research agenda.

Result: Constitutive definition of prompt graph engineering; four conditions: explicit structure, separation between structure and prompt content, executable semantics, and graph as a first-class engineering artifact; an inclusion/exclusion test; boundary with six neighboring concepts; empirical validation by matching six systems; closes with a research agenda.

Conclusion: Delivers an operational definition and shared vocabulary for a practice already used in industry, enabling clearer communication and reproducibility, and sets the stage for future methodological work via a four-axis design tension framework.

Abstract: Prompts stopped being isolated strings some time ago. In real systems, one model call feeds another, retrieval interleaves with generation, routers branch, and aggregators merge parallel results. Practice converged on a single structure to hold this together: the graph. Frameworks such as LangGraph, DSPy, and Prompt Flow expose it openly, and research systems already optimize it automatically. The vocabulary, however, lags behind. Graph names, variously, a reasoning topology inside one sampling strategy, a multi-agent conversation, or an orchestration artifact, while prompt engineering still evokes writing one good string. What is missing is a reference definition treating prompts as nodes of an explicit, executable, improvable graph. We build that definition through conceptual analysis over sources with persistent identifiers, complemented by primary grey literature. We reconstruct the genealogy of the idea, from dataflow graphs and build systems, through prompt chaining and the thought topologies (chain, tree, graph), to graphs compiled and optimized as artifacts. We then propose a constitutive definition of prompt graph engineering, state its four conditions (explicit structure, separation between structure and prompt content, executable semantics, and the graph as a first-class engineering artifact), and operationalize them as an inclusion and exclusion test. We draw the boundary against six neighboring concepts and apply the test to six real systems (LangGraph, DSPy, Prompt Flow, AutoGen, CrewAI, and Claude Code subagents); it includes and excludes consistently. We close with a research agenda organized along four design tension axes. The contribution is an operational definition and a shared vocabulary for a practice that industry already exercises daily without naming precisely.

</details>


### [131] [From Minds to Models: The Intersection of Psychology and LLM Behaviours](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27579)
*Oliver Guidetti,Reza Ryan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Weak, analysis-dependent evidence of racial sentiment differences in LLM prompts; results lack robustness and interpretability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether prompt-based IAT-style methods reveal racial sentiment biases in LLMs and contribute to understanding model bias in high-stakes domains.

Method: 14 base questions x 8 racial conditions + race-agnostic control (126 prompts); responses from GPT-3.5T, GPT-4, GPT-4T (n=378); sentiment scoring via categorical labels; two-way ANOVA; rank-transformed sensitivity check; Tukey-corrected post hoc analyses.

Result: Small main effect of racial condition in the original analysis; no main effect of model; no interaction; effect not retained after rank transformation; Tukey-corrected comparisons show no significant pairwise differences; one post hoc uncorrected European–Indigenous Australian difference reported as hypothesis-generating; overall evidence weak and analysis-dependent.

Conclusion: Highlights limitations of sentiment scoring for bias assessment; prompts the need for design improvements and interdisciplinary development of behavioural measures of model bias.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often compared with the human mind because their decision-making is complex, non-linear and difficult to interpret. Psychological methods developed to investigate unobservable mental processes may therefore help examine LLM behaviour, particularly in government and healthcare. Building on prompt-based adaptations of the Implicit Association Test, this study tested whether ChatGPT produced sentiment differences across racial conditions in open-ended text. Fourteen base questions were crossed with eight racial categories and a race-agnostic control, producing 126 prompts. Each was submitted once to GPT-3.5T, GPT-4 and GPT-4T, yielding 378 responses. Sentiment scores were derived from categorical labels and source scores: positive labels retained the source score, negative labels were assigned its negative, and neutral responses were coded zero. A two-way ANOVA found a small main effect of racial condition, F(8, 351) = 2.04, p = .042, partial-eta squared = .044, but no effect of model, F(2, 351) = 0.07, p = .933, and no interaction, F(16, 351) = 0.23, p = .999. However, the effect was not retained in a rank-transformed sensitivity analysis, F(8, 351) = 1.53, p = .145, and Tukey-corrected comparisons found no significant pairwise differences. An uncorrected European-Indigenous Australian comparison was significant, but was selected post hoc and is reported only as hypothesis-generating. Evidence for sentiment differences was therefore weak and analysis-dependent. Sentiment scoring also cannot distinguish evaluative bias from the valence of historical content elicited by a prompt. We outline design changes needed to address these limitations and argue for interdisciplinary development of behavioural measures of model bias.
  Keywords: Implicit Bias, Psychological Research Methods, Artificial Intelligence, ChatGPT, Large Language Models, Sentiment Analysis

</details>


### [132] [Wiring diagram extraction and gluing: a case study in classifying figure skating jumps using 3D dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27598)
*Jason Lo,Mohammadnima Jafari*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces a gluing wiring diagram theory to compose iterative Hasse clustering, achieving the same result as a single run; validated on figure skating jump videos.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Hasse clustering faces combinatorial explosion as the number of expected clusters grows, making it infeasible; a compositional framework is sought to scale clustering on sequential data.

Method: Develop a theory of gluing wiring diagrams that allows iterative applications of Hasse clustering to be equivalent to a single application; apply and test this approach on a dataset of videos of figure skating jumps.

Result: The framework shows that iterative, glued applications can reproduce the outcome of a single Hasse clustering run; the authors test and illustrate the approach on the task of classifying figure skating jumps in video data.

Conclusion: A scalable, compositional approach to Hasse clustering is presented via gluing wiring diagrams, enabling iterative composition to match one-shot results; demonstrated in a computer-vision classification task with potential applicability to other sequential data domains.

Abstract: Hasse clustering is an algorithm that extracts common patterns in sequential data and represents them in graphical forms. As the number of expected clusters grows, however, the algorithm can become infeasible to run due to combinatorial complexity. In this article, we describe a theory of gluing wiring diagrams, allowing iterative applications of Hasse clustering to achieve the same result as a single application. We test our theory in the context of classifying videos of figure skating jumps.

</details>


### [133] [World Action Planner: Generalizable Decision-Making with Action-Conditioned World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27599)
*Xiangcheng Zhang,Yilun Du*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces World Action Planner, a robot planning system that combines Vision-Language Model reasoning with a pose-image conditioned world model to plan and iteratively refine actions via imagined rollouts, achieving strong generalization to new scenes and tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the generalization gap of imitation-learning policies when facing novel scenes and tasks; need a planning+world-model approach that leverages perception-grounded reasoning.

Method: Use a Vision-Language Model for reasoning to propose initial action plans; employ a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model for physical grounding; iteratively refine plans through optimization and search over imagined rollouts.

Result: Outperforms state-of-the-art end-to-end policy models (e.g., VLAs, WAMs) across compositional tasks, novel layouts, and zero-shot generalization scenarios.

Conclusion: Integrating VLM-based reasoning with a grounded, conditioned world model and planning over imagined rollouts enhances generalization and task execution in robotic agents.

Abstract: Building generalizable agents for diverse applications remains a fundamental challenge. While imitation learning-based policies succeed in specific training environments, they often fail to generalize to novel scenes and tasks. In this work, we propose World Action Planner, a robot planning system that leverages the reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and the physical grounding of a multi-task pose-image conditioned world model. Our system enables an agent to propose initial action plans and iteratively refine them via optimization and search, reasoning over imagined world model rollouts. We demonstrate that our approach achieves superior performance across compositional tasks, new layouts, and zero-shot generalization scenarios, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art end-to-end policy models such as VLAs and WAMs. Project website at worldactionplanner.github.io

</details>


### [134] [CORE: In-Context Reconstruction for Unified Tabular Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27615)
*Yunfeng Zhao,Qingfeng Chen,Yue Tan,Shiyuan Li,Yili Wang,Yixin Liu,Shirui Pan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CORE introduces decorrelated feature alignment and in-context reconstruction for unified tabular anomaly detection, avoiding labeled/synthesized anomalies and aiming for generalization across unseen datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unified TAD suffers from semantic loss in alignment and reliance on binary classification with synthetic anomalies; a context-aware reconstruction approach can capture dataset-specific normal distributions without labels.

Method: Two modules: (1) decorrelated feature alignment to map heterogeneous features into a unified semantic space while preserving information; (2) in-context reconstruction that reconstructs each sample from normal context, using reconstruction error as anomaly score; no labeled or synthetic anomalies required; supports unseen datasets.

Result: Demonstrates improved cross-dataset generalization and robustness in anomaly scoring across unseen tabular datasets, by leveraging context-based normal distributions and semantic-preserving alignment.

Conclusion: CORE provides a principled unified TAD framework with semantic-preserving alignment and context-based reconstruction, enabling effective anomaly detection on arbitrary unseen tabular datasets without labeled anomalies.

Abstract: Tabular anomaly detection (TAD), which focuses on identifying abnormal samples that deviate from the majority in tabular data, has received growing attention. Recently, there has been an emerging trend towards unified TAD, which seeks to detect anomalies across different datasets using a single generalizable model. In unified TAD, aligning heterogeneous data remains challenging. While existing methods often rely on distance-based unified feature construction, they may obscure the semantics of the original features. Moreover, existing approaches typically formulate anomaly detection as a binary classification task, which may overlook diverse anomaly patterns from various datasets and be misled by unrepresentative synthetic anomalies. To address these challenges, we propose an in-COntext REconstruction approach for unified TAD (CORE for short). It introduces a decorrelated feature alignment module to directly align heterogeneous features into a unified representation space, which retains their semantic information. Meanwhile, CORE formulates unified TAD as an in-context reconstruction problem, eliminating the need for labeled or synthesized anomalies. Specifically, the in-context reconstruction module reconstructs each sample by leveraging contextual normal samples to capture dataset-specific distributions, such that reconstruction errors reflect its deviation from normality, facilitating unified TAD on arbitrary unseen datasets.

</details>


### [135] [HALO: Heterogeneous Admission through Localized Obligations for Safe Agentic Execution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27636)
*Taewoo Park,Kyeonghyun Yoo,Kiseok Kim,Seunghyun Yoo,Hwangnam Kim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HALO introduces a runtime protocol for agentic AI that preserves components with valid prerequisites, rechecks each action before dispatch, and replaces blocked actions with fresh candidates. It prevents stale or dependent actions from propagating and outperforms a whole-response policy across tests, including structured replay and robotic simulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic AI responses are heterogeneous and contain interdependent components. Prerequisites can become invalid as conditions change, so rejecting an entire response wastes usable parts and independent checks risk orphaned dependencies. HALO aims to maintain usable components while ensuring safety by reevaluating actions.

Method: HALO maintains support for components only if their declared prerequisites remain supported, performs a recheck of each exact action prior to dispatch, and substitutes blocked actions with new candidates rather than discarding them entirely. Evaluation includes structured-response replay and cold-start PX4/Gazebo experiments to test robustness against stale states.

Result: HALO matched all 96 admission expectations and passed all 20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay, it retained 248/248 components (128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes), while a whole-response policy retained 0/248. In ten cold-start PX4/Gazebo sessions HALO blocked every tested stale route, observed no matching stale setpoint, and completed all fresh recoveries.

Conclusion: HALO delivers robust, localized obligation management in agentic AI, preserving useful components despite changing prerequisites, and avoiding propagation of stale or unsafe actions. It demonstrates clear advantages over whole-response policies across multiple evaluation settings.

Abstract: Recent agentic AI systems may return a heterogeneous response containing notices, requests, handoffs, and actions. Conditions can change before external use, so components from the same response need not remain supported together. Rejecting the whole response discards useful components, whereas checking components independently can leave a dependent without its prerequisite. We present Heterogeneous Admission with Localized Obligations (HALO), a runtime protocol that preserves supported components whose declared prerequisites also remain supported, rechecks each exact action before dispatch, and allows blocked actions to be replaced only by fresh candidates. HALO matched all 96 admission expectations and passed all 20 protocol tests. In structured-response replay, it retained 248/248 supported components, including 128/128 unaffected by unrelated changes, while a whole-response policy retained 0/248. Across ten cold-start PX4/Gazebo sessions, HALO blocked every tested stale route, observed no matching stale setpoint, and completed all fresh recoveries.

</details>


### [136] [Hidden APIs in Language Models: Discovering Reusable Causal Interfaces from Forked Futures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27617)
*SiYuan Ma,Yiqin Luo,Zhangji,Canran Xiao,Albert Gao,Wei-Hsing Huang,Wei Wang,Qiwei Wu,Xinran Li,Jinfeng Wei,Qixin Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces forked futures to define an empirical causal quotient over LM hidden states; identifies Shared interface as the most economical and best in preserving future-signature fidelity across two LM families; experimental evidence includes two model evaluations, a backbone sweep, transplantation analysis, and a blind model-organism test, with results conditional on architectures and interventions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivated by the observation that identical model outputs can arise from different internal computations; seeks a reusable, architecture-conditional internal interface without relying on researcher-labeled latent variables.

Method: Proposes forked futures where future operations are sampled after a formed prefix state; compares hidden states by the response distributions to these operations. Evaluates four interface types (Shared, Local, Mixture, Distributed) under prequential causal description length while enforcing future-signature fidelity and capacity constraints. Two detailed model evaluations (Qwen2.5-1.5B and Llama-3-8B), a five-backbone sweep, figure-aligned transplantation analysis, API-aligned paths, and a blind four-class model-organism test.

Result: Shared interface yields the lowest held-out description length in both model evaluations (gains of 0.216 nats on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 0.294 nats on Llama-3-8B) while keeping future-signature distortion tightly clustered. Five-backbone sweep preserves the positive Sharedness Gain. Transplantation analysis shows Shared achieving the strongest joint target-correctness, locality, copy-preservation, and composite profile; API-aligned paths account for 0.749 of the target effect versus 0.150 for matched null paths. In the blind four-class model-organism test, 14/16 architectures are recovered with one non-Shared→Shared error among 12 non-Shared organisms.

Conclusion: The results support an economical, reusable causal interface within the tested operation banks, with conclusions conditioned on candidate architectures, interventions, and held-out futures.

Abstract: Identical language-model answers can arise from hidden states that support different future computations, so current-answer probes do not establish a reusable internal interface. We introduce forked futures: future operations are sampled only after a prefix state has formed, and states are compared through the response distributions induced by those operations. This yields an empirical causal quotient over hidden states without requiring researcher-specified latent labels. Shared, Local, Mixture, and Distributed interfaces then compete under prequential causal description length subject to future-signature fidelity and matched capacity constraints. In the two detailed model evaluations, Shared has the lowest held-out description length, with gains of 0.216 nats on Qwen2.5-1.5B and 0.294 nats on Llama-3-8B, while maintaining tightly clustered mean future-signature distortion; a five-backbone sweep preserves the positive direction of Sharedness Gain. The figure-aligned transplantation analysis gives Shared the strongest joint target-correctness, locality, copy-preservation, and composite profile, and API-aligned paths mediate 0.749 of the target effect versus 0.150 for matched null paths. In the blind four-class model-organism test, 14/16 architectures are recovered, with one observed non-Shared to Shared error among 12 non-Shared organisms. These results support an economical reusable causal interface within the tested operation banks, while keeping the claim explicitly conditional on the candidate architectures, interventions, and held-out futures.

</details>


### [137] [SCOPE: Synthetic Conditional Objectives for Policy Evolution in Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27630)
*Nguyen Viet Tuan Kiet,Nguyen Huu Duc,Le Cong Bang,Tran Cong Dao,Huynh Thi Thanh Binh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SCOPE introduces synthetic conditional objectives conditioned on search history to guide exploration in black-box combinatorial optimization, fostering diverse candidate policies and improved performance with limited evaluations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In black-box settings, the objective is unknown and expensive to evaluate. There is a need for surrogate objectives that reveal useful preferences to steer search while maintaining diversity and robustness.

Method: An outer loop learns and adaptively selects a set of synthetic objectives conditioned on accumulated search history. An inner loop evolves a portfolio of top policies that generate diverse candidate solutions. These policies are evaluated with the true black-box objective, and the surrogate objectives are updated based on their ability to discover promising regions.

Result: Empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks shows that SCOPE consistently improves performance under tight evaluation budgets and generalizes across diverse combinatorial structures.

Conclusion: Designing objective functions as exploration guides can robustly enhance black-box search, enabling efficient, diverse policy-driven exploration with minimal reliance on the unknown objective.

Abstract: Black-box combinatorial optimization requires systematically identifying high-quality solutions under a limited evaluation budget, yet the unknown objective function provides little guidance for deciding where the search should explore next. We introduce SCOPE, a general framework for Synthetic Conditional Objectives for Policy Evolution in Black-Box Combinatorial Optimization. Rather than directly optimizing the inaccessible objective, SCOPE learns a set of synthetic objectives conditioned on the accumulated search history, where each objective is designed to expose a distinct and potentially useful preference over candidate solutions. These objectives are then used to evolve search policies that generate diverse candidates, whose true quality is subsequently assessed through black-box evaluations. The outer loop adaptively updates and selects synthetic objectives according to how effectively their induced policies discover promising regions. In contrast, the inner loop returns a portfolio of top-performing policies to reduce the risk of relying on a single surrogate preference. This formulation reframes objective design as a mechanism for guiding policy exploration, enabling the search process to exploit observed evidence while maintaining structured diversity across discrete solution spaces. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark problems demonstrate that SCOPE consistently improves black-box search performance under limited evaluation budgets and generalizes well across diverse combinatorial structures.

</details>


### [138] [ReDiPPO: Reference-Guided Value Calibration and Discrepancy-Aware Token Reweighting for Mathematical Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27631)
*Zhenrong Zhang,Fei Wu,Jun Du,Jianshu Zhang,Si Wei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A PPO variant (ReDiPPO) improves mathematical reasoning by using a reference-guided critic plus a discrepancy-based reweighting of token-level advantages, yielding consistent performance gains over PPO, DAPO, and GSPO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon mathematical reasoning with sparse rewards makes token-level credit assignment unreliable; standard critics often misestimate intermediate states, leading to noisy advantages.

Method: Introduce a reference-guided critic that uses reference answers as privileged training-time signals for better value estimation. Retain a standard critic and measure the token-level discrepancy between the standard value and the reference-guided value. Use this discrepancy to reweight token-level advantages in PPO optimization.

Result: ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong policy optimization baselines (PPO, DAPO, GSPO) on final reasoning performance across diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks; code is available at the provided URL.

Conclusion: The combination of a reference-guided value estimator and discrepancy-aware reweighting enhances token-level credit assignment and overall reasoning performance in PPO-based policies for mathematical reasoning tasks; merits include robust improvements and practical availability of code.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning has emerged as an effective paradigm for enhancing the mathematical reasoning capabilities of large language models. Among existing policy optimization methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remains particularly appealing because its learned critic can, in principle, provide token-level credit assignment. However, in mathematical reasoning tasks characterized by long reasoning horizons and sparse outcome rewards, reliable token-level credit assignment remains challenging. The standard critic often fails to accurately evaluate intermediate reasoning states, resulting in noisy advantage estimates and suboptimal policy updates. In this paper, we propose ReDiPPO, a Reference-guided and Discrepancy-aware PPO framework for mathematical reasoning. ReDiPPO introduces a reference-guided critic that uses reference answers as training-time privileged signals to provide more accurate value estimation. Meanwhile, it retains a standard critic and quantifies the token-level reference-standard discrepancy between the standard value estimate and the reference-guided value estimate. This discrepancy serves as an indicator of difficult reasoning states and is used to reweight the corresponding token-level advantages during PPO optimization. Extensive experiments on diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ReDiPPO improves value-estimation accuracy and consistently outperforms strong policy optimization baselines, including PPO, DAPO, and GSPO, in final reasoning performance. Our code is available on https://github.com/cii030/ReDiPPO.

</details>


### [139] [HealthCAT: An Interpretable Encoder-only Transformer Framework for Health Indicator Prediction and Temporal Interpretation of Wearable Sensor Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27635)
*Xiaotong Yu,Joshua Y. Kim,HaeJin Lee,Kalina Yacef*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HealthCAT combines an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token to produce class-specific, time-step-level interpretations for wearable sensor data, enabling domain-aligned interpretability alongside predictive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address lack of interpretability in deep learning for wearable sensor data by providing temporally localized, domain-relevant explanations that map to behavioral cycles.

Method: Use an Encoder-only Transformer architecture augmented with an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to generate time-step-level explanations; map interpretations to domain cycles (e.g., time-of-day). Evaluated on two real-world datasets (n=306).

Result: HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17% in F1-score and 12% in accuracy (p<0.05). Time-step masking experiments show HealthCAT-identified steps are more predictive than random across conditions (p<0.05).

Conclusion: Elicits accurate health indicator predictions with interpretable temporal patterns, enabling health monitoring, behavioural analysis, and intervention design beyond aggregated metrics.

Abstract: Wearable sensors continuously capture fine-grained multivariate time-series data, providing opportunities to model behavioural patterns associated with health outcomes. However, existing deep learning methods prioritise predictive accuracy over interpretability, limiting their application in health research. In this study, we present HealthCAT, a flexible framework that integrates an Encoder-only Transformer with an Attentive Class Activation Token (AttentiveCAT) to generate class-specific, time-step-level interpretations. These interpretations can be mapped back onto behavioural cycles that are relevant to the domain (e.g., time-of-day), supporting individual-level analysis of wearable sensor data. We evaluated HealthCAT using two real-world wearable sensor datasets (306 participants in total). HealthCAT outperformed deep learning baselines by up to 17\% in F1-score and 12\% in accuracy on both datasets ($p<0.05$). In masking experiments, the time steps identified by HealthCAT carried significantly more predictive value than random selection across all masking conditions ($p<0.05$), indicating that the identified time steps are predictively informative. By coupling predictive performance with validated time-step-level interpretability, HealthCAT moves wearable sensor analysis beyond aggregated metrics towards temporal patterns that support health monitoring, behavioural pattern analysis, and intervention design in health research. The significance of this work is that it enables accurate prediction of health indicators from wearable sensor data while providing insights into when and how physical activity patterns occur, rather than relying solely on aggregated summary measures.

</details>


### [140] [Evaluating and Pricing Advertisements in AI-Generated Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27686)
*John L. Turner-Smith,Zimeng Huang,Yuhan Fu,Yihang Zhang,Tonghan Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A differentiable, agent-based evaluator for click-through intent and ad quality enables principled pricing (truthful bidding) for LLM-integrated ads, with strong validation, generalization, and potential as a training objective for ad generation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Advertising embedded in LLM-generated responses creates dual objectives (utility for users and commercial value). Traditional supervision of click-through signals is unavailable or noisy, and current judges conflate intent with fluency, hindering principled pricing. The work seeks a continuous, differentiable signal to support both evaluation and monetization.

Method: Develop a psychologically grounded agent-simulation framework to generate supervision for click-through intent; distill into a parameter-efficient, differentiable evaluator predicting click-through intent and three companion ad-quality dimensions; validate via perturbations; test on real and synthetic data; derive a pricing rule under which truthful bidding is optimal (best-of-k) and extend to non-monotone allocations; propose using the differentiable signal as a training objective for ad generation.

Result: The evaluator achieves 79% relevance sensitivity (outperforming frontier zero-shot judges at 60–67%), tracks graded content degradation, generalizes to 103 fictional products, and agrees with human preferences in 86% of pairwise judgments (five annotators), with higher agreement as confidence increases. A unique pricing rule enabling truthful bidding is derived and demonstrated for best-of-k allocations, with extensions to non-monotone allocations. The differentiable signal also serves as a training objective for ad generation.

Conclusion: A coherent framework that (i) provides a differentiable, supervision-based evaluation of click-through intent and ad quality, (ii) yields a principled pricing mechanism guaranteeing truthful bidding, and (iii) offers a training objective for ad generation, with strong validation and notable generalization.

Abstract: As search increasingly shifts toward LLM-driven answer engines, advertising is becoming embedded within the generated response itself and should therefore be evaluated for both user utility and commercial value. The key challenge is click-through intent: behavioural logs are unavailable, human annotation resists calibration, and frontier LLM judges conflate intent with linguistic fluency. These gaps compound, as principled pricing presupposes a continuous intent signal, while generating such a signal presupposes supervision that is currently unavailable. We construct the missing supervision through a psychologically grounded agent simulation framework, and distil it into a parameter-efficient evaluator that predicts click-through intent, together with the three companion dimensions of ad quality, as smooth, differentiable estimates. Validated through sign-certain behavioural perturbations, the evaluator surpasses frontier zero-shot judges on relevance sensitivity (79% versus 60-67%), tracks graded content degradation, generalises without error to 103 fictional products, and agrees with human preference in 86% of pairwise judgements across five annotators, with agreement rising in the evaluator's confidence. Upon its estimates we build the pricing layer directly, deriving the unique payment rule under which truthful bidding is optimal, demonstrating it on a best-of-k allocation, and extending the mechanism to non-monotone allocations. The same differentiable signal stands ready as a training objective for ad generation.

</details>


### [141] [Rehearse: Stepping Back from the Confidence Cliff in Self-Improving Autoresearch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27687)
*Jiazhen Ji,Shouhong Ding*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper(s) identify a 'confidence cliff' in autoresearch: pre-execution judgments degrade in reliability as iterations progress, hindering automatic code improvements. A memory-augmented approach, Rehearse, maintains focused past outcome memory to restore late-stage judgment accuracy and improve end-task performance under the same compute budget across domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficient autoresearch requires reliable pre-execution judgment to avoid costly full training runs. The authors show that judgment accuracy declines over iterations (the confidence cliff), creating suboptimal decision-making in the loop.

Method: Empirical analysis on AutoSOTA-like tasks: (1) measure how often proposed changes help across iterations; (2) evaluate LLM judges with rationales but no history on a 296-pair benchmark; (3) quantify selective accuracy on 366-pair benchmark; (4) introduce Rehearse: propose multiple ideas, compare pre-execution, run the most promising, and judge using focused memory of similar past attempts/outcomes; test across budgets and tasks.

Result: Key findings: helpful modification fraction drops from ~70% (early) to ~43% (late). LLM judge achieves 79.5% accuracy on pairs with strict consensus under no-attempt history. Overall late selective accuracy falls from 82.8% to 56.9%, despite the judge being willing to decide. Rehearse improves late selective accuracy to ~83.5% by using focused outcome memory. Across ~4,000 training runs over three loops and multiple tasks (nanochat, image classification, time-series forecasting), Rehearse yields better endpoints under the same budget.

Conclusion: The confidence cliff is a bottleneck in autoresearch loops. Augmenting the loop with a focused, memory-based evaluation (Rehearse) can sustain judgment quality and improve final performance across domains without increasing compute budget.

Abstract: Autoresearch improves machine-learning code by proposing changes, running full training jobs, and keeping changes that improve the metric. The efficiency of this loop depends not only on generating ideas, but also on the agent's ability to decide, before spending a training run, whether a proposed modification is likely to work. We study how the reliability of this pre-execution judgment changes over the course of an autoresearch trajectory. In public AutoSOTA logs (Li et al., 2026; Tsinghua FIB Lab, 2026), the fraction of helpful modifications falls from 70% in the first two iterations to 43% by iteration 6+. On 296 same-baseline modification pairs from 39 paper-derived AutoSOTA tasks, each containing one modification that improved the metric and one that did not, with measured outcomes hidden, an LLM judge given candidate rationales but no prior-attempt history reaches 79.5% accuracy on the pairs where strict consensus returns a verdict. On the full 366-pair benchmark, however, this ability weakens substantially late in the loop. As successful changes accumulate, selective accuracy - accuracy conditioned on a strict-consensus verdict - falls from 82.8% to 56.9%, while the judge remains willing to decide. We call this operational pattern the confidence cliff. Rehearse implements the loop change as a lightweight skill for autoresearch loops: propose several ideas, compare them before execution, run the most promising, and judge with a focused memory of similar past attempts and outcomes. This focused outcome memory raises late selective accuracy to 83.5%. Across 4,000 budgeted training runs over three loops, Rehearse improves the endpoint under the same training-run budget on nanochat, image classification, and time-series forecasting.

</details>


### [142] [Guiding Large Language Models with Genetic Programming-Evolved Heuristic Knowledge for Dynamic Multi-Mode Project Scheduling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27698)
*Yuan Tian,Yi Mei,Mengjie Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GP-evolved scheduling rules guide LLM decisions in dynamic multi-mode scheduling, improving performance and stability with varying token costs across integration strategies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Zero-shot LLM decisions lack domain knowledge and can consume many tokens; GP can automatically evolve high-quality heuristic rules; transferring GP-derived knowledge to guide LLM decisions can improve efficiency and consistency.

Method: Extract knowledge from high-quality GP rules and inject it into an online LLM decision maker via four mechanisms: Feature Selection, Feature Hint, Rule Reference, and Rule Follow. Evaluate scheduling performance, token consumption, decision stability, and feature focus in generated rationales.

Result: GP-derived guidance generally improves unguided LLM performance; representation of guidance matters; simplifying the decision context or providing explicit decision logic is more effective than merely highlighting important features. Feature Selection offers the best token efficiency; Rule Follow achieves strong performance at higher token cost. Guidance also improves decision stability and changes the features emphasized in generated rationales.

Conclusion: Knowledge transfer from GP to LLM is effective for guiding online scheduling decisions; the choice of guidance mechanism affects token efficiency and performance; optimizing representations (e.g., feature selection) yields meaningful gains while balancing token use.

Abstract: In dynamic multi-mode project scheduling, activities have alternative execution modes and uncertain durations, while precedence relations and limited resources constrain their execution. Heuristic priority rules support fast online decisions, but their design requires substantial domain expertise. Genetic programming (GP) hyper-heuristics can automatically evolve such rules. Large language models (LLMs), meanwhile, provide a flexible interface for interpreting scheduling information and explaining decisions. However, zero-shot LLM decisions may lack domain knowledge, consume many tokens, and vary across repeated queries. GP-evolved rules therefore provide a potential source of scheduling knowledge for guiding LLM decisions. Unlike existing LLM--GP hybrids that use LLMs to support heuristic evolution, we transfer knowledge in the reverse direction, using knowledge extracted from high-quality GP rules to guide an online LLM decision maker. We extract knowledge from high-quality GP rules and inject it through Feature Selection, Feature Hint, Rule Reference, and Rule Follow. These mechanisms are evaluated in terms of scheduling performance, token consumption, decision stability, and the feature focus expressed in generated rationales. GP-derived guidance generally improves the unguided LLM, but its representation matters. Simplifying the decision context or supplying explicit decision logic is more effective than highlighting important features. Feature Selection offers the best token efficiency, whereas Rule Follow achieves strong performance at greater token cost. Guidance also improves decision stability and changes the features expressed in generated rationales.

</details>


### [143] [SpatialCLI: Learning to Reason With Spatial Tools, Then Without Them](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27703)
*Yang Zhou,Zixuan Huang,Sunzhu Li,Zhuo Yang,Chen Zhang,Shunian Chen,Caijun Yan,Jianyao Xu,Shunyu Liu,Weijie Fu,Peiliang Li,Xiaozhi Chen,Yuxiang Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SpatialCLI introduces a three-stage framework that enables vision-language models to reason with external spatial tools provided by specialist vision models, progressively acquiring both tool-use ability and internalized perceptual capabilities. It is evaluated on a 516-sample SpatialCLI-Bench and shows large gains on MindCube (Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct: 29.3% to 84.6% with tools; 73.8% without tools after internalization), outperforming GPT-5.6 Sol with tools (72.1%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General VLMs excel at task-level reasoning but miss fine-grained visual details; specialist vision models capture such details but struggle to contribute to task-level decisions. SpatialCLI aims to bridge this gap by enabling VLMs to call specialized perceptual tools and progressively internalize their capabilities for robust, compositional perception in embodied tasks.

Method: Three-stage process: (1) Call to expose specialist vision models as spatial tools; (2) Learn using Cold-Start SFT and agentic reinforcement learning to improve tool use; (3) Internalize where the system verbalizes successful tool-use trajectories to embed perceptual capabilities within the VLM. A 516-example SpatialCLI-Bench assesses compositional perception across localization, segmentation, depth, and pose.

Result: Empirical gains on MindCube with Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct: 29.3% baseline improves to 84.6% with tools; 73.8% without tools after internalization. SpatialCLI also surpasses GPT-5.6 Sol with tools (72.1%). The benchmark demonstrates improved compositional perception across multiple perceptual tasks.

Conclusion: SpatialCLI provides a structured pathway to endow VLMs with robust, compositional perceptual reasoning by integrating external perceptual tools, leveraging staged training to improve tool use and internalize perceptual capabilities. This can enhance embodied agents' ability to translate fine-grained perception into task-level decisions.

Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used in embodied agents to interpret visual inputs, reason about spatial relationships, and make task-level decisions based on that reasoning. However, a fundamental capability mismatch remains: general VLMs can reason about the overall task but often miss the visual details that determine success, while specialist vision models can capture those details but cannot translate them into task-level decisions. In this work, we propose SpatialCLI, a framework that teaches VLMs to reason with spatial tools and progressively internalize the specialist perceptual capabilities they provide. SpatialCLI proceeds in three stages: (1) Call exposes specialist vision models as spatial tools to augment the VLM's perception; (2) Learn uses Cold-Start SFT and agentic RL to improve tool use; and (3) Internalize verbalizes successful tool-use trajectories to internalize specialist perceptual capabilities. We further introduce SpatialCLI-Bench, a 516-example benchmark for compositional perception across localization, segmentation, depth, and pose. On MindCube, SpatialCLI raises Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct from 29.3% to 84.6% with tools, surpassing GPT-5.6 Sol with tools (72.1%), while retaining 73.8% without tools after internalization.

</details>


### [144] [Albilich: Steerable Proof-State Orchestration for LLM-Based Mathematical Research with CAS Integration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27705)
*Ting Gong,Michael Ruofan Zeng,Yong Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Albilich: an open-source agentic framework for AI-assisted mathematical research integrating long-horizon reasoning, CAS, literature retrieval, and persistent context; strong performance on RealMath and Kourovka tasks, enabling human-guided proof search with CAS-driven efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address coordination, evaluation, and reproducibility challenges in long-horizon mathematical proofs and enable scalable, verifiable AI-assisted exploration.

Method: Integrates long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems (CAS), literature retrieval, and SQLite-based persistent context management; provides an advisor-like agent to guide autonomous math exploration; evaluated on RealMath benchmark and Kourovka Notebook problems; includes ablations to assess CAS impact and advisor necessity.

Result: RealMath: 10/10 with CAS; 9/10 without CAS. Kourovka: produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and a proof of strengthening of Problem 20.2. Ablations show 32.0% token reduction when CAS enabled; higher verifier-rejection rate and failure to synthesize proofs without the advisor. Overall supports Albilich as a CAS-boosted, human-steerable environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research.

Conclusion: Albilich provides a CAS-boosted, human-steerable environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research, improving proof synthesis, evaluation, and reproducibility and enabling coordinated long-horizon AI-driven mathematical exploration.

Abstract: Large language models can contribute useful ideas to mathematical research, yet long-horizon proof attempts remain difficult to coordinate, evaluate, and reproduce. We present Albilich, an open-source agentic harness for autoresearch in mathematics that combines long-horizon reasoning, computer algebra systems (CAS), literature retrieval, and persistent SQLite-based context management.
  We evaluate Albilich on the RealMath benchmark (Zhang et al. 2025) and on open problems in group theory from the Kourovka Notebook (Khukhro and Mazurov 2026). It solved 10/10 problems on RealMath with CAS and 9/10 with no CAS. On the Kourovka problems, Albilich produced a counterexample to Problem 21.142 and a proof of a strengthening of Problem20.2. Anablation on Problem 17.91 demonstrates 32.0% token reduction when CAS is enabled. An ablation on Problem 21.142 demonstrates higher verifier-rejection rate and failure to synthesize proof routes in the absence of the advisor agent. These results support Albilich as a human-steerable, CAS-boosted environment for scalable AI-assisted mathematical research.

</details>


### [145] [MECA: A Mechanism-Centered Agent for Constructing Well-Specified and Valuable Mathematical Conjectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27709)
*Wentao Long,Yunfei Zhang,Chenyi Li,Zaiwen Wen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MECA introduces a mechanism-centered multi-agent framework to generate well-specified conjectures by co-developing statements and their supporting mechanisms; evaluated against baselines and through automated provers, it yields concrete, challenging conjectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address underspecified conjectures that are difficult to connect to proofs/refutations; provide a structured mechanism to map assumptions to conclusions.

Method: Explorer agents propose and test mechanisms; critic agents assess validity and research value; feedback guides adjustments to assumptions, scope, and conclusion; two evaluation setups: reconstruction from target-conditioned sources; generation of 100 semi-open problems with automated prover evaluation.

Result: The approach produces well-specified, research-worthy conjectures that remain challenging for current provers; performance exceeds generate-and-revise baselines in targeted settings.

Conclusion: Mechanism-centered conjecture refinement is a promising direction for AI-assisted mathematical discovery, producing precise conjectures with explicit supporting mechanisms that preserve an unresolved core.

Abstract: Automatically constructing well-specified and valuable mathematical conjectures remains a central challenge in AI-assisted mathematical discovery. Many existing open problems and conjectures are often too broad, underspecified, or difficult to connect to plausible proof or refutation strategies. We view a mathematical mechanism as a structure or reasoning principle that connects the assumptions of a candidate problem to its target conclusion, such as an inequality, invariant, decomposition, or reduction to an intermediate claim. We present MECA (MEchanism-centered Conjecture Agent), a multi-agent framework that constructs conjectures by jointly developing candidate statements and their supporting mechanisms. Explorer agents propose mechanisms, test how they apply, and revise the candidate conjecture accordingly, while critic agents assess their mathematical validity and research value. Their feedback guides changes to the assumptions, scope, and conclusion. Through this process, MECA transforms broad research directions into precise conjectures with substantive mathematical support while retaining a clearly identified unresolved core. We evaluate MECA in two complementary settings. First, we compare it with a generate-and-revise baseline on reconstructing preselected target-paper conclusions from target-conditioned but article-blind source materials. Second, we construct 100 semi-open problems from literature-derived seeds and existing open problems and evaluate them through independent proof and refutation attempts by automated provers. Our results indicate that mechanism-centered refinement produces well-specified and research-worthy conjectures that remain challenging for current automated provers.

</details>


### [146] [New Synchronous Computation Dynamics for Hopfield Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27720)
*Francisco Requena-Domínguez,Rafaela Benítez-Rochel,Ezequiel López-Rubio*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduce Discrete Differential Filter (DDF) and SD-DDF, a synchronous Hopfield network dynamics that updates multiple neurons to maximize energy decrease per step, aiming at faster convergence with theoretical guarantees, plus four empirical experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reduce Hopfield network processing time by moving from asynchronous (sequential) updates to a synchronous/multi-update scheme while ensuring convergence and significant energy descent per step.

Method: Present the Discrete Differential Filter as a new tool to solve the combinatorial optimization of choosing the next state with maximal energy decrease; develop a corresponding SD-DDF synchronous dynamics; provide theoretical justification.

Result: Propose and validate, via four computational experiments, that the SD-DDF approach speeds up processing time compared to traditional asynchronous dynamics (no numerical figures given in abstract).

Conclusion: Original asynchronous dynamics are reviewed; a new tool (DDF) and a new synchronous dynamics (SD-DDF) are proposed with theoretical backing and empirical support for faster processing.

Abstract: The dynamics of the original Hopfield network is asynchronous (sequential) (updates the state of only one neuron per time step). In this paper, we propose a new tool and a new dynamics to reduce the processing time by updating one or more neurons simultaneously per instant while ensuring process convergence and aiming for the maximum energy decrease at each step, thus guaranteeing the shortest total processing time. From the point of view of synchronous dynamics, calculating the next network state at which energy decreases the most from the current state while ensuring convergence is itself a combinatorial optimization problem. We develop and use a new tool to solve it. We call this new tool Discrete Differential Filter (DDF) and, based upon it, we develop a new synchronous dynamics which we call SD-DDF (Synchronous Dynamics based upon Discrete Differential Filter). In this paper, we review the original asynchronous dynamics for Hopfield networks and present a new tool and a new synchronous dynamics with its theoretical justification and four computational experiments to assess the speed up in processing time empirically.

</details>


### [147] [Baikal: Structured Search for Deep Research over Data Lakes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27726)
*Dhruv Agarwal,Rishitha Guttapalle Mohan,Aarti Kumari,Ashi Sinha,Athulya Anil,Kavitha Srinivas,Horst Samulowitz,Andrew McCallum*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Baikal reframes data-lake research as a budgeted, region-based search and achieves substantial gains over baselines by organizing evidence into semantic regions and adaptively exploring them.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome inefficiencies of iterative retrieval that overexploit locally promising evidence and fail to cover distinct semantic regions within a fixed budget when researching heterogeneous data lakes.

Method: Cluster heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions; perform adaptive search over regions; within regions generate and investigate region-grounded subquestions; use finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates; explore with policies ranging from random and LLM-guided selection to Bayesian ε-greedy and UCB; evaluate on data lakes with thousands of tables and passages and assess with a GPT-5-mini-based rubric.

Result: Baikal's best configuration improves report scores over the strongest baselines by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA across 15 queries; gains attributed to organized exploration of semantic regions that enhances groundedness and diversity, yielding more useful findings under the same subquestion budget.

Conclusion: Structured semantic exploration better balances exploration and exploitation, improving groundedness, diversity, and utility in automated deep research over heterogeneous data lakes.

Abstract: Deep research over data lakes requires an LLM agent to investigate evidence across thousands of heterogeneous tables and passages to synthesize a report. Existing methods perform iterative retrieval and generation, letting accumulated context determine what to investigate next, which can overexploit locally promising evidence and fail to cover distinct semantic regions under a fixed budget. To address this, we cast deep research over data lakes as a budgeted search problem and present Baikal - a framework that clusters heterogeneous evidence into semantic regions, then searches over them adaptively to balance exploration and exploitation. Within each selected region, Baikal generates and investigates region-grounded subquestions, using finding quality as rewards to update region-level value estimates and guide search under policies ranging from random and LLM-guided selection to Bayesian $ε$-greedy and UCB. We evaluate Baikal on 15 queries each over HybridQA and TAT-QA data lakes containing 10,993 and 2,757 tables, respectively, together with 227K Wikipedia passages and 13K financial report passages. We assess research quality with a new rubric covering groundedness, relevance, diversity, and utility, and use GPT-5-mini to score Baikal and strong baselines, including DeepSearcher and an OpenCode research agent with retrieval and clustering variants. Across both data lakes, Baikal performs strongly under several region-selection policies; its best configuration improves report scores over the strongest baselines by 28% on HybridQA and 36% on TAT-QA. Our analyses attribute these gains to organizing and exploring semantic evidence regions, which improves groundedness and diversity and yields more useful findings under the same subquestion budget. These results demonstrate the value of structured semantic exploration for systematic research and discovery over heterogeneous data lakes.

</details>


### [148] [VeriSkill: A Self-Evolution Framework for Program Verification Skills](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27733)
*Changguo Jia,Tianqi Zhao,Zhiyou Xiao,Weiming Zhang,Minghui Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: VeriSkill is a self-evolution framework for program verification that distills skill deficiencies from verifier feedback into reusable, improved verification skills, iteratively refining them while preserving program semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable reliable, automated improvement of verification skills (e.g., specifications, annotations, lemmas, tool invocations) by tracing failures to skill gaps and extracting actionable signals from verifier feedback.

Method: Identify verification failures caused by skill deficiencies, distill diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, iteratively refine candidate skills, and only admit revisions that improve verification performance while preserving semantics.

Result: VeriSkill outperforms baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.

Conclusion: Self-evolving skill-based verification is effective and generalizes across tools and backends, enabling more robust, automated program verification.

Abstract: Automating program verification with LLM agents requires generating specifications, annotations, auxiliary lemmas, and tool invocations, all of which depend on reusable skills. A natural remedy is skill self-evolution: distilling skills from trajectories and refining them through feedback. However, existing evolution methods struggle with program verification tasks because they cannot reliably identify skill-specific failures or extract actionable signals from opaque verifier feedback. In this paper, we propose VeriSkill, a self-evolution framework built for program verification. It attributes verification failures to skill deficiencies, distills diagnostic signatures into reusable lessons, and iteratively refines candidate skills, admitting only revisions that improve verification performance while preserving program semantics. Experiments show that VeriSkill consistently outperforms all baselines across multiple verification tools, agent frameworks, and LLM backends.

</details>


### [149] [SpecCal: Ambiguity-Aware Candidate Calibration for Infrared Spectrum-Based Molecular Structure Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27788)
*Yixuan Chen,Bo Liu,Yusen Tan,Guokun Yang,Wenjie Du,Jun Xia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SpecCal is a training-free calibration framework that re-ranks and expands the candidate set from IR-to-molecule models to better satisfy spectral constraints, improving top-k reconstruction at SMILES and scaffold levels while being plug-and-play and model-agnostic.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IR spectra provide limited information and can map to multiple plausible structures; existing models’ outputs are biased by their generation preferences and may miss structures that better satisfy spectral constraints. A calibration step without training could address ambiguity and improve reconstruction.

Method: SpecCal operates on the candidate outputs of existing base models, re-ranking current candidates and introducing additional structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency. It is training-free, plug-and-play, and requires no parameter updates, enabling integration with diverse base models.

Result: Across multiple benchmarks and base models, SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction at both the SMILES and scaffold levels. Analyses show calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity yields practical improvements in molecular reconstruction from IR spectra.

Conclusion: A practical, model-agnostic, training-free calibration framework that enhances IR-to-molecule predictions by leveraging spectral consistency to re-rank and expand candidate sets, improving reconstruction performance without retraining.

Abstract: Inferring molecular structures from infrared (IR) spectra is a fundamental yet challenging problem. A key difficulty is that an IR spectrum provides limited structural information: different molecules may share similar functional groups and local vibrational patterns, leading to highly similar spectral responses. Thus, even when an observed spectrum has a unique underlying structure, reconstructing it from the spectrum remains ambiguous. Existing IR-to-molecule models usually generate a ranked set of candidate molecules, but this set is largely determined by the model's learned generation preference and may not fully capture the structures that best satisfy the observed spectral constraints. To address this limitation, we propose SpecCal, a training-free candidate calibration framework for IR-to-molecule prediction. SpecCal operates on the candidate outputs of existing base models and improves the prediction set by re-ranking current candidates while introducing additional structurally plausible alternatives guided by spectral consistency. The framework is plug-and-play and model-agnostic, requiring no parameter updates for integration with diverse base models. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that SpecCal consistently improves top-k reconstruction at both SMILES and scaffold levels across different base models. Further analyses demonstrate that calibrating candidate sets under spectral ambiguity provides a practical way to improve molecular reconstruction from IR spectra. The code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SpecCal-B18A.

</details>


### [150] [Annotating Topical Legal Insights from Case Proceedings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27792)
*Subinay Adhikary,Dwaipayan Roy,Debasis Ganguly,Shouvik Kumar Guha,Kripabandhu Ghosh*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces LeDA, a web-based system for annotating legal documents with dynamically creatable tags to build semantic bags of concepts for downstream tasks; demonstrated with Indian Supreme Court cases by 3 assessors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
