Motivation: Legal documents require structured representations beyond bag-of-words; existing ontologies are incomplete or absent, necessitating flexible, on-the-fly concept discovery during annotation.

Method: Develop and deploy LeDA, a web interface for annotating and adjudicating entities/concepts; supports dynamic creation of new tags; used to annotate legal concepts to form semantic representations (bags of concepts) for tasks like prior case retrieval and judgment prediction; demonstrated with Indian Supreme Court proceedings by 3 assessors.

Result: System demonstrated and used to annotate a set of concepts from legal documents, producing semantic bags of concepts; suitable for downstream tasks such as retrieval and prediction; validated by three assessors.

Conclusion: LeDA enables flexible annotation of legal data without a fixed ontology, facilitating the creation of semantic representations and improving downstream processing; demonstrated on Indian Supreme Court materials.

Abstract: In this paper, we mainly concentrate on finding concepts or topics from the legal case proceedings, since adopting a structured representation for legal documents, as opposed to a mere bag-of-words flat text representation, can significantly enhance processing capabilities. To achieve this objective, we put forward a set of diverse concepts for legal case proceedings. With this motivation, we propose LeDA, a system for Legal Data Annotation. The system offers the generic functionality of annotating and adjudicating entities or concepts within documents via a web-based interface. A novel feature of our system is that it allows to dynamic create new tags for annotation, which is a particularly useful provision for situations where there exists no pre-defined ontology for the entities (concepts) that need to be annotated - these being rather discovered by annotators as they continue examining more documents. The system that we demonstrate is currently in use to annotate a set of concepts from legal documents to construct semantic representations of documents as bags of concepts that can then be used for several downstream tasks, such as prior case retrieval, judgment prediction, and so on. Along with the system features in general, we also describe how LeDA was used by 3 assessors to annotate and adjudicate legal concept names from Indian Supreme Court case proceedings.

</details>


### [151] [MemeBench: What LVLMs Miss When Interpreting Culture-Dependent Memes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27798)
*Weihang Wang,Kainan Tu,Jielei Zhang,Run Yang,Boheng Sheng,Yuchen He,Yu Xie,Pengyu Chen,Peiyi Li,Huyang Sun,Longwen Gao,Zhouhui Lian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemeBench is a diagnostic, VIKR-based benchmark for meme interpretation, revealing a persistent Visual–Knowledge gap in LVLMs; KAR (entity-guided retrieval) partially closes the gap, but retrieval can trade off Visual coverage; MemeBench enables targeted diagnosis to guide model improvement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Memes require knowledge beyond pixels (cultural context, identities, community norms). Current LVLM benchmarks emphasize labels or holistic scores and lack fine-grained diagnostics. A structured VIKR (Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, Reasoning mechanisms) framework is needed to pinpoint failure modes and guide improvements.

Method: Construct MemeBench with 1,253 memes in Chinese and English across anime, comics, games, and related subcultures; provide human-written references and quality-controlled VIKR annotations; evaluate 26 LVLMs on Visual vs. Knowledge interpretation; develop KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline grounded in CultureBase; test four controlled models and compare with generic retrieval; measure VIKR Success and component-wise effects.

Result: Across models, visible content is more reliably interpreted than the necessary knowledge; the strongest model shows a 22.6% Visual–Knowledge gap. KAR improves VIKR Success by 3.6–7.4% and, compared with generic retrieval, repairs more answers and reduces errors, but improves Identity and Knowledge while reducing Visual coverage in all comparisons.

Conclusion: MemeBench provides a diagnostic lens to identify when interpretation succeeds, what is missing, and whether targeted evidence helps fill the diagnosed gaps. KAR demonstrates that entity-guided retrieval can enhance VIKR components, but fully bridging the Visual–Knowledge gap remains a challenge; the benchmark offers a path to targeted improvements in meme understanding for LVLMs.

Abstract: Large vision-language models have improved at describing visual content, but accurate descriptions do not ensure interpretation when meaning depends on knowledge beyond the pixels. Memes expose this gap because they rely on cultural entities, background knowledge, and community conventions. Most meme benchmarks reduce interpretation to labels or holistic scores, obscuring where an explanation breaks down. We introduce MemeBench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,253 Chinese and English memes with human-written references and quality-controlled VIKR annotations, centered on anime, comics, games, and adjacent online subcultures. Its VIKR schema decomposes explanations into Visual clues, Identity links, Knowledge units, and Reasoning mechanisms. Across 26 LVLMs, every model covers visible content more reliably than the knowledge needed to interpret it, and even the strongest retains a 22.6% Visual-Knowledge gap. To test whether this diagnosis can guide improvement, we introduce KAR, an entity-guided retrieval baseline built on CultureBase. Across four controlled models, KAR raises VIKR Success by 3.6-7.4% and, compared with generic retrieval, repairs more answers and breaks fewer. Yet both retrieval conditions improve Identity and Knowledge while reducing Visual coverage in every comparison. MemeBench reveals whether an interpretation succeeds, what is missing, and whether targeted evidence fills the diagnosed gap.

</details>


### [152] [STEREODISCO: Discovering Stereotypicality in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27824)
*Farane Jalali Farahani,Corina Dima,Mojtaba Nayyeri,Raphael H. Heiberger,Steffen Staab*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: STEREODISCO extends the semantic differential to LLM internal representations by deriving ~2k semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, probing LLM activations to recover axes, and identifying stereotypes via projections; applied to LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT; finds cross-model agreement with humans incomplete and uncovers novel axes (humble vs proud; narrow-minded vs broad-minded; cowardly vs brave).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the narrow scope of prior work that focused on a small set of semantic axes and word embeddings; systematically map the broader semantic axes and internal representations in LLMs to understand how stereotypes are encoded and organized.

Method: Construct ~2,000 candidate axes from WordNet antonym synsets; recover each as a geometric axis in the LLM activation space via probing; identify stereotypical axes with a statistical test on concept projections.

Result: Two LLMs (LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT) agree with each other on social group ratings more than with humans; LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from social psychology, and novel axes (e.g., humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, cowardly vs. brave) are discovered and independently confirmed by human annotators.

Conclusion: STER EODISCO provides a scalable framework to reveal the latent stereotype geometry in LLMs, showing alignment gaps with human stereotypes and uncovering axes not previously studied; implications for understanding, auditing, and potentially mitigating LLM biases.

Abstract: LLMs encode, convey, and perpetuate stereotypes. Prior computational research focuses on a small set of semantic axes investigated in social psychology, and operates on word embeddings produced by language models, leaving open which other semantic axes carry stereotypical associations in LLMs and how LLMs internally represent such axes. We introduce STEREODISCO, a framework that adapts the semantic differential method (Osgood et al., 1957) to the systematic study of stereotypes in LLM internal representations. STEREODISCO constructs approx. 2,000 candidate semantic axes from WordNet antonym synsets, recovers each as a geometric axis in the LLM's activation space via probing, and identifies stereotypical axes via a statistical test over concept projections. As a case study, we apply STEREODISCO to social group stereotypes with LLAMA-3-8B-INSTRUCT and MISTRAL-7B-INSTRUCT. We find that the two LLMs agree with each other on social group ratings more than with humans, suggesting that LLM-encoded stereotype content diverges from that documented in social psychology. We also discover stereotypical axes not investigated in prior work -- including humble vs. proud, narrow-minded vs. broad-minded, and cowardly vs. brave, which human annotators independently confirm.

</details>


### [153] [Sign Language Question Answering: A New Task, Benchmark, and Baseline for Sign Language Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27826)
*Shiwei Gan,Lichen Wang,Xiao Liu,Yafeng Yin,Kuizhuang Liu,Sanglu Lu,Lei Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA) as a new evaluation task to assess semantic understanding in sign language beyond recognition/translation; builds SignQA benchmarks on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily via template-generated QA pairs; proposes a baseline with Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling and in-domain knowledge transfer; baseline outperforms vision-language models across five question types; datasets released on HuggingFace.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the limitation of existing SLU tasks that focus on fixed mappings (gloss/translation) and do not thoroughly test semantic understanding and reasoning in sign language videos.

Method: Define SLQA task; automatically generate QA pairs from gloss/sentence annotations using designed templates; construct SignQA benchmarks with five question categories; propose a baseline model featuring a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling (QCMD) module and an in-domain knowledge transfer strategy to leverage existing SLU tasks for improved, question-aware temporal feature modeling.

Result: Extensive experiments show the proposed baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all five question categories on SignQA (PHOENIX14T/ CSL-Daily) datasets.

Conclusion: SLQA provides a flexible, comprehensive evaluation framework for sign language understanding and establishes challenging benchmarks for future research; the SignQA datasets are publicly available for reproducibility and further study.

Abstract: Recent advances in sign language (SL) understanding (SLU) have led to remarkable progress in tasks such as continuous SL recognition and SL translation. However, these tasks are designed with predefined objectives, requiring models to learn a fixed mapping from sign videos to glosses or spoken-language sentences. As a result, they provide only a limited assessment of whether a model truly understands the semantic content of SL videos. To address this limitation, \textbf{we first propose a new task, Sign Language Question Answering (SLQA)}, which evaluates SL understanding by requiring models to answer arbitrary natural language questions about SL videos. Unlike previous SLU tasks, SLQA provides a more flexible and comprehensive evaluation framework that assesses multiple reasoning capabilities beyond recognition and translation. To facilitate this task, \textbf{we further construct two SignQA benchmarks} based on PHOENIX14T and CSL-Daily by automatically generating question-answer pairs from existing gloss and sentence annotations using carefully designed templates. The resulting datasets cover five complementary question categories, including position reasoning, structural reasoning, visual search, gloss recognition, and translation understanding. \textbf{Finally, we propose a simple yet effective baseline model} equipped with a Question-Conditioned Modulated Temporal Downsampling module and an in-domain knowledge transfer strategy, enabling effective knowledge transfer from existing SLU tasks while enhancing question-aware temporal feature modeling. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our baseline consistently outperforms representative vision-language models across all question categories, establishing a strong benchmark for future research on SLQA. Datasets are available at:{https://huggingface.co/datasets/hulala/SignQA-2026}.

</details>


### [154] [MemTxn: A Transaction Boundary for Source-Supported Updates and Complete-State Recovery in Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27834)
*Hanshuai Cui,Zhiqing Tang,Zhi Yao,Fanshuai Meng,Qianli Ma,Weijia Jia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemTxn provides a transaction-like governance layer for persistent memory in long-running LLM agents, enabling verified updates, version selection, and robust recovery across sessions and tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Persistent memory errors can persist and corrupt future behavior; existing systems lack a transaction boundary for reliable updates and recovery.

Method: MemTxn introduces a governance layer outside the answer model with components: Ordered PatchTest to validate writes, Temporal Resolver to select the visible version, and a durable snapshot journal to recover state; it features an item-disjoint audit and fault-tolerant recovery under multi-key faults; evaluation across benchmarks.

Result: On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo, it restores the complete declared active map without knowing the actual physical write set. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, MemTxn achieves the highest average F1 across 12 answer-model configurations and outperforms Dense by 17.06–24.07 points in five representative settings.

Conclusion: MemTxn provides a robust governance mechanism for persistent memory in LLM agents, improving correctness, recoverability, and evaluation metrics across diverse benchmarks, and suggests substantial gains over Dense baselines while highlighting practical considerations for fault models and integration.

Abstract: Persistent memory lets long-running large language model agents reuse information across sessions and tasks. Yet errors in writable memory can persist and corrupt future behavior. Existing systems improve storage and retrieval, but they do not provide a transaction boundary for reliable updates and recovery. We therefore propose MemTxn, a governance layer outside the answer model. MemTxn verifies whether an update is supported by its source. It also selects the visible version when facts conflict and restores the application-visible state after a fault. The system uses Ordered PatchTest to validate writes, a Temporal Resolver to select versions, and a durable snapshot journal to recover state. On an item-disjoint audit, MemTxn accepts all 60 supported originals and rejects all 179 hard negatives. Under persistent multi-key faults on LongMemEval-S and LoCoMo states, it restores the complete declared active map without knowing the actual physical write set. On MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation, MemTxn achieves the highest average F1 across all twelve answer-model configurations. It outperforms Dense by 17.06--24.07 points in five representative settings.

</details>


### [155] [Crossing the Margin Cliff: Toward Relearn-Robust LLM Unlearning via Margin Calibration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27836)
*Xiangyu Yin,Jiaxu Liu,Zhen Chen,Chih-Hong Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The work analyzes fragility of LLM unlearning under relearn, identifies a per-token margin cliff across post-hoc forget methods, and proposes Margin Calibration (MC) to restore forget pressure. A single frozen configuration achieves superior forget robustness across multiple models/datasets with some retain-utility cost; deployment variants remove reliance on a retain reference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unlearning in large language models is fragile under relearn attempts. Existing post-hoc methods exhibit saturation and a geometry-induced fragility (margin cliff). The goal is to diagnose the phenomenon and develop a plug-in calibration to sustain forgetting pressure without excessive retraining.

Method: Extensive empirical study on TOFU (Llama-3 sizes, forget tiers) evaluating 14 post-hoc methods (gradient, preference, distillation families) using forget-set ROUGE and membership AUC. They identify a margin cliff where per-token answer margins collapse into a narrow band above the retain reference in 41/42 method-size cells. Introduce Margin Calibration (MC): a non-saturating margin hinge anchored at the reference margin plus a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus. They instrument gradient signatures to verify a gradient-dominance condition and test across TOFU, MUSE-News (Llama-2-7B-hf), and Phi-3.5 panels; compare configurations including a deployment variant without a retain-trained reference.

Result: MC restores forget-side pressure; under gradient-dominance, the stationary set lies on the cliff-crossing side, enabling an upper bound on relearn margin lift. A single frozen configuration surpasses all 14 forget-aggregates and 14 relearn cells (panel-mean post-attack ROUGE-L 0.41 vs 0.18) with reduced retain-side utility as the main cost. Results also hold for MUSE-News and Phi-3.5 panels; deployment variant matches gains without a retain reference.

Conclusion: Margin Calibration is an effective plug-in to mitigate the margin cliff in LLM unlearning, yielding robust forget reasoning across models and settings at a trade-off with retain utility. The approach provides a practical defense against relearn attacks and suggests a principled role for non-saturating margins and distributional probes in unlearning.

Abstract: Large language model unlearning is consistently fragile under relearn attacks. On TOFU, fine-tuning on twenty forget examples substantially recovers held-out forget-set ROUGE for every method we evaluate, and we trace this fragility to optimization geometry. The per-token answer margin of fourteen post-hoc methods spanning gradient, preference, and distillation families converges into a narrow band above the retain reference in 41 of 42 method--size cells, a regularity we call the margin cliff. We prove that this cliff follows whenever the retain coupling holds the diagnostic log-odds of forget content above a floor, a condition that token-saturating losses induce at stationarity and that we verify directly on 34 of 42 cells. Margin Calibration (\textsc{MC}) is a plug-in polish adding a non-saturating margin hinge anchored at the reference's per-token margin plus a KL probe on a disjoint instruction corpus, restoring forget-side pressure where the native loss saturates. Under a stated gradient-dominance condition, whose on-trajectory gradient signature we measure by instrumenting the polish, its stationary set lies on the cliff-crossing side, yielding an attack-budget upper bound on the relearn margin lift. Across TOFU (three Llama-3 sizes, three forget tiers), MUSE-News on Llama-2-7B-hf, and a Phi-3.5 panel, a single frozen configuration wins all 14 head-to-head forget aggregates and all populated relearn cells (panel-mean post-attack ROUGE-L $0.41$ to $0.18$) and lowers raw membership AUC on 13/14, with reduced retain-side utility as the main cost. A deployment variant matches these gains without a retain-trained reference.

</details>


### [156] [Virtual Process Dossier: A Process-Aware Data Catalogue](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27840)
*Lukas Kubelka,Alexander Bott,Frank Döhner,Saksham Kiroriwal,Georg Zeeb,Julia Butte,Julius Pfrommer,Jürgen Beyerer,Tobias Käfer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Virtual Process Dossier (VPD), a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue that captures workflow provenance for multi-stage manufacturing, enabling FAIR data access and explicit provenance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Downstream AI optimization requires distinguishing and tracing datasets across workflow steps; existing data catalogs often lack integrated provenance in production environments.

Method: Developed VPD ontology as the semantic core; designed a provenance framework to instantiate the ontology in production; built a human-centered UI; implemented as a Knowledge Graph.

Result: A complete VPD stack (ontology, provenance framework, and user interface) with an open-source repository at GitHub.

Conclusion: VPD enables FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, re-usable) datasets with explicit prospective and retrospective workflow provenance for AI-enabled manufacturing analytics.

Abstract: We propose the Virtual Process Dossier (VPD), a Knowledge Graph-based data catalogue that also captures workflow provenance. We developed VPD for multi-stage manufacturing use-cases where downstream AI-based optimization tasks require to distinct between datasets generated during individual workflow steps. VPD provides these datasets in a FAIR manner and makes both prospective and retrospective workflow provenance explicit. Our contributions are: (1) the VPD ontology that serves as the catalogue's semantic core; (2) the VPD provenance framework that integrates ontology instantiation into the production environment; and (3) the VPD user interface that provides human-centered interaction with the VPD Knowledge Graph. The ontology and code are available at https://github.com/kubeluk/VirtualProcessDossier .

</details>


### [157] [Simplifying Neural Networks During Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27854)
*Lorenzo Sciandra,Samuele Fonio,Roberto Esposito*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An NC-inspired framework simplifies deep networks mid-training by monitoring feature dynamics with the Inverse Fisher Criterion to identify where to split feature extraction from classification and when to prune trailing layers, replacing them with a lightweight head; experiments show substantial parameter reductions with accuracy close to the full model across MLP, VGG, and ResNet, with provided code.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address overparameterization and fragile generalization in deep nets by leveraging Neural Collapse (NC) and Tunnel Effect to dynamically simplify architectures during training without sacrificing performance.

Method: Track the Inverse Fisher Criterion to detect the split point between feature extractor and classifier and the training stage at which simplification is viable; once identified, substitute trailing layers with a lightweight classification head and continue training the reduced model; evaluate on image classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures.

Result: The method achieves substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to the full models, demonstrated across multiple architectures; code for reproduction is provided.

Conclusion: An NC-inspired early-stopping-like simplification strategy can reduce model size mid-training without significant loss in accuracy, offering a practical path toward efficient deep networks with readily reproducible results.

Abstract: Understanding and exploiting the training dynamics of overparameterized deep neural networks remains a central challenge in modern machine learning. Recent evidence on Neural Collapse (NC) shows that class representations and classifiers exhibit highly structured geometry, while the Tunnel Effect suggests that only a subset of layers is essential for feature extraction. We combine these two perspectives and propose an NC-inspired training framework for simplifying deep networks during training. Our method monitors representation dynamics through the Inverse Fisher Criterion, a stable and efficient proxy for the variability collapse behavior, to identify both the split point between feature extraction and classification and the training stage at which simplification becomes viable. We then replace the trailing layers with a lightweight classification head and continue training the reduced model. Experiments on image-classification benchmarks across MLP, VGG, and ResNet architectures show that the proposed method achieves substantial parameter reductions while maintaining accuracy comparable to that of the full model. Code to reproduce the experiments can be found at: https://github.com/LorenzoSciandra/NNS.

</details>


### [158] [Back to All-Entity Ranking: Sampler-Dependent Evaluation in Continuous-Time Dynamic Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27861)
*Minwoo Yu,Young-guk Ha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Negative sampling and candidate-set size alter rankings in CTDG next-destination prediction; all-entity ranking recommended for robust architecture evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how negative sampling strategy and candidate selection influence Bayes-optimal ranking and empirical model comparisons in continuous-time dynamic graphs.

Method: Factorial evaluation across repeated vs new positives and seen vs unseen negatives; minimal scorer based on pair-history; controlled representation interventions; six models evaluated on LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, Wikipedia; compare Uniform-20 with full catalog; introduce all-entity ranking.

Result: Non-uniform negative distributions shift Bayes-optimal ranking; even uniformly drawn finite candidate sets can destabilize rankings and module effects; the measured effect of modules varies with candidate-set size and training objective; in data, at least one model pair flips order on three of four datasets.

Conclusion: All-entity ranking eliminates negative sampling and sampling variation while preserving the original CTDG scorer; use all-entity ranking for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks with enumerable catalogs; sampling-based benchmarks yield conditional conclusions depending on candidate configuration.

Abstract: Next-destination prediction in continuous-time dynamic graphs (CTDGs) commonly ranks an observed interaction against sampled negative destinations. The resulting score is conditional on both the negative distribution and the number of candidates chosen by the researcher. We show that a non-uniform negative distribution changes the Bayes-optimal ranking, while even a finite candidate set drawn uniformly can destabilize model rankings and measured module effects.
  Time-varying source-destination history membership and model operations that use this information directly transmit the sampler's influence to the evaluation score. We examine this mechanism using a factorial evaluation of repeated and new positives against seen and unseen negatives, a minimal scorer based solely on pair-history membership, and controlled representation interventions. Across six models on LastFM, MOOC, Reddit, and Wikipedia, at least one model pair changes relative order between the expected Uniform-20 metric and the full catalog on three of the four datasets. The measured effect of the same module also changes in magnitude and direction with the candidate-set size and training objective.
  These results establish that model-superiority and ablation conclusions from sampled-negative benchmarks are conditional on the stated candidate configuration. All-entity ranking evaluates every destination in a fixed catalog, eliminating negative-selection freedom and sampling variation while retaining the original CTDG scorer. We therefore recommend all-entity ranking as the primary evidence for architecture comparisons on CTDG benchmarks with an enumerable, fixed destination catalog.

</details>


### [159] [Orca: Neural Operators for Causal Reasoning in Continuous Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27867)
*Gerrit Großmann,David A. Selby,Sebastian J. Vollmer*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Orca is a neural-operator-based causal framework for continuous-time dynamic systems where nodes are time-dependent functions and mechanisms are learned operators between function spaces, enabling counterfactual reasoning with reusable latent noise; demonstrated on synthetic data with code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard structural causal models are static and acyclic, limiting causal reasoning for systems that evolve over time, are irregularly observed, and contain feedback loops. A neural-operator approach provides a natural representation for function-valued dynamics and causal interactions.

Method: Extend neural operator architectures to causal graphs: each node is a function of time; each mechanism computes a node's function value from its parent functions using learned operators, respecting the arrow of time. Latent exogenous noise is modeled as a function that can be inferred and reused for counterfactuals. Formalize the model class and apply it to synthetic continuous-time examples to demonstrate counterfactual reasoning; code is released.

Result: Counterfactual reasoning is demonstrated on synthetic continuous-time examples; the work provides a formal model class and a public implementation for Orca.

Conclusion: Orca offers a principled framework to perform causal reasoning in continuous-time systems with feedback and irregular observations by leveraging neural operators to model time-dependent causal mechanisms; opens pathways for real-world applications and further research.

Abstract: Structural causal models are the standard language for reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals, but they describe static variables, typically measured once, and usually forbid cyclic dependencies. Many systems we care about, such as patients, climates, and economies, instead evolve continuously in time, are observed at irregular time points, and contain feedback loops. We argue that neural operator learning provides a natural foundation for causal reasoning in this setting, and propose Orca, a framework in which each node of the causal graph is a function of time and each mechanism is a learned map between function spaces. We extend existing neural operator architectures to express causal mechanisms: a mechanism computes the function value of a node from its parent nodes by taking several parent functions as input, respects the arrow of time, and treats latent exogenous noise as a function that can be inferred and reused for counterfactuals. We formalize the model class and demonstrate counterfactual reasoning on synthetic continuous-time examples. Code is available at https://github.com/gerritgr/orca

</details>


### [160] [Search as Computation Allocation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27871)
*Alexander Tuisov*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A unified framework for terminal decision-cost accounting: compute expensive observations to inform latent beliefs, maximize decision quality under budgets; connects VOC with information theory and search algorithms; shows multiple equivalences and limits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To formalize how expensive computations contribute to decision quality and how to quantify the value of information under budgeted or priced computation, linking VOC to information measures and common search procedures.

Method: Define terminal computation-allocation problems where costly observations update beliefs and only terminal loss matters. Derive Bellman equations for fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification. Relate VOC to information metrics (mutual information, knowledge-gradient). Illustrate with bandits, tree search, and node expansions; introduce frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model to derive that maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A* (and connects to standard A* and greedy best-first as limits).

Result: Establishes formal relationships between VOC and information measures: mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss; VOC equals knowledge-gradient under simple regret; information gain can misrank computations but upper-bounds VOC. Demonstrates that standard search/plan algorithms fit within the terminal computation-allocation framework.

Conclusion: A shared decision-theoretic problem under computation cost; no universal acquisition rule is optimal; the framework unifies valuation of computation, information, and search strategies, and explains why algorithms like weighted A*, A*, and greedy best-first arise as limits of approximate VOC maximization.

Abstract: Many algorithms spend an internal resource before returning a decision and are evaluated only by the quality of that terminal output. We formalize such procedures as terminal computation-allocation problems: costly computations produce observations, update beliefs about a latent environment, and matter only through terminal decision loss. Bellman equations characterize optimal allocation under fixed budgets, priced computation, and exact certification. We then relate value of computation (VOC) to information. Mutual information equals myopic VOC under log loss, whereas under simple regret VOC is a knowledge-gradient quantity; moreover, information gain can rank computations arbitrarily poorly, although it gives a one-sided upper bound on VOC. Bandit pulls, tree simulations, and node expansions illustrate the same model under different computation topologies. Finally, under an explicit frontier-resolution and heuristic-error model, maximizing approximate VOC recovers weighted A*, with A* and greedy best-first search as limiting cases. The theory identifies a shared decision problem without asserting that one acquisition rule is universally optimal.

</details>


### [161] [An Empirical Study of Coordination Mode as the First-Class Citizen in From-Scratch Multi-Agent Coding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27877)
*Yanyu Ren,Yunfeng Bai,Xizheng Wang,Li Chen,Dan Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A benchmark called MSEval evaluates multi-agent coding on real-world tasks using 10 authentic full-stack projects across 10 domains, with 10 collaboration topologies, a hierarchical rubric, and automated grading that measures functionality, latency, and token cost. Results show topology strongly influences speed, cost, and quality, sometimes more than model capability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address shortcomings of synthetic benchmarks in multi-agent coding that ignore real-world costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward superficial completion, by providing a realistic, reproducible evaluation that accounts time, money, and coordination dynamics.

Method: Ground the evaluation in 10 authentic full-stack projects across 10 domains. Use LegoGent to test 10 collaboration topologies with periodic syncs and native CI/CD deployment. Employ an automated grader TAgent that probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost. Run 100 trials to assess performance across topology-model-task combinations. Score via hierarchical, deterministic rubrics.

Result: Topology choice materially shapes performance: identical tasks and models see score differences >30 points and wall-clock time roughly doubles when switching topologies. Structured pipelines converge fastest with highest quality; heavy managerial oversight degrades performance. Across runs, organizational structure rivals model capability in determining speed-cost-quality trade-offs.

Conclusion: MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software, with open access at the provided repository.

Abstract: Multi-agent vibe coding promises to accelerate software development, yet existing benchmarks rely on synthetic environments that ignore practical time and monetary costs, conflate reasoning with communication, and reward only superficial completion. We introduce multi-agent from-scratch evaluation benchmark, MSEval, evaluating multi-agent coding on real-world tasks. Grounded in 10 authentic, full-stack projects across 10 domains, MSEval scores performance using hierarchical requirements and deterministic rubrics.
  Its execution engine, LegoGent, tests 10 collaboration topologies where agents coordinate via periodic sync intervals and deploy through native CI/CD pipelines. Concurrently, the automated grader TAgent dynamically probes implementations to jointly measure functional success, latency, and prefix-cached token cost. Across 100 runs, MSEval reveals that organizational topology rivals model capability in shaping the speed--cost--quality trade-off. For identical tasks and models, varying the topology shifts scores by over 30 points and doubles wall-clock time. Structured pipelines converge fastest with the highest quality, whereas heavy managerial oversight degrades performance. Ultimately, MSEval establishes a rigorous, reproducible standard for measuring how multi-agent teams actually build software. The benchmark is released at https://github.com/robinren03/MSEval.

</details>


### [162] [Not All Tokens Deserve Equal Credit: Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation for Long-CoT Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27888)
*Qiangqiang He,Zhongheng Wu,ZiJian Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CSCR extends GRPO by downweighting highly sensitive tokens to address unreliable privilege-induced directions in OPSD-based RLHF, yielding stable and improved long-CoT math reasoning performance over GRPO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve long-chain-of-thought (long-CoT) reasoning in large language models by RL with verifiable rewards, and to diagnose why on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) and critic-free methods like GRPO may misallocate credit across tokens.

Method: Perform a counterfactual sensitivity analysis of privileged shifts by re-scoring fixed trajectories under correct vs. incorrect outcomes; propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR) as an extension of GRPO that downweights highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes token-level advantages; evaluate on long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks with controlled policy updates and targeted ablations.

Result: Privileged shifts are largely unreliable for guiding token-level learning; most affected tokens are surface-form and highly substitutable, with problem-specific reasoning tokens less sensitive. CSCR yields consistent improvements over GRPO with the same update budget; moderate downweighting is most effective, while stronger modulation can destabilize optimization.

Conclusion: Privileged outcome-induced directions do not reliably encode answer-aligned information; reweighting by token sensitivity (CSCR) provides a stable and more effective credit allocation for long-CoT reasoning, improving performance over GRPO in the tested benchmarks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is central to improving long-CoT reasoning in large language models. Critic-free methods such as GRPO convert response-level rewards into advantages and uniformly broadcast them across tokens, overlooking their unequal contributions to the final outcome. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) instead provides dense distributional supervision by minimizing the forward KL divergence between an unprivileged policy and a privileged self-teacher, implicitly assuming that the resulting likelihood shifts encode reliable answer-aligned information. We test this premise by fixing each sampled trajectory and re-scoring it under two opposing outcome conditions, one asserting correctness and the other incorrectness. Most affected tokens shift in the same direction under both conditions, with few sign reversals and substantial overlap in the induced optimization signals. Large shifts also concentrate on highly substitutable surface-form tokens, whereas tokens carrying problem-specific reasoning content are less sensitive. These findings show that privileged shifts fail to provide reliable answer-aligned directions, while their magnitudes primarily reflect counterfactual sensitivity rather than token-level learning value. Based on these observations, we propose Counterfactual Sensitivity Credit Reallocation (CSCR), a simple extension of GRPO that reduces credit for highly sensitive tokens and renormalizes token-level advantages to preserve both the original credit budget and verifier-determined direction. On long-CoT mathematical reasoning benchmarks, CSCR consistently outperforms GRPO baseline with the same number of policy updates. Targeted ablations further corroborate our diagnosis: privilege-induced directions are unreliable, moderate downweighting is most effective, and stronger modulation destabilizes optimization.

</details>


### [163] [Dynamic Spectral Filtering for Temporal Graph Learning: Learning Evolving Propagation Operators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27891)
*Yan Kong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DSF proposes a time-evolving spectral filter for graph propagation using vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients treated as recurrent states; achieves strong, parameter-efficient temporal link prediction on MOOC, Wikipedia, Reddit.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate operator-centric temporal evolution of graph propagation to improve efficiency and performance, addressing gaps in predominant node-state evolution and history-encoding approaches.

Method: Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF) represents propagation at snapshot t with a Chebyshev polynomial filter whose coefficients are vector-valued and time-dependent. These coefficients form recurrent temporal states updated by a recurrent branch. Global and order-specific gates regulate magnitude. The temporal state is independent of the number of nodes.

Result: On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, DSF converged to AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860, respectively, with 93K–133K trainable parameters, 68–182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6–2.1 s per epoch. Compared with DEFT, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, modestly lower on Wikipedia, and uses 8.3–8.6x fewer parameters, 25–33x less GPU memory, and 5–19x less time per epoch. Relative to all measured alternatives, DSF uses 3.3–38.6x less GPU memory.

Conclusion: Spectral-response evolution provides a useful temporal inductive bias for temporal graphs when computational efficiency is a primary concern.

Abstract: Temporal graph learning is commonly organized around the evolution of node states or the encoding of interaction histories. We study an underexplored, operator-centric question: should the graph propagation mechanism itself evolve over time? We introduce Dynamic Spectral Filtering (DSF), which represents propagation at snapshot t by a Chebyshev polynomial filter with vector-valued, time-dependent coefficients. DSF explicitly treats these compact multi-order coefficients as recurrent temporal states. A recurrent branch proposes updates, while multiplicative global and order-specific gates regulate their magnitude. The temporal state is independent of the number of nodes. On MOOC, Wikipedia, and Reddit temporal link-prediction benchmarks, converged DSF runs attain AP scores of 0.7851, 0.9088, and 0.9860, respectively, with 93K to 133K trainable parameters, 68 to 182 MB peak GPU memory, and 1.6 to 2.1 seconds of training per epoch. Against the closely related DEFT baseline, DSF is better on MOOC, within 0.001 AP on Reddit, and modestly lower on Wikipedia, while using 8.3 to 8.6 times fewer parameters, 25 to 33 times less GPU memory, and 5 to 19 times less time per epoch. Relative to all measured alternatives, it uses 3.3 to 38.6 times less GPU memory. These results support direct spectral-response evolution as a useful temporal inductive bias when computational efficiency is a first-class requirement.

</details>


### [164] [MMHBench: A Multi-Perspective Benchmark for Mental Health Understanding in Long-Form Videos](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27895)
*Jinpeng Hu,Erqiang Wang,Shan Wang,Zhuo Li,Peipei Song,Xun Yang,Meng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MMHBench: a multimodal benchmark for long-form video mental health understanding with 268 videos and 2,184 questions, two perspective settings, and a MAQG-based question generation pipeline; 22 MLLMs show substantial challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks reduce mental health understanding in videos to coarse-grained tasks and miss nuanced interpretation across observable behavior, context, and latent states. There is a need for a comprehensive, multi-perspective benchmark to evaluate genuine understanding in long-form multimodal data.

Method: Introduce MMHBench with two settings (third-person interpretation from observable behavior; first-person perspective-taking). Develop MAQG to simulate diverse social roles to generate questions from multiple perspectives; iteratively refine questions via multi-role feedback and expert verification; evaluate 22 representative multimodal LLMs (open-source and closed-source).

Result: MMHBench enables diverse, perspective-aware questions; experiments show long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging for current MLLMs, highlighting gaps between surface cues and deeper psychological interpretation.

Conclusion: MMHBench provides a rigorous, multi-perspective benchmark for long-form mental health understanding in videos; the MAQG pipeline yields high-quality questions; results reveal substantial room for improvement in multimodal reasoning with respect to mental health phenomena.

Abstract: Mental health understanding in long-form videos requires nuanced reasoning over observable behavior, interpersonal context, and latent psychological states. Existing benchmarks largely reduce this task to coarse-grained classification, providing limited insight into whether models truly understand psychological phenomena or rely on superficial correlations. To address this limitation, we introduce MMHBench, a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for multi-perspective mental health understanding, comprising 268 long-form videos and 2,184 carefully curated questions. MMHBench organizes the evaluation into two complementary settings: (1) third-person assessment, consisting of 605 questions that focus on the interpretation of observable behaviors and multimodal evidence, and (2) first-person perspective-taking, comprising 1,579 questions that require perspective-conditioned reasoning to identify the interpretation of the mental state supported by the available multimodal evidence. We propose a Multi-Agent Question Generation (MAQG) framework that simulates diverse social roles to synthesize questions from multiple perspectives. The generated questions are refined through multi-role feedback and iterative optimization, followed by expert-guided verification to ensure quality and validity. Extensive evaluation of 22 representative multimodal large language models (MLLMs), spanning both open-source and leading closed-source models, demonstrates that long-form video mental health understanding remains highly challenging.

</details>


### [165] [A Cross-Architecture Audit of Direction-Based Inference-Time Defences in Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27910)
*Xiangyu Yin,Tora Bodin,Rohan Menon,Chih-Hong Cheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Five inference-time defenses for vision-language model jailbreaks were evaluated across 15 model/layer cells from four architectures under a magnitude-controlled protocol. No single method dominates both refusal recovery and utility preservation. Image-conditioning shift often preserves utility with minimal loss but is architecture- and model-specific and not transferable. CMRM shows alignment with image-conditioning direction. Results imply direction-based defenses require per-language-decoder calibration and reveal partial overlap in geometry between defense recipes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how different direction-based inference-time defenses fare against jailbreak attempts in VLMs, across diverse architectures and layers, and to assess transferability and geometry of the defense directions.

Method: Evaluate five defense candidates (mean image conditioning shift, CMRM-style refusal direction, ShiftDC-style attack-specific residual, prompt-instruction to ignore the image, and random control) under a magnitude-controlled protocol. For each prompt, pair the defense direction with a random equal-norm vector. Test across 15 model/layer cells from four architectural families. Measure refusal recovery and utility preservation. Analyze cosine alignment between the CMRM direction and the image-conditioning shift; report statistics and transferability.

Result: No single candidate dominates both refusal recovery and utility preservation. Image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and maintains utility close to measurement noise across all families. Prompt instruction dominates on Qwen2.5 VL; attack-specific residual dominates on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image-conditioning direction is direction-specific in 13 of 15 cells and largely non-transferable across LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B. The CMRM direction positively aligns with image conditioning across all cells (mean cosine 0.35; range 0.17–0.65; 15–25x the random vector; p ≈ 3e-5). The two recipes partly overlap in geometry; calibration is needed per language-decoder family.

Conclusion: Direction-based defenses exhibit architecture- and model-specific geometry; effective defense requires per-language-decoder calibration and careful consideration of transferability. There is partial overlap between defense directions, suggesting potential shared geometry but no universal, one-size-fits-all solution.

Abstract: Inference time defences against vision language model jailbreaks often subtract a calibrated direction from the residual stream at a chosen decoder layer. We compare five defence candidates across 15 model and layer cells from four architectural families under a magnitude controlled protocol that matches the intervention size for each prompt and pairs every direction with a random control of the same norm. The candidates are the mean image conditioning shift, a CMRM style refusal direction, a ShiftDC style attack specific residual, a prompt instruction to ignore the image, and a random control. No single candidate dominates on both refusal recovery and utility preservation. The image conditioning shift leads on LLaVA 1.5 and Pixtral 12B and is the only candidate whose utility loss remains at the measurement noise floor in every family. The prompt instruction leads on Qwen2.5 VL, while the attack specific residual leads on Qwen2 VL 2B. The image conditioning direction is direction specific in 13 of 15 cells, but strongly architecture specific and nontransferable across the only dimension compatible pair, LLaVA 1.5 13B and Pixtral 12B. We also connect text only and multimodal refusal geometry. The CMRM direction has positive cosine alignment with the image conditioning shift in all 15 cells, with mean 0.35, range 0.17 to 0.65, 15 to 25 times the random vector null, and a sign test p value of about 3e-5. These results show that the two recipes recover partially overlapping geometry and that direction based defences should be calibrated separately for each language decoder family.

</details>


### [166] [IFHierBench: Hierarchical Instruction Following for Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27912)
*Yuetian Mao,Chunyang Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IFHierBench is a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark with 600 prompts spanning four constraint depths and 35 constraints, each paired with deterministic, multi-scope checkers. It reveals that current models struggle with nested, hierarchical constraints, averaging ~50% prompt-level accuracy and deteriorating with depth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat constraints as a flat list that applies uniformly to the whole output, failing to assess adherence within specific sections or nested fields. Real-world LLM usage often requires multi-level compliance across structured artifacts.

Method: Create IFHierBench: 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints. Each prompt comes with a deterministic checker that verifies constraint satisfaction at every scope (artifact, sections, nested fields). Evaluate seven leading proprietary/open models on prompt-level accuracy under hierarchical constraints.

Result: Strongest model barely surpasses 50% prompt-level accuracy; accuracy declines sharply as constraint depth increases; reliably following nested constraints remains a substantial gap across models.

Conclusion: To close the gap, future work should explore training and prompting methods that enforce constraint adherence at finer granularity, enabling better instruction-following performance for structured outputs.

Abstract: Instruction-following ability is critical for deploying large language models in real-world applications, where downstream components depend on the output satisfying specific constraints. Modern deployments increasingly handle the full task in a single LLM call, with one prompt specifying a layered output whose overall artifact, structural sections, and nested fields must each satisfy concrete constraints. Existing instruction-following benchmarks treat the constraint set as a flat list applied uniformly to the response, so they cannot scope a check to a particular section of the output. We introduce IFHierBench, a hierarchical instruction-following benchmark of 600 prompts stratified across four constraint-tree depths and 35 distinct constraints, each prompt paired with a deterministic checker that verifies satisfaction at every scope. Evaluating seven leading proprietary and open-weight models, we find that even the strongest model only marginally exceeds 50% prompt-level accuracy and that accuracy degrades sharply as constraint depth grows. Reliably following nested constraints remains a substantial gap for current LLMs, motivating future training methods that consider constraint adherence at finer granularity to achieve better instruction-following ability.

</details>


### [167] [One Anchor for All: Unified Multilingual and Multimodal Safety Alignment for LVLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27917)
*Enyi Shi,Fei Shen,Chuancheng Shi,Linxia Zhu,Shuyi Miao,Jinhui Tang,Tat-Seng Chua*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: We propose MLS-Neurons, a neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework for LVLMs that identifies and aligns safety neurons across unimodal, multimodal, and multilingual dimensions, updating only a tiny subset (~0.03%) to transfer English safety supervision to multilingual/multimodal settings, achieving strong safety performance while preserving utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LVLMs face covert, compound attacks exploiting multilingual and multimodal inputs; existing defenses are siloed and require heavy data/fine-tuning; a minimal, cross-dimensional safety alignment is needed.

Method: 1) Identify monolingual/unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful vs benign samples and measuring functional saliency via activation strength and downstream impact. 2) Intersect unimodal neurons within each language to obtain MS-Neurons that respond to both visual and textual risks. 3) Use English as semantic anchor to intersect MS-Neurons across languages to obtain MLS-Neurons that are shared across modality and language. 4) Update only this small shared subset (~0.03% of parameters) with safety supervision to transfer English-only safety to multilingual/multimodal settings.

Result: Extensive experiments show significant improvements over state-of-the-art on diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility.

Conclusion: Minimal, cross-dimensional safety alignment via MLS-Neurons provides effective, transferable defenses with low fine-tuning cost, bridging safety gaps across languages and modalities.

Abstract: As large vision-language models (LVLMs) are deployed globally, the combination of multilingual instructions and visual information makes malicious attacks more covert and sophisticated than ever before. However, existing methods isolate language and modality defenses, which, coupled with the scarcity of safety data and high fine-tuning costs, makes it difficult for models to defend against compound attacks. To address this severe challenge, we propose a neuron-level cross-dimensional safety alignment framework driven by modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons). First, we identify monolingual and unimodal safety neurons by comparing responses to harmful and benign samples, quantifying functional saliency through activation strength and downstream impact. Then, by intersecting these unimodal neurons within each language, we extract modality-shared safety neurons (MS-Neurons) responsive to both visual and textual risks, bridging the safety representation gap between modalities. Furthermore, using English as a semantic anchor, we intersect MS-Neurons across languages to identify modality- and language-shared safety neurons (MLS-Neurons), serving as key defenses against compound attacks. Finally, we update only this minimal subset of shared neurons (~0.03% of parameters), transferring English-only safety supervision to multilingual and multimodal scenarios. Extensive experiments show that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse multilingual and multimodal safety benchmarks while preserving general utility.

</details>


### [168] [Meta-Task: Turning Terminal Task Synthesis into a Terminal Task for Scalable Agent Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27929)
*Zhihong Pan,Jiyuan He,Kai Zhang,Yupeng Han,Ze Liu,Yuze Zhao,Yongcong Ye,Zhaohua Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Meta-Task frames terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task executed in a real container, enabling iterative generation, execution, and verification with multi-phase task design and LLM-based filtering, achieving data-efficient downstream training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training terminal agents at scale requires diverse, verifiable terminal tasks and high-quality trajectories; existing synthesis approaches suffer from unreliable task generation due to misalignment with real execution and limited diversity due to repository dependence.

Method: An agent operates inside a real container to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks (Terminal-Bench-style). The approach decouples target task requirements across multiple dimensions, uses a multi-phase mechanism to design novel task specs prior to production of tasks, and optionally incorporates external materials. LLM-as-Judge filters the final training data.

Result: On Terminal-Bench 2.0, fine-tuning with 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories yields Avg Pass@1 of 22.5% for Qwen3-14B and 31.8% for Qwen3-32B, outperforming concurrent approaches with substantially more data.

Conclusion: Meta-Task improves reliability, diversity, and data efficiency in terminal task synthesis, enabling competitive downstream performance with far less synthetic data.

Abstract: Training terminal agents at scale requires diverse, verifiable terminal tasks and high-quality interaction trajectories, yet acquiring such data remains a significant challenge. Existing synthesis methods face two key limitations: (1) weak reliability caused by the disconnect between task generation and real execution, and (2) limited diversity and scalability due to dependence on existing repositories. We propose Meta-Task, a framework that redefines terminal task synthesis as a Terminal-Bench-format task itself: an agent operates within a real container environment to iteratively generate, execute, and verify tasks, so that synthesized components are checked for internal consistency and executability within the generation loop itself. Building upon this, we decouple the target task requirements along multiple dimensions, introduce a multi-phase mechanism that dynamically designs novel task specifications before producing the actual tasks, and incorporate optional external material support to enhance diversity and realism. We additionally apply LLM-as-Judge filtering to ensure the quality of the final training data. Experiments on Terminal-Bench 2.0 show that fine-tuning on only 3,221 Meta-Task synthesized trajectories achieves 22.5% and 31.8% Avg Pass@1 for Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B respectively, outperforming concurrent approaches with significantly less training data.

</details>


### [169] [The Geometric Nature and a Free Proxy for Flow-Matching Uncertainty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27933)
*Ziyang Rao,Yiren Zhao,Weiyu Guo,Ben Fei,Yandong Guo,Hui Xiong*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces denoising acceleration (accel), a zero-cost uncertainty proxy for Flow Matching (FM) in conditional generative models. It measures bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass to detect uncertainty and potential failures without extra evaluations, training, or resampling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reliable uncertainty estimation for FM-based controllers is crucial for safe deployment, but existing real-time methods incur extra training, high computation, and poor generalization. A lightweight, generalizable proxy would enable safer and more efficient operation under deployment budgets.

Method: Geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. Propose accel, which quantifies the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass, requiring no additional model evaluations, training, or resampling. The approach is supported by theoretical and empirical validation and is assessed for online failure detection.

Result: Accel acts as a faithful FM-uncertainty proxy, identifying failing rollouts well before termination and matching or surpassing costly resampling- and training-based baselines under realistic deployment budgets.

Conclusion: Accel enables cheap, generalizable, and effective uncertainty estimation for FM in real-time control, facilitating safer deployment and broader applicability without compromising performance or incurring substantial computational costs.

Abstract: Flow matching (FM) has become a popular action head paradigm for modern embodied models. However, as a conditional generative model, it does not explicitly expose its inherent uncertainty, producing faulty action chunks even when it misinterprets the scene or encounters out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. Therefore, determining when an FM-generated action can be trusted is essential for safe deployment, yet existing uncertainty estimation methods on real-time control suffer from several issues: extra training budget, high computational overhead, and low generalization ability. In this work, we provide a geometric interpretation of FM uncertainty in the velocity field, showing that uncertainty manifests as deviation from an ideal affine-isotropic contraction field. Building on this observation, we introduce denoising acceleration ($\mathrm{accel}$), a highly-generalizable and cost-free uncertainty proxy that measures the bending of the denoising trajectory from a single forward pass, without additional model evaluations, training, or resampling. We theoretically and empirically demonstrate that $\mathrm{accel}$ is a faithful proxy for FM uncertainty and further test its utility in online failure detection. Results show that $\mathrm{accel}$ identifies failing rollouts well before termination, matching or even outperforming costly resampling- and training-based baselines across settings under realistic deployment budget. Code and demos available at: https://github.com/rrrrrrzy/fm-geometry.

</details>


### [170] [Shapes from Examples: Foundations of Shape Learning in Recursive SHACL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27934)
*Bente Gortworst,Cem Okulmus,Magdalena Ortiz,Anni-Yasmin Turhan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Fitting SHACL shapes from positive/negative examples under an ELI-core fragment and three semantics (well-founded, stable, supported) is computationally characterized: existence and most-specific fitting are tight exponential-time, with polynomial bounds in several special cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Knowledge graphs rely on SHACL for validation. Automatic learning of shape expressions from labeled nodes (positive/negative) is essential for scalable schema induction and data validation, especially under logically constrained SHACL fragments.

Method: Formalize the fitting problem where a shape C (from a recursive catalogue of named shapes) validates all P and none of N, with C restricted to the core SHACL fragment corresponding to Description Logic ELI. Adopt three semantics for shape catalogues (well-founded, stable, supported). Prove decidability and compute-most-specific fittings, deriving upper bounds and identifying tractable subcases.

Result: Prove tight exponential-time upper bounds for the existence of a fitting and for computing the most specific fitting; derive polynomial-time bounds for relevant special cases.

Conclusion: The work delineates the computational boundary for learning SHACL shapes under ELI with several catalogue semantics, showing inherent exponential complexity in general, but enabling efficient solutions in important special cases, guiding practical shape learning for knowledge graphs.

Abstract: SHACL shapes enable data graph validation, making automatic shape learning essential for knowledge graph applications. We investigate the well-known fitting approach to this task: given sets P and N of positive and negative example nodes from an input graph, compute a shape expression C, possibly using shape names defined in a recursive shape catalogue, that validates at every node in P and none in N. We focus on the case where C is written in a core fragment of SHACL corresponding to the Description Logic ELI. For the catalogue, we consider the well-founded, stable, and supported semantics. We address fitting existence and most specific fitting computation, establish tight exponential-time upper bounds for both problems, and obtain polynomial bounds for relevant special cases.

</details>


### [171] [From Scoring to Acting: Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27937)
*Xu Xia,Jinghua Piao,Min Yang,Xiaochong Lan,Jiaju Chen,Yong Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation (OVCSD) for LLM agents: uses outcome-verified supervision on a prefix-tree of failed rollouts, adaptive skill-conditioned teacher invocation, and localized comparative learning at divergence; achieves large gains on ALFWorld/WebShop with minimal privileged training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address two limitations of on-policy self-distillation (OPSD): (1) teacher preferences lack grounding in environment outcomes, and (2) action-level scores underutilize information from student and teacher rollouts and their relations.

Method: Construct a prefix-tree of failed student trajectories; at student-reached states, adaptively invoke a skill-conditioned teacher; retain only outcome-verified successful continuations; perform localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence; distill the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior.

Result: Consistent improvements over skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines across three model scales on ALFWorld and WebShop; up to 29.7 percentage-point gains on ALFWorld and 5.4 on WebShop in absolute success-rate; privileged interaction during training is <3%.

Conclusion: Outcome-verified comparative supervision effectively internalizes capabilities in LLM agents, enabling efficient transfer of completion behavior with strong gains across tasks and model scales, using limited privileged data.

Abstract: Recent work on LLM agents is shifting from external capability elicitation to capability internalization, enabling agents to retain useful skills without retrieval at inference time. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) offers a promising direction, but many existing methods typically supervise students by scoring actions along student-generated trajectories. Such supervision has two limitations: teacher preferences are not validated by environment outcomes, and action-level scores underuse information from student rollouts, teacher rollouts, and their behavioral relationship. We therefore advocate outcome-verified teacher supervision and comparative learning over teacher-student trajectories. Based on this view, we propose Outcome-Verified Comparative Self-Distillation (OVCSD). OVCSD organizes failed student rollouts into a prefix tree, adaptively invokes a skill-conditioned teacher from student-reached states, and retains only outcome-verified successful continuations. It then applies localized comparative learning at the first state-aligned divergence and distills the post-divergence teacher suffix to transfer completion behavior. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop across three model scales show that OVCSD consistently outperforms skill-free RL and existing self-distillation baselines, achieving up to 29.7 and 5.4 absolute success-rate gains over the strongest baselines on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively, while adding less than 3% privileged interaction during training.

</details>


### [172] [MARS-RA: Rank Aggregation for Credit Assignment via Multimodal Comparisons in Embodied Multi-Agent Cooperation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27967)
*Dawei Wang,Di Zhao,Xinyuan Liu,Marci Chi Ma,Xiaoyang Liu,Chengming Zhou,Gary Ushaw,Richard Davison*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Reformulates MARL credit assignment as rank aggregation of pairwise agent contributions using LMMs; robust to changing agent counts and noise; uses potential-based shaping from contributions; convergence/robustness proven; Shapley values for interpretability; empirically improves cooperation across tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Credit assignment in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning under limited/delayed feedback and dynamic agent participation; absolute contribution estimates are fragile to noise and agent churn.

Method: Generate pairwise contributor assessments among agents via large multimodal models; aggregate these rankings to obtain relative contribution scores; convert scores into potential-based rewards for shaping; provide theoretical convergence/robustness analysis; use Shapley values as interpretive reference.

Result: Theoretical results indicate convergence and robustness of the framework; empirical results across diverse task types show improved cooperative behavior and guidance toward effective collaboration.

Conclusion: MARS-RA offers a robust, interpretable credit assignment mechanism for embodied AI with dynamic agent sets, leveraging rank-based contributions and Shapley-like interpretation to improve coordination and resilience to noise.

Abstract: Credit assignment is a fundamental challenge in cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, particularly in embodied AI settings characterized by limited and delayed feedback as well as dynamically changing numbers of active agents. We propose MARS-RA, a framework that reformulates credit assignment as a rank aggregation problem using contribution-based pairwise comparisons among agents generated by large multimodal models. This shift from absolute to relative estimation ensures robustness against noise and dynamic agent participation, converting comparison results into contribution scores for potential-based reward shaping. We provide theoretical justification for the convergence and robustness of the proposed framework, and show that Shapley values can be used as an interpretive reference. Experimental results on challenging tasks of different types indicate that MARS-RA can guide agents toward effective cooperation.

</details>


### [173] [Share the Judge, Learn the Deferral: Where Specialization Helps LLM Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27984)
*Weining Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Shared learning of judgment is typically better than splitting evaluation across multiple specialized judges, and domain-specific adaptation should be placed in an audited release boundary rather than in evaluator weights; when data justify a split, use accredited structures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Agentic systems create a persistent gap between generating candidate outputs and evaluating them. The paper investigates where to introduce domain specialization—either into evaluator weights or into the trust/deferral rules—using large-scale rubric-conditioned evaluation and ablations to assess accuracy, auditability, and compute implications.

Method: Experimentally, the authors study 99,952 rubric-conditioned examples. They compare using the correct rubric versus an unrelated one; they partition the training corpus into eight criterion-family LoRA judges; they examine capacity matching with a single rank-64 adapter; they initialize family adapters from a shared judge; they explore a deferral-versus-judgment specialization; they evaluate a learned-correctness-headed cascade (0.6B-4B-8B) on RewardBench 2 across 20 locked repartitions with risk audits; they compare against a fixed 8B baseline and report compute-normalized results.

Result: Key findings include: (1) correct rubric improves locked-test accuracy by 2.11 points; an unrelated rubric costs 2.66 points. (2) Splitting into eight LoRA judges causes a 10.05-point drop in accuracy and reduces audited coverage at 5% risk from 24.44% to 5.43%. (3) Matching the bank’s capacity with a single rank-64 adapter does not reproduce the loss. (4) Initializing the family adapters from a shared judge recovers accuracy to 76.85%, about 19.94 points above scratch training (95% CI 18.88–21.02). (5) If specialization governs deferral instead of judgment, a learned-correctness cascade improves RewardBench 2 accuracy to 89.40% (vs 84.75% for 8B) at 0.415 normalized parameter compute, with all runs passing a one-sided 95% audit; margin-based rules stay near 84.8% with at least 0.94 compute. (6) The overall design rule: share judgment learning until data justify a split, then place domain-specific adaptation in an audited release boundary.

Conclusion: The results support a qualified design principle: delay specialization in judgment until there is sufficient data to justify division; when splitting, constrain domain-specific adaptation to an audited release boundary to preserve auditability and coverage while controlling compute.

Abstract: Agentic systems have widened the gap between producing candidate outputs and reviewing them. This paper asks a practical architectural question: should domain specialization be built into an evaluator's weights, or into the rule that decides when its judgment can be trusted? We study 99,952 public, rubric-conditioned examples. Supplying the correct rubric improves locked-test accuracy by 2.11 points over a response-only control; replacing it with an unrelated rubric costs 2.66 points. Dividing the same training corpus among eight criterion-family LoRA judges, however, loses 10.05 points and cuts audited coverage at a 5% risk target from 24.44% to 5.43%. Matching the bank's stored capacity with one rank-64 adapter does not reproduce this loss. Nor is the result explained by learning rate or optimizer steps. Initializing the family adapters from a shared, trained judge recovers test accuracy to 76.85%, 19.94 points above scratch training at the same learning rate (95% interval 18.88-21.02). The result changes when specialization governs deferral rather than judgment. On RewardBench 2, learned correctness heads route examples through a 0.6B-4B-8B cascade without changing any reward score. Across 20 locked repartitions, the cascade attains 89.40% accuracy, compared with 84.75% for 8B alone, at 0.415 normalized parameter compute. Every run passes an exact one-sided 95% risk audit; margin-based rules remain near 84.8% accuracy while using at least 0.94 compute. These results suggest a qualified design rule: share the learning of judgment until there is enough data to justify a split, and place domain-specific adaptation in an audited release boundary.

</details>


### [174] [SKIMIX: Multi-Agent Harness-Time Scaling with Skill Mixture for Dynamic Harness Engineering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27994)
*Jia Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SKIMIX enables collaboration among agents with diverse skill portfolios via embedding-based skill retrieval, anti-dilution routing, and adaptive skill evolution; it improves open-ended reasoning but not necessarily multiple-choice tasks; gains are non-monotonic with agent count, with most improvements in the first refinement round.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the challenge of selecting, combining, and maintaining large skill libraries for autonomous agents and to improve reasoning through multi-agent collaboration.

Method: Iterative refinement among agents with different skill portfolios, using embedding-based retrieval to fetch relevant skills, submodular anti-dilution routing to balance cross-skill usage, and adaptive evolution of skills over rounds; evaluated across six reasoning benchmarks on open-ended and multiple-choice tasks.

Result: Multi-agent collaboration substantially improves open-ended mathematical reasoning, but yields limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks. Agent-count scaling is non-monotonic, and most improvements occur during the first refinement round.

Conclusion: Task characteristics determine the usefulness of skill-level ensembles; the work provides practical guidance for designing scalable, multi-skill agent systems and when to deploy collaborative ensembles.

Abstract: AI agents increasingly rely on large skill libraries, but selecting, combining, and maintaining skills remains difficult. We propose SKIMIX, a multi-agent framework in which agents with different skill portfolios collaborate through iterative refinement. SKIMIX combines embedding-based skill retrieval, submodular anti-dilution routing, and adaptive skill evolution. Across six reasoning benchmarks, multi-agent collaboration substantially improves open-ended mathematical reasoning but offers limited or negative gains on multiple-choice tasks. Agent-count scaling is non-monotonic, and most improvements arise during the first refinement round. These results show that task characteristics determine whether skill-level ensembles help and provide practical guidance for scalable agent design.

</details>


### [175] [MMLDSum-LLM: Multimodal Long-Document Summarization with Visual-Alignment and Keyword-Aware](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28006)
*Xianpeng Zhang,Jiahua Yang,Dongyu Chen,Lei zhang,Jian Ma,Xu guohuan,Haonan Lu,Tianhuang Su,Chuangchuang Wang,Kai Tang*

Main category: cs.AI
