TL;DR: Introduces MMLDSum-Bench benchmark and MMLDSum-LLM framework for multimodal long-document summarization, addressing information omission and cross-modal hallucinations via improved long-range attention, inter-modal alignment, and multi-objective optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivated by sparse critical evidence distributed across long, multimodal documents, which leads to information omissions and cross-modal hallucinations in existing multimodal LLM summarization due to attention drift and alignment gaps.

Method: Two-stage training: (1) supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss; (2) GRPO (goal-driven reinforcement policy optimization) with multi-objective reward (keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, length control); evaluation against baselines under a unified protocol using LLM-based judgments, atomic-claim precision/recall, ITA, and ROUGE.

Result: Empirical results show significant improvements in key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency on MMLDSum-Bench, outperforming leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models under a unified evaluation protocol.

Conclusion: Benchmark and training framework offer reproducible, scalable improvements for multimodal long-document summarization across domains and context lengths, reducing omissions and cross-modal misalignment while maintaining quality metrics.

Abstract: Multimodal long documents are core carriers of professional knowledge, where critical evidence is sparsely distributed across paragraphs and modalities. This easily causes key information omission and cross-modal hallucinations in summarization by multimodal LLMs. These issues stem from attention drift in long-range dependency modeling and gaps in inter-modal alignment. To address this, we introduce MMLDSum-Bench, a high-quality benchmark for multimodal long-document summarization, covering multiple domains, context-length scales, and visual-textual modality distributions. We further propose MMLDSum-LLM, a reproducible two-stage training framework that combines supervised fine-tuning with visual-alignment weighted loss and keyword-aware weighted loss, followed by GRPO with a multi-objective reward (keyword coverage, image-text alignment, ROUGE, and length control). Extensive experiments on MMLDSum-Bench, comparing against leading closed-source and open-source multimodal models under a unified evaluation protocol - including LLM-as-a-judge scoring, atomic-claim precision/recall, image-text alignment (ITA), and ROUGE - demonstrate that our approach significantly improves key-information coverage and cross-modal consistency.

</details>


### [176] [MUL-T: Decoding Spatial Cellular Architecture in Multiplexed Tissue Images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28030)
*Farzaneh Seyedshahi,Kai Rakovic,Adalberto Claudio Quiros,John LeQuesne,Ke Yuan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MUL-T is a lightweight transformer that reframes tissue architecture as masked contextual prediction over discrete cell tokens, achieving strong performance with low compute.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome scalability and generalization issues in multiplexed imaging where handcrafted features fail across heterogeneous marker panels; enable robust modeling of tissue organization.

Method: A masked contextual prediction framework over discrete cell tokens, learning contextualised [CLS] embeddings without task-specific supervision; a compact transformer with substantially fewer parameters and lower training cost than large ViT models.

Result: MUL-T outperforms classical feature-based baselines across core-level tumor pattern classification, patient-level grading, PD-L1 positivity prediction, and cross-dataset treatment response prediction; its performance approaches that of a foundation ViT model while using far fewer parameters and less training data.

Conclusion: MUL-T provides scalable, generalizable modeling of spatial cellular context in multiplexed imaging, enabling robust clinical predictions with efficient computation.

Abstract: Understanding tissue organisation in multiplexed imaging requires modelling both cellular phenotypes and their spatial context. Existing approaches typically rely on handcrafted features, such as marker intensity statistics or cell-type proportions, which often fail to scale or generalise across cohorts with heterogeneous marker panels. We introduce MUL-T, a lightweight transformer framework that reframes tissue architecture as a masked contextual prediction task over discrete cell tokens. By learning contextualised [CLS] embeddings without task-specific supervision, the model captures higher-order cellular interactions while remaining computationally efficient. We evaluate MUL-T on several clinically relevant downstream tasks, including core-level tumour pattern classification, patient-level grading, PD-L1 positivity prediction, and cross-dataset treatment response prediction. Across tasks, MUL-T consistently outperforms classical feature-based baselines and achieves performance comparable to a foundation ViT model, despite substantially fewer parameters and lower training cost.

</details>


### [177] [DataClawEval: A Benchmark for Data Engineering Agents in Real Industrial Harness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28033)
*Debin Meng,Jiaming Yang,Zefang Zong,Tengyue Xu,Haining Xie,Yang Li,Peng Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A new benchmark, DataClawEval, assesses end-to-end autonomous data engineering across five engines using production-grade tasks, with deterministic sandbox-based evaluation across 16 agents; results show no single model dominates and domain specialization is evident.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current benchmarks largely target simplified tasks (Text-to-SQL, data analysis), leaving end-to-end data engineering underexplored. There is a need for realistic, end-to-end evaluation with production-grade code to measure autonomous agent capabilities in data engineering workflows.

Method: Develop DataClawEval comprising 100 end-to-end tasks spanning PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, and FlinkSQL. Tasks run in isolated sandboxes with deterministic, rule-based scoring. Evaluate 16 frontier agents on the tasks; release dataset, containerized environments, and evaluation scripts.

Result: Best-performing model achieves 74.9 overall; no model dominates across engines, with each model excelling on different engines. The study reveals strong domain specialization and remaining challenges in autonomous data engineering.

Conclusion: End-to-end autonomous data engineering remains a difficult problem. DataClawEval provides a realistic, reproducible benchmark and evaluation framework to quantify progress and identify domain-specific gaps across data engines.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly being deployed to automate complex workflows, promising to revolutionize data management and processing. However, existing benchmarks predominantly focus on simplified Text-to-SQL translation or data analysis, leaving the critical and complex domain of end-to-end data engineering largely unexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce DataClawEval, the first comprehensive benchmark designed specifically to evaluate the end-to-end task completion capabilities of autonomous agents in real-world data engineering scenarios. Built upon production-grade code authored by professional enterprise data engineers, it comprises 100 rigorous, end-to-end tasks spanning five execution engines: PySpark, MySQL, HiveSQL, PrestoSQL/Trino, and FlinkSQL. Rather than non-deterministic LLM-as-a-judge scoring, each task is executed within a case-specific, isolated sandbox and graded by deterministic, rule-based scripts. Evaluating 16 frontier agents exposes critical limitations: The strongest model attains only 74.9 overall, and no single model dominates, as each excels on a different engine, revealing strict domain specialization rather than omnipotent proficiency. Thus, autonomous data engineering remains a formidable, unresolved challenge. We release our dataset, containerized environments, and deterministic evaluation scripts at https://github.com/Dicemy/DataClawEval/tree/master

</details>


### [178] [SKILL-KD: Contrastive Skill Distillation for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28048)
*Qiming Shi,Yibo Dou,Jiawen Zhu,Yulong Tao,Linbo Jin,Zhaolu Kang,Yunfan Zhou,Di Weng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SKILL-KD introduces a contrastive skill distillation framework that treats skills as explicit textual patches distilled from teacher-student discrepancies, with drift-aware consolidation to prevent patch drift and improve weak student agents without full model fine-tuning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address the mismatch between how skills are represented (as implicit demonstrations or representations) and the needs of weaker student agents, where failing trajectories may not reveal the correct behavior, by using explicit, reusable textual patches as the distillation medium.

Method: Given a student failure and the teacher trajectory on the same task, SKILL-KD extracts actionable discrepancies as textual skill patches, tests them by re-running the student, and iteratively refines patches. It maintains trace-linked edit histories and applies Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation to decide whether to add, modify, delete, or skip patches, ensuring stability across updates.

Result: Empirical evaluation across five agent benchmarks and two student settings shows that SKILL-KD consistently improves frozen student agents compared to fixed-model adaptation baselines.

Conclusion: Explicit textual skill patches with drift-aware consolidation provide a robust mechanism to distill actionable improvements from teacher trajectories to weaker students, enhancing their performance without full fine-tuning.

Abstract: Skill-based prompting has become a practical mechanism for improving large language model (LLM) agents, yet existing skill acquisition methods often treat skills as experience summaries, memory entries, or direct summaries of successful demonstrations. This creates a mismatch for weaker student agents: when a student fails because it lacks task knowledge or operational strategy, its failed trajectory may not contain enough evidence to infer the missing behavior, while the teacher trajectory may be too implicit to be internalized as reusable guidance. We propose SKILL-KD, a contrastive skill distillation framework that treats skills as an explicit distillation medium between agents of different capabilities. Given a student failure and the teacher trajectory on the same task, SKILL-KD distills their actionable discrepancy into a textual skill patch, evaluates the patch by re-running the student, and iteratively refines the patch when the student still fails. To prevent repeated local updates from causing skill drift, SKILL-KD further maintains trace-linked edit histories and performs Drift-Aware Skill Consolidation, deciding whether each patch should add a new rule, delete or modify an existing rule, or be skipped. Across five agent benchmarks and two student settings, SKILL-KD consistently improves frozen student agents over fixed-model adaptation baselines.

</details>


### [179] [IndustryForge-27B: A Domain-Enhanced Multimodal Foundation Model for Industrial CAD](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28050)
*Nianchen Deng,Jiaxin Ai,Tao Hu,Shu Zou,Yurui Dong,Siqi Li,Xinyu Cai,Xuemeng Yang,Licheng Wen,Hongbin Zhou,Hairong Zhang,Pinlong Cai,Botian Shi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IndustryForge-27B is a domain-specific multimodal foundation model built on Qwen3.5-VL-27B, trained with ~52k industry-CAD multimodal samples across CAD-VQA, parametric CAD code, assembly code, and COM API scripts; it achieves large gains on CAD benchmarks (+33.65 pp) while preserving general capabilities (+1.56 pp) and outperforms GPT-5.4 on four CAD benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Industrial CAD design and manufacturing demand multimodal understanding across engineering drawings, 3D geometry, and code for parametric modeling and Windows COM APIs. General models underperform on these tasks; a single-task fine-tuned model is too narrow to support diverse interactions. A unified, multi-task approach on domain data is needed.

Method: Curated six industrial-CAD sub-corpora totaling ~52k multimodal samples (CAD-VQA; text2cadquery; text2cadquery-assembly; com_2d; com_3d; com_assembly); integrated with the Qwen3.5-VL-27B base; trained with a unified multi-task supervised fine-tuning (SFT) objective to cover parts-to-assemblies and CAD-to-COM workflows.

Result: On four CAD-domain benchmarks, IndustryForge-27B improves by +33.65 percentage points and outperforms the strong closed-source GPT-5.4 across all four. On eleven general-capability benchmarks, it preserves and slightly improves the base ( +1.56 pp mean ) with no catastrophic forgetting.

Conclusion: IndustryForge-27B provides a unified substrate for downstream industrial-agent projects, enabling a full-stack industrial agent across CAD design to software operation, from parts to assemblies, and from single-shot generation to closed-loop self-improvement.

Abstract: Automating industrial CAD design and manufacturing places distinctive demands on multimodal foundation models: the model must see engineering drawings and 3D geometry screenshots, write correct parametric-modelling scripts and Windows COM API code, and cover the full range from single parts to assemblies. General-purpose multimodal models fall short on these tasks, while single-task fine-tuning is too narrow to support the diverse calls that upper-layer agents issue. We build IndustryForge-27B on top of Qwen3.5-VL-27B by curating and integrating six industrial-CAD sub-corpora totalling $\sim$52k multimodal samples---CAD Visual QA (CAD-VQA), parametric CAD code (text2cadquery), assembly-level CAD code (text2cadquery-assembly), and three COM sub-corpora for Inventor / SolidWorks (com_2d / com_3d / com_assembly)---and training with a unified multi-task SFT recipe. Across four CAD-domain benchmarks IndustryForge-27B lifts the base model by $+33.65$~pp on average and outperforms the strong closed-source model GPT-5.4 on all four; across eleven general-capability benchmarks it retains, and slightly improves upon, the base model ($+1.56$~pp mean, no catastrophic forgetting). IndustryForge-27B will serve as the common substrate for downstream industrial-agent projects, providing a unified starting point for a full-stack industrial agent that spans from CAD design to industrial-software operation, from parts to assemblies, and from single-shot generation to closed-loop self-improvement.

</details>


### [180] [SemPIC: Learning Semantic Position-Independent KV Caches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28069)
*Hui Xie,Peng Xiao,Yutong Deng\textsuperscript,Shuoran Dou,Jian Yang,Jinyang Guo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SemPIC leverages a LoRA Writer to build native per-layer document KV representations via behavioral distillation, enabling offline cache construction that preserves the standard KV interface; it improves micro-F1 from 0.53 to 0.60 on 3-model/4-task evaluation, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62, with KV Gradient Checkpointing reducing training memory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-context retrieval and agentic workloads repeatedly reuse documents; existing prefix caching and PIC fail to exploit reuse or context future; need adaptive document representations to reduce attention misalignment across reusable blocks.

Method: Train a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile per-layer document KVs through behavioral distillation, keeping the pretrained decoder as Reader; offline cache construction; preserve KV interface and decoding path; introduce KV Gradient Checkpointing for memory savings; evaluation across three models and four tasks.

Result: Mean micro-F1 over KV Packet improves from 0.53 to 0.60; close to Full Recompute 0.62; demonstrates effectiveness of SemPIC and memory-saving technique.

Conclusion: Adapting document representations via SemPIC plus KV Gradient Checkpointing yields substantial gains in long-context retrieval with offline caching, narrowing the gap to full recomputation while maintaining compatibility with standard KV interfaces.

Abstract: Long-context retrieval and agentic workloads repeatedly reuse the same documents under changing instructions, histories, and document orders. Prefix caching cannot exploit this reuse, while position-independent caching (PIC) remains unreliable because independently compiled KV states lack the future context in which they will be consumed. Our diagnostics show that a learned boundary-conditioned baseline sharply reduces attention deviation near reusable-block boundaries but leaves interior and task-level residuals, motivating adaptation of the document representation itself. We present \emph{SemPIC}, which trains a LoRA-enabled Writer to compile native per-layer document KVs through behavioral distillation while retaining the pretrained decoder as an unchanged Reader. Adaptation is confined to offline cache construction, preserving the standard KV interface and cache-hit decoding path. We further introduce KV Gradient Checkpointing, which reduces peak training memory without severing gradients through cached KVs. Across three models and four tasks, SemPIC raises mean micro-F1 over KV Packet from 0.53 to 0.60, approaching Full Recompute at 0.62.

</details>


### [181] [Echoverse: Deep, Evolving Environments for Training Computer-Use Agents at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28074)
*Yash Pandya,Sahil Gupta,Sarthak Harne,Archana Yadav,Kavyansh Chourasia,Hussein Mozannar,Vibhav Vineet,Sara Abdali,Corby Rosset,Yash Lara,Ahmed Awadallah,Ece Kamar,Akshay Nambi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Echoverse compiles specifications into stateful applications for training agents, uses a co-evolution loop to repair environments and training signals, and demonstrates substantial gains on large models. It identifies three properties—behavioral depth, failure-targeted tasks, and model-aligned improvement—as key drivers, and releases a four-environment benchmark with graders.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Training agents that act on real or simulated apps requires interactive, gated, and stateful environments. Bulk generation shifts bottlenecks from quantity to content; thus understanding how environmental properties affect learning is essential.

Method: Convert specifications into stateful applications. Use a co-evolution loop: graded rollouts inform repairs to the environment, tasks, and verifier, and provide training signals to the model. Evaluate on twelve environments with a 9B model; additionally frame environments as RL with a verifier and per-step judge for rewards. Release four environments with seed data and graders.

Result: 9B model improves from 36.5% to 67.1% across fourteen evaluation splits, approaching frontier model; shallow environments degrade live-site accuracy, while deep ones improve; single interface control generalizes; repairing environments boosts model performance; RL reward raises held-out score from 58.8% to 68.0%.

Conclusion: Depth and targeted failure, coupled with co-evolved verifiers, tasks, and environments, yield substantial gains; Echoverse provides a benchmark suite and code to advance research on synthetic stateful environments.

Abstract: Computer-use agents learn from what their actions change, so training one needs applications it can act on, break and reset. The applications that matter most are login-gated and stateful, so synthetic environments stand in for them. Recent pipelines generate such environments in bulk, which moves the bottleneck from how many exist to what is inside each one. The returns, we find, come from three properties: how much behavioural depth an environment carries, whether it targets the interaction an agent actually fails, and whether it improves alongside the model. We present Echoverse, which compiles specifications into stateful applications whose tasks are graded against the application's own database, and a co-evolution loop that reads every graded rollout twice: as repairs to the environment, its tasks and its verifier, and as training signal for the model. Trained on twelve such environments, a 9B model improves from $36.5\%$ to $67.1\%$ across fourteen evaluation splits, within fourteen points of the much larger frontier model that taught it. We examine each property in turn. On the same domains, shallow environments push live-site accuracy below the base model ($80.0 \to 75.0$) while deep ones raise it ($80.0 \to 85.0$ and $48.0 \to 65.0$); drilling one interface control across many renderings transfers to held-out widget families and to the open web; and repairing a single environment lifts the model trained on it from $16.2\%$ to $38.5\%$. The same worlds serve as reinforcement-learning environments, where a reward combining the grounded verifier with a dense per-step judge raises held-out score from $58.8\%$ to $68.0\%$. We release four environments as a benchmark, with their applications, seed data and grounded graders. Code: https://aka.ms/echoverse

</details>


### [182] [Group-Reflective Self-Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28076)
*Binbin Zheng,Zijun Xie,Guanqun Zhao,Enlei Gong,Xing Ma,Xiaoliang Fu,Zeyu Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GRSD introduces group-reflective self-distillation to derive capability-aligned, outcome-discriminative guidance from the policy's own verified rollouts, improving credit assignment and robustness across tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides coarse trajectory-level supervision; existing self-distillation relying on external skills or single-trajectory extraction risks misalignment or path-specific bias.

Method: For each prompt, the policy reflects on each verified trajectory within an on-policy group. A stop-gradient snapshot contrasts the reflections from successful vs. failed rollouts to create group-level privileged guidance. A self-teacher uses this guidance to modulate turn-level credit assignment while preserving the verifier-based learning direction.

Result: GRSD outperforms competitive baselines across multiple agentic environments and scales, and generalizes better to unseen tasks.

Conclusion: GRSD offers a scalable, on-policy, verification-aligned self-distillation mechanism that improves credit assignment and robustness in LLM agents trained with verifiable rewards.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is effective for training large language model agents. However, terminal rewards provide only coarse trajectory-level supervision, leaving successful behaviors, recurring mistakes, and incidental choices entangled in the same outcome signal. Existing agentic self-distillation methods enrich sparse supervision with natural-language skills, but skills retrieved externally or extracted from a single trajectory by stronger models may mismatch current experience, exceed the policy's capability, or remain path-specific. We propose Group-Reflective Self-Distillation (GRSD), which derives capability-aligned and outcome-discriminative guidance from the policy's own verified rollouts. For each prompt, the policy reflects on each verified trajectory in an on-policy group, and a stop-gradient snapshot contrasts the resulting reflections from successful and failed rollouts to construct group-level privileged guidance. Conditioned on this guidance, a self-teacher refines turn-level credit assignment by modulating outcome-based advantages while preserving the verifier-determined learning direction. Experiments across multiple agentic environments and model scales demonstrate that GRSD consistently outperforms competitive baselines and generalizes more effectively to unseen tasks.

</details>


### [183] [Distilling Answer Set Programming Theories from Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28086)
*Nelson Higuera Ruiz,Markus Hofmarcher,Claudiu Leoveanu-Condrei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A neurosymbolic prompting protocol distills complete ASP theories within 1 hour using a fixed solver loop; evaluated on VQA benchmarks CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER; frontier models achieve near-perfect performance; GPT-5 shows mixed results; adding handwritten references modestly helps frontier models but hurts GPT-5; code and theories released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate whether large language models can distill complete and correct Answer Set Programming theories from scratch, using a fixed agent with a solver in the loop, in a dataset-agnostic protocol.

Method: Prompt-based distillation with empty starting file, 1-hour time limit, fixed agent with solver in the loop; evaluation across nine models (four frontier, two mid-tier, three open weights) on three VQA benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER); comparison to handwritten reference theories; release of code/prompts/theories.

Result: Frontier models reach 100% on CLEVR and 92.8%-98.8% on GQA; on CLEVRER, Sonnet/Opus/DeepSeek V4 Pro score 92.7%-95.3%; GPT-5 achieves 98.7% on CLEVR but 41.8% on GQA and 86.7% on CLEVRER; adding handwritten references changes other frontier models by up to ±3.4pp but reduces GPT-5 accuracy by 3-19pp; code, prompts, and theories distilled are released.

Conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of neurosymbolic ASP theory distillation with a solver-in-the-loop protocol; model scale is crucial; protocol is dataset-agnostic and reproducible via released materials.

Abstract: Writing Answer Set Programming (ASP) theories from scratch is a difficult and time-consuming task. We take a neurosymbolic approach to study whether a model can distill complete and correct theories, given a fixed agent harness with the solver in the loop. The protocol is dataset-agnostic: with a single prompt and an empty file as the starting point the model is given a 1-hour time limit to derive a complete theory. We chose VQA as the application domain, three benchmarks (CLEVR, GQA, CLEVRER), as these are publicly available and non-trivial. In order to study the model scale required for solving this task we nine different models: four frontier (Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Opus 4.7, GPT-5, DeepSeek V4 Pro), two mid-tier (DeepSeek V4 Flash, gpt-oss-120b), and three open-weights (qwen3.6-27b, gpt-oss-20b, qwen3.5-9b). Three of four frontier models reach 100% on CLEVR and 92.8%-98.8% on GQA; on CLEVRER, Sonnet, Opus, DeepSeek V4 Pro score 92.7%-95.3%. GPT-5 reaches 98.7% on CLEVR but drops to 41.8% on GQA and to 86.7% on CLEVRER. Adding handwritten reference theories from other datasets moves the other three frontier models by at most +/-3.4 pp but reduces GPT-5's accuracy by 3-19 pp. We release the code, prompts, and theories distilled.

</details>


### [184] [Diversifying Personalized Research Ideation against AI-Induced Homogenization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28087)
*Rui Xu,Yunke Wang,Linwei Tao,Wenjie Xuan,Yong Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DivAlign is a four-stage pipeline that personalizes ideation directions by extracting fine-grained researcher profiles, generating profile-conditioned directions, scoring them on Executability, Comprehensibility, and Growth Potential, and surfacing diverse, low-redundancy directions while preserving researcher-direction alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current ideation systems favor generic, high-probability directions, risking misalignment with individual researcher constraints and homogenization of the community portfolio. The paper aims to align suggestions with fine-grained researcher representations and reduce portfolio redundancy.

Method: 1) Extract fine-grained researcher profiles; 2) generate profile-conditioned candidate directions; 3) score directions on three alignment dimensions; 4) surface researcher-local directions and reduce community redundancy; benchmark built from 95 AI researchers across five subfields.

Result: DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy compared to coarse single-shot ideation (average pairwise similarity 0.331→0.294; nearest-neighbor similarity 0.704→0.608). Compared with independent top-choice variant, NN similarity 0.663→0.608 while retaining 99.9% of researcher-direction fit. Code/data released.

Conclusion: Alignment-preserving de-homogenization is feasible: fine-grained profiles and multi-dimensional scoring can diversify researcher directions without sacrificing individual fit; the approach yields measurable reductions in redundancy in a real-world-inspired benchmark.

Abstract: AI-assisted research ideation has emerged as a promising paradigm for accelerating scientific discovery, with systems now capable of generating research directions conditioned on papers, topics, or lightweight researcher contexts. Yet current systems largely optimize individual suggestions in isolation. This leaves two blind spots. First, coarse researcher representations may elicit mainstream directions that appear broadly feasible, but lack sufficient researcher-specific grounding. Second, independent recommendations can concentrate a community's portfolio around recurring high-probability themes. To address these blind spots, we propose DivAlign, a four-stage pipeline for alignment-preserving de-homogenization. DivAlign extracts fine-grained researcher profiles, generates profile-conditioned candidate directions, scores them along three alignment dimensions (Executability, Comprehensibility, and Growth Potential), and surfaces researcher-local directions while reducing redundancy across the community portfolio. On a benchmark we construct from 95 AI researchers across five subfields, DivAlign reduces community-level redundancy while preserving researcher-direction fit. Compared with coarse single-shot ideation, it lowers average pairwise similarity from 0.331 to 0.294 and nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.704 to 0.608. Compared with the independent top-choice variant, DivAlign reduces nearest-neighbor similarity from 0.663 to 0.608 while retaining 99.9% of the researcher-direction fit score. Code and data are available at https://github.com/Ruixxxx/DivAlign.

</details>


### [185] [PerturbMap: Cross-Context Transfer of Single-Cell Perturbation Responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28090)
*Panpan Cui,Yiqi Liu,Wenhao Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PerturbMap predicts missing recipient-context perturbation effects by combining a recipient-local low-rank base with transport proposals from source contexts using source-to-recipient ridge experts; weights are set by route reliability via validation anchors, improving predictive accuracy and cross-context retrieval on Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma data, approaching centralized references.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Single-cell perturbation atlases rarely measure every intervention across all contexts; ignoring measured responses discards evidence and naive transfer risks signal contamination. A principled transport-based approach is needed to leverage source-context measurements while preserving recipient-context specificity.

Method: Construct a recipient-local low-rank base; generate proposals that transport the same perturbation’s measured source responses through ridge regression experts trained on paired training perturbations (source→recipient). Combine base and proposals with weights determined by route reliability estimated on validation anchors.

Result: On Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma data, PerturbMap reduces full-effect MSE by 4.1% relative to the recipient-local low-rank base and outperforms FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. It reaches within 2.82e-6 MSE of a centralized token-matched pooled reference. A diagnostic shows improved same-recipient top-10 counterpart retrieval (cosine) from 74.5% to 80.5%.

Conclusion: PerturbMap provides a robust, data-driven mechanism to infer missing recipient-context perturbation effects by transporting source-context responses while guarding against incorrect signal transfer, achieving superior cross-context predictive performance and retrieval accuracy.

Abstract: Single-cell perturbation atlases rarely measure every intervention in every cellular context: a query perturbation is often observed in one or more source contexts but missing in the recipient context where its effect is needed. Ignoring those measured responses discards query-specific experimental evidence, whereas copying or weakly calibrating them across contexts risks transferring the wrong signal. We propose PerturbMap, which predicts a missing recipient-context effect by combining a recipient-local low-rank base with accepted proposals that transport the same perturbation's measured source responses through source-to-recipient ridge experts fit on paired training perturbations, with proposal weights determined by route reliability estimated on validation anchors. On the Perturb-CITE-seq melanoma cohort, PerturbMap improves full-effect MSE by 4.1\% over a recipient-local low-rank base and achieves lower MSE than FedAvg, zero-response, raw-copy, calibrated-copy, and identity-shuffled affine controls. It remains within $2.82\times10^{-6}$ MSE of our centralized token-matched pooled reference, which uses a stronger training interface. A condition-mean specificity diagnostic shows the same direction: same-recipient top-10 counterpart retrieval by cosine increases from 74.5\% for the low-rank base to 80.5\% for PerturbMap.

</details>


### [186] [An Instrument to Evaluate Governance Proposals: AI Policy Analysis at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28094)
*Paulo Carvao,Claudio Mayrink Verdun,Isabel Adler,Jeffrey Zhou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A multidimensional, rubric-based framework for transparent AI governance policy analysis that surfaces tradeoffs, using mixed methods and rubric-calibrated LLM benchmarks to assess relevance and alignment with normative commitments across policies.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the opacity and binary framing in AI governance debates by providing a transparent, explicit-assumption framework that highlights tradeoffs and enables cross-policy comparison without prescribing outcomes.

Method: A mixed-methods approach that combines qualitative insights from subject-matter experts with computational text analysis to inform policy attribute rubrics. It quantifies the relative emphasis of policy objectives and uses comparative visualizations for interpretability. The framework benchmarks outputs of commercial LLMs against a domain-trained, rubric-calibrated model with explicit analytical assumptions, and emphasizes relevance and alignment over effectiveness or desirability.

Result: Produces quantifiable emphasis across policy attributes and comparative visuals to enable cross-policy comparison. Demonstrates benchmarking of general-purpose LLMs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model, and surfaces how well outputs align with embedded analytical assumptions.

Conclusion: The framework makes analytical assumptions explicit (attribute selection, rubric construction, weighting) and shows that users can assess whether embedded priorities align with their normative commitments. It is jurisdiction-agnostic and aims to support policymakers, analysts, and researchers navigating complex AI governance landscapes.

Abstract: This paper introduces a policy analysis framework for systematic, transparent assessment of AI governance proposals in an evolving and contested regulatory landscape. AI policy debates often collapse into binary positions that obscure underlying tradeoffs and normative assumptions. The framework structures policy analysis around multiple policy attributes, allowing users to surface priorities and tensions without prescribing outcomes. We use a mixed-methods approach that integrates qualitative insights from subject matter experts with computational text analysis to inform the design of policy attribute rubrics. This quantifies the relative emphasis of different policy objectives and presents them through comparative visualizations that support interpretability and cross-policy comparison. The paper also examines the use of commercial LLMs for rubric-based policy analysis, benchmarking their outputs against a domain-trained rubric-calibrated model with explicitly defined analytical assumptions. Rather than assessing policy effectiveness or desirability, the framework focuses on relevance and alignment across attributes. By making analytical assumptions explicit, including attribute selection, rubric construction, and weighting schemes, the framework enables users to evaluate whether its embedded priorities align with the users' own normative commitments. The approach is jurisdiction-agnostic and intended to support policymakers, analysts, and researchers navigating complex AI governance environments.
  Contributions: (1) multidimensional policy assessment through empirically grounded rubrics that surface tradeoffs rather than resolving them; (2) a transparent hybrid methodology combining feedback from subject-matter experts with computational validation; and (3) use of domain-trained rubric-calibrated models as a benchmark for comparing different general-purpose large language models.

</details>


### [187] [SciDataSailor: Deep Scientific Data Exploring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28098)
*Jiyong Rao,Yicheng Qiu,Chi Zhang,Chunfeng Song,Runkai Zhao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Proposes SciDataSailor: an MCTS-based agent framework enabling LLMs to interact with hierarchical scientific data assets to perform exploration, cross-file evidence integration, and grounded conclusions; introduces SciDataSailor-SFT-2K and SciDataSailor-Bench for training and evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Scientific data are stored in hierarchical, heterogeneous repositories; LLMs excel at reasoning but struggle with real data interaction; need executable environments and embodied tool use to inspect and analyze datasets.

Method: Deep Scientific Data Exploration paradigm; SciDataSailor framework; Monte Carlo Tree Search-based trajectory synthesis with four mechanisms: difficulty-stratified seeds, dual-feedback first-play urgency, hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, entropy-guided branching; two artifacts: SciDataSailor-SFT-2K (supervised fine-tuning) and SciDataSailor-Bench (evaluation) comprising 627 meta-information tasks and 586 QA tasks across 27 datasets in life, earth, physical sciences.

Result: Introduces the framework and two artifacts; provides evaluation bench; no reported quantitative results in abstract; demonstrates ability to synthesize tool-interactive trajectories and grounded conclusions, enabling evaluation of LLM agents on scientific data tasks.

Conclusion: The work presents a viable paradigm and concrete framework for agentic exploration of scientific data assets, enabling integration of heterogeneous evidence and executable analyses, with potential to reduce reliance on domain expertise and improve reproducibility.

Abstract: Scientific datasets are commonly organized as hierarchical repositories containing heterogeneous and interdependent files, making their inspection, integration, and analysis labor-intensive and reliant on domain expertise. Although large language model (LLM) agents have advanced substantially in planning, reasoning, and tool use, existing research has largely overlooked their ability to interact with real scientific data assets through executable environments. We introduce Deep Scientific Data Exploration, an agentic task paradigm in which agents navigate repositories, interpret heterogeneous files and schemas, execute analyses, integrate cross-file evidence, and produce conclusions grounded in executed observations. To operationalize this paradigm, we present SciDataSailor, a framework for synthesizing tool-interactive trajectories by balancing broad exploration with targeted exploitation. SciDataSailor instantiates trajectory synthesis as Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) with four task-specific mechanisms: difficulty-stratified exploration seeds, dual-feedback first-play urgency, hierarchical strategy-to-tool action generation, and entropy-guided branching. Using this framework, we construct SciDataSailor-SFT-2K for supervised fine-tuning and SciDataSailor-Bench for evaluation, with the latter comprising 627 meta-information summarization tasks and 586 scientific question-answering tasks across 27 datasets spanning the life, earth, and physical sciences.

</details>


### [188] [MIND: Lightweight and Effective Memory Injection Defense for LLM Agents via Intent-Aware Information Bottleneck](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28103)
*Dongyi Liu,Haixing He,Xiaobao Wu,Jia Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces MIND, a lightweight defense for memory injection in memory-augmented LLM agents using an intent-aware Information Bottleneck to extract compact intent-behavior representations and a detector to flag malicious memories, reducing attack success while maintaining accuracy and efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Protect memory-augmented LLM agents from memory injection attacks without incurring high computational cost or information redundancy in multi-turn contexts.

Method: Apply an intent-aware Information Bottleneck to derive compact cross-turn representations from the initial user intent and turn-level behavior; use a lightweight detector to identify poisoned memories from these representations; avoids repeated LLM auditing and mitigates redundancy.

Result: Empirical evaluation shows substantial reductions in attack success rates (ASR) on ReAct-StrategyQA (mean ASR-r and ASR-a ~55%), while preserving average accuracy and latency comparable to undefended agents.

Conclusion: Intent-aware representation learning via a memory denoising framework can defend memory-augmented LLMs against injection attacks with lower overhead and maintained task performance.

Abstract: Memory-augmented LLM-based agents are vulnerable to memory injection attacks: Agents may retrieve poisoned memory from attackers, which diverts their behavior from initial user intent and finally causes task failure. However, existing defense mechanisms either incur high computational cost or suffer from information redundancy in multi-turn contexts. To address these challenges, we propose Memory Intent-Aware Neural Denoising(MIND), a lightweight defense framework for memory injection attack. Our preliminary analysis reveals that benign and poisoned trajectories exhibit distinguishable relationships between the initial user intent and subsequent behavior. Building on this observation, MIND employs an intent-aware Information Bottleneck(IB) to extract compact intent--behavior representations from the initial intent and turn-level behavior. The IB preserves intent-relevant cross-turn attack signals while filtering task-irrelevant and repetitive information, and a lightweight detector identifies malicious memories from the resulting representations. As such, MIND mitigates information redundancy in multi-turn contexts while avoiding the overhead of repeated LLM auditing. Extensive experiments show that MIND reduces attack success rates while preserving task accuracy and inference efficiency. Notably, on ReAct-StrategyQA, MIND reduces mean ASR-r and ASR-a by 55.4% and 55.3%, respectively, while matching the undefended agent in average accuracy and latency.

</details>


### [189] [Beyond Rephrasing: Book-Level Organization Improves Synthetic Textbook Data for Mid-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28109)
*Jiawen Tao,Miao Peng,Yaoming Li,Xiaokun Yuan,Mengzhou Wu,Wenhan Yu,Guoan Wang,Nuo Chen,Tong Yang,Maxm Pan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Organizing synthetic textbook data into coherent book-level documents during pre-training yields measurable improvements over baselines that treat content as independent sections or simply rewrite/reuse natural books; a scalable pipeline demonstrates gains across scales and models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether the organizational structure of source content (book-level coherence) influences LM pre-training benefits, beyond content quality or rewriting style.

Method: A scalable synthesis pipeline: retrieve material from pre-training corpus, cluster into topics, plan hierarchical tables of contents, assemble sections into complete, book-grounded documents (Full setting). Evaluate by replacing natural books in mid-training, and performing ablations: content-matched Split, length-matched RandomConcat, retrieval-pool-matched Rephrase; test on Llama3-8B.

Result: Full yields average +1.09 improvement; Split shows +1.02 gain; RandomConcat under Full; Rephrase yields +1.17 improvement; results hold for Llama3-8B.

Conclusion: Book-level organization of synthetic textbooks is a useful axis for synthetic pre-training data design; structured synthesis provides additional gains beyond content quality or rewrites, suggesting data curation guidelines that favor coherent, source-grounded book-like documents.

Abstract: Synthetic textbook data has improved language model pre-training, but prior work largely treats the benefit as a property of generated content or local rewriting style. We study a different factor: whether related content is organized into coherent book-level documents. We contribute both a scalable synthesis pipeline and controlled evidence that this organization matters. The pipeline retrieves source material from a pre-training corpus, clusters it into topical units, plans hierarchical tables of contents, and assembles source-grounded sections into complete books (our Full setting), yielding 686K textbooks (32B tokens) across 15,000+ disciplines. Replacing natural books in a mid-training mix with this corpus improves downstream performance by +1.09 on average. Controlled comparisons then disentangle the relevant design factors. A content-matched Split condition holds generated text and tokens fixed but treats each section as an independent document; Full's +1.02 mean gain isolates document packaging. A length-matched RandomConcat control that joins sections from different books remains below Full, ruling out document length alone. A retrieval-pool-matched Rephrase condition independently rewrites individual retrieved documents under the same audience-by-style scheme, without clustering, TOC planning, or book assembly; Full's +1.17 gain demonstrates the value of structured synthesis. On Llama3-8B, Full likewise outperforms both RandomConcat and Natural Books, supporting book-level organization as a useful axis for synthetic pre-training data design.

</details>


### [190] [BlueprintRepair: Typed Local Edits for Failed Lean Proof Blueprints](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28110)
*Ruslan Khrulev*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces BlueprintRepair and BlueprintTrace for Lean proofs: a schema-checked, node-specific repair interface to modify proof graphs; benchmarks show typed edits are cost-effective, with similar success to patch/rewire interfaces; Free-form interfaces lag, while model choice affects outcomes across proof-authoring vs. localisation tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Improve robustness and verifiability of LLM-guided lean proving by enabling safe, trackable edits to dependency graphs, and to systematically compare repair interfaces under realistic constraints.

Method: Define ten schema-checked local edit operations that name the edited node; require edits to declare every blueprint lemma used; Lean validates each change; create BlueprintTrace benchmark with 142 controlled failures and complete accepted/rejected repair trajectories; compare three interfaces (typed edits, exact source patches, complete module rewrites) under matched source, feedback, model, budget; evaluate with DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen3.6-Flash; measure solved state counts and per-state costs.

Result: Across interfaces, all solve a similar number of localized failures; typed repair is cheapest per solved state (patching 1.30x, rewriting 2.06x more expensive); within 10,000 tokens per task, typed repair achieves near-complete final coverage while free-form interfaces perform worse; Qwen3.6-Flash solves fewer states but keeps typed repair cheapest and leads in proof-authoring states, showing pattern repetition across models.

Conclusion: Schema-checked, node-specific typed repairs offer the most cost-efficient path for repairing Lean proof graphs, with free-form interfaces lagging in coverage. The benchmarks and cross-model results underscore the value of constrained repair interfaces for reliable, budget-conscious proof development, while model choice shifts strengths between localization and authoring tasks.

Abstract: LLM-based Lean proving systems increasingly organize a proof as a blueprint: a dependency graph of formal statements. We introduce BlueprintRepair, a repair interface that lets a model change this graph through ten schema-checked local operations. An operation names the node it edits, so the target theorem cannot be changed. Lean checks every applied change, and an accepted repair must declare every blueprint lemma its proof uses. We also construct BlueprintTrace, a benchmark of 142 controlled failures with complete accepted and rejected repair trajectories. We compare typed edits, exact source patches, and complete module rewrites under matched source, feedback, model, and budget, one episode per state and interface. With DeepSeek-V4-Flash, the three interfaces solve almost the same number of the benchmark's localized failures. Typed repair is the cheapest per solved state (patching is 1.30x as expensive, rewriting 2.06x), and within 10,000 completion tokens per task it reaches almost all of its final coverage, while both free-form interfaces are well behind. A second model, Qwen3.6-Flash, solves fewer states but keeps typed repair cheapest, puts it ahead on the proof-authoring states, and repeats the localized pattern.

</details>


### [191] [ConMem: Contribution-Aware Memory for Long-Horizon Manufacturing Inspection Logs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28126)
*Bingchen Liu,Yuanyuan Fang,Lei Liu,Guangyuan Dong,Xing Fu,Yuanyuan Gao,Shuyue Wei,Xin Li,Xiangtian Meng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: ConMem is a contribution-aware memory framework for long-horizon, LLM-assisted steel-equipment inspection that segments logs into functional evidence units, estimates each unit's diagnostic contribution via Shapley-style valuation, and retaining high-value evidence within a memory budget; it enables early risk detection and efficient retrieval.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-horizon inspection requires reasoning over heterogeneous, temporally distributed records; existing retrieval systems treat logs as a static corpus and do not quantify diagnostic value, delaying or missing early risk signals.

Method: Segment inspection logs into functional evidence units; estimate each unit's contribution to downstream diagnosis using Shapley-style valuation; prune and retain high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget for LLM-assisted inspection with human-in-the-loop screening.

Result: On real-world data, ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy, surpassing baseline; reduces input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6% compared to naive 8K-context LLM baselines; ablations show functional segmentation and contribution-based valuation improve prioritization of weak degradation signals.

Conclusion: ConMem preserves weak early signals across inspection cycles, enabling early-stage wear alerts for on-site inspectors and validating the value of contribution-aware memory for long-horizon, human-in-the-loop diagnostic tasks.

Abstract: Long-horizon steel-equipment inspection requires reasoning over heterogeneous records accumulated across repeated inspection cycles. Existing retrieval-augmented generation systems treat historical logs as a static corpus and retain records without estimating their diagnostic value, failing to report early risk. To this end, we propose ConMem, a contribution-aware memory framework for LLM-assisted equipment inspection, supporting a human-in-the-loop early-risk screening system. Specifically, our ConMem first segments inspection logs into functional evidence units, then estimates each memory unit's contribution to downstream diagnosis through a Shapley-style estimation, and finally retains high-value evidence under a constrained memory budget. In experiments, we evaluate ConMem on real-world dataset and ConMem achieves 76.0% QA accuracy, exceeding the strongest directly comparable baseline. Relative to the naive 8K-context LLM baselines, it reduces the average number of input tokens by 88.2% and response time by 86.6%. Ablation studies also show that the functional-role-aware segmentation and contribution-based valuation are helping prioritize weak degradation signals for targeted field inspection. Practical deployments further confirm that ConMem retains the weak early signal across three inspection cycles, providing an early-stage seal-wear alert targeted for on-site inspectors.

</details>


### [192] [AgenticASR: Refining Speech Recognition in Real-World Scenarios via an Agentic Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28175)
*Zixuan Jiang,Binghao Qiang,Jiaying Chi,Yanqiao Zhu,Kai Yu,Xie Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A novel streaming ASR paradigm (AgenticSR/AgenticASR) that revises emitted text online to remove disfluencies and preserve speaker intent, using a Refiner over a bounded active context. Evaluated with a bilingual AASR-Bench showing top performance; human–AI agreement aligns with experts; ablations highlight trade-offs (context length, Refiner capacity, latency). Code/benchmarks will be released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Verbatim ASR transcripts contain disfluencies, false starts, and self-corrections that hinder readability and downstream tasks. Existing pipelines process static audio or transcripts and cannot revise past output as new speech arrives. A streaming, revision-enabled transcription aims to yield clean, intent-preserving text in real time.

Method: AgenticASR uses an ASR–Refiner architecture that repeatedly transforms a bounded active context and replaces the corresponding output span as audio streams in. It enables continual emission and revision over arbitrarily long streams. The approach is evaluated with AASR-Bench (bilingual, fine-grained rubrics) across multiple front ends, plus ablations on Refiner capacity, context length, and online vs offline latency.

Result: AgenticASR achieves the highest AASR-Bench scores among evaluated systems. A human–AI agreement study shows rubric judgments align with expert assessments. Ablations reveal the impact of Refiner capacity, context length, and the quality–latency trade-off between online and offline inference.

Conclusion: AgenticASR provides a practical framework for intent-preserving, clean transcription during ongoing speech, with publicly released code, AASR-Bench, and a demo.

Abstract: Automatic speech recognition (ASR) has achieved substantial gains in transcription accuracy, yet verbatim transcription does not necessarily produce readily usable text. It retains fillers, repetitions, false starts, and self-corrections that increase reading effort, obscure the speaker's final intent, and propagate unresolved or abandoned content to downstream tasks. Existing spoken-to-written methods process completed audio or transcripts but cannot revise emitted text when later speech changes how preceding content should be interpreted. We therefore formulate Agentic Speech Recognition (AgenticSR), an audio-to-clean-text task that removes disfluencies, resolves self-corrections, and normalizes written form while preserving the speaker's final intent. AgenticASR implements this task through an ASR--Refiner architecture that repeatedly transforms a bounded active context and replaces its corresponding output span as audio arrives. This enables continual emission and revision over streams of arbitrary duration. We also introduce AASR-Bench, a bilingual benchmark with fine-grained atomic rubrics. Across multiple ASR front ends, AgenticASR attains the highest AASR-Bench scores among evaluated systems. A human--AI agreement study shows that rubric-based judgments align with independent expert assessments. Ablations characterize Refiner capacity, context length, and the quality--latency trade-off between online and offline inference. Together, these results establish AgenticASR as a practical framework for intent-preserving clean transcription during ongoing speech. Code, AASR-Bench, and a demo will be released at https://github.com/AnXMuy/AgenticASR.

</details>


### [193] [Old Tricks, New Models: How Simple Image Transformations Break Modern AI-based Content Moderation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28187)
*Marco Alecci,Francesco Marchiori,Iyiola Emmanuel Olatunji,Tegawendé F. Bissyandé,Jacques Klein*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Foundation-model-based image moderation APIs alone are not robust: inexpensive image transformations can bypass three commercial services, and robustness varies by dataset and harm type, especially multimodal content and self-harm. A layered moderation pipeline is recommended over standalone filters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether shifting from task-specific classifiers to broad foundation-model-based multimodal moderation improves robustness and policy coverage, and whether these APIs provide a reliable security boundary.

Method: Large-scale black-box evaluation of three commercial image-moderation services. The study applies seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations across multiple providers, datasets, harm categories, perceptual-similarity constraints, and transformation intensities to test robustness.

Result: All three services can be bypassed using inexpensive transformations that require no gradients or surrogate models. Fixed transformations (e.g., color inversion, grayscale) can flip decisions while preserving recognizable content. Robustness varies by dataset and harm category, with multimodal content and self-harm showing pronounced vulnerabilities.

Conclusion: Replacing traditional moderation classifiers with foundation-model-based APIs does not guarantee a robust safety boundary. These systems should be evaluated under realistic transformations and deployed as one component of a layered moderation pipeline rather than as standalone safety filters.

Abstract: While automated content-moderation systems have become essential for screening harmful content at scale, conventional task-specific classifiers often provide limited policy cov- erage and contextual understanding. Recently, commercial multimodal moderation APIs built on large foundation models have been introduced with the promise of providing broader and more capable safety filters. In this work, we analyze whether this shift also yields more robust image moderation. We conduct a large-scale black-box evaluation on three established commercial image-moderation services and compare their robustness. By evaluating seven simple, model-agnostic image transformations across multiple providers, datasets, harm categories, perceptual-similarity constraints, and transformation intensities, we find that: (1) all three commercial services can be bypassed using inexpensive image transformations that require no gradients, surrogate models, or knowledge of the target system; (2) even fixed transformations such as color inversion and grayscale conversion induce unsafe-to-safe decision changes while preserving content that remains recognizable to humans; (3) their robustness varies substantially across datasets and harm categories, with multimodal content and self-harm exhibiting pronounced vulnerabilities. This yields the conclusion that replacing conventional moderation classifiers with foundation-model-based APIs does not, by itself, provide a reliable security boundary. Such systems must be evaluated under realistic transformations and deployed as one component of a layered moderation pipeline rather than as standalone safety filters.

</details>


### [194] [Qwen-UI-Agent Technical Report: Toward Next-Generation Real-World Centric Foundation GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28227)
*Hanzhang Zhou,Panrong Tong,Xu Zhang,Quyu Kong,Chenglin Cai,Tianyu Xia,Gongjie Zhang,Jianan Zhang,Long Li,Long Chen,Lei Wang,Gaole Dai,Pengxiang Li,Liangyu Chen,Yue Wang,Steven Hoi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Qwen-UI-Agent is a real-world centric foundation GUI agent across mobile, computer, web, and DeepSearch that unifies GUI and CLI actions, uses an AutoResearch data flywheel and online RL to achieve state-of-the-art mobile performance and competitive results elsewhere, with scalable training and proactive service capabilities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable GUI agents to operate reliably on real devices, across platforms and workflows, handle long-horizon tasks, proactively initiate useful services, and autonomously improve with minimal human input.

Method: A unified action space combining GUI operations with CLI execution, real-device mobile runtime plus sandbox environments, a data-flywheel (AutoResearch) to construct tasks, diagnose failures, and plan iterations, online reinforcement learning trained on trajectories over 100 turns across more than 10,000 concurrent environments, and a lightweight harness layer for proactive service initiation and stateful cross-device workflows.

Result: Outperforms state-of-the-art on mobile-use benchmarks and remains competitive on computer- and browser-use tasks when compared to frontier models (Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, GPT-5.6 Sol). Mobile metrics: MobileWorld 82.1%, MobileWorld-Real 92.2%, AndroidDaily 97.5%. Computer metrics: OSWorld-Verified 79.5%, OSWorld-v2 partial-progress 40.0%. Browser/GUI grounding: WebArena 73.6%, ScreenSpot-Pro 81.5%.

Conclusion: The work demonstrates strong real-world cross-domain GUI-agent capabilities and scalable training infrastructure, with a notable emphasis on mobile performance and broad applicability. It suggests promise for deployment and cross-platform automation, though further details on ablations, safety, generalization to unseen apps, efficiency, and ethical considerations would strengthen the evaluation.

Abstract: GUI agents have the potential to become a general purpose executor over existing digital devices. To advance them toward real-world use, we envision agents that operate reliably on real devices, execute workflows across platforms, combine GUI interaction with CLI execution, complete long-horizon tasks, proactively initiate useful services, and autonomously improve their capabilities with minimal human effort. Guided by this vision, we present Qwen-UI-Agent, a real-world centric foundation GUI agent spanning mobile, computer-use, web, and DeepSearch environments. Qwen-UI-Agent combines diverse sandbox environments with a large-scale real-device mobile runtime. Its unified action space interleaves GUI operations with CLI execution and generates batched actions in a single model turn. An AutoResearch-style data flywheel uses agents to construct tasks and environments, diagnose failures, and plan subsequent iterations. Online RL supports training on trajectories exceeding 100 turns, with over 10,000 concurrent environments accelerating rollout. A lightweight harness layer supports proactive service initiation and stateful workflows across mobile and computer.
  Across a broad suite of evaluations, Qwen-UI-Agent sets state-of-the-art performance on mobile-use benchmarks while delivering competitive performance on computer- and browser-use tasks against frontier models, including Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.1 Pro, and GPT-5.6 Sol. On mobile use, it achieves 82.1% on MobileWorld, 92.2% on MobileWorld-Real, and 97.5% on AndroidDaily. On computer use, it achieves 79.5% on OSWorld-Verified and a 40.0% partial-progress score on OSWorld-v2. On browser use and GUI grounding, it achieves 73.6% on WebArena and 81.5% on ScreenSpot-Pro, respectively.

</details>


### [195] [CDAE: Enhancing Perturbation Robustness in Pretrained Language Models with Contrastive Denoising](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28236)
*Sina Heydari,Amirreza Abbasi,Mohsen Hooshmand,Majid Ramezani*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Lightweight CDAE refines BERT embeddings by jointly optimizing contrastive and reconstruction objectives to produce perturbation-invariant sentence representations, outperforming BERT and SimCSE under semantic-preserving perturbations; code released.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pre-trained language models' sentence embeddings are fragile under perturbations that preserve semantics; resilience to synonym substitution, masking, and word dropout is needed.

Method: Introduce Contrastive Denoising Autoencoder (CDAE) that refines fixed BERT embeddings by denoising via reconstruction while aligning perturbed views via contrastive loss; evaluate with multiple perturbation strategies and compare to BERT and SimCSE.

Result: CDAE yields higher embedding similarity under perturbations than baselines; gains grow with perturbation strength; demonstrates perturbation-invariant learning improves stability while preserving semantics.

Conclusion: Perturbation-invariant learning via joint contrastive-reconstruction objectives is promising for robust sentence embeddings; code available at provided GitHub.

Abstract: Pre-trained language models have significantly improved sentence representation learning, yet their embedding remain sensitive to semantic preserving textual perturbations such as synonym substitution, masking and word dropout. This work proposes a lightweight Contrastive Denoising Autoencoder (CDAE) that refines pre-trained BERT embedding by jointly optimizing contrastive and reconstruction objective to learn perturbation-invariant representation. We evaluate the proposed framework using multiple perturbation strategies with varying strengths and compare it against the original BERT embeddings and SimCSE. Experimental results show that CDAE consistently preserves higher embedding similarity under perturbations, with the improvements becoming more pronounced as framework effectively enhances representation stability while preserving semantic information, highlighting perturbation-invariant learning as a promising direction for improving sentence embeddings. The source code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ComputationIASBS/CDAE

</details>


### [196] [AI and Authenticity in Islamic Research: A Critical Evaluation of Generative AI Reliability, Hallucination, and Source Fidelity in Quranic, Hadith, and Fiqh Knowledge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28237)
*Muhammad Sajjad Akbar*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Six leading generative AI systems were evaluated on fifty realistic Islamic questions to assess their reliability, accuracy, and trustworthiness. Findings show AI can aid introductory learning but is not yet suitable as an authoritative source for religious rulings, given issues with hallucinations, incomplete citations, and divergent jurisprudence; verification by primary sources and scholars is essential.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: With increasing use of generative AI for Islamic guidance and education, there is a need for empirical evidence on the authenticity, verifiability, and trustworthiness of AI-provided Islamic knowledge in high-trust religious contexts.

Method: Six leading generative AI systems were tested using fifty open-ended questions spanning Qur’anic interpretation, Hadith, Fiqh, ethics, pastoral advice, and Madhhab-sensitive topics. Data were collected under real-world conditions from participants in Australia and the United Kingdom and analyzed with a mixed-method framework focusing on domain accuracy, citation verification, hallucinations, jurisprudential consistency, uncertainty handling, source provenance, and geographical variation.

Result: AI systems function well as assistive tools for introductory Islamic learning but cannot be trusted as authoritative sources for religious rulings or scholarly research without verification. Common issues include hallucinations, incomplete or unverifiable citations, inconsistent handling of jurisprudential disagreement, and geographic variation in responses.

Conclusion: This study provides a pioneering empirical evaluation of AI reliability in Islamic knowledge, offering practical guidance for researchers, educators, AI developers, and the Muslim community on using AI responsibly in religious education and guidance.

Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used by Muslims for religious guidance, Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith explanation, jurisprudential rulings, and Islamic education. Despite its growing adoption, there is limited empirical evidence on whether current AI systems provide authentic, verifiable, and trustworthy Islamic knowledge suitable for high-trust religious contexts. This study evaluates six leading generative AI systems using fifty realistic open-ended Islamic questions covering Qur'anic interpretation, Hadith, Fiqh, ethics, pastoral advice, and Madhhab-sensitive topics. Responses were collected under real-world conditions from participants in Australia and the United Kingdom and analysed using a mixed-method framework examining domain accuracy, citation verification, hallucinations, jurisprudential consistency, uncertainty handling, source provenance, and geographical variation.
  The study addresses four research questions: (1) How accurate and authentic are AI-generated responses across major Islamic knowledge domains? (2) To what extent do AI systems produce hallucinations, incomplete citations, or unverifiable religious references? (3) How consistently do models handle jurisprudential disagreement, Madhhab diversity, and uncertainty? (4) Are current AI systems sufficiently reliable for religious guidance, Islamic education, and scholarly research?
  Overall, current generative AI systems are valuable as assistive tools for introductory Islamic learning but should not be treated as authoritative sources for religious rulings or Islamic research without verification against authenticated primary sources and qualified scholarly expertise. This study provides one of the first comprehensive empirical evaluations of AI reliability within Islamic knowledge, offering practical guidance for researchers, educators, AI developers, and the wider Muslim community.

</details>


### [197] [Operationally Guided Placement-Aware Learning for Industrial Online 3D Bin Packing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28257)
*Dheeraj Poolavaram,Aanchal Rajesh Chugh,Sebastian Dorn*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: OPAL provides an operationally guided, placement-aware learning framework for online 3D-BPP that couples an OG-EMS candidate generator, an xLSTM-based placement encoder, and a masked PPO-ranked policy, achieving substantial gains in space utilization on BED-BPP.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gaps in prior work: policy optimization often overlooks candidate generation and representation; industrial settings demand space-efficient, stable, compact, and balanced packings; geometry-driven candidate generation limits performance.

Method: OG-EMS evaluates multiple anchors within each free-space region, prioritizes low, well-supported, compact, and spatially diverse placements; an xLSTM-based placement encoder models dependencies among geometric and operational candidate attributes; a lightweight recurrent core combines embeddings with current item/pallet state to rank feasible actions; policy trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO).

Result: On BED-BPP, OPAL achieves mean space utilization of 0.49, with improvements of 15.1% from operationally guided candidate generation and 6.3% from learned ranking, while maintaining robust inference-time performance.

Conclusion: OPAL demonstrates that integrating operation-guided candidate generation with a learned ranking significantly improves space utilization in online 3D-BPP and is suitable for industrial deployment due to modular, efficient components.

Abstract: The online three-dimensional bin packing problem (3D-BPP) is a longstanding challenge in logistics and industrial palletizing. Recent learning-based methods use a learned policy to select among feasible candidate placements. Performance depends on the candidate generator and representation, especially in industrial settings where packings must be space-efficient, stable, compact, and balanced. However, prior work has mainly optimized the policy, while candidate generation and representation remain largely geometry-driven. We address this gap with OPAL, an operationally guided placement-aware learning framework for industrial online 3D-BPP which combines an Operationally Guided Empty-Maximal-Space generator (OG-EMS), an operational representation for each candidate placement, and a masked ranking policy trained with proximal policy optimization. OG-EMS evaluates multiple anchors within each free-space region and prioritizes low, well-supported, compact, and spatially diverse placements. An xLSTM-based Placement Encoder models dependencies among geometric and operational candidate attributes, while a lightweight recurrent core combines the resulting embeddings with the current item and pallet state to rank feasible actions. On the BED-BPP benchmark, OPAL achieves a mean space utilization of 0.49, with improvements of 15.1% from operationally guided candidate generation and 6.3% from learned ranking, while maintaining robust inference-time performance.

</details>


### [198] [LLM-Guided Evolutionary Search for Constraint Model Reformulation to Improve Solver Efficiency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28268)
*Kostis Michailidis,Dimos Tsouros,Nguyen Dang,Tias Guns*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: LLMs can automate performance-oriented reformulation of declarative constraint models via an evolutionary AHD framework; a Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR) strategy using MMR diversifies retained attempts; evaluated on eight CSPLib problems, yielding substantial held-out speedups and showing that diversity and validation-based selection improve results.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Constraint-solver performance is highly sensitive to modelling choices; while LLMs can generate correct models from natural language, performance optimization requires automated reformulation. The paper extends Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD) with diversity-aware retention to improve search efficiency.

Method: An evolutionary loop where an LLM proposes reformulations of a given constraint model; each candidate is verified and benchmarked against a user baseline. The study compares AHD-adapted search strategies that control which prior attempts, instructions, and feedback enter prompts. It introduces Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR) by applying Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) to instance-level runtime vectors to retain behaviorally diverse attempts. Evaluation on eight CSPLib problems with validation-based final model selection.

Result: Iterative reformulation yields substantial held-out speedups. Strategies that preserve a diverse set of retained attempts outperform those favoring recency or the fastest results. Validation-based selection improves held-out speedups for every strategy.

Conclusion: Diversification via PDR and validation-based model selection enhances the effectiveness of LLM-assisted reformulation for performance-oriented constraint modelling, demonstrating that automated, diversified reformulation can achieve notable speedups across problems.

Abstract: Combinatorial problems appear in numerous industrial applications. A common approach is to formulate these problems as declarative constraint models that can subsequently be compiled to and solved by a range of back-end solvers. Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can produce correct models from natural language, but even a correct model can be expensive to solve because performance remains sensitive to modelling choices. In this work, we investigate whether LLMs can automate performance-oriented model reformulation. Inspired by Automatic Heuristic Design (AHD), we use an evolutionary framework in which an LLM proposes candidate reformulations that are verified and benchmarked against the user-defined baseline model. We compare AHD-adapted search strategies that control which prior attempts, instructions, and measured feedback enter each prompt. Existing retention strategies prioritize recency or performance, but do not explicitly diversify the context. To cover this gap, we introduce Profile-Diverse Retention (PDR), which applies Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) to instance-level runtime vectors to retain behaviourally diverse attempts. We systematically evaluate the strategies on eight CSPLib problems using validation-based final model selection. The results show that: (i) iterative reformulation can produce substantial held-out speedups; (ii) strategies that keep the retained context diverse outperform those that retain only recent or the fastest attempts; and (iii) validation-based selection improves the held-out speedup of every strategy.

</details>


### [199] [MemHarness: Memory Is Reconstructed, Not Replayed](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28272)
*Rong Wu,Daocheng Fu,Licheng Wen,Xuemeng Yang,Shu Zou,Jianbiao Mei,Yuxin Wang,Hairong Zhang,Yu Yang,Tao Hu,Cong Zhang,Botian Shi,Pinlong Cai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MemHarness uses a context-grounded reconstructive policy to reorganize retrieved experiences before action, improving LLM agent decision-making and robustness to distribution shifts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome negative transfer from verbatim memory replay by aligning retrieved experiences with the current state, emulating human memory adaptation.

Method: At each decision step, a unified policy model critiques and reconstructs retrieved experiences conditioned on the current state, producing context-grounded guidance before acting. End-to-end training with GRPO. Evaluations on ALFWorld and WebShop.

Result: Significant performance gains over pure RL and static memory baselines; robust in out-of-distribution scenarios; the reconstruction objective reduces negative transfer and provides latent guidance that enhances intrinsic reasoning.

Conclusion: Reconstruction-based memory harnessing improves reasoning and transfer, offering a general approach to context-aware memory use in LLM agents that mitigates negative transfer and enhances adaptability.

Abstract: Retrieving past experiences has become a common strategy to enhance large language model agents. However, most existing memory-augmented agents treat retrieved experiences as static records to be replayed verbatim, injecting them into the context regardless of whether they align with the agent's current situation.
