This ``replay'' paradigm ignores the gap between the abstract, general nature of stored experience and the concrete, ever-changing states encountered at decision time, frequently causing negative transfer. In contrast, humans rarely recall past experiences verbatim; instead, they reorganize and adapt retrieved memories to fit the present context. Inspired by this, we propose MemHarness, a framework that equips LLM agents to actively harness and reconstruct past experiences based on the present context. At each decision step, a unified policy model critiques and reconstructs the retrieved experience conditioned on the current state, producing context-grounded guidance before acting. This reconstructive ability emerges naturally through end-to-end training with GRPO. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop show that MemHarness substantially outperforms pure RL and static memory-augmented baselines, demonstrating strong robustness in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios. Furthermore, our analyses reveal that this reconstruction objective not only prevents negative transfer but also serves as latent guidance during training, fundamentally improving the agent's intrinsic reasoning capabilities.

</details>


### [200] [Tycho: Active Abstraction with Programmatic World Models for ARC-AGI-3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28287)
*Jens Lehmann,Andrei Aioanei,Sahar Vahdati*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces Tycho, a coding-agent system for active abstraction in ARC-AGI-3; formalizes environments as parameterized Moore machines; evaluates four orchestration policies showing model-building delegation yields high action efficiency; automatic repair improves fidelity but not action efficiency; defines active abstraction as deciding when to construct/repair/use models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Efficiently learning unfamiliar game's rules, hidden state, and goals under tight interaction budgets requires separating actionable observations from non-actionable frames and enabling executable hypotheses and planning.

Method: Formalize environments as parameterized rendered deterministic Moore machines. Tycho constructs and uses game-specific models during interaction, separating actionable observations from animation/level-progress frames. Evaluate four orchestration policies on 25 public games using Claude Opus 4.8 with matched inference budgets; compare RHAE and human-replay baselines; assess automatic repair.

Result: Actor-requested delegation to a model builder yields the highest mean RHAE (88.49). With this policy, GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 achieve 100.00 RHAE and complete all 183 levels; game-balanced first-run human-replay midranks are 98.5 and 100.0. Opus 5 uses 61% fewer scored actions than aggregate official human baselines. Automatic repair after verification failures yields models that reproduce observed transitions more accurately but reaches only 83.07 RHAE. Transition match measures fidelity of dynamics, not goal identification or action improvement.

Conclusion: Active abstraction is a joint, cost-aware problem: deciding when to construct, repair, use, or bypass a model is essential for Strong play. The Tycho framework demonstrates that structured modeling and selective model usage can achieve near-perfect action efficiency, while automatic repair enhances fidelity without guaranteeing action gains. This supports treating model-building and evaluation as integral components of interactive skill acquisition.

Abstract: ARC-AGI-3 turns abstraction into an interactive problem of skill acquisition. A player must infer an unfamiliar game's rules, hidden state, and goal while maintaining action efficiency because every move counts. We formalize these environments as parameterized rendered deterministic Moore machines and introduce Tycho, a coding-agent system that constructs and uses game-specific models during interaction. Tycho separates actionable observations from intermediate animation, level-completion, and game-over frames. From this structured history, an agent can model, test, plan with, repair, or bypass a free-form executable hypothesis.
  In one matched public-set run per policy, we compare four orchestration policies on all 25 public games using Claude Opus 4.8 under matched inference budgets. Actor-requested delegation to a model builder obtains the highest observed mean Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), 88.49. With this selected policy, GPT-5.6 Sol and Opus 5 both reach 100.00 RHAE and complete all 183 levels. Their game-balanced first-run human-replay midranks are 98.5 and 100.0. Opus 5 uses 61% fewer scored actions than the aggregate official human baselines.
  Automatic repair after verification failures produces models that reproduce observed transitions much more accurately, yet reaches only 83.07 RHAE. Transition match indicates whether a simulator reproduces observed dynamics, not whether it has identified the objective or improves the next action. Strong play also requires deciding when to construct, repair, use, or bypass a model. We call this joint problem active abstraction: generating a testable model from costly interaction and deciding when acquiring or using it is worth its cost.

</details>


### [201] [One Human, $N$ Agents: Audit-Budget Allocation for LLM Agent Fleets under Miscalibrated, Correlated Confidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28317)
*Cesare Zavattari,Alessandro Tommasi,Giuseppe Prencipe*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Under budgeted auditing of N LLM agents with B audits per round, self-reported confidence can be adversarially miscalibrated and correlated errors can render confidence-ranked auditing worse than random; there exists a miscalibration threshold δ*; δ* grows as budget shrinks; cross-family correlation is strong; five open-weight LLMs show near-constant confidence while a proprietary model remains informative; a quantitative criterion for vacuous oversight is provided; replay on traces confirms the ordering.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand when self-reported confidence is a reliable signal for auditing multiple LLM agents under strict audit budgets, accounting for miscalibration and error correlations.

Method: Model the problem as budgeted noisy inspection over a two-level Gaussian copula; derive the miscalibration threshold δ* beyond which confidence-ranked auditing performs worse than random; analyze how δ* depends on budget B and on cross-family correlations; empirically evaluate five open-weight LLMs and one proprietary model, reporting confidence estimates, confidence intervals, and ordering via replay on recorded traces.

Result: Identification of a miscalibration threshold δ* with respect to budgeted auditing; δ* increases as budget B decreases; strong cross-family correlation dominates error structure; five open-weight LLMs exhibit near-constant confidence with point estimates at or beyond δ* while their CIs may straddle it; a proprietary model remains informative and lands below δ*; a quantitative criterion for vacuous oversight is provided; replay experiments validate the inferred ordering.

Conclusion: Self-reported confidence is unreliable for auditing LLM agents under budget constraints when miscalibration and correlated errors are present; there exists a quantifiable threshold directing when confidence is vacuous; robust auditing requires moving beyond naive confidence ranking, especially in settings with multi-family, correlated errors.

Abstract: A single human must audit $N$ LLM agents under a budget of $B \ll N$ audits per round, guided by self-reported confidence that may be adversarially miscalibrated and by correlated errors. We model this as budgeted noisy inspection over a two-level Gaussian copula and locate the miscalibration threshold $δ^*$ past which confidence-ranked auditing is \emph{worse} than random. Two a-priori expectations reverse: $δ^*$ \emph{rises} as the budget shrinks, and cross-family correlation is not low---shared difficulty dominates lineage. Five open-weight LLMs show operationally useless (near-constant) confidence, point estimates at or beyond the flip though CIs straddle it; a proprietary model is informative and lands below it. We give a quantitative criterion for \emph{vacuous} oversight, and replaying policies on recorded traces confirms the ordering.

</details>


### [202] [PathView-Bench: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Achieve Fine-grained Multiscale Understanding of Pathology Images?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28318)
*Zongyi Chen,Yu Liang,Jie Lin,Liansheng Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PathVU is a vision-anchored, multiscale pathology benchmark enabling fine-grained evaluation of MLLMs across region and slide FOV with 14 VQA tasks over 28 organs; reveals gaps in current models and provides a reproducible evaluation framework.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current pathology benchmarks emphasize final outputs (diagnosis, captions) and overlook fine-grained, multiscale visual reasoning needed for pathology; a standardized, reproducible suite is required to assess and drive development of explicit multiscale understanding.

Method: PathVU aggregates 23 public pathology datasets with human-supervised labels and spatial annotations, defines two focal views (Region FOV for high-resolution regions and Slide FOV for macro views), converts annotations into deterministic task targets, and includes 14 VQA-style tasks with 61,673 images and 308,070 samples across 28 organs and 7,253,526 annotations. It evaluates 18 MLLMs (general-purpose, medical-domain, and pathology-focused), focusing on region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, spatial reasoning, and insufficient-context judgment.

Result: The study finds substantial limitations in even advanced MLLMs on fine-grained, multiscale pathology tasks, demonstrating the necessity of PathVU for reproducible, multiscale evaluation and guiding development of stronger pathology MLLMs.

Conclusion: PathVU offers a robust, reproducible benchmark for evaluating and accelerating the development of pathology MLLMs with explicit multiscale visual understanding, addressing a key gap in current evaluation practices.

Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to analyze pathology images. However, dominant multimodal benchmarks in pathology mainly score final diagnostic answers, captions, or reports. These evaluations provide limited insight into whether a model understands the multiscale visual content needed for pathology reasoning and decision-making. We introduce PathVU, a vision-anchored benchmark for fine-grained and multiscale visual understanding in computational pathology. Built from 23 public pathology imaging datasets with human-supervised labels and spatial annotations, PathVU evaluates MLLM understanding in two fields of view: Region FOV for high-resolution local regions and Slide FOV for macro whole-slide views. By converting raw annotations into deterministic task targets, PathVU enables programmatic scoring of region localization, visual recognition, quantity estimation, spatial reasoning, and insufficient-context judgment. The benchmark contains 14 VQA-style tasks, 61,673 images, and 308,070 samples across 28 organs and 7,253,526 annotations. Evaluating 18 representative general-purpose, medical-domain, and pathology-oriented MLLMs, we observe substantial limitations even in advanced models on fine-grained visual tasks across multiscale pathology images. PathVU provides a reproducible basis for developing and evaluating pathology MLLMs with explicit multiscale visual understanding.

</details>


### [203] [Paying for Honesty Without Knowing the Truth: Reputation-Penalty Design for LLM Marketplace Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28330)
*Mingdai Yang,Shicheng Fan,Kejing Yu,Duohao Wang,Li Sun,Hao Peng,Philip S. Yu,Zhiwei Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CARP uses a reputation-penalty with a deadband and state-dependent severity to suppress dishonest LLM sellers without ground-truth, paired with SPARC to induce penalty-driven self-correction; it improves consumer welfare toward a perfect-information oracle while resisting gaming.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM agents fabricating product attributes undermines trust on platforms that cannot verify truth, so a ground-truth-free mechanism is needed to deter dishonest listings without false-positive harms.

Method: Design CARP: a reputation-penalty mechanism with a deadband to forgive complaint noise and a state-dependent severity to prevent erosion of reputation from false signals; operates without product-level ground truth and is robust to strategic manipulation. Pair with SPARC, a byte-clean, code-gated reflection mechanism that ties fabrication costs to sales outcomes, inducing behaviorally binding self-correction reasoning. Evaluate welfare relative to a perfect oracle and compare with alternative policies; report confidence intervals.

Result: CARP+SPARC reduces the consumer-welfare gap with a perfect oracle, suppressing sales of low-rated liars while sparing honest sellers; evidence of behaviorally binding penalty via SPARC across models with consistent results and confidence intervals.

Conclusion: A ground-truth-free reputation-penalty framework (CARP) paired with SPARC can closely approximate oracle-level consumer welfare by deterring lying in LLM-driven listings; the mechanism appears robust to gaming and generalizable across models, with penalty-driven self-correction as the key behavioral driver.

Abstract: LLM agents increasingly act as autonomous merchants that write their own product listings, and under competitive pressure, they fabricate attributes to win sales. Even under instructions to be honest, they fabricate attributes in a majority of listings across models. A platform's obvious remedy---verifying each claim against the truth---is unavailable, because it observes only a noisy, biased complaint signal, never the ground truth. We design CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism with a deadband that forgives complaint noise and a state-dependent severity that counters reputation-driven detection erosion. CARP requires no product-level ground truth and is robust to strategic gaming. CARP protects consumers by suppressing the sales volume of low-rated liars while sparing honest sellers. Paired with SPARC, it closes most of the consumer-welfare gap relative to a perfect-information oracle, without ever accessing the truth. It also achieves the best welfare of the policies we compare. We further show that this felt penalty becomes behaviorally binding through SPARC, a byte-clean code-gated reflection mechanism: LLM merchants fabricate when lying is free but restrain themselves when fabrication costs them sales, a self-interested response rather than compliance. We trace this distinction to penalty-gated self-correction reasoning, and observe the binding across models, with supporting confidence intervals.

</details>


### [204] [Correcting What You Cannot See: Credit Assignment for Perception Distillation in Multimodal Reasoners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28336)
*Feng Xiong,Leyan Xue,Hongyu Lin*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Perception-Correction Distillation (PCD) is a label-free approach that identifies and fixes correctable perception failures in on-policy multimodal distillation by multiplying signals from downstream failure and teacher–student disagreement to gate distillation, yielding state-of-the-art gains across eight benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Distinguish whether errors come from perception or reasoning in multimodal reasoning. Perception Success Rate is ambiguous when multiple reasonings share a single perception; on-policy distillation lacks a direct mechanism to target perception corrections.

Method: PCD uses separated perception and reasoning rollouts, collects two witnesses: downstream failure and teacher–student disagreement; computes a multiplicative (soft AND) gate (their product) to decide when to apply distillation corrections; justify via Bayesian evidence combination; use mean-preserving weights to keep the original reasoning objective unchanged.

Result: Empirical gains: 8B 2B macro average improves from 44.50 (OPD) to 47.28; 32B 8B from 56.94 to 61.22; ablation studies show that removing PCD or separated rollout degrades performance by 2.22 and 0.88 points on held-out averages, respectively, across matched 2B settings.

Conclusion: Effective multimodal distillation hinges on identifying when perception is the appropriate target of correction; PCD’s multiplicative gate effectively combines complementary witnesses to target perception corrections without altering the reasoning objective, and its benefits generalize across multiple benchmarks.

Abstract: On-policy distillation provides dense supervision for multimodal reasoners, but its trajectory-level reward cannot determine whether a failed answer arose from perception or subsequent reasoning. Perception Success Rate (PSR), estimated from multiple reasonings sharing one perception, remains ambiguous because low success conflates perceptual insufficiency with reasoning difficulty. We introduce \textbf{Perception-Correction Distillation (PCD)}, a label-free method that identifies correctable perception failures using downstream failure and teacher--student disagreement as complementary witnesses. Their product, , forms a soft AND gate that strengthens distillation only when both witnesses are present. We motivate this rule through Bayesian evidence combination and show that multiplication is the unique normalized bilinear gate that vanishes when either witness is absent. PCD uses separated perception--reasoning rollouts and mean-preserving weights, leaving the reasoning objective unchanged. Across eight benchmarks, PCD improves the 8B 2B macro average from 44.50 with OPD to 47.28 and the 32B 8B result from 56.94 to 61.22. In matched 2B ablations, removing PCD and separated rollout reduces held-out average by 2.22 and 0.88 points, respectively. Effective multimodal distillation therefore depends not only on what the teacher predicts, but also on identifying when perception is the appropriate target of correction.

</details>


### [205] [How Benchmarks Mis-Score Computer-Use Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28367)
*Zihan Dong,Zhiyuan Ma,Zekun Wang,Yunqing Li,Zirou Liu,Ruixuan Deng,Qishi Zhan,Rui Qian*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Reliability issues plague CUA benchmarks; an audit of 150 failure-scored trajectories across five benchmarks reveals 15.3% incorrect FAIL verdicts (10.7% evaluator false negatives, 4.7% broken tasks); a three-tier taxonomy shows verification/feedback and planning failures dominate; single scalar success rates are insufficient; stage-specific design rules and connections to long-horizon benchmarks are proposed.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ensure trustworthy evaluation of computer-use agents by diagnosing where current benchmarks and scoring pipelines fail and how to fix them.

Method: Audited 150 public failure-scored trajectories across five benchmarks in web, enterprise-workflow, and desktop-control; reassessed verdicts; classified failures into a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy; quantified error rates; mapped findings to broader benchmark design.

Result: Found 15.3% wrong FAIL verdicts; 10.7% evaluator false negatives; 4.7% broken tasks; (three-tier taxonomy): verification/feedback and planning failures dominate execution/ grounding; scalar scores insufficient; stage-specific design rules derived; linkage to long-horizon benchmarks.

Conclusion: Propose stage-specific design rules for CUA evaluation and a reliability framework spanning task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting; encourage better benchmarks for long-horizon CUA tasks.

Abstract: Computer-use agents (CUA) are being deployed to browse the web and operate desktop software, yet their benchmark scores are still commonly produced by brittle scripted oracles. A score is the output of a pipeline in which tasks can be stale, trajectories can omit decisive visual evidence, evaluators can reject valid alternatives, and aggregate reports can hide the cause of failure. We organize these problems into a reliability framework spanning task construction, trajectory observation, scoring, and reporting. We then audit 150 public failure-scored trajectories from five web, enterprise-workflow, and desktop-control benchmarks, find that 15.3\% of FAIL verdicts are wrong: 10.7\% are evaluator false negatives and 4.7\% are broken tasks. For genuine failures, a three-tier diagnostic taxonomy shows that verification/feedback and planning failures dominate execution/grounding errors, while a single scalar success rate can not explain. We connect these findings to newer long-horizon CUA benchmarks and derive stage-specific design rules for CUA evaluation.

</details>


### [206] [HyperClaim: Fine-Grained Cross-Modal Hypergraph Reasoning for Video Misinformation Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28375)
*Xiangbo Wang,Jiasheng Zhang,Xingtong Yu,Luoqiang Lei,Delvin Ce Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HyperClaim uses a discriminative temporal hypergraph to capture higher-order cross-modal dependencies for video misinformation detection, outperforming baselines on FakeSV/TT/VV with interpretable incidence/attention weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Global multimodal fusion and pairwise graphs under-represent localized authenticity cues that arise from coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal frame spans; higher-order interactions are more effectively modeled by hypergraphs.

Method: Construct a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames; apply confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units; perform adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration; aggregate textual, visual, and hyperedge states via a discrepancy-aware readout; operates under the FactGuard temporal protocol without external rationales or tools.

Result: Achieves 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, FakeVV respectively, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning baselines; learned incidence and attention weights reveal token- and frame-level structure.

Conclusion: HyperClaim preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure that global fusion tends to flatten, demonstrating effective sample-level authenticity classification using a hypergraph-based representation.

Abstract: Video misinformation detection is often approached through global multimodal fusion or free-form multimodal reasoning. Both paradigms can under-represent localized authenticity cues that arise from coupled interactions among query phrases, contextual text, and short temporal spans of frames. Because such interactions are inherently higher-order, pairwise graph formulations are insufficient to capture multi-way cross-modal dependencies, whereas hypergraphs offer a suitable representation for these relations. We propose HyperClaim, a discriminative temporal hypergraph framework for sample-level authenticity classification. Using the title or benchmark-provided paired text as a claim-like query, HyperClaim constructs a sparse heterogeneous hypergraph over query tokens, evidence tokens, and sampled frames; applies confidence-aware filtering and source budgeting to form compact text-frame and short-range temporal evidence units; performs adaptive soft-incidence reasoning with residual text-video calibration; and aggregates textual, visual, and hyperedge states through a discrepancy-aware readout. Without relying on generated rationales or external tool calls, HyperClaim preserves fine-grained cross-modal and temporal structure that global fusion tends to flatten. Under the FactGuard temporal protocol, it achieves 83.7%, 82.0%, and 87.3% accuracy on FakeSV, FakeTT, and FakeVV, respectively, outperforming strong discriminative and reasoning-centric baselines. Learned incidence and attention weights further reveal token- and frame-level structure.

</details>


### [207] [When Specifications Conflict: A Symmetry-Based Framework for Measuring LLM Preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28384)
*Tairan Wang,Liang Zhou,Zikang Zhan,Pingchuan Yan*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A framework to study how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing specifications, using a symmetry-based experimental design and multiple representation types; shows systematic preferences and broad applicability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a lack of controllable, attributable methods to analyze how models resolve conflicting specifications; understanding model preferences helps interpret decisions when confronted with inconsistent information.

Method: Construct explicit conflicting specifications and apply a symmetry-based design to minimize confounds. Evaluate on an executable mathematical benchmark with 550 conflict instances across 11 function families, comparing four representation types (pure natural language, formal language, naturalized formal language, and input–output examples). Extend framework to heterogeneous specification conflicts in Boolean algebra, code generation, and clinical domains.

Result: Results reveal systematic preference patterns rather than random behavior: Formal ≈ Naturalized Formal > Pure Natural Language > Input–Output Examples. Example effects depend on model capability and function family.

Conclusion: The framework provides a unified, transferable approach for measuring how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing sources of information and demonstrates applicability across diverse tasks and specification forms.

Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly required to integrate multiple sources of information that may be inconsistent or conflicting. However, there is still a lack of controllable and attributable methods for analyzing how models resolve conflicts between competing specifications. We propose a controlled experimental framework for studying model preferences under conflicting specifications. By constructing specifications with explicit conflicts, the framework enables model choices between competing specifications to be directly observed and analyzed. A symmetry-based design further reduces confounding factors, allowing preferences across representation types to be compared systematically.
  We evaluate the framework on an executable mathematical benchmark with 550 conflict instances spanning 11 function families, comparing four representation types: pure natural language, formal language, naturalized formal language, and input--output examples. Results show systematic preference patterns rather than random behavior, with a consistent ordering: $ \text{Formal} \approx \text{Naturalized Formal} > \text{Pure Natural Language} > \text{Input--Output Examples} $. Example effects further depend on model capability and function family.
  We extend the framework to heterogeneous specification conflicts in Boolean algebra, code generation, and the clinical domain, demonstrating its applicability across diverse tasks and specification forms. The framework provides a unified approach for measuring how LLMs resolve conflicts between competing sources of information.

</details>


### [208] [GLM-RAG: Graph Language Models for Graph-Based Retrieval-Augmented Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28397)
*Maya Arseven,Anette Frank,Beni Egressy,Johann Higl,Moritz Plenz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A GLM-based retriever for retrieval-augmented generation over knowledge graphs is proposed and evaluated against GNN-based and vector-search retrievers. Finetuned GLM retrievers generalize better out-of-domain and achieve state-of-the-art on two multi-hop benchmarks, with in-domain multi-hop QA on par with prior work. GNN-based retrievers offer higher graph coverage with efficient training, while vector-search excels on single-hop tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve retrieval in RAG over knowledge graphs by leveraging graph language models (GLMs) and to compare GLM-based, GNN-based, and vector-search retrievers across single- and multi-hop settings, with a focus on transferability to unseen domains.

Method: Introduce a GLM-based retriever for RAG over knowledge graphs and conduct a systematic comparison against GNN-based and vector-search retrievers. Evaluate on single-hop and multi-hop datasets, including cross-domain transfer scenarios, adjusting for model size and subgraph coverage.

Result: Finetuned GLM retrievers generalize better out-of-domain and achieve state-of-the-art on two multi-hop benchmarks. On in-domain multi-hop QA datasets, GLM retrievers are comparable to prior work, with scaling suggesting improvements as parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with efficient training, whereas the vector-search baseline excels on single-hop datasets.

Conclusion: GLM-based retrievers offer strong cross-domain generalization and competitive in-domain performance for RAG over knowledge graphs. GNN-based retrievers provide higher graph coverage with efficient training, and vector-search remains strong for single-hop tasks. The results indicate that choosing the retrieval paradigm should depend on the task (multi-hop vs. single-hop) and domain transfer considerations, and potential future work could explore hybrid or ensemble strategies.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs requires retrievers that can effectively capture both graph structure and semantic information. Recent approaches have explored graph neural network (GNN)-based retrievers to model graph topology in multi-hop reasoning tasks. In parallel, graph language models (GLMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm that integrates graph reasoning and the semantic capabilities of language models. In this work, we introduce a GLM-based retriever and investigate the comparative strengths of GLM-based, GNN-based, and traditional vector-search-based retrievers in single- and multi-hop RAG settings, and with a particular focus on transferability to unseen domains. Our findings suggest that finetuned GLM retrievers generalize better out of domain, achieving SOTA on two multi-hop benchmarks. On in-domain multi-hop QA datasets they remain comparable to prior work, with promising scaling as parameters and subgraph coverage increase. GNN-based retrievers achieve higher graph coverage with an efficient training setup, whereas the vector-search baseline excels at single-hop datasets.

</details>


### [209] [QuantWAMs: Calibrating at the Right Granularity for World Action Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28405)
*Jiacheng Zhou,Jinfan Lv,Ruixuan Li,Longtai Zhang,Yan Wang,Wenqiang Zhang,Lizhe Qi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: QuantWAMs presents calibration-aware post-training quantization for World Action Models, using three strategies to align quantization with rollout, structure, and task objectives, achieving substantial memory savings and speedups with minimal accuracy loss in simulation and real-robot tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: WAMs require iterative denoising and closed-loop execution, making deployment costly. Existing PTQ methods misalign with deployment context due to open-loop objectives, homogeneous assumptions, and calibration distributions that do not reflect real use.

Method: 1) Shared-basis outlier calibration: pool activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules. 2) Co-training-objective saliency: compute empirical-Fisher scores from joint video–action gradients and allocate weight precision per calibration-stable layer. 3) Fixed-intervention rollout auditing: adjust denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states without changing the overall precision budget.

Result: Under W4A4-dominant settings, simulation means differ from FP16 by only 0.2–0.7 percentage points. Real-robot trials show deployment feasibility on three manipulation tasks. For targeted video/action blocks, peak weight-and-activation memory reduces to ~29% of FP16, with 1.4–1.6× block-level speedups across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-robot setups.

Conclusion: QuantWAMs demonstrates effective, deployment-friendly PTQ for WAMs by tailoring quantization to model structure, rollout, and task objective, achieving substantial memory and speed gains with minimal accuracy loss in both simulation and real-robot environments.

Abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) jointly predict future observations and actions, but their iterative denoising and closed-loop execution make efficient deployment costly. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods are poorly suited to WAMs because they rely on open-loop objectives, homogeneous model assumptions, and calibration distributions that do not reflect deployment. We present QuantWAMs, a PTQ framework that aligns quantization decisions with the calibration context defined by model structure, rollout distribution, and task objective. QuantWAMs introduces three strategies: shared-basis outlier calibration, which pools activation evidence only across coordinate-compatible modules; co-training-objective saliency, which computes empirical-Fisher scores from the joint video--action gradient and assigns weight precision at a calibration-stable layer granularity; and fixed-intervention rollout auditing, which revises denoising-step protection schedules using reachable closed-loop states without changing the precision budget. We evaluate QuantWAMs on Fast-WAM and LingBot-VA across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-robot manipulation with an AgiBot G2. Under a W4A4-dominant setting, the reported simulation means differ from FP16 by 0.2--0.7 percentage points. Real-robot trials further establish deployment feasibility on three manipulation tasks. For the targeted video and action blocks, QuantWAMs reduces peak weight-and-activation memory to about 29\% of FP16 and provides 1.4--1.6$\times$ block-level speedups.

</details>


### [210] [WIDE: Boosting Adaptive LLM Inference via Token-level Dynamic Width Pruning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28418)
*Haozhe Hu,Hao Wu,Peiran Yin,Chao Han,Yunpu Ma,Xiaoyu Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: WIDE introduces end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning for LLMs, enabling per-token selection of attention-head and FFN channels, with a two-stage training pipeline and a pruning–kernel co-design to achieve substantial end-to-end speedups and better accuracy at 50% sparsity compared to prior dynamic pruning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static structured pruning yields hardware-friendly but input-agnostic sparsity that degrades accuracy under aggressive pruning; dynamic sparsity methods improve quality but are coarse-grained and struggle to realize real-world speedups. There is a need for fine-grained, input-aware, end-to-end pruning that can be efficiently implemented on hardware.

Method: Two-stage training to learn token-wise sparse execution; per-token selection of attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups (neuron-block granularity). Pruning-kernel co-design: mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, hardware-dependent intra-block skipping, to enable efficient execution across granularities.

Result: At 50% sparsity, 55.1% performance boost versus state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. For prefill and decoding inference, near-theoretical kernel-level speedups: up to 1.98x (prefill) and 4.95x (decoding); end-to-end acceleration 1.68x (prefill) and 1.55x (decoding).

Conclusion: Token-level dynamic width pruning is viable for LLMs, delivering substantial efficiency gains with maintained accuracy; WIDE's two-stage training plus pruning–kernel co-design enables practical end-to-end acceleration. Code available at the provided GitHub repo.

Abstract: Pruning is a promising approach for improving the efficiency of LLMs. Existing static structured pruning methods are hardware-friendly and can deliver practical throughput gains, but their input-agnostic computation allocation often causes substantial accuracy degradation under aggressive sparsity. Recent dynamic sparsity methods improve quality retention by adapting computation to individual inputs, yet they remain largely limited to coarse-grained structural decisions and their practical acceleration under real-world inference scenarios remains challenging. To address these challenges, we present WIDE, the first end-to-end differentiable token-level dynamic width pruning framework designed for both prefill and decode scenarios. WIDE enables fine-grained computation allocation by allowing each token to dynamically select attention-head groups and FFN-channel groups, extending dynamic pruning beyond layer-level decisions to neuron-block-level granularity. Through a two-stage training pipeline, WIDE learns effective token-wise sparse execution patterns and achieves substantially better quality retention than existing approaches. To make such fine-grained dynamic pruning practical, we further propose a pruning--kernel co-design framework that decomposes dynamic sparsity acceleration into mask reordering, hardware-agnostic block-level skipping, and hardware-dependent intra-block skipping, enabling efficient execution across different granularities. At 50% sparsity, WIDE provides 55.1% performance boost when compared to the state-of-the-art dynamic depth pruning under calibration-only settings. Under prefill and decoding inference workloads, WIDE achieves close-to-theoretical kernel-level speedups of up to 1.98x for prefill and 4.95x for decoding, as well as 1.68x and 1.55x end-to-end acceleration. Our code is available at https://github.com/EIT-NLP/LLM-Pruning/tree/main/WIDE.

</details>


### [211] [When Derived Measurements Mislead: Quantifying and Mitigating LLM Over-Trust with Privileged-Modality Reliability Evidence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28421)
*Zongheng Guo,Tao Chen,Tianli Li,Mingzhe Cui,Yang Jiao,Lei Xie,Yi Pan,Xiao Hu,Manuela Ferrario*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Defines and quantifies Derived-Feature Over-Trust (DFOT) in LLM pipelines; introduces five estimands (COTR, CIR, CRR, ESRM, UHR) and evaluates them on PPG-ECG data via a privileged distillation baseline vs PPG-only inference; shows modest gains in repair/specificity and mixed UHR results; provides code for replication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the risk that derived measurements (e.g., physiological signals) are treated as facts by LLMs regardless of their validity scope, enabling systematic evaluation and mitigation of DFOT.

Method: Formalize DFOT and two test scenarios (D1/D2) where LLMs receive derived measurements with conflicting or misleading context. Use ECG as supervision/reference not exposed to the LLM. Define five estimands to capture conflict, context-induced error, repair capability, evidence-matching repair margins, and unnecessary verification. Validate on 50k paired PPG-ECG records with ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as a baseline and compare to a PPG-only inference on a protocol-locked 187-patient test.

Result: Quantitative results show a 1.82–6.69 percentage point improvement across four repair/specificity endpoints with all CIs excluding zero; UHR increases by 0.67 percentage points with a 95% CI spanning from -0.4 to +1.7 (not conclusively positive). Code available for replication.

Conclusion: DFOT offers a common, modality-agnostic evaluation target to drive development of mitigation strategies for when derived measurements are misused as direct facts in LLM pipelines.

Abstract: Derived measurements increasingly enter large language model (LLM) pipelines as direct facts despite their instance-dependent validity. We define derived-feature over-trust (DFOT) as the failure in which a downstream LLM assigns such a measurement the epistemic status of a direct fact or uses it outside its valid scope. Using physiological sensing as a case study, D1 tests acceptance of a PPG-derived rhythm contradicted by offline ECG, whereas D2 tests rejection of an offline-confirmed reliable PPG rhythm under misleading severe history. ECG supplies training supervision and offline reference construction but is never shown to the LLM. Five estimands quantify this chain: conflict over-trust rate (COTR) and context-induced error rate (CIR) characterize D1/D2; correct repair rate (CRR) measures frozen-error repair; evidence-specific repair margin (ESRM) contrasts matched and patient-disjoint shuffled evidence; and utility harm rate (UHR) measures unnecessary verification among HIGH-reliability cases used without verification at baseline. The framework does not depend on a particular reliability generator. We demonstrate it on 50,000 paired PPG-ECG records using ECG-to-PPG privileged distillation as an illustrative baseline and PPG-only inference. On a protocol-locked 187-patient test, the baseline improves four repair and specificity endpoints by 1.82-6.69 percentage points, with all paired confidence intervals excluding zero; UHR increases by 0.67 percentage points (95% CI: -0.4 to +1.7). DFOT provides a common evaluation target for stronger mitigation methods. The code is available at https://github.com/Zongheng-Guo/When-Derived-Measurements-Mislead.

</details>


### [212] [A foundation model of numerical intelligence with cross-disciplinary generalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28432)
*Chenghan Wu,Zongmin Yu,Liu Yang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: UNICON is a foundation model that demonstrates numerical intelligence by learning a shared predictive relation from graph-based context and applying it to new queries across disciplines, including unseen ones; its generalization improves with diverse training data and when combined with language-model agents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill the gap in AI beyond language: develop models that acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context to solve problems across scientific and social systems, including disciplines not seen during training.

Method: UNICON uses graph-based context as input to infer a universal predictive relation shared across graphs within a system; it applies this relation to new queries from the same system; evaluated across diverse scientific and social domains, including unseen disciplines; integration with language-model agents enhances performance.

Result: UNICON approaches specialist performance without retraining across multiple domains, including disciplines absent from training; combining with LM agents yields state-of-the-art performance in unseen disciplines; training-corpus diversity improves generalization to unseen areas.

Conclusion: UNICON positions numerical intelligence as a foundational capability and provides a building block for a broader AI ecosystem, enabling cross-domain reasoning and generalization without task-specific retraining.

Abstract: Intelligence is commonly understood as the ability to acquire and apply knowledge, adapt to unfamiliar situations and solve new problems. Large language models exhibit this capacity by inferring task-relevant knowledge from textual context and applying it to new tasks. Yet intelligence need not be confined to language. For scientific and social systems, we need models that acquire and apply knowledge from numerical context-an ability we call numerical intelligence. Here we introduce UNified In-Context Operator Networks (UNICON), a foundation model that exhibits numerical intelligence across disciplines. Using graph-based examples from a system as context, UNICON infers the predictive relation shared across them and applies it to queries from the same system. Across scientific and social systems, including those from disciplines absent from training, the same model approaches specialist performance without retraining. Combining UNICON with language-model agents yields further gains, enabling it to surpass state-of-the-art specialists in a discipline unseen in training. We further show that training-corpus diversity improves generalization to unseen disciplines. Together, these results establish UNICON as a foundation model of numerical intelligence and position it as a building block for a broader ecosystem of artificial intelligence.

</details>


### [213] [Metaphor Tracer: A Theory-Informed Analysis of Hidden States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28434)
*Marc Heimann,Roxana Assadi Moghaddam,Olga Brovkina,Mark Pettifor,Lutz Goetzmann*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Introduces two relational, position-based metrics (aggregator and differentiator) derived from a single forward pass to characterize a token's role in a text; demonstrates these align with independent ground truths (engineered registers, psychoanalytic transcripts) across multiple models and transfer tests; claims structural value depends on token position within a text rather than vector content.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand how hidden states encode global text structure within a single pass and without training; connect interpretability with discourse-level organization; validate across models and ground-truth references.

Method: Compute per-token aggregator and differentiator scores in a forward pass, freezing constants on a discovery text and treating others as confirmatory; test across three unrelated models; assess against engineered registers and psychoanalytic transcripts; perform transfer tests comparing lexical type structure and base/instruction tuning.

Result: Aggregator tracks a token's place in the text independent of classic information measures; when a signifier repeats, surprisal and attention drain increase while aggregator score remains; transfer results reveal token structure travels with lexical type, and tuned models improve fidelity without altering type-transfer; strong cross-model and cross-ground-truth alignment.

Conclusion: Structural value is relational to a token's position within the current text rather than an intrinsic property of its vector; supports a relational reading of hidden states and aligns with pre-existing theory; findings show robustness across models and grounding tests though rely on a specific experimental setup.

Abstract: What do a language model's hidden states say about the organization of a single text? From one forward pass, without training, we score every token position on two properties. The *aggregator* measures whether the position consolidates the whole text into a stable configuration. The *differentiator*, whether other tokens are transiently carried into its subspace as the model reads: metaphor in its root sense, transport. Constants were frozen on one discovery text; every other is confirmatory.
  The aggregator is not, in the classic sense, an information measure, nor a measure of salience. Across three unrelated models, as a signifier repeats, its surprisal and its attention drain while its aggregator score holds: the channel marks a token's place in the text. That this tracks a reading rests on independent ground truth: an engineered register the aggregator follows across its boundaries (6/6 cells), and a psychoanalyst's marking of clinical transcripts, fixed before the instrument existed, in 34/36 cells, with a graded increment above lexical controls and dissociations no type-level measure reproduces. A transfer test gives the result its shape: the model whose token structure travels with lexical type reads the singular discourse worst, and in a matched base/instruct pair tuning raises fidelity without moving type-transfer. Structural value is a property of a token's place in *this* text, not of its vector alone: a relational rather than essentialist reading of hidden states, operationalizing theory that predated the instrument.

</details>


### [214] [SVR: Self-Verifying Refinement via Joint Verdict-Confidence Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Test-Time Compute](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28457)
*Hongyu Chen,Liang Lin,Guangrun Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SVR uses an internal self-verification signal to control multi-turn reasoning without external feedback, achieving better compute efficiency and accuracy on seven math benchmarks (macro-avg 0.563, ~3 turns).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce wasted compute on easy inputs and dependence on external feedback by learning a self-verification policy that governs whether to stop or refine.

Method: Train with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories where each turn outputs a solution, a discrete correctness verdict, and a confidence score. Retain the answer only if verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold; otherwise continue refinement using self-verification. Ground-truth correctness is used only to shape training rewards and is never exposed during refinement or inference. Adaptive stopping is enabled only at inference. Rewards promote solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready states.

Result: On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks using Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves a macro-average accuracy of 0.563 with an average of 2.99 inference turns. In complete-system comparisons, it surpasses standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference, while using fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference.

Conclusion: Learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation.

Abstract: Scaling test-time computation can improve language-model reasoning, but uniform budgets waste computation on easy inputs, while verifier-guided refinement relies on external feedback. We introduce Self-Verifying Refinement (SVR), an oracle-free multi-turn reinforcement learning framework that learns to use self-verification as a compute-control policy. At each turn, the model produces a solution together with a discrete correctness verdict and a confidence score; it retains the current answer only when the verdict is Correct and confidence exceeds a threshold, and otherwise continues refinement using its own self-verification. Ground-truth correctness is used only to construct training rewards and is never exposed to the policy through refinement prompts or required at inference. SVR is trained with GRPO on fixed-horizon trajectories using rewards that promote solution correctness, calibration-aware self-verification, and stop-ready correct states; adaptive stopping is activated only at inference. On seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks with Qwen3.5-2B, SVR achieves a macro-average accuracy of 0.563 with only 2.99 inference turns on average. In the evaluated complete-system comparison, it exceeds standard GRPO, strong multi-turn baselines, and a fixed-budget oracle-guided score-feedback reference while requiring substantially fewer turns than fixed ten-turn inference. These results demonstrate that learned self-verification can serve as an effective internal control signal for answer retention and adaptive test-time compute allocation.

</details>


### [215] [LeanCSP: A Framework for Certifying Constraint Reformulation and Solving in Lean](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28459)
*Pablo Manrique,Stefan Szeider*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Lean-based end-to-end verification for constraint programming, proving reformulation properties and validating solver certificates across problem families with backends to MiniZinc/SMT-LIB/OPB; achieves large practical speedups and keeps Lean certification tractable.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To provide guarantees for both reformulations and solver results in constraint programming, ensuring semantic preservation and solver correctness without trusting external solvers.

Method: A Lean framework enabling parametric, formulation-level proofs (equivalence, equisatisfiability, symmetry-breaking correctness) for problem families, plus translation backends to external formats to check solver-produced certificates for individual instances.

Result: Verified symmetry breaking reduces solver search dramatically (up to 2×10^7 speedups across problem families); Lean-based certification remains affordable, taking minutes for largest instances.

Conclusion: An end-to-end, trust-preserving constraint programming workflow is achievable by combining parametric reformulation proofs with solver certificates validated via external backends, yielding both theoretical guarantees and practical performance gains.

Abstract: Constraint programming is a core technology for solving complex combinatorial problems in scheduling, planning, configuration, and verification. Trusting its results therefore demands guarantees at two levels: that reformulations applied beforehand are semantics-preserving, and that solvers produce correct answers. In this work, we introduce a framework that addresses both verification levels in the Lean theorem prover: it can be used to prove formulation-level properties, such as equivalence, equisatisfiability, and the correctness of symmetry-breaking constraints, parametrically for entire problem families; and to check solver-produced certificates for individual instances via translation backends to external formats such as MiniZinc, SMT-LIB, and OPB. Combining both levels yields an end-to-end workflow that establishes the satisfiability or unsatisfiability of a constraint problem without trusting the external solver. Experimental results show that our framework's verified symmetry breaking also pays off in practice: a single parametric proof per problem family, reused across all instance sizes, reduces solver search effort by a factor of up to 2x10^7, while the entire in-Lean certification stays affordable, taking at most a few minutes for our largest instances.

</details>


### [216] [A report-grounded vision-language foundation model for colonoscopy from 280000 routine reports](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28466)
*Jia Yu,Yan Zhu,Yili He,Zilong Wang,Xinyang Jiang,Peiyao Fu,Ruijie Yang,Tianyi Chen,Siyuan Li,Zhihua Wang,Fei Wu,Quanlin Li,Xian Yang,Pinghong Zhou,Shuo Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: EndoCLIP is a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image–text pairs recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records, achieving strong zero-shot and linear-probe performance on lesion-level retrieval, report generation, and six multi-centre classification tasks; its linear probe for benign-versus-malignant classification rivals expert readers in a blinded study of 12 endoscopists.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision–language models are underutilized in colonoscopy due to lack of frame-level annotations; routine reports summarize procedures rather than individual frames, weakening the link between findings and images. Recovering finding-to-frame correspondence could unlock scalable supervision from existing documentation.

Method: Construct EndoCLIP by progressively recovering lesion-level image–text pairs from routine colonoscopy records (≈125k pairs from ≈281k records). Evaluate on lesion-level image–text retrieval, structured report generation, and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks using zero-shot and linear-probe settings.

Result: EndoCLIP consistently outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision–language encoders across tasks in zero-shot and linear-probe settings; in benign-versus-malignant classification its linear probe nearly matches expert readers in a blinded study with 12 endoscopists.

Conclusion: Recovering finding-to-frame correspondence enables scalable supervision from routine documentation, allowing clinical targets to be specified in language rather than needing task-specific frame-wise annotations.

Abstract: Vision-language models remain underused in colonoscopy despite the rich expert descriptions recorded in routine reports. These reports document lesion appearance, size and location but summarise entire procedures rather than caption individual frames, leaving clinical findings only weakly linked to the corresponding images. Here we develop EndoCLIP, a colonoscopy vision-language foundation model trained on 125,756 lesion-level image-text pairs progressively recovered from 280,476 routine colonoscopy records. Across lesion-level image-text retrieval, structured report generation and six multi-centre clinical classification tasks, EndoCLIP outperforms general-purpose and biomedical vision-language encoders in both zero-shot and linear-probe settings. On benign-versus-malignant classification, its linear probe approaches the performance of expert readers in a blinded study involving 12 endoscopists. These results suggest that recovering finding-to-frame correspondence can transform routine documentation into scalable supervision, enabling clinical targets to be specified in language rather than separately annotated for each task.

</details>


### [217] [Towards Autonomous Aircraft Surveillance from Nanosatellites through On-Board Inference and Generative Data Augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28470)
*Antonio Delgado-Rosa,David Muñoz-Valero,Enrique Adrian Villarrubia-Martin,Juan Moreno-Garcia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: On-board inference plus diffusion-based data augmentation on a 6U CubeSat enables real-time aircraft detection with improved robustness to rare classes, addressing downlink and data scarcity bottlenecks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Nanosatellite downlink budgets limit raw-image transmission and open datasets for aircraft are scarce and severely class-imbalanced. This hampers timely decision-making and robust learning of rare classes.

Method: Deploy on-board inference with a low-power edge tensor accelerator on a 6U CubeSat; fine-tune a diffusion model via low-rank adaptation to generate synthetic minority-class aircraft imagery; auto-annotate via an intermediate detector; pseudo-label and merge with classically augmented data; use a quantised detector that fits on-chip and runs at 25–30 frames per second.

Result: Balanced dataset improves global mAP from 77.9% to 82.2%; minority-class F1 rises from 0.683 to 0.811; on-board detector achieves 25–30 fps on orbit.

Conclusion: The proposed workflow demonstrates real-time, autonomous airborne surveillance capability from nanosatellites and offers a decision-support tool that outperforms passive bent-pipe architectures.

Abstract: Airborne surveillance from low Earth orbit is hindered by two interconnected bottlenecks: nanosatellites have a limited downlink budget, yet the conventional approach still transmits terabytes of raw imagery to the ground for processing, and open satellite datasets for aircraft are scarce and severely class-imbalanced. These limitations either delay timely decision-making or prevent standard detectors from learning robust representations of rare aircraft classes. In this paper, a workflow that combines on-board inference with generative data augmentation is proposed to address both limitations jointly. Inference is executed on a 6U CubeSat equipped with a low-power edge tensor accelerator, while a diffusion model fine-tuned through low-rank adaptation generates synthetic minority-class imagery. This synthetic output is automatically annotated, pseudo-labelled, by an intermediate detector and merged with classically augmented samples. The results show that the balanced dataset increases global mean average precision from 77.9% to 82.2%, with the minority class rising from F1=0.683 to F1=0.811, and that the quantised detector fits the on-chip memory and projects 25-30 frames per second on orbit. This approach contrasts with the conventional bent-pipe architecture, in which the satellite acts as a passive data collector. Therefore, the computational tests support the proposed workflow as a decision-support tool for real-time, autonomous airborne surveillance from nanosatellites.

</details>


### [218] [A Fuzzy Rule-based Neuro-Symbolic Approach for Pipe Severity Prediction in Sewer Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28481)
*Ngoc Thai Le,Thanh Ma,Umberto Straccia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A modular neuro-symbolic framework for sewer pipe severity assessment that decouples neural perception from symbolic reasoning, combining a Swin Transformer for multilabel CODE degree prediction with a J48-derived rule set and fuzzy inference to produce interpretable severity evidence, showing notable improvements over image-only classification on a 3,244-image dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the opacity of end-to-end image classification for sewer pipe severity by introducing interpretable, traceable reasoning that links predicted defect codes to severity decisions.

Method: Perception: Swin Transformer predicts 14 multilabel CODE degrees from images. Reasoning: Train Weka J48 decision tree on ground-truth CODEs and severity labels; convert its paths into 19 fixed IF-THEN rules. Inference: apply fuzzy logic with t-norm activations weighted by rule confidence and combined with s-norms to form evidence. Evaluate operator pairs (Product, Lukasiewicz, Hamacher) on a dataset of 3,244 images across five imbalanced severity classes. Ground-truth labels generated via consensus from five independent LLMs analyzing inspector notes.

Result: Compared to image-only classification, the framework improves accuracy by 17.9%, balanced accuracy by 12.2%, Macro F1 by 23.0%, and MCC by 17.3%. Overall, it achieves competitive class-balanced performance with traceable reasoning from predicted CODE degrees to rule supports and severity evidence.

Conclusion: The proposed neuro-symbolic, fuzzy-rule framework provides improved, interpretable severity assessment with transparent linkage from neural predictions to symbolic rules and evidence, addressing the black-box limitation of standard image-only approaches.

Abstract: Standard automated sewer pipe severity assessment relies on direct image classification, creating a "black box" where the link between visual defects and final severity scores remains implicit. This study introduces a modular, fuzzy rule-based neuro-symbolic framework that bridges this gap by decoupling neural perception from symbolic reasoning. The perception module utilizes a Swin Transformer to predict 14 multilabel inspection CODE degrees directly from images. For reasoning, a DT, specifically Weka's J48, algorithm is trained on ground-truth CODEs and severity labels, and its paths are converted into 19 fixed IF--THEN rules. Inference operates via fuzzy logic: t-norm activations from CODE conditions are weighted by rule confidence and combined with corresponding s-norms to produce interpretable class evidence. We assessed Product, Łukasiewicz, and Hamacher operator pairs using a dataset of 3,244 images spanning five highly imbalanced severity classes. Ground-truth labels were robustly generated via consensus from five independent large language models analyzing original inspector notes. Our results show an improvement of accuracy, balanced accuracy, Macro F1 and MCC by 17.9%, 12.2%, 23.0%, and 17.3%, respectively, over image-only based classification.
  Overall, the framework combines competitive class-balanced performance with traceable reasoning from predicted CODE degrees to rule supports and severity evidence.

</details>


### [219] [SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28488)
*Yunhao Liang,Xianqi Cao,Pujun Zhang,Yuan Qu,Yongzhi Qi,Ningxuan Kang,Max Z. J. Shen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Unified cross-coupled policy framework (SCOPE) for end-to-end replenishment that outperforms stage-wise optimization on real urban fresh-retail data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Supply chains exhibit strong operational couplings across assortment, sourcing, replenishment frequency, and routing; decoupled decisions cause inefficiencies and stockouts; need a framework to coordinate multiple decision stages.

Method: Introduce SCOPE: a composite policy model where entities are tokens, share a common representation, and decision interfaces map to token types; decisions are incremental and evaluated by a system-level utility. Apply to urban fresh-retail replenishment; evaluate on real data from Dingdong and JD.com across replenishment echelons.

Result: SCOPE consistently outperforms stage-wise optimization methods and practical baselines in both datasets, indicating benefits of cross-department coupling and end-to-end learning.

Conclusion: End-to-end coordination via coupled policies improves replenishment outcomes; the token-based, interconnected framework can generalize to other supply-chain settings.

Abstract: Can supply-chain AI move beyond isolated decision modules toward unified operational planning? A complete replenishment plan specifies which products each location carries, which upstream facility supplies it, how often it is replenished, and how deliveries are routed. These decisions are operationally coupled: the selected assortment changes the demand and load passed to later stages; source assignment and replenishment frequency reshape the delivery requests; and route feasibility and cost, in turn, determine the system value of the earlier choices. Yet in modern supply chains, these decisions are often handled by separate departments and optimized through separate systems, which can lead to stockouts, inventory exposure, and avoidable transportation. We propose SCOPE: Supply-Chain Operations through Coupled Policies for End-to-End Coordination, a composite policy model that represents supply-chain entities as tokens, contextualizes them through a shared operational representation, and maps each token type to the corresponding decision interface. Each decision builds on the partial plan formed by earlier decisions while the completed plan is evaluated using a shared system-level utility. We instantiate this framework in urban fresh-retail replenishment, where service frequency, assortment, capacity pressure, and road-network routing interact strongly, and evaluate it on real operational data from Dingdong and JD.com, two large-scale supply chains operating at different replenishment echelons. Across both settings, SCOPE consistently outperforms methods that optimize each decision stage separately, as well as practice-oriented baselines commonly used in supply-chain operations. These results show that learning and coordinating cross-department operational couplings lead to more effective end-to-end supply-chain decisions.

</details>


### [220] [InfoOps Bench: A live information operations safety benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28503)
*Dorian Quelle,Lisa-Maria Neudert,Jonathan Bright,John Gallacher*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: An actively updated AI benchmark to assess whether frontier language models can be used for state-backed information operations; shows wide variability in refusal rates and model behaviors; highlights safety-usability trade-offs and cross-model differences, especially with Chinese models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To counteract the risk of frontier LMs being co-opted for state-backed information operations by creating a dynamic, live benchmark that tracks real-world manipulation patterns.

Method: Leverage a live monitoring pipeline of 2,100+ state-backed information operations; evaluate 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings; measure integrity as the percentage of refused requests; analyze output characteristics and fact-checking rates; publish a companion website updated weekly.

Result: Integrity/refusal rates range from 8.8% to 94.5%, an 85.7-point spread not explained by model size; model choice alters the nature of the operation; some models fabricate details or increase harm; others defuse while complying; fact-checking rates vary 2.9% to 72.9%; with one exception (GLM 5.2), Chinese-developed models sharply reduce compliance on China-critical claims (48-70 percentage points vs benign).

Conclusion: The study provides a dynamic benchmark that reveals gaps between usability and safety, shows that model and prompt design significantly influence resistance to information operations, and underscores the need for ongoing evaluation and guardrails in frontier models.

Abstract: In this paper we present an active, constantly updated AI benchmark which measures the integrity of frontier language models against being co-opted for state-backed information operations. We draw on over 2,100 information operations from a live monitoring pipeline which tracks Russian, Chinese and Iranian state-backed information assets. Alongside this paper, we release a companion website that tracks the most prominent claims spread by state-backed media outlets, updated weekly, available from: pattrn.ai/research/infoopsbench. The dynamic nature of the benchmark makes it resistant to saturation.
  In the benchmark, we test 17 models from 8 providers across four prompt framings. We find that most models can be co-opted for information operations. Integrity scores, defined as the percentage of refused requests, range from 8.8% to 94.5%, an 85.7-percentage-point spread not explained by model size. Model choice also changes the character of the resulting operation. Some models fabricate details and produce output more harmful than the source material, others defuse claims even while complying, and fact-checking rates vary from 2.9% to 72.9%.
  Integrity against information operations is at least partly related to refusal to produce content even for benign claims, illustrating the challenge of balancing model usability with safety. With one exception (Z.ai's GLM 5.2), the Chinese-developed models sharply cut compliance on factually grounded but China-critical claims, dropping 48-70 percentage points relative to matched benign claims.

</details>


### [221] [Selective Credibility-Limited Belief Update](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28523)
*Theofanis Aravanis,Costas D. Koutras*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Selective credibility-limited belief update (SCLBU) introduces per-source input weakening before credibility-limited transitions, unifying and extending KM and CRL updates by enabling source-dependent selective acceptance; two well-behaved sub-classes are identified.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome the indivisibility of epistemic inputs in credibility-limited updates, enabling partial realization of compound inputs and source-dependent reasoning; to provide a unified, expressive framework for belief update.

Method: For each source world, apply a transformation that maps the original epistemic input to a weaker proxy; perform a credibility-limited transition on that proxy. Provide semantic and axiomatic characterizations of the resulting operators. Identify two sub-classes: consistency-preserving update operators (proxy credible whenever original input is consistent) and maximal consistency-preserving update operators (proxy maximally informative among credible consequences).

Result: A general class of update operators is obtained; two well-behaved sub-classes are characterized; credibility-limited belief update is recovered as a special case, and KM belief update is recovered when credibility restrictions are removed and transformations are identities; the framework subsumes existing approaches and supports source-dependent selective acceptance.

Conclusion: The framework offers a unified, strictly more expressive account of belief update, unifying KM and CRL approaches while enabling selective, source-driven acceptance of epistemic inputs; suggests broad applicability and potential for further refinement.

Abstract: Belief update concerns changes in an agent's beliefs induced by changes in the underlying world. Standard Katsuno-Mendelzon update assumes that an epistemic input can be incorporated from every initially possible world, whereas credibility-limited belief update restricts, for each source world, the successor worlds regarded as credible or reachable. Nevertheless, existing credibility-limited approaches treat the epistemic input as an indivisible whole, and therefore cannot represent cases in which only part of a compound epistemic input can be realized. We introduce selective credibility-limited belief update, in which the epistemic input is transformed, relative to each source world, into a weaker proxy before the credibility-limited transition is performed. We provide semantic and axiomatic characterizations of the resulting class of update operators. We then identify two well-behaved sub-classes; namely, consistency-preserving update operators, which require every transformed epistemic input to be credible from its source world whenever the original epistemic input is consistent, and maximal consistency-preserving update operators, which additionally require the selected proxy to be maximally informative among the credible consequences of the original epistemic input. Finally, we establish the generality of the proposed framework by showing that credibility-limited belief update is recovered as a special case, while Katsuno--Mendelzon belief update emerges when credibility restrictions are removed and the transformation functions are taken to be identities. These results demonstrate that the framework provides a unified and strictly more expressive account of belief update, encompassing established approaches while supporting source-dependent selective acceptance.

</details>


### [222] [MANTA: Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation for Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28527)
*Mao-xun Huang,Jerry Wang,Yi-Cheng Lai,Zhengxin Zhang,Claire Cardie,Hen-Hsen Huang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: MANTA enables inference-time adaptation of multi-agent communication topology for LLM-based systems, improving problem-solving by evolving agent roles, links, and validation pathways during deployment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current multi-agent systems often fix the communication topology, limiting coordination. There is value in evolving collaboration structures at inference time to sustain or improve performance.

Method: Initialize a task-conditioned topology using prior structural experience; during deployment, monitor collaboration traces and apply bounded structural updates when organization is insufficient. Updates can modify agent roles, communication links, execution order, information visibility, and validation pathways while preserving the task interface and budget.

Result: Evaluated on five benchmarks across information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, and mathematical reasoning. MANTA achieves an average score of 74.0, outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points and achieving the best result on PlanCraft.

Conclusion: Inference-time self-improvement can extend to the architecture of collaboration, enabling dynamic topology evolution to sustain or improve multi-agent performance.

Abstract: Large language model-based multi-agent systems improve complex problem solving through task decomposition, agent specialization, information exchange, and intermediate validation. However, existing systems typically treat communication topology as a fixed design choice or an offline optimization target. We introduce MANTA, a framework for Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation that enables communication structures to self-evolve at inference time. Before execution, MANTA initializes a task-conditioned topology from prior structural experience. During deployment, it monitors collaboration traces and applies bounded structural updates when the current organization becomes insufficient. These updates can modify agent roles, communication links, execution order, information visibility, and validation pathways while preserving the task interface and agent budget. We evaluate MANTA against representative single-agent and multi-agent baselines on five benchmarks spanning information seeking, tool use, planning, workflow execution, and mathematical reasoning. MANTA achieves the highest average score of 74.0, outperforming the strongest baseline by 5.8 percentage points and obtaining the best result on PlanCraft. These results show that inference-time self-improvement can extend to the architecture of collaboration itself.

</details>


### [223] [Rethinking Inference-Time Scaling in Local Computer-Use Agents: Failure Modes and Compute Tradeoffs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28573)
*Woongkyu Lee,Jungwook Choi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Inference-time scaling for local computer-use agents yields limited gains and shifts failure modes under hardware constraints; effectiveness depends on scaling type, suggesting selective compute, failure-aware control, and agentic designs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how inference-time scaling translates to performance improvements for privacy-preserving, resource-constrained local CUAs.

Method: Systematic empirical study across contextual, temporal, structural, and parallel dimensions evaluating Qwen3-VL-8B/30B-A3B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, and OpenCUA-7B on the OSWorld benchmark, measuring task success, stability, stalls, and failure modes.

Result: Additional computation often yields diminishing returns and changes failure modes. Contextual scaling improves trajectory stability and accuracy but saturates with higher token costs and shifts failures from repetitive/stalled trajectories to premature false successes. Temporal scaling reduces max-step stalls but does not substantially improve task success, often extending erroneous trajectories. Structural decomposition adds planning/formatting overhead in two-stage local agents. Parallel scaling mitigates some failures but at a substantial computational cost.

Conclusion: Efficient local CUAs require selective compute allocation, failure-aware control mechanisms, and agentic frameworks designed around the capabilities and limitations of local models.

Abstract: Deploying autonomous computer-use agents (CUAs) locally is increasingly important for privacy, cost efficiency, and practical usability, yet improving their performance under strict hardware constraints remains challenging. While recent studies show that inference-time scaling can improve frontier computer-use agents through additional computation during execution, its effectiveness for resource-constrained local models remains poorly understood. We present a systematic empirical study of inference-time scaling in local CUAs across contextual, temporal, structural, and parallel dimensions. We evaluate Qwen3-VL-8B/30B-A3B, UI-TARS-1.5-7B, and OpenCUA-7B on the OSWorld benchmark. Our results show that additional computation often yields diminishing returns while changing failure modes. Contextual scaling provides historical grounding that improves trajectory stability and task accuracy, but its gains saturate as token cost increases and failures shift from repetitive or stalled trajectories toward premature false successes. Temporal scaling similarly reduces max-step stalls, yet does not substantially improve task success, indicating that longer horizons often extend erroneous trajectories rather than correct them.
