We propose Aging-Aware Autonomous Intelligence (AAAI), a framework that integrates hardware health directly into reasoning, planning, and mission execution. AAAI is built on three pillars: hardware self-awareness, which continuously estimates the health of power, sensing, memory, and computation subsystems using physics-of-failure models; self-adaptive reasoning, which adjusts inference complexity, planning horizon, and task priorities according to remaining hardware capability; and survival-centric intelligence, which allocates remaining operational life across mission objectives through performance optimization, resource conservation, and graceful degradation. Rather than introducing new hardware, AAAI unifies prognostics, lifecycle management, and hardware-aware computing into a closed-loop cognitive architecture. We argue that such integration is essential for autonomous systems operating in inaccessible or safety-critical environments, including space missions, marine robotics, and implantable medical devices. By enabling machines to recognize and respond to their own aging, AAAI improves resilience, extends operational lifetime, and supports safer, more graceful mission completion.

</details>


### [249] [TEA-AgriVLN: Traversability Estimation Alarm for Agricultural Vision-and-Language Navigation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28474)
*Xiaobei Zhao,Xingqi Lyu,Xin Chen,Xiang Li*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: The TEA-AgriVLN framework introduces a Traversability Estimation and Alarm (TEA) module that predicts image traversability and flags actions that conflict with it, yielding state-of-the-art results for agricultural VLN-CE (A2A): SR 0.54 (up from 0.47) and NE 2.70 m (down from 2.91 m), with ablation and case studies validating effectiveness and limitations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: VLN-CE in indoor environments benefits from clear traversability signals, but agricultural scenes present ambiguity (e.g., unripe crops may be traversable for robots but not for humans). This ambiguity motivates a traversability-aware navigation module to reduce action-perception mismatch.

Method: Introduce TEA module that (1) estimates traversability from camera images, and (2) issues an alarm to rethink the predicted action if it conflicts with the traversability map. TEA is integrated into the AgriVLN backbone to form TEA-AgriVLN.

Result: Empirical gains on A2A: Success Rate increases from 0.47 to 0.54; Navigation Error decreases from 2.91 m to 2.70 m, achieving state-of-the-art performance in agricultural VLN-CE. Ablation studies and case analyses elucidate the conditions under which TEA helps and its limitations.

Conclusion: TEA effectively reduces action-environment mismatch in agricultural VLN-CE by incorporating traversability awareness, though limitations remain (e.g., ground-category and scene-class variability). The work provides ablations, case studies, and publicly available code (GitHub).

Abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires an agent to follow a natural language instruction, predicting a sequence of low-level actions to navigate a robot from a starting point to a target location. The A2A benchmark and the AgriVLN method pioneeringly extended VLN-CE from indoor scenes to agricultural scenes, while we observed a challenging distinction: In indoor scenes, whether a zone is traversable tends to be clear to classify, such as wood floors are traversable but concrete walls are not. In agricultural scenes, however, this issue tends to be ambiguous, such as an unripe cornfield might be traversable for a robotic dog but might be non-traversable for a human. To address this issue, we propose the TEA module, which estimates the traversability of the camera image, then alarm the decision-maker for rethinking when the predicted action does not align with the traversability map. We integrate it into the AgriVLN backbone to build our TEA-AgriVLN method. When evaluated on A2A, it improves Success Rate (SR) from 0.47 to 0.54 and Navigation Error (NE) from 2.91 m to 2.70 m, showing the state-of-the-art performance in the agricultural VLN-CE domain. We further implement the ablation studies and the case study, discussing the effectiveness and limitations of TEA on different ground categories and scene classes. Code: https://github.com/AlexTraveling/TEA-AgriVLN.

</details>


### [250] [X-NavDP: Generalizing Navigation Diffusion Policy to Novel Behavior and Embodiments with Group Q-score Reweighted Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28560)
*Tianyu Yang,Yiming Zeng,Wenzhe Cai,Yuqiang Yang,Jiaqi Peng,Hui Cheng,Jiangmiao Pang,Tai Wang*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: A data-efficient diffusion RL post-training framework, GQRM, improves cross-embodiment visual navigation by self-bootstrapped exploration and group Q-score reweighting, achieving substantial gains in simulation and real-world hard cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Pretraining on expert demonstrations from a single, fully-informed planner limits generalization to diverse robot embodiments and challenging scenarios that require diverse local reactive behaviors with only onboard observations. RL post-training can help, but diffusion-policy RL is hampered by intractable likelihood, unstable policy gradients, and inefficient exploration.

Method: Twofold design: (i) self-bootstrapped exploration with behavior perturbation that preserves the pretrained policy prior; (ii) group Q-score normalization computing per-trajectory values on each state for efficient reweighted score matching. Training is distributed online across heterogeneous embodiments to fine-tune the policy, resulting in X-NavDP.

Result: X-NavDP achieves state-of-the-art cross-embodiment visual navigation performance, improving success rate from 61.20% to 84.28% in simulation and from 10% to 65% in real-world hard cases.

Conclusion: The proposed GQRM framework enables data-efficient diffusion RL post-training and yields strong cross-embodiment navigation performance (X-NavDP); code and model are publicly available.

Abstract: Pretraining navigation diffusion policies rely on large-scale expert demonstrations. These data are typically generated by a fully-informed oracle planner suited to a single nominal robot. This limits the policy's generalization to diverse embodiments and challenging scenarios (e.g., escaping dead ends or detouring long obstacles) that demand diverse local reactive behaviors with only onboard local observations. Post-training the policy with reinforcement learning (RL) offers a principled remedy. However, previous RL for diffusion approaches lead to only marginal improvements. This is because the intractable likelihood of diffusion policies renders policy gradients unstable in addition to inefficient policy exploration. To address these challenges, we propose a data-efficient diffusion RL post-training framework - GQRM (Group Q-score Reweighted Matching). Our framework introduces two complementary designs: (i) a self-bootstrapped exploration strategy with behavior perturbation that preserves the pretrained policy prior, and (ii) a group Q-score normalization mechanism that computes per-trajectory values on each state for efficient reweighted score matching. By conducting distributed online RL training across heterogeneous embodiments, the resulting fine-tuned policy, X-NavDP, achieves state-of-the-art cross-embodiment visual navigation performance, improving the overall success rate from 61.20% to 84.28% in simulation and 10% to 65% in real-world hard cases. The code and model are publicly available at https://yty-sky.github.io/x-navdp-project-page.

</details>


### [251] [FA-RDP: A Frequency-Adaptive Reactive Diffusion Policy for Contact-Rich Manipulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28596)
*Lifeng Zhuo,Wendi Chen,Han Xue,Shirun Tang,Jun Lv,Cewu Lu,Chuan Wen*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: FA-RDP is a frequency-adaptive diffusion policy for contact-rich manipulation that preserves pre-contact action multimodality and improves reactivity via dynamic frequency switching guided by a multimodality indicator, complemented by Manifold Consistency Distillation to align diffusion with the robot action manifold.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard diffusion policies fix inference frequency, forcing a tradeoff: low-frequency sampling preserves pre-contact multimodality but is slow to respond to force feedback; high-frequency sampling improves reactivity but collapses pre-contact modes. A frequency-adaptive approach is needed to handle distinct phases (pre- and post-contact) of manipulation.

Method: FA-RDP introduces a shared multi-frequency Visual-Force Transformer that predicts action chunks at both low and high frequencies. A learned multimodality indicator dynamically selects low-frequency sampling before contact (to preserve multimodality) and one-step high-frequency sampling as action ambiguity declines after contact. Manifold Consistency Distillation (MCD) reparameterizes the diffusion network to predict actions on the robot action manifold while preserving DDPM-based residual supervision.

Result: Experiments on three contact-rich manipulation tasks show FA-RDP achieves the highest success rate while preserving diverse pre-contact trajectory modes.

Conclusion: The proposed frequency-adaptive diffusion policy, together with manifold-consistent distillation, resolves the fundamental tradeoff between multimodality preservation and rapid force-feedback reactivity, yielding superior performance in contact-rich manipulation; code and videos are available.

Abstract: In contact-rich manipulation, action multimodality and reactivity dominate different stages of a single episode. Before contact, multiple trajectories might be equally valid, making it important to preserve diverse action modes. After contact, geometric constraints and force limits narrow the solution space, while successful execution demands rapid responses to force feedback. However, standard diffusion policies use a fixed inference frequency and sampling steps throughout the episode, forcing a fundamental compromise: low-frequency, multi-step sampling better preserves pre-contact multimodality but responds slowly to force feedback, whereas high-frequency sampling improves reactivity but tends to collapse distinct pre-contact modes. To resolve this tradeoff, we present FA-RDP, a frequency-adaptive reactive diffusion policy. A shared multi-frequency visual-force Transformer predicts action chunks at both low and high frequencies, while a learned multimodality indicator dynamically selects multi-step low-frequency sampling before contact and one-step high-frequency sampling as action ambiguity decreases. We further introduce Manifold Consistency Distillation (MCD), which reparameterizes the diffusion network to predict actions on the robot action manifold while retaining DDPM-based residual supervision. Experiments on three contact-rich manipulation tasks show that FA-RDP achieves the highest success rate while preserving diverse pre-contact trajectory modes. Code and videos are available at https://fa-rdp.github.io.

</details>


### [252] [PAC-MAN: Perception-Aware CBF-RL for Whole-Body Safety in Humanoid Dodgeball](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28623)
*Lizhi Yang,Junheng Li,Aaron D. Ames*

Main category: cs.RO

TL;DR: PAC-MAN is a perception-aware CBF-RL framework for whole-body humanoid dodgeball that couples safety barriers with deployment-time perception. It achieves near-oracle evasion in controlled benchmarks and demonstrates robust zero-shot real-world deployment on a Unitree G1 with 95% success, leveraging semantic segmentation to dodge various balls.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Enable safe, perception-limited, real-time control for dynamic humanoid tasks by integrating barrier-based safety with learning from perception-constrained observations.

Method: Integrates control-barrier functions (CBF) with reinforcement learning (RL). Deployment uses segmentation-masked depth from a head-mounted camera; training-time CBF guidance provides clearance to every body link; an adversarial motion prior regularizes evasive reflexes. Evaluation on an any-link benchmark with seeded throws in single-throw and deployment-loop regimes; zero-shot deployment on Unitree G1 uses semantic segmentation.

Result: Policy nears privileged-state oracle performance; usable barrier structure depends on perceptual observability: Joint-CBF best with accurate ball states; degrades when used only as training guidance with fixed-camera; recovers with ball-tracking gimbal or privileged runtime filter. Real-world deployment yields 95% success rate and robust dodge of different balls.

Conclusion: Perception-aware CBF-RL enables robust, safe, perception-constrained dodgeball control in both simulation and real hardware, with barrier design and observability playing crucial roles; real-world deployment is feasible and effective under imperfect perception.

Abstract: We present PAC-MAN, a perception-aware CBF-RL framework that couples control-barrier safety with deployment-realistic onboard sensing for whole-body humanoid dodgeball. The deployed policy sees the ball only as segmentation-masked depth from a head-mounted camera, while training-time CBF guidance represents clearance to every body link, and an adversarial motion prior regularizes the resulting evasive reflexes. We evaluate on a controlled any-link contact benchmark with seeded throws in two regimes: single throws and a deployment loop in which the robot walks back to its station and recovers between throws. On this benchmark, the policy comes within a few points of a privileged state oracle: a fixed onboard camera alone is adequate for evasion. We find that usable barrier structure depends on perceptual observability: Joint-CBF gives the best performance with accurate ball states, degrades under fixed-camera observations when used only as training guidance, and recovers with a ball-tracking gimbal or privileged runtime filter. We therefore deploy a lightweight Link-CBF policy zero-shot on the Unitree G1 in the real world, where it tolerates imperfect perception, succeeds on 95% of throws, and uses semantic segmentation to dodge different balls.

</details>


<div id='cs.CG'></div>

# cs.CG [[Back]](#toc)

### [253] [Minimum-Width Drawing of Trees with Sized Vertices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27445)
*Markus Wallinger,Oscar Navarro,Stephen G. Kobourov*

Main category: cs.CG

TL;DR: NP-hard problem (MWD) with rectangles; reordering improves layered tree drawing width; MILP provides exact solutions for moderate sizes; a fast heuristic delivers good results; width reductions: median ~20%, up to ~55%; heuristic runs under 1s and is within 25% of optimal width in 75% of cases when MILP is optimal.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In layered tree drawings, vertices are rectangles with given widths and heights. With arbitrary child order, width can be reduced by reordering siblings. This work studies the complexity and provides exact and heuristic approaches to minimize width.

Method: Prove NP-completeness of MWD (even on binary trees with unit widths). Develop a mixed-integer linear programming formulation for exact optimization. Design a fast heuristic. Empirically compare against a baseline on synthetic and real-world datasets.

Result: MWD is NP-complete. The MILP solves moderate-sized instances exactly. The heuristic is fast and yields good layouts. Reordering reduces drawing width by a median of about 20% and up to about 55% on some instances. The heuristic runs in under a second; when MILP proves optimal, the heuristic width is within 25% of optimal in 75% of instances.

Conclusion: Reordering significantly impacts width minimization in layered tree drawings with rectangles. Despite NP-hardness, practical exact and heuristic methods enable substantial width reductions, with reliable performance across datasets. The combination of MILP and heuristic provides a robust toolkit for MWD.

Abstract: Trees arise in many applications and computing nice tree layouts is a classical problem in information visualization. In many practical settings, vertices need to be represented as rectangles with a given width and height rather than as points. When an order over the children of each vertex is given, polynomial-time algorithms are known that produce drawings adhering to various drawing conventions. However, in many applications, the order of children carries no semantic meaning, and choosing it well can significantly reduce the drawing's width. In this paper, we study the problem \textsc{Min-Width Tree Drawing with Reordering} (\textsc{MWD}): given a rooted tree whose vertices have prescribed widths, find a sibling order at each internal vertex that minimizes the width of the resulting layered drawing. We show that the problem is \textsf{NP}-complete, even on binary trees with unit-width vertices. We present a mixed integer linear program that solves \textsc{MWD} exactly on moderately sized instances, and a heuristic that is fast and delivers good results in practice. We evaluate both approaches against a baseline on synthetic and real-world datasets, where reordering reduces drawing width by a median of $\approx20\%$ and by up to $\approx55\%$ on individual instances. The heuristic computes its layouts in under a second and, when the MILP proves optimality, it stays within $25\%$ of the optimal width in three-quarters of all instances.

</details>


### [254] [Tight UGC Thresholds for Geometric Stabbing Problems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28062)
*Khaled Elbassioni,Rishikesh Gajjala,Saurabh Ray*

Main category: cs.CG

TL;DR: A transfer theorem under the Unique Games Conjecture (UGC) for fixed-arity covering LP formulations of geometric stabbing problems, yielding tight UGC thresholds for three problems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Bridge LP-based integrality gaps for geometric stabbing to UGC-hardness, and to identify exact thresholds matching known approximations; extend the strict-CSP rounding framework to geometric trace structures.

Method: Use the strict-CSP framework (Kumar, Manokaran, Tulsiani, Vishnoi) to construct connected local distributions via randomized rounding and full-support perturbation. For a fractional vector x on a block, rounding selects candidate i with probability x_i, and hits each consecutive trace T with probability min{1, x(T)}; the construction yields local distributions consistent with the LP constraints.

Result: Three tight UGC thresholds: (1) For fixed d≥2, stabbing arbitrary-size axis-parallel d-cubes with coordinate hyperplanes has threshold d; for d=2, hardness holds for squares and yields threshold 2 for rectangle/square stabbing (matching the 2-approximation of Gaur, Ibaraki, Krishnamurti). (2) Stabbing horizontal segments with horizontal and vertical lines has threshold e/(e−1), matching Kovaleva and Spieksma’s e/(e−1)-approximation. (3) Separated d-interval transversal has threshold d for fixed d≥2.

Conclusion: Under UGC, the authors show that each fixed finite, bounded-arity integrality-gap instance of the stated form yields a matching hardness ratio; the results provide tight hardness thresholds that align with existing approximations and close gaps in three geometric stabbing settings.

Abstract: Many geometric stabbing problems admit natural covering LPs in which each constraint is a union of consecutive traces on ordered candidate sets. We prove a transfer theorem showing that every fixed finite, bounded-arity integrality-gap instance of this form yields a matching hardness ratio under the Unique Games Conjecture. Using the strict-CSP framework of Kumar, Manokaran, Tulsiani, and Vishnoi [SODA 2011], we construct the required connected local distributions by randomized rounding and a full-support perturbation. Given a fractional vector $x$ on a block, the rounding selects candidate $i$ with marginal probability $x_i$ and hits each consecutive trace $T$ with probability $\min\{1,x(T)\}$.
  We obtain three tight UGC thresholds. First, for every fixed $d\ge 2$, stabbing arbitrary-size axis-parallel $d$-cubes with coordinate hyperplanes has threshold $d$. For $d=2$, the hardness holds for arbitrary-size squares and establishes threshold $2$ for rectangle and square stabbing, matching the $2$-approximation of Gaur, Ibaraki, and Krishnamurti [ESA 2000]. Second, stabbing horizontal segments with horizontal and vertical lines has threshold $e/(e-1)$, matching the $e/(e-1)$-approximation of Kovaleva and Spieksma [ESA 2004]. Third, separated $d$-interval transversal has threshold $d$ for every fixed $d\ge 2$, closing under UGC the gap left by the $d$-approximation of Ben-David, Grant, Ma, and Sharpe [CCCG 2012].

</details>


<div id='cs.LG'></div>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [255] [Recursive transformers for semiconductor thermo-mechanical reliability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27251)
*Kart-leong Lim*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Recursive transformer surrogates offer a parameter-efficient, compute-centric alternative to conventional transformers for small engineering datasets. Hardware-aware, they compare three recursive paradigms under resource constraints for thermo-mechanical surrogates and a PDE solver, yielding guidelines for architecture selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address over-parameterization and overfitting of large transformers on small, costly engineering design datasets by prioritizing compute over learnable parameters and leveraging weight-sharing across depth to reduce memory and compute overhead.

Method: Hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms: Tiny Recursive Model, Depth Recursive Transformer, and Simple Recursive Transformer. Compare predictive performance (Recall, MRR), parameter count, and FLOPs on two low-dimensional engineering tasks: 1) thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of advanced semiconductor packages (stress/warp under thermal cycling with FEA), and 2) Laplace PDE iterative solver for capacitance field. Derive practical design guidelines for resource-constrained surrogate modeling.

Result: Recursive weight-sharing transformers provide a favorable balance between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small-data engineering surrogate modeling. The study validates the trade-offs on two tasks and offers guidelines for selecting recursive transformer architectures under hardware constraints.

Conclusion: Weight-sharing recursive transformers are effective for small-data engineering surrogates, enabling reduced parameters and compute without compromising accuracy, suitable when data is limited and compute is constrained.

Abstract: Transformer-based surrogate models are increasingly used to replace expensive first-principles simulation in engineering design. But conventional transformer architectures are often over parameterized for the small, low-dimensional datasets typical of engineering design spaces, where large simulation data is expensive to generate. Under these conditions, excess parameter capacity leads to overfitting rather than improved accuracy, while also incurring unnecessary memory and compute overhead. This motivates a shift towards architectures that focus on additional compute rather than additional learnable parameters. This paper presents a hardware-aware evaluation of three recursive transformer paradigms for surrogate thermo-mechanical analysis of advanced packages: a)Tiny Recursive Model, b) our proposed Depth Recursive transformer, c) and a simple recursive transformer. We systematically compare their predictive performance (Recall, Mean Reciprocal Rank), parameter count, computational complexity (FLOPs), providing practical design guidelines for selecting recursive transformer architectures under resource-constrained scenarios. We validate this principle on two low-dimensional engineering prediction tasks: 1) thermo-mechanical reliability analysis of advanced semiconductor packages, where stress and warpage from thermal cycling must be evaluated repeatedly across a design-of-experiments sweep under costly finite element analysis (FEA). 2) Laplace PDE iterative numerical solver for capacitance field. Overall, recursive weight-sharing transformers provide an effective and generalizable trade-off between prediction accuracy, parameter efficiency, and computational cost for small data engineering surrogate modeling.

</details>


### [256] [Regularizing modality contribution drift in multimodal continual learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27260)
*Zhen Zhang,Jielei Chu,Bin Liu,Tianrui Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes CMCDR to address Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) in multimodal continual learning by preserving modality contribution structure via replay-based or replay-free regularization; validated on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual VQA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MMCL methods emphasize cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity but ignore potential drift in the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions across incremental tasks, risking accumulated forgetting of contribution patterns.

Method: Introduce MCD score combining contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled modality-subset interventions. Provide theoretical and empirical analyses showing why existing MMCL methods fail to mitigate drift. Propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR) to preserve the modality contribution structure of previously learned tasks. Two variants: (1) replay-based CMCDR uses modality-subset interventions on stored old samples to compare current vs frozen old-model contribution profiles and constrains changes in old-sample modality-specific and interaction contributions; (2) replay-free CMCDR uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses to regularize the observed contribution profile without exemplars.

Result: Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering demonstrate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR in mitigating Modality Contribution Drift and preserving contribution structures across tasks.

Conclusion: CMCDR provides a principled mechanism to stabilize modality contributions in MMCL, addressing a previously overlooked source of forgetting, with demonstrated applicability to replay-based and replay-free continual learning scenarios.

Abstract: Multimodal continual learning (MMCL) aims to learn emerging knowledge from multimodal data while preserving knowledge. To mitigate forgetting, current MMCL methods usually focus on cross-modal representation alignment or semantic similarity, but they overlook whether the relative contributions of individual modalities and their interactions remain stable across incremental tasks. We term this decision-level shift Modality Contribution Drift (MCD) and quantify it with the MCD score, which combines contribution-strength and relative-reliance changes under controlled interventions on modality subsets. Theoretical and empirical analyses further explain why current MMCL methods cannot reliably mitigate this drift. To this end, we propose Continual Modality Contribution Drift Regularization (CMCDR), which preserves the modality contribution structure of previously learned tasks. Since MMCL settings differ in whether old exemplars are available, CMCDR includes both replay-based and replay-free versions. The replay-based version uses modality-subset interventions as diagnostic probes on stored old samples, compares their contribution profiles between the current model and a frozen previous model, and constrains changes in old-sample modality-specific and interaction contributions. The replay-free version uses current-task samples as probes and distills the frozen model's old-task contribution responses, thereby regularizing the observed contribution profile without exemplars. Experiments on multimodal class-incremental learning and continual visual question answering validate the generality and effectiveness of CMCDR.

</details>


### [257] [DoTime: A Synthetic Benchmark Generator for Interventional and Counterfactual Time Series](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27263)
*Dennis Thumm,Billy Tim Anthony,Ying Chen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Open-source DoTime tool for generating multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions; introduces continuous-time intervention windows, counterfactual sampling with positivity guard, regime-switching (generalizing interrupted time series), non-stationary dynamics via switching parameters, and deterministic ramp/sinusoidal interventions; ships evaluation suites and baseline implementations to assess interventional priors versus observational models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Fill a gap in causal inference for time series by providing scalable, intervention- and counterfactual-ready benchmarks with ground truth, enabling robust evaluation and serving as a prior for causal foundation models.

Method: Develop DoTime as a PyPI package that generates TSCMs with interventions; adds: continuous-time intervention windows; counterfactual sampling with a positivity guard; regime-switching SCMs; non-stationary dynamics via parameter switching; deterministic ramp and sinusoidal intervention profiles; four frozen evaluation suites; a training-scale snapshot of 100,000 trajectories across eight identification structures; paired interventional trajectories and shared-noise counterfactuals; ships reference baselines and an evaluation harness.

Result: Demonstrates DoTime as a suitable prior for a causal foundation model reference; interventional prior-fitted network (PFN) exhibits a positive gap (direction-accuracy advantage) over an observational model of identical capacity across all tested structures, trajectory lengths, and seeds (three seeds per arm) in structure-matched held-out evaluation.

Conclusion: Interventional training yields a measurable direction-accuracy advantage; DoTime offers a scalable, theory-grounded framework with rich evaluation resources to advance causal inference in time series and to support causal foundation-model development.

Abstract: Most benchmarks for causal inference over time series are observational, small, or domain-specific, leaving interventional and counterfactual estimation under-served exactly where it matters most, such as in healthcare, policy evaluation, and climate science. We introduce \textbf{DoTime}, an open, scalable, and theoretically grounded generator of multivariate temporal structural causal models (TSCMs) with interventions, released as the \code{dotime} PyPI package together with four frozen evaluation suites. Beyond existing work, it adds capabilities absent from prior generators: continuous-time intervention \emph{windows}, counterfactual sampling modes with a positivity guard, regime-switching SCMs as a strict generalization of interrupted time series, non-stationary dynamics by construction with switching SCM parameters, and deterministic ramp and sinusoidal intervention profiles that place trends and structural breaks \emph{inside} the evaluation window. Moreover, it demonstrates the suitability of the generator as a prior for a causal foundation model reference implementation. The released suites span a training-scale snapshot of $100{,}000$ trajectories and eight named identification structures, each with exact ground truth: paired interventional trajectories from the same SCM throughout, and shared-noise counterfactuals in the continuous-time suite. We ship reference baseline implementations with an evaluation harness, and pose a falsifiable claim: interventional training buys a measurable direction-accuracy advantage over an observational model of identical capacity. It is tested across three training seeds per arm. Under structure-matched evaluation on held-out episodes, the interventional prior-fitted network's (PFN) gap is positive in every structure, trajectory length, and seed tested.

</details>


### [258] [PlatformBid: An Auto-Bidding Benchmark from a Unified Advertising Platform's Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27265)
*Shengtian Yang,Yewen Li,Peng Jiang,Zhiyi Lyu,Bo An,Peng Jiang,Qingpeng Cai,Lei Feng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PlatformBid is introduced as a platform-centric benchmark for auto-bidding in real-time bidding, with three competition settings, evaluation across classical, RL, and generative methods, plus BidFlow flow-matching method; online validation on Kuaishou shows a +0.68% target cost improvement, indicating offline-online consistency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Addresses the absence of platform-centric evaluation frameworks for auto-bidding in real-time bidding. Modern ad platforms increasingly integrate SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange, making platform revenue a core objective alongside advertiser conversions.

Method: Define three representative competition settings (homogeneous, heterogeneous, promotional); evaluate a broad set of auto-bidding methods including classical control, RL-based, and generative approaches; introduce BidFlow, a flow-matching-based auto-bidding method; conduct offline evaluations and online experiments on Kuaishou to assess deployment feasibility and offline-online consistency.

Result: PlatformBid provides the first comprehensive benchmark from a unified platform perspective; BidFlow demonstrates competitive performance within the benchmark; online Kuaishou experiments show a +0.68% improvement in target cost, supporting offline-online consistency of PlatformBid results.

Conclusion: PlatformBid fills a gap in platform-centric auto-bidding research, offering a standardized evaluation framework and a novel flow-matching method. The results suggest practical viability and invite further exploration of platform-revenue-oriented bidding strategies.

Abstract: Real-time bidding is central to computational advertising, comprising three elements: Supply Side Platform (SSP) selling ad impressions, Demand Side Platform (DSP) bidding for advertisers, and Ad Exchange conducting auctions between them. Traditional auto-bidding algorithms focus solely on the DSP side, maximizing advertiser conversions by adjusting bids against competitors. However, current big ad platforms, such as social media and e-commerce companies, now integrate SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange functions internally. From such ad platforms' perspective, the goal of the auto-bidding algorithms is not only to maximize the advertisers' conversions, but also the total revenue of the platform. Given the lack of platform-centric evaluation frameworks and the pressing need to advance auto-bidding research, we propose PlatformBid - the first comprehensive benchmark designed from a unified ad platform's perspective. To accurately reflect the real-world auto-bidding scenarios, we define three representative settings: (1) homogeneous competition with identical algorithms across advertisers, (2) heterogeneous competition with diverse algorithmic strategies, and (3) promotional competition where some advertisers surge budgets for boosting sales during promotional events like Black Friday. We systematically evaluate a broad spectrum of existing auto-bidding methods across these settings, encompassing classical control methods, RL-based methods, and recent generative methods. Besides these methods, we further propose a novel auto-bidding method based on flow-matching, termed BidFlow, which leverages the flow-matching method's expressive policy representation to effectively handle dynamic competitive environments. Online experiments on Kuaishou further show a +0.68\% improvement in target cost, providing deployment evidence for the offline-online consistency of PlatformBid.

</details>


### [259] [Beyond KV Reconstruction: Functional Reconstruction for MLA Draft Models in Speculative Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27269)
*Weiye Shi,Fanxu Meng,Muhan Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Presents a converter-agnostic end-to-end Functional Reconstruction method to transform MHA/GQA into MLA for long-context LLM inference, preserving cache/inference graph and improving draft-acceptance in speculative decoding without requiring verifier signals.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Direct MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion introduces attention-function errors (due to low-rank factorization and RoPE handling) that hurt draft-token acceptance. A reconstruction-based approach aims to preserve the target post-output-projection response, enabling MLA cache benefits without retraining.

Method: End-to-end Functional Reconstruction: optimizer per converted MLA attention module to match the post-output-projection response of the original MHA/GQA on calibration hidden states; converter-agnostic, preserves cache and inference graph; requires no verifier logits or supervision.

Result: Evaluated 192 configurations over four Llama/Qwen target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA, HF and vLLM, across four 200-prompt tasks. With a 0.5 percentage-point tolerance, functional reconstruction improved draft acceptance in 37 of 64 matched cells, left 26 unchanged, and materially decreased one.

Conclusion: Functional Reconstruction provides a practical, converter-agnostic post-conversion strategy to retain MLA cache benefits and improve speculative-draft acceptance without additional verifier data, demonstrated across multiple backends and task sets; code and data are available.

Abstract: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) is increasingly important for long-context LLM inference because compact latent states replace the growing key-value (KV) cache and reduce decoding memory traffic. Yet most capable open checkpoints use multi-head or grouped-query attention (MHA/GQA), so conversion is needed to obtain MLA's cache efficiency without retraining from scratch. Speculative decoding offers complementary acceleration, but its speedup depends on agreement between draft proposals and target verification. We find that direct MHA/GQA-to-MLA conversion can sharply reduce this agreement: low-rank factorization and RoPE handling introduce attention-function errors that may be tolerable for standalone generation but substantially lower draft-token acceptance. We therefore formulate MLA draft construction as functional reconstruction rather than cache compression. Our end-to-end (E2E) method optimizes each converted MLA attention module to reproduce the post-output-projection response of its original MHA/GQA counterpart on calibration hidden states. This converter-agnostic post-conversion procedure preserves the converted cache and inference graph and requires neither verifier logits nor verifier supervision. We evaluate 192 model-converter-backend-method-task configurations spanning four Llama/Qwen draft-target pairs, TransMLA and MHA2MLA, HF and vLLM, and four 200-prompt tasks. With a 0.5-percentage-point reporting tolerance, Functional Reconstruction materially improves acceptance in 37 of 64 matched task cells, leaves 26 practically unchanged, and materially decreases one. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/swyhahaha/FunctionalMLA.

</details>


### [260] [RLPF: Reinforcement Learning from Performance Feedback for Code Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27271)
*Huihao Jing,Haozhe Cui,Wenbin Hu,Shaojin Chen,Haochen Shi,Changxuan Fan,Yuxuan Liu,Hanyu Yang,Sirui Zhang,Ziyi Chen,Haoran Li,Yangqiu Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes RLPF, reinforcement learning from performance feedback, to train code agents to prefer faster correct solutions; demonstrates large gains on PerfCodeBench.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Code models are trained mainly for correctness, but runtime is crucial for systems code. Execution-based signals are fragile and inconsistent, yet essential to guide efficiency.

Method: RLPF converts execution outcomes into staged rewards: failed programs are ordered by execution progress; correct programs are ranked by improvement from the baseline toward an expert reference. This feedback precedes correctness and, once correct, provides performance-sensitive guidance. The method is applied to fine-tune Qwen3-32B on PerfCodeBench, with additional analysis on EffiBench-X and model-generated references.

Result: Correct-and-runnable solutions rise from 11.1% to 54.6%. Relative efficiency improves from 8.1% to 38.6%. The model becomes competitive with stronger open-weight systems and shows some transfer to EffiBench-X. Model-generated references offer useful but weaker supervision; the full composite reward outperforms correctness-only or runtime-only baselines.

Conclusion: Code agents can be trained to optimize performance, not just pass tests. A composite, staged reward enables effective learning from execution feedback and aligns model optimization with runtime efficiency.

Abstract: Code models are increasingly trained with execution feedback, but most training signals still stop at correctness. This leaves an important gap for systems code: two programs can pass the same tests while differing greatly in runtime. We study how to train code agents to prefer faster correct implementations, rather than treating efficiency only as an evaluation metric. The key difficulty is that runtime is a fragile reward. It is meaningful only after a program is correct, varies across tasks, and gives little guidance when most sampled programs fail to compile or run. We propose \textbf{RLPF}, reinforcement learning from performance feedback, which turns execution outcomes into a staged reward. Failed programs are ordered by execution progress, while correct programs are ranked by their relative improvement from the baseline toward the expert reference. This gives useful feedback before correctness and performance-sensitive feedback after correctness. Fine-tuning Qwen3-32B with RLPF on PerfCodeBench raises correct-and-runnable solutions from $11.1\%$ to $54.6\%$ and improves relative efficiency from $8.1\%$ to $38.6\%$. The trained model becomes competitive with stronger open-weight systems, and its optimization behavior transfers modestly to EffiBench-X. Additional studies show that model-generated references provide useful but weaker supervision, and that the full composite reward is more reliable than correctness-only or runtime-only baselines. These results suggest that code agents can be trained not only to pass tests, but also to optimize the programs they write.

</details>


### [261] [SDO: Structure-Aware Data Organization for Efficient LLM Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27273)
*Jinliang Gao,Ning Yang,Hai Wang,Baili Xiao,Pin Lyu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SDO introduces a structure-aware, exposure-driven data organization for LLM fine-tuning that dynamically shapes mini-batches and per-sample exposure using frozen embeddings, improving convergence and gradient coherence without additional warm-up.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Static data organization in large-model fine-tuning leads to redundant updates for over-exposed samples and under-optimized updates for others; there is a need for dynamic, structure-aware data organization that adapts exposure across training.

Method: SDO operates epoch-by-epoch on frozen external embeddings; within each epoch, locality-aware batching forms coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal; across epochs, exposure-balanced scheduling tracks per-sample participation and reduces sampling probability of over-exposed samples to maintain long-term coverage; it is plug-and-play and does not require model warm-up.
Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO scenarios, it reorganizes data to accelerate convergence.

Result: Accelerates convergence, especially in early-to-mid phases; yields more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across diverse question types; maintains long-term coverage by not permanently excluding samples; achieves gains without increasing warm-up overhead.

Conclusion: Structure-aware data organization with exposure-driven feedback is an effective, plug-and-play approach to improve training efficiency and sample balance during LLM fine-tuning across multiple training objectives.

Abstract: Post-training of large language models is expensive, and existing efficiency improvements mainly focus on selecting informative samples or designing training schedules. However, data organization itself is usually treated as a static preprocessing step: embedding-based grouping methods construct fixed partitions before training and cannot adapt to the evolving sample exposure during optimization. As a result, all samples receive similar exposure despite their different optimization needs, leading to redundant updates for some samples while leaving others under-optimized. To address this problem, we propose SDO (Structure-Aware Data Organization), a plug-and-play data organization framework with an exposure-driven feedback mechanism that organizes mini-batch composition and sample exposure according to representation-space structure. SDO operates epoch by epoch on frozen external embeddings, avoiding model warm-up training overhead: within each epoch, locality-aware batching forms coherent mini-batches via KNN neighborhood traversal; across epochs, exposure-balanced scheduling records per-sample participation and reduces the sampling probability of over-exposed samples to preserve long-term coverage. Across SFT, DPO, and GRPO, SDO accelerates convergence, with the largest gains observed in the early-to-mid phase, producing more coherent gradients and more balanced accuracy across question types without permanently excluding training samples.

</details>


### [262] [Rethinking EEG-Based Disease Diagnosis: Decoupling Instance Representation Learning from Subject-Level Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27274)
*Zhiyuan Ma,Zeyuan Li,Zhiyi Lu,Jiacheng Hao,Youlang Du,Zhen Jiang,Xinche Zhang,Yuhao Sun,Sen Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: BridgeMIL is a two-stage MIL framework for EEG disease diagnosis that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy across multiple datasets and backbones.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Typical EEG pipelines assign disease labels to individual short windows, assuming equal informativeness; MIL helps but is limited by far fewer subjects, so end-to-end MIL can underutilize abundant instance data. A two-stage approach better aligns supervision with subject-level prediction.

Method: Stage 1: self-supervised pretraining of encoder by aligning temporally nearby windows and within-subject sub-bags, with variance and covariance regularization to prevent collapse and redundancy. Stage 2: transfer to an attention-based MIL aggregator, apply supervision at the subject level, and constrain representation drift via feature retention.

Result: BridgeMIL achieves the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone combinations across three EEG datasets and five backbones; overall mean accuracy 76.57%, 4.28 pp above strongest baseline.

Conclusion: Inherited-label reliability varies across instances; performance is more sensitive to subject scarcity than instance scarcity; representation space becomes more structured with subject-wise clusters and better class separation, underscoring the importance of subject-level supervision for EEG-based diagnosis while leveraging abundant instance data without per-instance labels.

Abstract: EEG-based disease diagnosis requires one prediction per subject, yet common pipelines segment recordings into short instances, inherit the subject label for every instance, and train instance-level classifiers. This assumes that all instances provide equally reliable diagnostic evidence. Multiple instance learning (MIL) avoids inherited labels by treating each subject as a bag. However, EEG datasets contain far fewer subjects than instances, which can limit the quality of the representations learned by end-to-end MIL. We propose BridgeMIL, a two-stage framework that decouples instance representation learning from subject-level supervision. Stage 1 pretrains the encoder without inherited instance labels by aligning temporally nearby windows and independently sampled within-subject sub-bags. Variance and covariance regularization prevent collapse and reduce redundancy without negative pairs. Stage 2 transfers the encoder to an attention-based MIL aggregator, applies supervision only to subject predictions, and limits representation drift through feature retention. Across three EEG disease datasets and five representative backbones, BridgeMIL attains the highest mean accuracy in 14 of 15 dataset-backbone settings and an overall mean accuracy of 76.57%, 4.28 percentage points higher than the strongest baseline. Further analyses reveal substantial variation in inherited-label reliability across instances, greater performance sensitivity to subject scarcity than to instance scarcity, and a more structured representation space with distinct subject-wise clusters and improved separation between diagnostic classes. Together, these findings underscore the importance of aligning supervision with the subject-level prediction objective while learning from abundant EEG instances without assigning disease labels to individual instances.

</details>


### [263] [Flat Score, Amplified Failures: How the Error Budget Masks Damage in Quantized LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27275)
*Jiwon Jang,Kisu Yang,Heuiseok Lim,Hyunwoo Park*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: 4-bit post-training quantization is near-lossless on standard metrics for multi-turn tool-calling agents, but amplifies preexisting failures; targeted repair prompts can fix damage; report per-channel error rate and budget-sensitivity metrics alongside task reward.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Assess whether aggressive quantization degrades complex agent behaviors that rely on tool-use and multi-turn reasoning, beyond standard accuracy metrics.

Method: Evaluate two open-weight model families (dense and MoE) in two domains across eight cells and 456 episodes each, at 16-, 8-, 4-bit weights on τ^2-bench. Use standard scores, multiple-comparison corrections, equivalence testing bounds, per-channel error rate, and budget-sensitivity analysis; test a targeted error-repair prompt.

Result: Standard metric shows no meaningful score change; equivalence bounds within ±7.5; but quantization increases existing failure volume up to 2.5x (+17.6 points per task) and maintains the same failure set; 10-error budget hides the gap; reducing budget to 2 reveals a 17-point gap in the quantized condition; targeted repair prompts remove damage exactly in telecom models.

Conclusion: Report per-channel error rate and budget-sensitivity diagnostics alongside task reward; consider prompt-based repair as a practical mitigation when quantization is used for model deployment.

Abstract: Post-training quantization to 4-bit weights is widely reported to be nearly lossless. We test this claim for multi-turn, tool-calling agents, where it now matters most. On $τ^2$-bench, across two open-weight model families in dense and MoE variants and two domains (eight cells, 456 episodes each, at 16-, 8-, and 4-bit weights), quantization indeed looks free on the standard metric. No cell shows a score change that survives multiple-comparison correction, and in the cell that carries the largest process damage, equivalence testing bounds the change within $\pm$7.5 points. The process tells a different story. Quantization amplifies the failure the model already exhibits at full precision (tool-name hallucination in telecom, with the same directional trend in retail entity errors) by up to 2.5$\times$ in volume (+17.6 points per task), while creating essentially no new failures. The failure set is the same at every precision (rank correlation $\geq$ 0.94, 0.18% novel events). The score stays flat because the benchmark's ten-error budget absorbs the extra failures. Shrinking the budget to two errors re-exposes a score gap of 17 points, and it does so only in the one cell where quantization added error volume, exactly as the masking account predicts. A targeted error-repair prompt, run for five telecom models at every precision, removes the damage exactly and only where it lives. Both diagnostics, the per-channel error rate and success under a shrinking budget, come from logs benchmarks already collect; we suggest reporting them alongside task reward.

</details>


### [264] [The Kinetics of Training: A Driven-Nucleation Rate Law for Emergence, Plasticity Loss, and Circuit Control in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27281)
*Lei Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: No-partial-credit alignment is the rate-limiting constraint for capability formation in transformers; partial credit fails to capture learned capabilities, while total alignment emerges only when all required parts align. Evidence from ablations and gating shows missing parts govern ignition delays; a cure via reinitializing only query-key slices restores learnability. A rate-equation framing (forward/backward/completed) underpins the dynamics, with forward ignition datable from a precursor and backward delays blind to standard monitors. Validation across Pythia and a controlled gated-attention model. Scope: conjunction circuits up to 1.4B parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To identify the structural bottleneck in emergent capabilities of language models, testing whether full, joint, no-partial-credit alignment is essential, and to locate potential mechanisms and remedies through targeted ablations and controlled models.

Method: (1) Ablation/ablation-like experiments on five-part vs three-part circuits in shortcut-free transformers; measure wait-times and the effect of missing parts. (2) Large-scale evaluation on Pythia across seven capabilities and three scales, examining how ablating one part affects capability presence in discriminating cells and comparing to partial-credit predictions. (3) Propose a rate-equation framing and analyze forward ignition, backward learning delays, and completed dynamics with preregistered constants. (4) Intervention experiments: re-initializing only the query-key slices versus value slices; evaluate learnability restoration across models. (5) Controlled gated-attention model proofs to establish a mechanism. (6) SGD noise experiments to adjust fluctuation-dissipation behavior and apply annealing/pinning. 

Result: (a) No-partial-credit joint alignment is the rate-limiting step in capability formation. Ablations show missing three parts in a five-part circuit affect wait times equivalently to three missing parts in a three-part circuit; wait counts track missing parts, not circuit size. (b) In Pythia, ablating one part leaves a median 17% of the capability in all discriminating cells (32/32), while partial credit would predict 50–83% (p=2e-10); a random non-part head leaves 100%. (c) A rate equation with three factors (sites × attempts × drive × exp(-βK)) minus destruction accounts for forward ignition and other dynamics; forward ignition occurs after crossing a concentration floor and can be dated to 5% median error across six held-out models. Backward learning delays grow with waiting and eventually capability never ignites, though validation loss declines smoothly. (d) Damage localization implicates base data; curing by reinitializing only query-key slices fully restores learnability (6/6 experiments) whereas value-slices do not (0/6). (e) A controlled gated-attention model proves the mechanism: occupation enforces a deadline without mixing assumptions. (f) SGD noise is insufficient for fluctuation-dissipation; adding noise and annealing/pinning circuits on schedule completes the methodology. 

Conclusion: Capability emergence in transformers is governed by a deadline-driven, no-partial-credit alignment process. The critical bottleneck is the joint alignment across all required parts, not mere circuit size. Targeted interventions—particularly reinitializing query-key components—can restore learnability after damage. The dynamics admit a rate-equation framing and reveal monitoring blind spots, informing both interpretability and training design for robust emergent capabilities.

Abstract: A capability appears in a language model when the last parts of its circuit align in one stochastic attempt, and getting all but one right is worth nothing. We show this no-partial-credit joint alignment is the rate-limiting step of capability formation. Two fingerprints: in a shortcut-free apparatus a five-part circuit missing three waits as long as a three-part circuit missing three (1.19-1.37), so the wait counts missing parts, not size; and on Pythia across seven capabilities and three scales, ablating one part leaves a median 17% of the capability in 32 of 32 discriminating cells, where partial credit predicts 50-83% (p = 2e-10), while a random non-part head leaves 100%.
  One rare event whose barrier grows with missing parts yields a rate equation -- sites x attempts x drive x exp(-beta*K), minus destruction -- read three ways, each preregistered with frozen constants. Forward: a capability flat at baseline ignites at a step of our choosing once the mix passes a concentration floor (10/10 above, 0/12 below), and while still flat its arrival is datable from its precursor to 5% median error on six held-out models. Backward: the delay to learn a withheld capability grows with waiting until, past a critical step, it never ignites -- yet validation loss falls smoothly throughout, so standard monitors are blind to it. We locate the damage (heads commit to the base data) and isolate the cure: re-initializing only the query-key slices restores learnability (6/6) while the value slices do nothing (0/6). We prove the mechanism in a controlled gated-attention model: occupation forces a deadline whose consequences need no mixing assumption. Completed: SGD's noise fails the fluctuation-dissipation test, so we install one and anneal, melt and pin circuits on schedule. Scope: conjunction circuits in transformers to 1.4B.

</details>


### [265] [Benchmarking the Residual: What Long-Horizon Evaluations Add Beyond Matched Short-Task Performance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27283)
*Chao Peng,Zhiheng Lyu,Peijie Dong,Hande Dong,Qiang Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Defines horizon residual to diagnose long-horizon failures by comparing full-task success to a baseline from short stages, addressing trajectory-induced degradation and context rot.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long tasks often fail more, but it's unclear whether failures come from longer horizons, harder decisions, or accumulation of context. A principled baseline is needed to attribute failures to long-horizon effects.

Method: Proposes a log-ratio (horizon residual) between actual full-task success and a baseline prediction built from short, individual stages. Requires identical agent configuration and pre-specified stage choices, information, and budgets. Uses trajectory-induced degradation and context rot as mechanisms to explain differences.

Result: As a position paper, provides a definitional framework and experimental protocol rather than empirical results; emphasizes need for targeted experiments to attribute causes.

Conclusion: Horizon residual offers a principled metric to assess long-horizon failures; interpretable only when pre-defined baselines and configurations are fixed; further experiments required to uncover underlying causes.

Abstract: Long-horizon benchmarks often show that agents fail more as tasks become longer. This observation is useful for deployment, but it does not by itself explain why failure occurs. More stages create more opportunities for ordinary errors to compound; longer tasks may also contain harder individual decisions or become harder as conversation history, tool outputs, and environment changes accumulate. We use trajectory-induced degradation to mean this last possibility: earlier execution makes later work harder. When the harmful accumulation is specifically the text visible to the model, it is often called context rot. In this position paper, we argue that to claim a "long-horizon failure", benchmarks must compare actual full-task success against a baseline prediction built from short, individual stages. We call the log-ratio between this prediction and actual success the horizon residual. The comparison must use the same agent configuration and specify in advance how stages, checkpoints, information, and budgets will be chosen. The residual shows that the full rollout differs from the chosen baseline; targeted experiments are still needed to explain why.

</details>


### [266] [TIER-MoE: Trust-Informed Expert Routing via Conditional Modality Risk for Multimodal Fusion in Biomedical Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27289)
*Yu Chang,Anzhe Cheng,Chenwei Wu,Zhuoran Wang,Jiahao Chen,Tamoghna Chattopadhyay,Sophia I. Thomopoulos,Paul M. Thompson,Liyue Shen,Paul Bogdan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces TIER-MoE, a risk-guided subspace Mixture-of-Experts for multimodal fusion that estimates modality reliability via out-of-fold unimodal losses to route samples, improving predictive performance, calibration, and zero-shot generalization on biomedical tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Multimodal fusion often assumes all modalities contribute beneficially, but in practice modalities can be unreliable, redundant, or mismatched to specialized experts. Existing fusion strategies lack explicit, sample-specific modality reliability signals.

Method: Estimate a modality's risk from out-of-fold unimodal predictions (not trained on the sample). Use this risk with expert-subspace compatibility to perform sparse modality-expert routing, plus an always-active shared path to maintain multimodal complementarity.

Result: Evaluated on four public multimodal biomedical datasets (Alzheimer's status, skin-lesion malignancy, retinal classification). TIER-MoE achieves superior predictive performance and probability calibration (notably Macro-F1 and Brier score) and shows strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.

Conclusion: Risk-guided, subspace routing in a Mixture-of-Experts framework improves multimodal fusion by identifying reliable modalities per sample, yielding better performance and calibration across diverse biomedical tasks and enabling robust external generalization.

Abstract: The promise of multimodal fusion lies in combining complementary sources of evidence, yet more evidence does not always yield a better prediction. Recent multimodal models have advanced fusion through richer cross-modal interaction and sample-adaptive fusion. However, the influence assigned to a modality during fusion does not reveal whether that source is unreliable, redundant, or poorly matched to a specialized expert. To address this limitation, we introduce TIER-MoE, a risk-guided subspace mixture-of-experts model that defines sample-specific modality reliability as the prediction loss its unimodal predictor is expected to incur. This risk is learned from out-of-fold predictions generated by models that were not trained on the corresponding sample. TIER-MoE combines the estimated risk with expert-specific subspace compatibility for sparse modality-expert routing, while an always-active shared path preserves multimodal complementarity. We evaluate TIER-MoE on four public multimodal biomedical datasets spanning Alzheimer's disease status, skin-lesion malignancy, and retinal classification. Results demonstrate its superiority over state-of-the-art methods in predictive performance and probability calibration, with consistent improvements in Macro-F1 and Brier score and strong zero-shot generalization to an external cohort.

</details>


### [267] [EvoCause: LLM-Guided Evolution of Causal Graphs for Root Cause Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27290)
*Lei Zan,Keli Zhang,Shifeng Xie,Jiale Zheng,Zehao Xiao,Zhiwei Dong,Ke Zhang,Ruichu Cai,Malik Tiomoko,Lujia Pan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: EvoCause refines learned causal graphs for root-cause analysis by using an LLM to propose plausible edge edits under expert constraints, validating edits deterministically and selecting the best graph on a labeled set; at test time only the refined graph is used. A TeleRCA benchmark from production data is released. On synthetic data, EvoCause with PC improves Node F1, Case EM, Graph F1, and reduces nSHD; on TeleRCA, anonymizing alarm titles reduces predictive performance, showing alarm-name information aids refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learned causal graphs from observational logs are fixed and do not leverage expert knowledge from historical incidents. Incorporating expert diagnoses can refine structure and improve RCA accuracy while maintaining transparent predictions.

Method: Use a large language model to propose semantically plausible graph edits that align with expert-provided source-node constraints; deterministic code validates node identities and acyclicity; select the best graph based on alignment to expert labels; at test time rely on the refined graph without invoking the LLM.

Result: Synthetic data: Node F1 +11.59 pp, Case EM +9.40 pp, Graph F1 +4.59 pp; nSHD −0.2379. TeleRCA: replacing alarm titles with anonymous IDs lowers Node F1 by 6.12 pp and Case EM by 8.04 pp, indicating alarm-name information aids refinement.

Conclusion: LLM-guided, expert-constrained graph edits can meaningfully improve causal RCA graphs and predictive performance, with a practical, transparent test-time model; the TeleRCA benchmark demonstrates real-world utility and highlights the value of descriptive alarm names for graph refinement.

Abstract: Modern telecommunication, cloud, and microservice systems emit correlated alarm cascades when components fail. Root cause analysis (RCA) aims to identify the small set of alarms that initiate each cascade. A common approach learns a causal graph from observational logs and predicts all zero-in-degree alarms in each incident-induced subgraph. However, the learned graph remains fixed and cannot benefit from expert diagnoses of historical incidents. We close this loop with EvoCause. Expert labels constrain which alarms should be source nodes but do not specify the edge edits needed to satisfy those constraints. EvoCause uses a large language model (LLM) to propose semantically plausible graph edits, while deterministic code validates node identities and acyclicity and retains the best graph on a labeled alignment set. At test time, the refined graph alone produces transparent predictions without an LLM call. We also release TeleRCA, an expert-annotated benchmark from a production telecommunication network containing $485{,}681$ alarm events spanning $194$ alarm types over $5{,}621$ resources. On synthetic data, EvoCause initialized with the PC causal discovery algorithm outperforms the unrefined PC baseline, raising Node F1, Case EM, and Graph F1 by $11.59$, $9.40$, and $4.59$ percentage points, respectively, while reducing nSHD by $0.2379$. On TeleRCA, replacing human-readable alarm titles with anonymous identifiers lowers Node F1 and Case EM by $6.12$ and $8.04$ percentage points, respectively, indicating that alarm-name information contributes to graph refinement.

</details>


### [268] [THGFM: Dual-Branch Temporal Heterogeneous Graph Fusion Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27303)
*Yixin Peng,Diego Collarana,Er Jin,Stefan Decker*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: THGFM is a dual-path fusion model for temporal heterogeneous graphs with shared-space cross-type transfer and relation-aware specialization, incorporating rotary temporal attention, achieving multi-task gains on several benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To unify parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization while directly modeling time within attention, addressing heterogeneity and temporal dynamics in temporal heterogeneous graphs.

Method: THGFM uses a Shared-Space Temporal Attention branch to enable parameter-efficient cross-type transfer and a Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention branch for relation-aware specialization. These are fused via Dual-Path Relational--Shared Fusion using Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion, enabling independent, type-conditioned feature-wise gates for both branches. It introduces Rotary Temporal Attention by rotating queries and keys by half-phases of relative time to incorporate temporal information directly into the attention score.

Result: THGFM consistently outperforms baselines on academic-graph benchmarks, achieving a six-task mean gain of +3.25%, with peak relative gains of +12.37% (OAG-CS PV), +4.87% (PF-L2), +1.18% (PF-L1); and gains of +4.24%, +3.73%, +4.61% on OGBN-MAG, HTAG-ArXiv, HTAG-DBLP respectively.

Conclusion: THGFM effectively reconciles cross-type transfer and relation-aware specialization through dual-path fusion, with time integrated into attention via rotary temporal attention, delivering strong performance on diverse temporal heterogeneous-graph benchmarks.

Abstract: Temporal heterogeneous graphs offer a natural abstraction for dynamic relational systems in which diverse node and relation types co-exist and evolve over time. Learning on such graphs requires jointly modeling cross-type structural heterogeneity and the temporal dynamics of interactions, yet existing methods still struggle to reconcile parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with relation-aware specialization, and typically inject time only as additive features outside the attention kernel. We propose \textbf{THGFM}, a web-scale temporal heterogeneous graph fusion model that addresses both limitations within a unified dual-path architecture. THGFM couples a \textit{Shared-Space Temporal Attention} branch for parameter-efficient cross-type transfer with a \textit{Relational Type-Partitioned Temporal Attention} branch for relation-aware specialization, and integrates them through \textit{Dual-Path Relational--Shared Fusion}, instantiated with \textit{Type-Conditioned Non-Competitive Gated Sum Fusion}: a adaptive mechanism that assigns independent, type-conditioned feature-wise gates to the shared and specialized branches, allowing both to be amplified or suppressed without zero-sum competition. To directly incorporate relative time into the attention score, THGFM further introduces \textit{Rotary Temporal Attention}, which rotates queries and keys by half-phases of relative time before matching. THGFM consistently outperforms baseline graph transformer models on academic graphs benchmarks, delivering a $+3.25\%$ six-task mean gain, with peak relative gains of $+12.37\%$ on OAG-CS PV, $+4.87\%$ on PF-$L_2$, and $+1.18\%$ on PF-$L_1$, and $+4.24\%$, $+3.73\%$, and $+4.61\%$ on OGBN-MAG, HTAG-ArXiv, and HTAG-DBLP, respectively.

</details>


### [269] [Position, Not Provenance: Separating Reasoning Mediation from Sycophancy in Medical Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27304)
*Supratik Bhowal,Subhrajyoti Basu,Aritra Gir Mahanta,Anik Pal Chowdhury*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoT-Mediate introduces a framework to test causal influence of generated reasoning in medical VLMs by perturbing a single clinically meaningful attribute in the model's own chain-of-thought and measuring changes in predictions, using a dual-arm protocol and provenance-controlled interventions; evaluated on two models on VQA-RAD; findings show prefix-forced continuation yields higher faithfulness, contextual position matters, and visual evidence absence shifts reliance on injected reasoning; laterality is poorly tracked.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To establish whether model-generated chain-of-thought causally affects predictions in medical VLMs and to disentangle reasoning mediation from sycophancy.

Method: Dual-arm protocol combining re-prompted evidence vs prefix-forced continuation; provenance-controlled intervention varying only the attributed source of identical reasoning; evaluation on LLaVA-Med and MedGemma with 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each.

Result: Prefix-forced continuation achieves higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting; provenance analysis reveals model-specific deference; removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning; laterality least faithfully tracked; context position is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use generated reasoning.

Conclusion: The way reasoning is injected materially affects faithfulness; contextual position overrides stated provenance in determining whether models utilize their generated reasoning; the framework enables disentangling mediation from sycophancy and reveals model-specific behaviors.

Abstract: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) generate chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning before answering clinical questions, but whether this reasoning causally influences predictions remains unclear. We present CoT-Mediate, a behavioral framework that perturbs a single clinically meaningful attribute within a model's own generated reasoning and measures whether the resulting prediction follows the edited reasoning. Our framework combines a dual-arm protocol comparing re-prompted evidence with prefix-forced continuation, together with a provenance-controlled intervention that varies only the attributed source of identical reasoning to disentangle reasoning mediation from sycophancy. We evaluate LLaVA-Med and MedGemma on 1,000 VQA-RAD samples each. Prefix-forced continuation consistently yields higher mediation faithfulness than re-prompting, while the provenance analysis reveals distinct model-specific deference behaviors. Across both models, removing visual evidence increases reliance on injected reasoning, whereas laterality is the least faithfully tracked clinical attribute. These results show that the mechanism used to inject reasoning substantially affects measured faithfulness and that contextual position, rather than stated provenance, is the primary determinant of whether medical VLMs use their generated reasoning.

</details>


### [270] [ZUNA1.1: A more flexible EEG foundation model for Denoising and Super-resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27308)
*Christopher Warner,Jonas Mago,JR Huml,Beren Millidge*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder (ZUNA1.1) for flexible EEG signal reconstruction, enabling variable-length sequences up to 30s, arbitrary channels/locations, and interval-specific restoration; matches the prior ZUNA1 performance, outperforms conventional methods, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To enable flexible, high-quality reconstruction of EEG data across arbitrary channel configurations and partial temporal intervals, addressing limitations of standard interpolation methods (e.g., spherical spline) and rigid prior models.

Method: Diffusion autoencoder architecture with 380M parameters that accepts variable-length, multi-channel EEG input and can reconstruct arbitrary temporal intervals within channels as well as entire channels.

Result: On par with the original ZUNA1 in performance while offering much greater flexibility; substantially superior to spherical spline interpolation for denoising/reconstruction; open-source under Apache 2.0.

Conclusion: ZUNA1.1 extends EEG reconstruction capability to flexible, channel/interval-aware tasks, with strong empirical performance and broad usability due to its open-source release.

Abstract: We introduce ZUNA1.1, a 380M-parameter diffusion autoencoder for flexible EEG signal reconstruction. ZUNA1.1 is capable of reconstructing variable length sequences of up to 30s, with an arbitrary number of EEG channels at arbitrary scalp locations, and can reconstruct arbitrary temporal intervals within channels in addition to reconstructing entire channels. We demonstrate that ZUNA1.1 performs at least on par with our earlier ZUNA1 model, while being far more flexible and capable of handling a wide range of reconstruction tasks. ZUNA1.1 continues to substantially outperform standard EEG denoising and reconstruction methods such as spherical spline interpolation, which is ubiquitously deployed in the MNE package. The ZUNA1.1 model is released open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license.

</details>


### [271] [Modeling Decisions in Blockchain Analytics: A Leakage-Aware Evaluation of Tree-Based vs. Sequential Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27350)
*Michał Bartnicki,Jarosław A. Chudziak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Leakage-aware evaluation of Ethereum actor classification shows XGBoost with a Transaction Grammar representation outperforms Transformer/BiLSTM sequence models, delivering lower latency and energy use for real-time Sybil bot detection; introduces a leakage-resilient framework (Blind-Spot protocol and Transaction Grammar).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address potential label leakage that inflates deep-sequence model performance and assess whether sequential models are necessary for real-time detection; understand how organic users, Sybil bots, and MEV bots differ in transaction history structure; evaluate practical deployment constraints.

Method: Introduce Blind-Spot protocol to remove high-signal shortcuts; develop Transaction Grammar capturing wallet rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent; compare Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines for Ethereum actor classification; assess latency and energy implications.

Result: Under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models, with lower latency and estimated energy use, indicating tree-based models with grammar features can match or exceed deep sequence models in this setting.

Conclusion: A leakage-aware framework and Transaction Grammar representation enable practical, low-latency Ethereum actor classification; tree-based models provide competitive performance with better deployment efficiency, challenging the default preference for deep sequential models in this domain.

Abstract: Sybil bots are Ethereum actors that imitate legitimate users to extract airdrop rewards or influence governance. Recent Sybil detection methods increasingly use deep learning and treat blockchain activity as a quasi-linguistic sequence. However, complex sequence models are computationally expensive for real-time monitoring, and their reported performance may be inflated by label leakage from high-signal smart contracts. We ask whether and how organic users, Sybil bots, and MEV bots differ in the structural complexity of their transaction histories; whether sequential models outperform tree-based tabular models once leakage is reduced; whether transaction order or timing provides the stronger behavioral signal; and whether the resulting models are practical for low-latency deployment. Our approach to leakage-aware Sybil bot detection consists of a Blind-Spot protocol and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior.
