The former eliminates shortcuts associated with high-signal contracts, whereas the latter models wallets using rhythm, EVM execution structure, and intent. We evaluate this approach on Ethereum actor classification by comparing Transformer and BiLSTM sequence models against XGBoost and SVM baselines. We contribute a framework for leakage-aware Ethereum actor classification and a Transaction Grammar representation of wallet behavior. Our results demonstrate that, under leakage-aware evaluation, XGBoost outperforms Transformer-based sequence models while providing lower latency and estimated energy use.

</details>


### [272] [Compression-Based Behavioral Similarity for Open-World Sybil Discovery on Ethereum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27370)
*Michał Bartnicki,Jarosław A. Chudziak*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A training-free, compression-based framework for Sybil detection on Ethereum that uses a symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM traces and a Blind-Spot Protocol to filter high-signal contracts, building a gzip-based NCD behavioral graph for open-world discovery without funding links, robust to drift and evasion.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Limitations of graph-based Sybil detection that relies on token transfers and the vulnerability of closed-set ML classifiers to evolving attack strategies; need training-free, leakage-aware, open-world auditing methods that do not require explicit funding links.

Method: Construct a symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM traces capturing rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent; filter high-signal contracts with the Blind-Spot Protocol; compute gzip-based Normalized Compression Distance (NCD) to build a behavioral graph for Sybil discovery; evaluate against supervised ML baselines, with temporal split and synthetic camouflage stress tests; focuses on leakage-aware, training-free local discovery rather than formal open-set recognition.

Result: Demonstrates a leakage-aware behavioral framework where the core NCD primitive requires no supervised training and can expand suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links; validated against ML baselines and stress tests, indicating robustness to temporal drift and camouflage in an open-world audit setting.

Conclusion: The approach offers a training-free, local discovery primitive suitable for open-world blockchain audits, emphasizing leakage-aware behavior comparison and avoiding dependence on explicit financial links; not framed as a formal open-set classifier but as a practical tool for adversary discovery.

Abstract: Sybil attackers are Blockchain actors that adopt the characteristics of regular users to exploit airdrops or influence governance. Current methods of Sybil actor detection include constructing graphs, which requires token transfers between examined wallets. Machine learning algorithms have been employed as well, but they treat the task as a closed-set classification problem, making them vulnerable to frequent changes in attack strategies or evasion tactics. We address the following questions: can compression-based similarity differentiate Sybil bots, organic users, and arbitrage bot wallets without direct financial links? What is the effect of high-signal contracts on the discovery of Sybils, and how robust are behavioral graphs under temporal drift and adversarial perturbations? Our approach synthesizes a symbolic Transaction Grammar from EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) traces, capturing separately transaction rhythm, execution structure, and functional intent. The high-signal contracts are filtered with our own protocol, called the Blind-Spot Protocol. Gzip-based NCD is used to construct a behavioral graph for Sybil discovery. We validate this framework against supervised machine learning baselines, a temporal split, and synthetic camouflage stress tests. Ultimately, we contribute a leakage-aware behavioral framework for Sybil candidate discovery. Its core NCD primitive requires no supervised training and can expand suspicious seed wallets without explicit funding links. We position the method as a training-free local discovery primitive for open-world blockchain audits, rather than as a formal open-set recognition system.

</details>


### [273] [Explorative Modeling: Unlocking a Third Pretraining Axis and End-to-End Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27372)
*Alexi Gladstone,Heng Ji,Yilun Du*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces Explorative Modeling (XMs): a training paradigm that samples K candidate generations per data point and trains on the best match, enabling end-to-end, multi-modal generative modeling with notable efficiency and scalability gains across domains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: End-to-end generative modeling is hampered by multi-modal distributions; existing approaches decompose generation into hand-designed stages. XM proposes to treat exploration as a third pretraining axis that selects among multiple candidate generations to preserve mode structure and improve efficiency.

Method: During training, for each data instance the model generates K candidate outputs; these are evaluated against the data, the best-performing candidate is chosen, and only its pathway is backpropagated to update model parameters. This creates a new training axis—exploration—alongside parameters and data. The approach is demonstrated across continuous and discrete domains (images, video, language) and includes end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling.

Result: Scaling exploration yields significant efficiency and performance gains: FLOP efficiency ~4.1x, sample efficiency ~6.2x, parameter efficiency ~47%. Gains with data scale rise from 7% to 36% and with model scale from 13% to 23%; compute-efficiency gains more than double at 3x compute. Achieves near-state-of-the-art 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance. Enables end-to-end scaling of existing models and broader generalization, and in reconstructive tasks matches diffusion with 16–256x fewer inference steps.

Conclusion: XMs represent a new pretraining axis and a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm, enabling scalable, multi-modal generation and efficient end-to-end reconstructive modeling across domains.

Abstract: The deep learning revolution, kicked off by AlexNet, taught us that end-to-end training beats decomposing a problem into hand-designed stages. Generative modeling, however, has remained the exception-despite generative models being remarkably capable, they are still not trained end-to-end. This is because, at its core, generative modeling is about handling distributions with many modes, and existing scalable approaches handle this the same way, by factoring the generation procedure, which prevents end-to-end generation. In this work, we introduce Explorative Modeling, a new paradigm that instead factors the training loop, exploring K candidate matches between model generations and data, and training on the best, so predictions commit to modes rather than blurring them. We find Explorative Models (XMs) useful in two settings. First, increasing exploration adds a third pretraining axis beyond parameters and data for existing generative models-where scaling exploration monotonically improves performance across both continuous and discrete domains (images, video, and language). Notably, gains from exploration increase with scale, climbing from 7% to 36% as data scales and from 13% to 23% as models grow, with efficiency gains more than doubling at 3x the compute. Concretely, exploration improves FLOP efficiency by 4.1x, sample efficiency by 6.2x, parameter efficiency by 47%, lifts the strongest of image-generation recipes to a near-state-of-the-art 1.43 FID on ImageNet without guidance, enables scaling how end-to-end existing models are, and unlocks scaling generalization. Second, XMs enable end-to-end reconstructive generative modeling, matching diffusion on control tasks with 16-256x fewer inference steps. Together, these results establish XMs as both a new pretraining axis for existing generative models and a standalone end-to-end generative modeling paradigm.

</details>


### [274] [The Convergence Behavior of Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27383)
*Yijiang Pang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: First convergence guarantees for plain Adam under heavy-tailed noise; converges to stationary points but with suboptimal iteration complexity unless the domain radius is known; extends online-to-nonconvex framework to heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand Adam's behavior when stochastic gradients have only bounded p-th moment for p in (1,2], a regime common in deep learning.

Method: Generalize the online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise and derive a discounted regret analysis for Adam without restrictive parameter coupling.

Result: Adam converges to (ρ, ε)-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise but with suboptimal iteration complexity and p-dependent convergence; if the domain radius is known and used to control the online-learner output, the rate matches the optimal complexity.

Conclusion: Shows robustness and limitations of Adam in heavy-tailed regimes; domain-radius knowledge can recover optimal rates; provides theoretical insight into nonconvex optimization with heavy-tailed stochastic gradients.

Abstract: We establish the first convergence guarantees for the plain vector-form \emph{Adam} optimizer under heavy-tailed stochastic noise. While several Adam variants are known to achieve optimal iteration complexity in bounded-variance nonconvex optimization, little is understood about their behavior when stochastic gradients admit only a bounded $p$-th central moment for some $p \in (1,2]$, a setting increasingly observed in modern deep learning. To address this gap, we generalize the recent online-to-nonconvex conversion framework to accommodate heavy-tailed martingale-difference noise. Building on this generalized framework, we develop a discounted regret analysis for Adam, without restrictive parameter coupling. Our results show that Adam converges to $(ρ,ε)$-stationary points under heavy-tailed noise. However, it exhibits a suboptimal iteration complexity and $p$-dependent convergence, a suboptimality that persists even in the bounded-variance case ($p=2$). When the domain radius is known and used to control the online-learner output, a standard setup in related literature, the convergence rate improves to match the optimal complexity. These findings provide new theoretical insight into the robustness and limitations of Adam in heavy-tailed regimes.

</details>


### [275] [FunL2O: LLM-Guided Feature Function Design for Learning to Optimize](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27389)
*Bingheng Li,Junyang Cai,Yupeng Zhang,Bistra Dilkina,Jayant Kalagnanam,Dzung T. Phan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FunL2O automates feature design for learning-to-optimize by evolving feature functions with LLMs in a FunSearch loop, outperforming hand-crafted features on continuous and discrete tasks across multiple LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Feature design is a critical bottleneck in L2O pipelines and is typically manual and domain-specific. Automating feature design with LLM-driven program evolution promises broader applicability and better representations.

Method: In a FunSearch-style loop, an LLM proposes executable feature functions. A fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model and measures downstream optimization performance. The approach is evaluated on linear and quadratic programming tasks (solution prediction and warm-starting) and on mixed-integer optimization tasks using GNN-guided backdoor branching and Predict-and-Search, across continuous and discrete tasks and four LLMs.

Result: Across tasks and LLMs, the evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations, demonstrating the generality and effectiveness of LLM-driven feature evolution for L2O.

Conclusion: LLM-driven feature evolution is a general and effective approach to automating representation design in learning-to-optimize, reducing manual feature engineering and improving performance across domains.

Abstract: Learning-to-optimize (L2O) methods accelerate repeated optimization by training models to predict solutions, warm starts, branching decisions, or other forms of solver guidance. A critical yet largely overlooked component of these pipelines is the feature function that maps problem instances to inputs for machine learning models. Existing L2O methods typically rely on hand-crafted features, making representation design manual and largely fixed across domains. We introduce FunL2O, the first unified framework for automating feature design through LLM-driven program evolution for L2O. In a FunSearch-style loop, an LLM proposes executable feature functions, while a fixed evaluation process retrains the original L2O model and measures downstream optimization performance. We evaluate FunL2O on linear and quadratic programming tasks involving solution prediction and warm-starting, as well as on mixed-integer optimization tasks using GNN-guided backdoor branching and Predict-and-Search. Across continuous and discrete optimization tasks and four LLMs, the evolved features consistently outperform hand-crafted representations. These results establish LLM-driven feature evolution as a general and effective approach to automating representation design in L2O.

</details>


### [276] [ECG-InterpBench: Benchmarking the Interpretability of ECG Foundation Models with Matched-Scale Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27404)
*Yixuan Duan,Wei Qiu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ECG-InterpBench provides a capacity-controlled benchmark to evaluate interpretability of ECG foundation-model representations using sparse autoencoders, revealing distinct interpretability profiles and cross-dataset reproducibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current ECG foundation-model benchmarks focus on predictive performance and do not systematically assess whether internal representations are interpretable, decomposable, or reproducible across analyses.

Method: Evaluate six frozen ECG foundation models across five encoder depths, five matched dictionary widths, and three random seeds using sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments; build a 450-cell interpretability atlas with 75 exactly matched six-model blocks; assess sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility and coverage of 49 clinically meaningful ECG measurements, and cross-seed reproducibility; quantify patient-sampling uncertainty, depth- and seed-dependent variation, and sparsity-parameter sensitivity; replicate on MIMIC-IV-ECG.

Result: Found distinct interpretability profiles across models; leading models differ depending on the interpretability metric; a replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG confirms that reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility can nominate different top models; provides executable evaluation code, standardized manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits.

Conclusion: ECG-InterpBench offers a capacity-controlled, reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across interpretability dimensions, complementing performance-focused benchmarks.

Abstract: Existing benchmarks for electrocardiogram foundation models primarily evaluate downstream predictive performance, providing limited insight into whether their internal representations can be faithfully decomposed, clinically interpreted, or reproduced across independent analyses. We introduce ECG-InterpBench, a benchmark designed to systematically evaluate the interpretability of ECG foundation-model representations. ECG-InterpBench uses sparse autoencoders as standardized measurement instruments and matches their capacity across models to enable controlled comparisons. We evaluate six frozen ECG foundation models across five standardized encoder depths, five matched dictionary widths, and three random seeds, producing a 450-cell interpretability atlas comprising 75 exactly matched six-model comparison blocks. The benchmark evaluates complementary dimensions of representation interpretability, including sparse reconstruction fidelity, single-feature accessibility and coverage of 49 clinically meaningful ECG measurements, and cross-seed feature reproducibility. The evaluation further quantifies patient-sampling uncertainty, depth- and seed-dependent variation, and sensitivity to the sparsity parameterization. The benchmark reveals that ECG foundation models exhibit distinct interpretability profiles. A matched replication on MIMIC-IV-ECG confirms that reconstruction fidelity and clinical accessibility identify different leading models. The benchmark is accompanied by executable evaluation code, standardized manifests, cell-level metrics, and reproducibility audits. ECG-InterpBench complements performance-centered ECG benchmarks by providing a capacity-controlled and reproducible framework for comparing ECG foundation models across distinct dimensions of representation interpretability.

</details>


### [277] [Context-Informed Ship Trajectory Prediction via Conditional Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27418)
*Yuan Guan,Chandler Squires,Timothy Hu,Pradeep Ravikumar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes Conditional Informer, an encoder–decoder that models ship trajectories as conditional on environmental context via a dedicated conditional attention mechanism, augmented by Modality Masking to handle sensor dropouts; achieves 15.4% accuracy gains with robust fallback performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-term maritime trajectory prediction should respect the directional physical dependence of dynamics on weather and vessel characteristics, not treat environmental variables as mere features or treat dynamics as independent from context.

Method: An encoder–decoder architecture named Conditional Informer with a Conditional Attention module where the vessel state queries environmental contexts; explicit physical prior that weather modulates but is not generated by vessel dynamics; Modality Masking training strategy to mitigate data intermittency and prevent shortcut learning.

Result: Empirical evaluation on AIS and ERA5 shows 15.4% improvement over kinematic and concatenation-based baselines when context is available; Modality Masking reduces fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.

Conclusion: Explicit conditioning on environmental context via cross-attention enhances long-horizon trajectory forecasting accuracy and robustness to modality dropouts, highlighting the importance of physics-informed conditioning in maritime prediction.

Abstract: Long-term ship trajectory prediction is a fundamental capability for maritime safety and autonomous navigation. While recent Transformer-based architectures have improved forecasting horizons, they predominantly rely on historical kinematic states, treating vessel motion as an isolated system. In reality, maritime navigation is profoundly modulated by extrinsic factors like weather and constrained by static vessel characteristics. Existing multimodal approaches fundamentally model the joint distribution over states and contexts, treating environmental variables as peer features rather than encoding the directional physical dependence of vessel dynamics on environmental conditions.
  In this work, we propose the Conditional Informer, a novel encoder-decoder architecture that formulates trajectory prediction as a conditional generation task. We employ a dedicated Conditional Attention mechanism where the vessel state explicitly queries environmental contexts through cross-attention, encoding the physical prior that weather modulates - but is not generated by - vessel dynamics. Furthermore, to address the intermittency of real-world data, we introduce a Modality Masking training strategy to prevent catastrophic degradation during sensor fallback. Extensive experiments on AIS and ERA5 data demonstrate that our approach outperforms kinematic and concatenation-based baselines by 15.4% in prediction accuracy when context is available. Crucially, Modality Masking prevents shortcut learning, reducing fallback error by nearly an order of magnitude compared to unconstrained models.

</details>


### [278] [Good Rankers, Bad Objectives: Bilinear Contrastive Critics under Expressive Policy Search](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27422)
*Ayushman Singh,Siddharth Aphale*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Contrastive critics exhibit norm-drift and score-saturation that degrade action ranking, failing to reliably order actions off-support; they are useful as compatibility rankers, but robust action selection requires a calibrated value function (e.g., Bellman TD-Q).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate whether contrastive, value-like critics can guide best-of-K decisions, planning, or generation, and identify failure modes due to unbounded scores, norm drift, and calibration.

Method: Empirical evaluation across navigation tasks (PointMaze, AntMaze, HumanoidMaze) and a toy exact-Q*; compare unbounded bilinear, cosine-bounded, and hybrid/contrastive critics; analyze training/readout decomposition and inference-time normalization; measure realized costs via simulator rollouts; assess calibration of top decile and fixed-query ordering; test parameter-matched function-class controls.

Result: Unbounded bilinear scores permit norm drift that inflates off-support values; cosine bounding does not eliminate this; cosine and hybrid critics still select off-support actions and incur similar regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top score decile and fail to order fixed-query actions by value. Bellman-trained TD-Q succeeds, including in a parameter-matched function-class control. Task-dependent costs emerge: PointMaze may show single-step costs; the exact-Q* toy shows clear gains; AntMaze and HumanoidMaze often yield nulls where the controller self-corrects. A training/readout decomposition traces the lost ordering to the cosine training objective; raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization. Candidate maximization can exploit false positives from norm drift, score saturation, or in-support misranking. Contrastive critics remain useful compatibility rankers for navigation/manipulation tasks, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar.

Conclusion: Treat contrastive critics as compatibility/ranking aids; employ a calibrated value function for action selection (e.g., TD-Q), since training objective and normalization critically affect ordering. A hybrid approach that preserves contrastive signals while providing a stable value-based scalar is recommended.

Abstract: Good action rankings do not make a contrastive critic safe to maximize. These critics increasingly act as value-like objectives for best-of-$K$ selection, planning, and critic-guided generation. Unbounded bilinear scores can let large embedding norms inflate off-support values, but cosine bounding does not remove the failure. A controlled support decomposition attributes most raw bilinear regret to norm drift. Cosine and hybrid critics nevertheless select off-support actions from most pools and incur comparable regret. Contrastive scores are weakly calibrated or inverted in the top score decile across four OGBench navigation tasks, and they fail to order fixed-query actions by value. Bellman-trained TD-Q succeeds, including in a parameter-matched function-class control. Realized costs depend on the task: simulator rollouts reveal single-step selection costs on PointMaze and the exact-$Q^*$ toy but well-powered nulls on AntMaze and HumanoidMaze, where the controller can self-correct. A training/readout decomposition traces the lost ordering to the cosine training objective; raw-trained embeddings retain weak ordering after inference-time normalization. Candidate maximization can therefore exploit false positives caused by norm drift, score saturation, or in-support misranking. Contrastive critics remain useful compatibility rankers on navigation and manipulation tasks, but action selection requires a value-calibrated scalar.

</details>


### [279] [SE(3)-MeanFlow: Few-Step Protein Backbone Generation on Lie Groups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27431)
*Yikun Bai,Binghang Lu,Yikai Liu,Elaheh Akbari,Soheil Kolouri,Linxuan Wang,Ping He,Shuchan Wang,Ruqi Zhang,Guang Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SE(3)-MeanFlow extends MeanFlow to the Lie group of protein frames to enable few-step, simulation-free training for protein backbone generation, reducing inference cost while maintaining or improving quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing diffusion/flow-matching models operate on SE(3)^N and require costly ODE integration with Lie group exponentials, hindering high-throughput protein backbone design. A faster, simulation-free method on the Lie group is needed.

Method: Builds SE(3)-MeanFlow by working in the Lie algebra so(3) and R^3, deriving closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations/translations, and introducing SE(3) alpha-Flow as a Jacobian-vector-product-free warm-up. A small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss is used for rest of pretraining and rectification-based post-training. Evaluates on protein backbone generation, comparing to flow-matching baselines with fewer sampling steps.

Result: SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use more steps, with a pronounced advantage in the few-step regime. Rectification-based post-training enables it to lead at every budget, at a modest cost to diversity.

Conclusion: SE(3)-MeanFlow provides efficient, high-quality protein backbone generation with significantly reduced inference steps, leveraging Lie-group geometry and closed-form velocity identities; effective for high-throughput design due to simulation-free training and robust few-step performance.

Abstract: Generative modeling of protein backbones promises the de novo design of proteins with prescribed structural and functional properties. Existing diffusion and flow-matching models produce high-quality backbones on SE(3)^N, but inference requires numerically integrating an ODE over hundreds of network evaluations, each involving a Lie group exponential map - a bottleneck for high-throughput design campaigns. We introduce SE(3)-MeanFlow, a few-step generative framework that extends MeanFlow from Euclidean space to the Lie group geometry of protein frames. Working natively in the Lie algebra so(3) and in R^3, we derive closed-form average-velocity identities for rotations and translations, giving simulation-free training targets. We further introduce an SE(3) alpha-Flow objective that removes the Jacobian-vector product from the rotation branch and serves as a warm-up stage, after which training switches to a small-t stabilized MeanFlow loss that is used for the remainder of pretraining and for rectification-based post-training. In protein backbone generation, SE(3)-MeanFlow matches or exceeds flow-matching baselines that use several times more sampling steps, and its advantage widens in the few-step regime, where rectification lets it lead at every matched budget - at a modest cost in diversity.

</details>


### [280] [Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN for Channel Modeling in Low-SNR Regimes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27450)
*Chaofan Deng,Linyu Sun,Jaeho Lee,Arijit Raychowdhury*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: NN-CLEAN is a hybrid neural-network–assisted CLEAN algorithm that replaces exhaustive grid search with parallel neural passes inside the iterative CLEAN loop, while using exact physical models for residual subtraction. It achieves GS-CLEAN–level accuracy at low SNR with massively reduced computational complexity and favorable batch scalability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional CLEAN-like methods are accurate but computationally expensive due to grid search; purely data-driven networks lack physical grounding and generalization to variable multipath densities and off-grid parameters. A hybrid approach aims to combine high-resolution physics-based estimation with fast learned components.

Method: Embed a multi-head residual network directly into the CLEAN iterative loop. Replace exhaustive grid search with rapid, parallelizable forward passes through the network, while encoding residual subtraction with exact, physical models to preserve physical interpretability and accuracy.

Result: Monte Carlo simulations show NN-CLEAN achieves >96% estimation accuracy at 5 dB SNR, matching GS-CLEAN, with a drastic reduction in computational complexity. It outperforms subspace methods and standalone neural networks. Batch-size scaling is near-flat for runtime and memory, enabling real-time operation in MIMO channel estimation.

Conclusion: NN-CLEAN provides a robust, real-time, physically grounded hybrid solution for high-resolution multipath parameter estimation in challenging wireless environments, with strong performance parity to GRID-SEARCH CLEAN and substantial efficiency gains.

Abstract: Accurate multipath parameter estimation is critical for modern wireless communication systems, particularly in challenging low-SNR environments. Traditional Maximum Likelihood Estimation algorithms, such as CLEAN, provide high-resolution parameter extraction but suffer from prohibitive computational complexity due to exhaustive grid search. Conversely, purely data-driven deep learning approaches lack physical grounding and struggle to generalize across variable multipath densities and off-grid parameters. To address these limitations, this paper proposes Neural Network-Assisted CLEAN (NN-CLEAN), a hybrid framework that embeds a multi-head residual network directly into the iterative CLEAN extraction loop. By replacing the exhaustive grid search with rapid, parallelizable forward passes while delegating residual subtraction to exact mathematical models, NN-CLEAN isolates physical multipath parameters without accumulating non- physical errors. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate that NN-CLEAN achieves estimation accuracy exceeding 96% at 5 dB SNR, matching the traditional Grid-Search CLEAN (GS- CLEAN) baseline, while providing a massive reduction in computational complexity and substantially outperforming subspace methods and standalone one-shot neural networks. Crucially, NN-CLEAN exhibits a near-flat scaling in execution runtime and memory consumption as batch sizes increase. This highly efficient parallelization establishes NN-CLEAN as a robust, real- time solution for channel estimation in MIMO systems.

</details>


### [281] [FADEx: Feature Attribution and Distortion-based Explanation of Dimensionality Reduction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27463)
*Lucas Greff Meneses,Evandro S. Ortigossa,Claudio Silva,Luis Gustavo Nonato*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FADEx provides local, per-instance feature attributions for dimensionality reduction (DR) explanations using a local linear model built from a Taylor expansion and SVD, making the method agnostic to the DR technique and capable of distortion analysis; it claims robust explanations and improved performance over prior methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Non-linear DR methods are opaque and hinder interpretability of how original features influence positions in the reduced space. Existing DR explanation methods are limited by multiple attributions per feature and narrow applicability across DR methods.

Method: Construct local linear models around each data point using first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition. Use weighted least squares to fit the local model, without requiring out-of-sample data mapping, making the approach agnostic to the specific DR method. Extract per-feature attributions and distortion analyses from the local models.

Result: Qualitative and quantitative evaluations, comparisons with existing methods, and case studies show FADEx yields robust and reliable explanations that outperform existing approaches in several aspects.

Conclusion: FADEx provides versatile explanations and analytical resources for analyzing DR behavior, improving interpretability of DR methods across different techniques and datasets.

Abstract: Dimensionality Reduction (DR) is a fundamental tool for high-dimensional data exploration, reducing the complexity of latent spaces of machine learning models, and assisting in the explanation of complex opaque models. However, non-linear DR techniques often function as opaque transformations themselves, making it challenging to understand how individual features influence instance positioning in the reduced space. This lack of transparency complicates the analysis and interpretation of structural patterns, hindering the ability to reason about the organization of high-dimensional data based on the projected layout. In order to address this challenge, dimensionality reduction explanation methods have shown promise in improving the understanding of the observed groups and cluster structures. Unfortunately, existing DR explanation approaches tend to suffer from limitations such as multiple attributions per feature and restricted applicability to specific dimensionality reduction methods, which hinder their use. In this work, we propose FADEx, a novel local per-instance feature attribution method that leverages local linear approximation via first-order Taylor expansion and Singular Value Decomposition to provide explanations. FADEx computes the local linear models via weighted least squares, eliminating the need for out-of-sample data mapping, making it agnostic to the DR method, while simultaneously providing local feature attributions and distortion analysis. Through qualitative and quantitative evaluations, comparisons with existing methods, and case studies, we demonstrate FADEx's effectiveness and versatility in providing explanations and analytical resources for analyzing the behavior of DR methods. The results indicate FADEx yields robust and reliable explanations, outperforming existing approaches in several aspects.

</details>


### [282] [Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27479)
*Aryan Mishra,Randy Martinez,Lizhen Lin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A graph rewiring method (SCGR) augments the input graph with a Schreier-Coset graph from a special linear group to improve information flow in GNNs by reducing effective resistance and increasing spectral gap, claimed to preserve key graph properties and achieve competitive accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Over-squashing in GNNs bottlenecks long-range information propagation; existing rewiring methods introduce structural/computational bottlenecks and often distort original graphs. A principled, scalable rewiring that preserves key properties is needed.

Method: Construct a Schreier-Coset graph derived from a special linear group and augment the input graph with it. This yields a graph with a spectral gap and bounded effective resistance, providing a low-resistance bypass for long-range communication. The approach is presented as a group-theoretic rewiring technique named Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring (SCGR).

Result: Empirical evaluations show SCGR reduces effective resistance by 5-40% across diverse tasks, mitigating connectivity bottlenecks while maintaining competitive accuracy.

Conclusion: SCGR offers theoretical guarantees (spectral gap, bounded effective resistance) and practical gains (lower effective resistance, improved information flow) with competitive accuracy, representing a principled alternative to existing graph rewiring methods.

Abstract: The information flow in the graph neural networks (GNNs) is fundamentally constrained by over-squashing, where structural bottlenecks impede long range information propagation. Graph-rewiring methods, which modify graph topology, have been extensively used to alleviate this. However, existing approaches often introduce prohibitive structural and computational bottlenecks, fail to preserve the critical properties of original graphs, and increase the edge counts massively. We introduce a novel method Schreier-Coset Graph Rewiring , a group-theoretic rewiring method that augments the input graph with a Schreier-Coset graph derived from a special linear group. Our method provides theoretical guarantees, a graph that exhibits spectral gap and a bounded effective resistance, creating a low-resistance bypass for long-range communication. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that SCGR reduces effective resistance by 5-40% across various learning tasks, effectively mitigating connectivity bottlenecks while maintaining competitive accuracy.

</details>


### [283] [Latent States in Neural Networks: Recovering the Temporal Structure of Drifting Data from Model Weights](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27482)
*Kevin Guan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Hidden Markov modeling of weight trajectories reveals discrete regime states in drifting data streams; within-state transfer improves generalization across two tasks, indicating regime-relevant transfer beyond data distribution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate if discrete, temporally drifting regimes can be recovered from the sequence of model weights and whether these regimes predict transfer performance.

Method: Train classifiers on consecutive temporal windows; align and collect their weights; fit an HMM to the trajectory of these weights to infer latent regime states; evaluate within-state vs cross-state transfer; control for temporal proximity; residualize class divergence and lag; replicate on Fakeddit and Yelp.

Result: Within-state transfer advantage replicated on both tasks; advantage modestly exceeds equal-sized contiguous state partition; states align with shifts in data distribution more than with weight-space geometry; after residualization, the effect remains above permutation null; Yelp shows weaker effects due to more temporally stable label distribution.

Conclusion: Discrete regimes in temporally drifting data are recoverable from model-weight trajectories and meaningfully predict transfer performance; the phenomenon generalizes across tasks but is sensitive to label drift magnitude.

Abstract: A temporally drifting data stream may pass through discrete regimes rather than changing continuously. We ask whether such regimes are recoverable from the weights of models trained on the stream, using a hidden Markov model (HMM) fit to the chronologically ordered trajectory of those weights. We study this question in two domains known to drift over time: multimodal misinformation detection, using the Fakeddit dataset; and sentiment analysis, using the Yelp dataset. We train classifiers on consecutive temporal windows and fit an HMM to the trajectory of their aligned weights, recovering latent states that partition each timeline into coherent phases. On both datasets, classifiers generalize better to data from windows sharing the state of their training window than to windows across state boundaries. This within-state transfer advantage survives a control for temporal proximity and modestly exceeds the advantage recovered by a naive partition into contiguous states of equal size. Although the states are estimated solely from model weights, they correlate more strongly with shifts in the data's class distribution than with the weight-space geometry used to estimate them. After class divergence and lag are residualized out, the within-state advantage exceeds its permutation null on both tasks, indicating that the states recover structure relevant to transfer beyond the data distribution. Every effect replicates on both tasks but is attenuated on Yelp, whose label distribution is more temporally stable.

</details>


### [284] [ODEWorld: A Continuous Predictive Architecture via Physical-Time Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27924)
*Dongxiu Liu,Haoyi Niu,Peng Cheng,Yuan Gao,Xirui Kang,Sangli Teng,Koushil Sreenath,Xianyuan Zhan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PT-Flow and ODEWorld propose a continuous-time latent world model using a latent velocity field and ODE dynamics, enabling future prediction via ODE solvers, arbitrary timing, backward prediction, and planning-friendly representations; claimed to improve long-horizon video generation and robotic control.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Discrete-time world models struggle to capture continuous physical dynamics efficiently and suffer from representation collapse over long horizons; a continuous-time latent framework aims to improve fidelity, temporal flexibility, and planning utility.

Method: Introduce PT-Flow: learn a continuous latent velocity field in physical time governed by ODEs in latent space; predictions obtained by integrating the latent state with an ODE solver. Build ODEWorld: enforce time-variant latent features and ODE-consistent dynamics to mitigate representation collapse, enable long-horizon and backward predictions, and provide planning-oriented cues.

Result: Empirical results indicate ODEWorld achieves high-fidelity video generation and effective robotic control, with the ability to operate at arbitrary temporal resolutions and perform backward prediction; demonstrates improved balance between realistic visuals and planning-relevant dynamics.

Conclusion: Continuous-time latent world models with ODE-based dynamics offer a versatile, efficient framework for world modeling that enhances long-horizon prediction and planning capabilities, with broad applicability to video synthesis and control.

Abstract: In the physical world we inhabit, space and time are fundamentally continuous. However, existing machine learning paradigms for world modeling are largely confined to discrete-time prediction, thereby exhibiting significant inefficiency in capturing the dynamics of physical world. We introduce Physical-Time Flow (\textbf{PT-Flow}), a novel approach that learns a continuous latent velocity field operating in physical time. Crucially, the underlying dynamics of sequential data are parameterized by an ordinary differential equation (ODE) embedded in a well-structured representation space. Under this paradigm, the prediction of future can be recast as temporal integration via an ODE solver in the compressed latent space. Building upon PT-Flow, we construct \textbf{ODEWorld}, a continuous-time latent world model that is both efficient and versatile. By extracting time-variant features and enforcing ODE properties on both the dynamical representation space and the latent velocity field, ODEWorld effectively addresses the long-standing representation collapse issue in latent world model literature. This also enables high-quality image reconstruction even after long-horizon prediction. Moreover, its continuous nature allows for arbitrary temporal resolution and even backward prediction, which is impossible for most discrete-time models. Lastly, ODEWorld can provide rich planning-oriented information to facilitate downstream policy learning. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that ODEWorld successfully reconciles planning-conducive dynamics abstraction with visual realism, excelling in both video generation and robotic control. \href{https://dstate.github.io/odeworld_website/}{Project Website}.

</details>


### [285] [A Lightweight Foundation Model for Collider Physics with Multi-Domain Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27501)
*Liangyu Wu,Qibin Liu,Alexander Yue,Julia Gonski*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A lightweight ~3M-parameter autoencoder pre-trained on LHC collision data functions as a foundation model, boosting collider downstream tasks with limited labeled data and generalizing to other scientific domains, while offering greater efficiency than transformer-based approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To reduce data and compute demands of foundation models in science by leveraging abundant unlabeled collider data to learn transferable representations, enabling efficient, edge-friendly deployment and cross-domain applicability.

Method: Train a fully connected autoencoder with ~3 million parameters on unlabeled charged-particle track features from LHC collision data. Use pre-trained weights for downstream collider tasks such as kinematic regression and event classification with limited labeled data. Perform latent-space analysis and test transferability to non-collider domains (gravitational waves, flood forecasting, neural activity). Compare computational efficiency against transformer-based baselines at similar scale.

Result: Achieves improved accuracy on collider tasks when labeled data are scarce compared to models trained from scratch. Latent-space interpretation provides insights into learned representations. Demonstrates cross-domain applicability to gravitational waves, flood forecasting, and neural activity. Shows that the approach is computationally simpler than transformer models at comparable scale, suggesting suitability for real-time or edge deployments.

Conclusion: A lightweight, unsupervised pre-training strategy with a small autoencoder can function as a foundation model for scientific data, delivering strong downstream performance with limited labels and enabling efficient, cross-domain, and edge-friendly deployment.

Abstract: We present a lightweight approach to foundation modeling (\textbf{NEXUS}) that leverages pre-trained learning from collider physics data towards out-of-domain tasks in other scientific datasets, using a fully connected autoencoder model with approximately 3 million parameters. The model pre-trains with no supervision over a large-scale collision dataset from the Large Hadron Collider modeled by charged particle track features. Downstream tasks for collider analyses, such as kinematic regression and event classification, are developed on pre-trained model weights and achieve improved accuracy with only small labeled datasets when compared to equivalent architectures trained from scratch. The benefits of pre-training are additionally investigated through latent space interpretation and application to other domains, including gravitational waves, flood forecasting, and neural activity. Furthermore, the relative computational simplicity of NEXUS is demonstrated compared to transformer approaches at comparable scale, opening the door to power-efficient inference and real-time or edge applications of foundation models in scientific experiments.

</details>


### [286] [Sparsity Induced Identifiability in Matrix Tri-Factorisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27507)
*Tingting Mu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: First rigorous theory for sparsity-induced identifiability in real-valued matrix tri-factorisation, via a novel two-stage decomposition into coupled auxiliary factorizations; establishes recovery guarantees, convergence behavior, spectral error bounds, and structure preservation, with Monte Carlo validation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap in theoretical guarantees for sparsity effects in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation, where two-factor results are well-studied but tri-factorisation lacked rigorous theory.

Method: Introduce a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the tri-factorisation into two coupled auxiliary factorisations, preserving the relevant structure. Use this to derive recovery guarantees, structural consistency results, convergence properties, spectral approximation error bounds, and high-probability bounds. Validate theory with comprehensive Monte Carlo experiments.

Result: Derives recovery guarantees and structural consistency results showing how coefficient sparsity shapes sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behaviour, spectral error, and high-probability bounds. Empirical experiments demonstrate close agreement with the theory.

Conclusion: Presents the first rigorous theoretical framework for sparsity-induced identifiability in real-valued matrix tri-factorisation, providing actionable insights into how sparsity influences recovery and structure preservation, supported by extensive simulations.

Abstract: Matrix factorisation is a fundamental tool for exploiting low-dimensional structure in high-dimensional data, with applications such as data compression, denoising, structure discovery, interpretable representation learning, and dimensionality reduction. Compared to conventional two-factor models, matrix tri-factorisation provides greater modelling flexibility, while sparsity constraints often improve both interpretability and recovery performance. Although the role of sparsity has been extensively studied for two-factor matrix factorisation, rigorous theoretical guarantees for general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation remain largely unexplored. To address this gap, we establish, to the best of our knowledge, the first rigorous theoretical study for sparsity-induced identifiability in general real-valued matrix tri-factorisation. Our analysis is enabled by a novel decomposition strategy that transforms the original problem into two coupled auxiliary factorisation problems, while preserving the structural information necessary to the recovery of the original factor matrices from the observations. Building upon this decomposition, we derive recovery guarantees and structural consistency results that characterise how coefficient sparsity influences the sufficient recovery conditions, convergence behaviour, spectral approximation error, high-probability bounds, and structure preservation. Comprehensive Monte Carlo experiments validate the proposed theory and demonstrate close agreement between the theoretical results and empirical observations.

</details>


### [287] [QQWorld: Quantile-Quantile Matching for World Model Regularization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28415)
*Zhoushun Yu,Xiaoyu Hu,Xiangyu Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QQWorld replaces EP with quantile-quantile matching for latent Gaussian alignment, improving tail control and planning in LeWM; cross-batch QQ expands ranking pool; empirical gains in four control tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: EP objective yields vanishing corrective gradients for heavy-tailed tails, leading to suboptimal regularization of latent distributions; improving tail alignment should enhance planning performance.

Method: Introduce QQWorld, a quantile-quantile (QQ) matching objective that aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles; replace Epps-Pulley with QQ; develop cross-batch QQ by using detached samples from previous batches to enlarge the ranking pool and analyze its bias-variance trade-off.

Result: Across four control environments, QQWorld improves the average planning success rate of LeWM and achieves better Gaussian alignment with thinner latent tails compared to EP-based regularization.

Conclusion: Quantile-based latent matching provides stable gradient signals in the tails, improving latent distribution regularization and planning performance; cross-batch QQ offers robustness by widening the ranking pool at a potential bias-variance trade-off.

Abstract: Latent world models enable efficient planning by predicting future states in a compact representation space, but their performance depends critically on the quality of the learned latent distribution. LeWorldModel (LeWM) regularizes its latents toward an isotropic Gaussian using the Epps-Pulley (EP) objective. We show that the corrective gradients of EP rapidly vanish for isolated tail samples, leaving heavy-tailed deviations insufficiently controlled. To address this limitation, we propose QQWorld, which replaces EP with a quantile-quantile matching objective that directly aligns projected latent samples with rank-matched Gaussian quantiles, thereby maintaining effective corrective gradients in the tails. We further develop cross-batch QQ, which enlarges the effective ranking pool using detached samples from previous batches, and characterize its bias-variance trade-off. Across four control environments, QQWorld effectively improves the average planning success rate of LeWM, while consistently yielding better Gaussian alignment and thinner latent tails.

</details>


### [288] [Expanding Data-Agnostic Pivotal Instances Selection Models with Proximity Trees and Ensemble Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27522)
*Alessio Cascione,Mattia Setzu,Cristiano Landi,Paolo Maria Mancarella,Riccardo Guidotti*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A pivot-based, hierarchical, interpretable model selects representative pivots to build an interpretable predictor. It extends to pivot pairs and ensembles, is data-modality-agnostic via pre-trained feature transforms, and achieves competitive results with few pivots across diverse data types.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Interpretable decision-making remains a challenge as ML models grow more complex. The work seeks a naturally interpretable approach by using a small set of pivots—representative examples—to guide predictions, inspired by decision trees.

Method: A hierarchical pivot-selection model that measures similarity between pivots and inputs to construct predictions. Functions as both a pivot selector and standalone predictor. Extends to pivot pairs (proximity and oblique trees) and ensembles. Data-agnostic through pre-trained networks for data transformation, enabling application across modalities.

Result: Empirical evaluation across tabular, text, image, and time-series datasets shows the method outperforms other instance-selection strategies and is competitive with state-of-the-art interpretable models, while using a minimal number of pivots.

Conclusion: The proposed pivot-based method provides a versatile, interpretable, modality-agnostic predictive framework that delivers strong performance with few pivots and adapts to various data types and ensemble configurations.

Abstract: As decision-making processes grow more complex, machine learning tools have become essential for tackling business and societal challenges. However, many existing methods rely on decision-making procedures that are difficult to interpret. Since humans naturally make decisions by comparing new cases with a few representative examples, we aim to design an approach that selects such pivots to construct an interpretable predictive model. Inspired by decision trees, we propose a hierarchical, interpretable-by-design pivot selection model based on the similarity between pivots and input instances. Our method functions both as a pivot selection technique and a standalone predictive model. Extending beyond single pivots, we incorporate pairs of pivots that are used by proximity and oblique trees, as well as ensembles, which enhance the versatility and effectiveness of our proposal. Additionally, our approach is data modality-agnostic, leveraging pre-trained networks for data transformation. Experiments across diverse datasets, including tabular data, text, images, and time series, demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, outperforming alternative instance selection strategies and achieving competitive results against state-of-the-art interpretable models while maintaining a minimal number of pivots.

</details>


### [289] [Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps for Few-Step Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27529)
*Mansoor Ahmed,Yue-Tsz Fan,Hemanth Venkateswara,Murray Patterson*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF) introduce a latent-conditioned mixture of factorized flow kernels to model cross-token dependencies in discrete diffusion for text generation, enabling native correlated steps and improved perplexity without teacher models; MDLM corresponds to M=1, and larger M yields stronger gains (e.g., M=8 surpasses distilled/rectified few-step samplers); code available.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Discrete diffusion models for text traditionally factorize transitions across positions, treating tokens independently. This hinders few-step generation when targets require strong inter-token correlations (e.g., subject-verb agreement). Existing few-step methods rely on teacher distillation/rectification and hit a quality ceiling. A model that expresses correlations directly could unlock better efficiency and quality without reliance on teachers.

Method: Propose Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF): a mixture of M factorized components tied by a single shared latent. Conditioned on the latent, each component is cheap; the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form for small M. One latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire denoising trajectory, giving the same per-step time complexity as factorized models. The MDLM is a special case of LKF with M=1.

Result: Empirical evaluation on unconditional text generation (LM1B and WikiText-103) shows LKF learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1x to 3.3x over likelihood baselines without sacrificing diversity. Gains grow with M; at M=8, LKF surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers.

Conclusion: LKF provides a native mechanism to express cross-position correlations in discrete diffusion for text. Increasing the number of latent components M yields stronger performance gains; MDLM is a special case (M=1). Code is available at the linked GitHub repository.

Abstract: Discrete diffusion and flow-matching models denoise a sequence over many steps, but to keep each step cheap, they factorize the transition across positions and decide every token independently. This makes few-step generation challenging for text when the target couples two positions, such as a subject and a verb that must agree. An independent update commits to them separately, and many function evaluations are spent repairing the mismatch. Existing few-step methods buy back the lost correlation by distilling or rectifying a slow teacher, and so inherit the teacher's quality ceiling. We ask instead whether a model can express correlated steps natively, and answer with Latent-Kernel Discrete Flow Maps (LKF), a from-scratch flow-map kernel that is a mixture of M factorized components tied by a single shared latent. Conditioned on the latent, each component is cheap, and the mixture is summed over the latent in closed form for small M. We show that a single step places mass on correlated completions with the same sampling time complexity as a factorized model, since one latent is drawn per sequence and reused across the entire denoising trajectory. We also show that the Masked Diffusion Language Model (MDLM) is a special case of our LKF model at M=1. The experiments for unconditional text generation on the One-Billion-Word (LM1B) and WikiText-103 benchmarks show that our LKF model learns strongly heterogeneous components and improves generative perplexity by 2.1x to 3.3x over the likelihood baselines without losing diversity. The gain grows with M, and at M=8, it surpasses distilled and rectified few-step samplers. The source code is available at: https://github.com/mansoor181/lkf.git

</details>


### [290] [When Does Explicit View Routing Work? A Controlled Study of Multi-View Graph-Text Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27530)
*Xiao Yue,Guangzhi Qu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A controlled MV-GTA study distinguishes architectural channelization from semantic routing in graph-text retrieval, showing externally grounded routing can improve performance, but evidence for free-form semantic routing is limited.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate whether multi-head graph-text retrieval truly routes meaning content versus relying on architectural channels; establish causal routing via controlled data and external relevance signals.

Method: Introduce a controlled MV-GTA variant with deterministic text segments, isolated encoders, view-specific graph heads, and external-label/RDKit-based relevance; perform causal tests comparing correctly routed vs deranged routing; evaluate on BBBP and BACE; compare joint multi-head model against single-specialist baselines; assess property paraphrase augmentation.

Result: Correct routing improves label/property nDCG by 0.305–0.685 over deranged training; the expected graph head outperforms the best wrong head by 0.303–0.453; topology effects vary across datasets; in a matched three-seed setup a joint model attains 0.720/1.000/0.877 vs three specialists at 0.633/0.976/0.859; property paraphrase augmentation raises unseen-template nDCG by ~0.140–0.147; consistency and hard-template methods can hurt canonical retrieval in some cases.

Conclusion: Evidence supports externally grounded routing and multi-interface consolidation under constrained conditions but does not establish free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to specialists, or universal performance gains; conclusions are dataset- and setting-dependent.

Abstract: Graph-text retrieval typically maps a graph and its description to a single embedding, even when a query concerns only one semantic aspect, such as a class label or molecular property. Multiple heads can separate these aspects, but a change in the query head may alter retrieval even when the wrong text is sent to that head. Such behavior demonstrates architectural channelization, not necessarily semantic routing. We examine the conditions under which this distinction can be resolved. Our controlled version of MV-GTA uses deterministic, verifiable text segments; isolated text encoders; view-specific graph heads; and relevance derived from external labels or RDKit descriptors. Correct routing and per-sample derangements form a causal test of whether retrieval depends on content. On BBBP and BACE, correct routing improves label and property nDCG by 0.305 to 0.685 over deranged training. The expected graph head exceeds the best wrong head by 0.303 to 0.453. Topology does not specialize consistently across the two datasets. In a matched three-seed comparison, one joint model obtains mean topology, label, and property nDCG of 0.720/1.000/0.877; three separately trained Single specialists obtain 0.633/0.976/0.859. Property paraphrase augmentation also improves unseen-template nDCG by 0.140 and 0.147 over a matched-exposure canonical control. Consistency and hard-template extensions, however, reduce canonical retrieval in some settings. The evidence is therefore limited to explicit, externally grounded label and property routing and observed multi-interface consolidation. It does not establish free-form routing, consistent three-view specialization, statistical equivalence to specialists, or superior downstream prediction.

</details>


### [291] [Subtract or Replay? Exact Deletion from Language-Model Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27539)
*Vishwajith Ramesh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Exact deletion from persistent LM memory depends on memory representation; deletion can be achieved by subtracting addressable records and replaying entangled writes, with measurable trade-offs across architectures.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To determine whether deletion is architecture-independent and whether memory representations constrain deletion, informing privacy guarantees and robustness to redaction attacks.

Method: Experiment 1: Replace Gemma 3's global-attention with support-vector memory; perform low-rank recovery at 1B; compare algebraic decrement vs retained-key refit for 31 deletions; measure next-token KL, perplexity; assess masked-refit vs never-ingested floor; test at 4B and 12B for changes in certificate ordering and utility costs. Experiment 2: In a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid, analyze additive writes (fixed decrement) and diagonal decay (corrected), vs delta-rule (suffix dependence); use checkpointed rewind-and-replay to delete real records up to 18,842 tokens; verify logit and recurrent-state bit-for-bit equality; replay correction to amend.

Result: Experiment 1 yields median KL of 5.4e-15 across 31 deletions; +2.0% perplexity relative to a matched fine-tune; masked-refit indistinguishable from never-ingested floor under elicitation, relearning, sampling, and LiRA attacks; at 4B and 12B, certificate ordering persists but utility costs rise to 11.2% and 44.3%. Experiment 2 shows additive writes give fixed decrement and diagonal decay a corrected one, while delta rule yields 12–49% of a record’s contribution being suffix-dependent. Checkpointed rewind-and-replay deletes real clinical records up to 18,842 tokens, matching never-ingested logits and bit-for-bit recurrent states in a deterministic MLX; replaying a correction provides exact amendment.

Conclusion: Exact deletion is a property of memory representation: one can subtract addressable records and replay entangled writes to achieve redaction or amendment of memory contents.

Abstract: Exact deletion from persistent language-model memory depends on how that memory represents a record. Addressable influence can be removed by algebraic decrement; influence transformed by later writes inside shared recurrent state requires rebuilding from before the write. We test this distinction in two pretrained models against explicit record-omitted references. First, we replace Gemma 3's global-attention layers with support-vector memory. After low-rank recovery at 1B, decrement and retained-key refit agree at the next-token output to median KL $5.4\times10^{-15}$ over 31 support-token deletions, with $+2.0\%$ perplexity relative to a matched fine-tune. A masked-refit proxy is indistinguishable from the never-ingested floor under elicitation, relearning, sampling, and LiRA attacks. At 4B and 12B, certificate ordering persists but utility cost rises to $11.2\%$ and $44.3\%$. Second, in a 48B Kimi Linear hybrid, additive writes admit a fixed decrement and diagonal decay a corrected one, whereas the delta rule makes $12$--$49\%$ of a record's contribution suffix-dependent. Checkpointed rewind-and-replay deletes real clinical records at contexts up to 18,842 tokens, matching never-ingested logits and all recurrent states bit for bit within a deterministic MLX implementation; replaying a correction provides exact amendment. Exact deletion is therefore a property of memory representation: subtract addressable records and replay entangled writes.

</details>


### [292] [Memory Efficient Tabular Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27546)
*Shuting Luo,Monika Mikhail Kanaan,Cameron Gordon,Anna Leontjeva,Simon Lucey*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Compression of TabPFN-like Tabular Foundation Models yields substantial memory savings (up to 7.6x) with negligible performance loss, reducing deployment requirements by about 87%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Practical deployment constraints for tabular foundation models are underexplored; this study quantifies memory requirements and investigates compression to enable real-world use.

Method: Apply model compression techniques to TabPFN variants; evaluate memory usage and accuracy to characterize memory–performance trade-offs.

Result: Memory reductions up to 7.6x demonstrated; deployment memory needs decreased by ~87%; performance preserved relative to uncompressed baselines.

Conclusion: Model compression enables efficient deployment of tabular foundation models without significant performance degradation; provides actionable guidance for practitioners.

Abstract: Tabular Foundation Models, such as TabPFN, have received a large amount of recent attention due to their performance on in-context tabular machine learning tasks, which often exceeds classical baselines. However, practical deployment considerations of these models has received less attention. In this paper we investigate the memory requirements for these models. We demonstrate that employing model compression approaches can enable memory reductions of up to 7.6 with similar levels of performance, reducing deployment requirements by nearly 87%. Our work provides insight to practitioners seeking efficient deployment of these models in practical settings.

</details>


### [293] [Strategies for Milestone-driven Start-ups in Multi-activity Settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27563)
*Zhengli Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A diffusion-based stochastic control model for milestone-driven startups with multiple controls shows that the optimal strategy uses an efficient frontier of controls ordered by riskiness and cost-effectiveness; frontier types vary with parameters, producing qualitatively different policies; provides intuitive evaluation measures and foundational insights for entrepreneurial decision-making.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand how start-up firms should allocate effort across multiple activities under milestone targets, using tractable continuous-time stochastic control when several controls affect drift, diffusion, and cost.

Method: Model the firm state as a diffusion process controlled by multiple actions that change drift, diffusion, and cost. Solve a continuous-time stochastic control problem with fixed success/failure boundaries. Introduce an efficient frontier curve ranking controls by drift-to-volatility (riskiness) and drift-to-cost (cost-effectiveness). Derive the optimal policy and its structure explicitly, showing frontier-type dependent qualitative differences.

Result: Explicit optimal policy characterized; optimal controls lie on the efficient frontier, with the frontier type (varying by parameters) determining the policy's qualitative form. The paper provides intuitive activity measures and shows a foundational block for entrepreneurial decision-making.

Conclusion: This work yields a complete analytical solution for a milestone-oriented startup model with multiple controls, reveals that frontier curves of different types can arise and shape policy, and offers foundational insights and practical evaluation tools for entrepreneurial strategy.

Abstract: New venture start-ups need to ``survive'' through multiple stages of reaching milestone targets. We investigate the strategies for start-ups in a milestone-oriented setting. We examine a model of an entrepreneurial start-up firm, where its state is captured by a diffusion process. The entrepreneur can choose between multiple activities (or controls), which incur different cost and determine the drift and the variance of the process. Depending on whether the process reaches a fixed upper boundary or a lower one, the start-up firm succeeds or fails. Continuous-time stochastic models with multiple ($\ge 3$) controls are typically very challenging to deal with. In this work, we are able to completely solve for the optimal policy and provide an explicit characterization of its structure. In particular, the optimal policy only uses controls from a set characterized by a so-called efficient frontier curve that orders the controls by two intuitive measures: riskiness (drift-to-volatility ratio) and cost-effectiveness (drift-to-cost ratio). A unique feature of our model is that depending on the model parameters, the efficient frontier curves can be of different types, resulting in qualitatively different structures of the optimal policy. As far as we know, this is the first study that analyzes a stochastic control model which admits efficient frontier curves of different types. Our work provides start-up firms with intuitive measures to evaluate their activities and offers valuable insights on how the optimal strategies in a milestone-oriented setting change qualitatively contingent upon the specific scenario. We believe the results provide a foundational block in the study of entrepreneurial decision-making.

</details>


### [294] [A Montage-Agnostic Encoder for Calibration-Light Cross-User Gesture Recognition from Surface Electromyography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27565)
*Jethro Odeyemi,W. J. Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A montage-agnostic, electrode-coordinate-based encoder for EMG-based prosthesis control generalizes across users and channel counts, surpassing per-user baselines on two datasets but not on a third; ablation shows three components drive most performance; cross-subject training exhibits a flat margin across a wide range of training subjects; self-supervised pretraining offers no gains when supervised data is adequate.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-subject transfer in myoelectric pattern-recognition is poor and per-subject calibration is burdensome. A montage-agnostic, scalable encoder that can ingest varying channel counts without montage-specific parameters could enable practical, multi-gesture control.

Method: A montage-agnostic encoder with shared weights per electrode is defined by physical coordinates rather than index. Trained across users and evaluated on multiple EMG datasets (DB1, DB2, DB5). 3-shot macro-F1 as primary metric. conducts ablation studies to assess three key components, performs a subject-count sweep to study cross-subject training stability, and compares against Hudgins feature-based classifiers and an LDA baseline. Also evaluates self-supervised pretraining versus supervised models.

Result: The encoder exceeds the per-user Hudgins and LDA baselines by 0.234 macro-F1 on DB1 and 0.108 on DB2, but falls below it on DB5. Each of its three key components accounts for more than half of its 3-shot macro-F1 in ablation. The cross-subject training margin is nearly flat from nine to thirty-nine training subjects, indicating a stability floor; cross-dataset direction of the comparison is governed by the strength of the per-user baseline. LDA comparisons depend on training budget and baseline quality, and self-supervised pretraining provides no advantage when supervised data is sufficient.

Conclusion: Montage-agnostic encoding can achieve cross-subject generalization in EMG-based control with stability across a wide training set, but gains are dataset-dependent. The architecture's robustness to montage and channel counts is demonstrated, though some datasets (e.g., DB5) reveal limits; training pool size matters for convergence and cross-subject transfer relies on baseline fidelity.

Abstract: Pattern-recognition control promises a myoelectric prosthesis that responds to many intended gestures rather than one or two, but the promise has stayed in the laboratory. A recogniser trained on one person rarely transfers to the next, and useful performance usually demands a fresh round of labelled calibration from the end user. A montage-agnostic encoder is introduced that reads each electrode with shared weights and locates it by its physical coordinate rather than its index, so one architecture ingests any channel count without montage-specific parameters. Trained across users, it exceeds a per-user Hudgins and linear-discriminant classifier by 0.234 macro-F1 on DB1 for every held-out subject and by 0.108 on DB2, and falls below it on the ten-subject DB5. Each of the encoder's three key components individually accounts for more than half of its 3-shot macro F1 in an otherwise budget-matched ablation study. A controlled subject-count sweep shows the margin is close to flat from nine training subjects to thirty-nine, so the training pool binds only as a stability floor below which cross-user training fails to converge; what tracks the direction of the comparison across the three databases is instead the strength of the per-user baseline, which signal fidelity sets. Comparing against an LDA baseline depends on budget spent training models and on how good that baseline is, and self-supervised pretraining had no benefits once a supervised model was adequately trained.

</details>


### [295] [Recognition and Label-Free Adaptation Across Recording Sessions in Surface-EMG Gesture Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27568)
*Jethro Odeyemi,W. J. Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A montage-agnostic encoder enables cross-session transfer for myoelectric pattern recognition, outperforming per-user baselines on macro-F1 and approaching baselines on per-window metrics; however, memory of performance is highly sensitive to adaptation technique, with feature-statistic alignment being the only reliable test-time method.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address day-to-day EMG variability that breaks cross-session recognition, without onerous per-session recalibration.

Method: Train a montage-agnostic encoder on data from a single recording session (NinaPro DB6, ten intact subjects) and apply unchanged to later sessions; compare to a per-user LDA baseline and two published session-only baselines; evaluate five label-free test-time adaptations (e.g., feature-statistic alignment, batch-normalisation re-estimation).

Result: Encoder retained macro-F1 of 0.688 across sessions vs 0.540 for per-user LDA; on the per-window metric, the baselines sit roughly two points above the encoder (i.e., the encoder is near but not clearly superior). Among adaptations, only feature-statistic alignment consistently improved all subjects; batch-normalisation re-estimation collapsed the model; alignment recovers performance close to a single labelled calibration repetition.

Conclusion: Cross-session transfer is feasible with a montage-agnostic encoder; effective adaptation should target feature-statistic alignment rather than normalization re-estimation to preserve cross-session robustness.

Abstract: Recognition accuracy obtained during a recording session does not persist when a user puts on the electrodes again after the electrodes had previously been removed. The electrodes may have moved slightly, the skin may be drier or wetter, or the elbow may be positioned differently; these factors all contribute to day-to-day variability and therefore represent a major obstacle to implementing successful pattern-recognition based myoelectric control systems in daily practice. However, simply recalibrating a user's hand for 20 min at every doff/don event is a clearly unrealistic expectation. A montage-agnostic encoder built for cross-user, cross-montage transfer is trained here using data collected during a particular recording session, and then applied to data collected later in a different recording session without adjusting anything, on the ten intact subjects of NinaPro DB6. The performance of this approach is compared to that of a per-user LDA classification pipeline, and to that of two published approaches that only rely on source data collected from the same recording session. Carried unchanged across recording sessions, the encoder retains 0.688 macro-F1 against 0.540 for the per-user pipeline, and, on the per-window metric the published baselines use, sits above both published source-only results, a band of two points that locates the encoder rather than ranking it. Of five label-free test-time adaptations, only feature-statistic alignment improves every subject; batch-normalisation re-estimation, a standard method in the domain-adaptation literature, collapses this architecture entirely. Aligning the encoder's feature statistics to the new session recovers about what a single labelled calibration repetition would.

</details>


### [296] [Policy Gradient Steering: Interventions from Behavioral Objectives](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27574)
