*Yoann Poupart,Aurélie Beynier,Nicolas Maudet*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Policy Gradient Steering (PGS) treats steering as a reinforcement learning problem, accumulating gradient signals from short rollouts or demonstrations to form removable, task-specific vectors that temporarily alter model behavior. Demonstrations across gridworld, chess puzzles, and football show calibration, reversibility, and constructive composability across objectives and opponents.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Activation-based steering methods often fail to influence simple policies and lack a natural, reversible interface for temporary behavior changes across diverse domains, motivating a gradient-based, composable solution.

Method: Formulate steering as an RL objective and accumulate gradients of a temporary behavioral objective over a small set of rollouts or demonstrations to construct a removable task vector. Evaluate independently fitted PGS vectors in isolation and in combination, and test transferability across opponents.

Result: PGS demonstrates calibration and reversibility in a two-route gridworld. In chess puzzles, independently fitted vectors are effective alone and can combine constructively when compatible. In competitive football, PGS can alter specific team behaviors with transfer of effects across opponents.

Conclusion: Policy gradients provide a natural interface for constructing temporary and composable behavioral adaptations across diverse decision-making domains.

Abstract: Activation steering has emerged in large language models as a lightweight alternative for dynamically changing a model's behavior at inference time. However, we show that existing steering methods fail to steer even a simple policy in a two-route gridworld environment. To address this limitation, we propose Policy Gradient Steering (PGS), which formulates steering as a reinforcement learning problem. PGS accumulates gradients of a temporary behavioral objective over a small set of rollouts or demonstrations to construct a removable task vector. We first demonstrate the calibration and reversibility of PGS in a two-route gridworld environment. Using chess puzzles, we then evaluate independently fitted PGS vectors both in isolation and in combination, finding that compatible tactical objectives accumulate constructively. Finally, in competitive football, we show that PGS can alter specific team behaviors and that its effects transfer across opponents. Together, these results show that policy gradients provide a natural interface for constructing temporary and composable behavioral adaptations across diverse decision-making domains.

</details>


### [297] [MUGEN: A Unified Framework for Efficient Motion Understanding and Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27581)
*Zhankai Ye,Yukai Jin,Bingyang Wei,Bofan Li,Yusen Wu,Fangyi Li,Shangqian Gao,Xin Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: MUGEN is a no-codebook, single-draw unified motion–language model. It uses an adaptive-length autoencoder to compress motions into a few continuous latent slots, which a language model can generate and interpret in one pass, enabling efficient text-to-motion and motion understanding without the heavy decoding machinery of discrete token approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantization in prior unified motion–language systems (discrete codebooks, stacked residuals, diffusion heads) incurs high decoding cost and can hurt generation quality and efficiency. A continuous, single-slot representation could simplify the pipeline and improve both generation and understanding.

Method: Propose MUGEN: a single adaptive-length autoencoder compresses any-length motion into a few continuous latent slots (the only motion representation). A language model generates these slots for text-to-motion and reads them back for understanding. Depth-routed hidden states allow each latent slot to read from the appropriate transformer depth; a calibrated head predicts a joint distribution over the full latent set, enabling a single draw to encode cross-slot variation conditioned on text. Decoding cost is a fixed K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass.

Result: MUGEN achieves state-of-the-art results: surpasses LM baselines on FID for HumanML3D; retrieves more accurately than real-motion reference under standard evaluator; achieves best CIDEr and BLEU@4; outperforms discrete-token SOTA on SnapMoGen for retrieval and alignment metrics.

Conclusion: A continuous, single-draw, adaptive-length autoencoder latent representation suffices for unified motion–language tasks, offering competitive or superior performance with significantly reduced decoding cost compared to prior discrete-token approaches.

Abstract: Grounding human motion in language, and language in motion, is a central step toward physical AI systems that can understand, generate, and communicate human behavior. Unified motion--language systems first coupled the two directions through a shared discrete motion codebook, but quantization limits generation quality. The strongest generators buy quality back at growing cost: stacked residual codebooks enlarge the representation; masked decoding stages, long autoregressive rollouts, and denoising chains of tens to hundreds of steps stretch inference; even the continuous-latent designs among them reach their latent only through an iterative diffusion head; and none of this decoding machinery serves understanding. We therefore propose MUGEN, a unified motion--language framework that pays neither cost: no codebook, one draw. A single adaptive-length autoencoder compresses any-length motion into a few continuous latent slots, the system's only motion representation: the language model generates them for text-to-motion and reads them back for motion understanding. Depth-routed hidden states let each slot read from the transformer depth it needs, and a calibrated head predicts a joint distribution over the full latent set, so a single draw carries the text-conditional, cross-slot variation a description permits. At a decoding cost of K language-model steps, one draw, and one decoder pass, MUGEN leads language-model baselines on FID on HumanML3D while raising retrieval precision above the real-motion reference under the standard evaluator, achieves the best CIDEr and BLEU@4 scores, and surpasses the discrete-token state of the art on every retrieval and alignment metric on SnapMoGen.

</details>


### [298] [Prox: Training-Free FFN Activation Sparsity via Approximate Intermediate-Channel Salience in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27591)
*Jinyi Liu,Wei Chen,Pengyu Chen,Xinyi Yuan,Minghe Bai,Guoquan Wu,Jun Wei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Two-stage training-free sparse SwiGLU FFN method (Prox) constructs a channel mask from SwiGLU's intermediate state magnitude, enabling sparse execution with up to ~2x speedup at 70% FFN sparsity, compatible with quantization and sparse attention.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Activation sparsification in LLMs is hampered by poor channel-selection strategies in training-free methods; the SwiGLU intermediate state is a strong signal for channel importance but is expensive to compute densely.

Method: Stage 1 builds a shared channel mask using input sparsity and quantized proxy weights; Stage 2 computes the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections. The mask is derived from the magnitude ranking of the SwiGLU intermediate state's entries rather than their exact values, enabling sparse computation.

Result: Empirical evaluation across ten LLMs from six model families shows Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels, achieving up to 1.99× end-to-end decoding speedup at 70% FFN sparsity, and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention.

Conclusion: Prox provides an effective training-free approach for sparse SwiGLU FFNs, delivering substantial speedups with broad compatibility; it leverages a magnitude-based channel mask derived from the SwiGLU intermediate state to enable efficient sparse execution.

Abstract: Feed-forward networks (FFNs) dominate memory traffic and computation in large language model (LLM) inference, making them a primary target for activation sparsification. However, existing training-free methods suffer substantial model-quality degradation at high sparsity due to limitations in their channel-selection strategies. We observe that the SwiGLU intermediate state provides a highly effective channel-selection signal, but obtaining it requires costly dense computation. To address this, we present \emph{Prox}, a two-stage training-free framework for sparse SwiGLU FFNs. Prox hinges on the key insight: sparse execution requires only the channel mask induced by the intermediate state, which can be constructed from the magnitude ranking of its entries rather than their exact values. Specifically, Stage 1 uses input sparsity and quantized proxy weights to construct a shared mask; Stage 2 computes the selected channels exactly, enabling sparse execution of all three projections. Across ten LLMs from six model families, Prox outperforms training-free baselines at all sparsity levels, achieves up to a $1.99\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup at 70\% FFN sparsity, and is compatible with quantization and sparse attention.

</details>


### [299] [Compliance2LoRA: On-Demand Safety Alignment on Arbitrary Policy Subsets via Hypernetwork-Generated LoRA Adapters](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27594)
*Pankayaraj Pathmanathan,Furong Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes ours, an adaptive hypernetwork that generates policy-specific LoRA adapters conditioned on safety policies, enabling on-demand multi-policy compliance for LRMs without retraining separate models and with preserved task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There's a growing need to personalize large reasoning models (LRMs) to user-specific safety policies. Training distinct LRMs per policy subset is combinatorially expensive; in-context methods incur long-context costs and may not scale well. A unified adaptive mechanism, via a hypernetwork that outputs policy-conditioned adapters, offers scalable multi-policy compliance.

Method: A hypernetwork takes safety policy inputs and outputs LoRA adapter weights to be applied to the downstream LRM. These weights steer generation to comply with the specified policy subsets. The hypernetwork is trained to map policy subsets to corresponding adapters, enabling on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM across models of different sizes and datasets.

Result: Training the hypernetwork enables on-demand policy adjustments without sacrificing task performance across reasoning models of varying sizes and evaluation datasets, demonstrating the practicality and effectiveness of adaptive hypernetwork-based alignment for multi-policy compliance.

Conclusion: Adaptive hypernetwork-based alignment is a practical and effective approach to achieving multi-policy compliance in LRMs, reducing combinatorial overhead while maintaining performance.

Abstract: Post-training alignment in large reasoning models (LRMs) has significantly improved their adaptability to diverse safety compliance settings. However, as LRMs personalization for downstream users takes center stage, the demand for varying levels of policy compliance grows as different user-specific LRMs must adhere to distinct subsets of safety policies. Training a separate LRM for each policy subset introduces severe combinatorial overhead. While in context learning methods overcome this combinatorial overhead, they introduce additional computational challenges associated with long context generation. To address this challenge, we propose \ours, a unified adaptive hypernetwork-based framework for multi-policy compliance. In our framework, safety policies serve as customizable inputs to a LoRA adapter generator, which learns to produce policy compliant LoRA weights for downstream LRM. When added to the LRM these weights enable the generation of responses compliant with the specified policy subsets. In this work, we demonstrate that training such a hypernetwork enables on-demand policy adjustments on a single LRM without sacrificing task performance across reasoning models of different sized and different evaluation datasets. This highlights the effectiveness and practicality of adaptive hypernetwork based alignment in LRMs.

</details>


### [300] [Back from the Future: Key-Value Cache Management by Counter-Causal Surprise](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27600)
*Stephen Gould,Anton van den Hengel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Counter-causal KV eviction for LLM cache to reduce memory footprint and speed up inference without training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: KV caches in LLMs grow linearly with context length, causing memory pressure during long prompts or outputs; efficient eviction is needed to maintain performance within hardware limits.

Method: Score eviction by re-running the model on the cached tokens with a counter-causal mask that attends only to future context, reusing existing KV representations. Also propose a fast single-layer approximation limiting the counter-causal pass to the last transformer layer to speed up refresh cycles.

Result: Demonstrates competitive or improved performance vs. state-of-the-art KV eviction strategies across multiple open-source LLMs and benchmarks, with reduced compute for refresh cycles.

Conclusion: Counter-causal KV eviction is an effective, training-free mechanism for managing KV caches, offering memory savings and speedups with minimal accuracy loss; a lightweight single-layer variant provides substantial speedups with marginal accuracy cost; code is available at the provided GitHub link.

Abstract: Key-value (KV) cache management through compression and eviction strategies has emerged as an important research direction in recent years. Computational demands of large language models (LLMs) and their multi-modal variants during output generation can be partially alleviated by caching previous key and value calculations needed by subsequent scaled dot-product attention operations. However, this leads to another problem: the size of the resulting KV cache grows linearly with context length and quickly consumes all available GPU memory when either the prompt or the generated output are long. KV cache management periodically prunes entries from the cache thereby reducing its memory footprint while attempting to retain sufficient information for accurate generation. A by-product is faster inference speed. We propose a simple yet effective KV eviction scheme motivated by the insight that past tokens which can be well-predicted from more recent tokens are redundant and their associated keys and values can be removed from the cache. To score entries for eviction we run the model on the tokens in their original order, reusing the key and value representations already stored in the KV cache, and applying a counter-causal attention mask so that each position attends only to its future context. This is in-distribution, tied directly to the actual cache contents, and requires no additional training. To further reduce cost, we additionally propose a fast single-layer approximation that restricts the counter-causal pass to the last transformer layer, achieving a significant speedup per refresh cycle at marginal accuracy cost. We evaluate our strategy on various open-source LLMs and benchmark datasets showing competitive or improved performance over other state-of-the-art methods. Reference code is available at https://github.com/metacognitionai/counter_causal.

</details>


### [301] [Kalman Meets Curriculum: Efficient Dynamic Prompt Selection for Adaptive RL Finetuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27610)
*Haodong Zhu,Yangyang Ren,Yanjing Li,Sheng Xu,Haiguang Liu,Linlin Yang,Baochang Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Kalman-Guided Prompt Selection (KGPS) tracks each prompt's latent success rate with a linear-Gaussian state-space model in logit space; a Kalman filter updates a Gaussian posterior of prompt difficulty with process noise tied to policy update magnitude; prompts are chosen by maximizing a posterior-expected training utility, favoring intermediate difficulty and revisiting uncertainty. Shows consistent improvements in final accuracy and rollout efficiency across math, planning, and geometry benchmarks and multiple RL algorithms, achieving state-of-the-art among online prompt selection methods (e.g., 83% fewer rollouts on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B with +0.12 average score).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Prompt difficulty evolves during RL finetuning of LLMs, making fixed or stationary-prediction-based selection ineffective. There is a need for an online, non-stationary prompt selection method that adapts to policy drift without extra rollouts.

Method: Model each prompt's latent success rate in logit space using a linear-Gaussian state-space model. The process noise scales with policy update magnitude, capturing non-stationarity. Use a Kalman filter to maintain a Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty. Select prompts by maximizing a posterior-expected training utility, which favors intermediate difficulty and revisits uncertain prompts; requires no extra rollouts beyond standard policy training.

Result: KGPS consistently improves final accuracy and rollout efficiency across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks and multiple RL algorithms, setting state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods.

Conclusion: KGPS provides an adaptive, data-efficient prompt selection mechanism robust to policy drift in RL-finetuned LLMs, with strong empirical gains and wide applicability to online prompting strategies.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) finetuning significantly enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), yet its effectiveness critically depends on selecting prompts of appropriate difficulty for the current policy. This is challenging because prompt difficulty evolves throughout training. Existing online methods therefore face a trade-off: evaluation-based approaches are accurate but expensive, while prediction-based approaches are efficient but typically assume stationary difficulty, making them ill-suited to RL's non-stationary training dynamics. To address these issues, we propose a Kalman-Guided Prompt Selection method (KGPS), which reformulates prompt selection as a dynamic state estimation problem rather than static difficulty prediction. KGPS models each prompt's latent success rate in logit space using a linear-Gaussian state-space model, with process noise coupled to the magnitude of policy updates so that uncertainty increases when the policy changes more substantially. A Kalman filter then maintains a calibrated Gaussian posterior over prompt difficulty, and prompts are selected by maximizing a posterior-expected training utility that favors intermediate-difficulty prompts while naturally revisiting uncertain ones. The resulting procedure is adaptive to policy drift and requires no additional rollouts beyond standard policy training. Extensive experiments across mathematics, planning, and geometry reasoning benchmarks, as well as multiple RL algorithms, show that KGPS consistently improves both final accuracy and rollout efficiency over strong baselines, establishing state-of-the-art performance among online prompt selection methods. For example, on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B, KGPS uses 83% fewer rollouts than DS while even improving the average performance by 0.12 point across six math reasoning benchmarks.

</details>


### [302] [Real-Time Hard Peak Age-of-Information Safety with No-Regret Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27626)
*Wentao Zhang,Wentao Mo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Transforms hard per-slot AoI deadlines into affine half-space constraints on a resource-allocation vector, formulating time-varying constrained online convex optimization (OCO) over a polyhedral safe set. Proposes a strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop with a single Euclidean projection per slot, achieving no-regret and zero modeled-state deadline violations under adversarial conditions, plus matching lower bounds and competitive ratios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety-critical IoT systems require strict per-slot AoI deadlines rather than mere long-term averages. Existing methods fail to guarantee per-slot feasibility under adversarial or uncertain channels; there is a need for algorithms with hard guarantees and theoretical optimality in online settings.

Method: Model the fractional peak-AoI deadline as an affine half-space constraint on the allocation vector. Solve a time-varying constrained online convex optimization problem over a polyhedral safe set using a strictly causal loop: at each slot, perform a gradient step and project onto the safe set (one Euclidean projection). The virtual queue is repurposed as an a-posteriori certificate. Provide static/dynamic regret bounds, a minimax Omega(sqrt(T)) lower bound, a margin-safe variant, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio.

Result: The approach achieves zero modeled-state deadline violations on a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel across ten seeds. Baselines exhibit nonzero slot violations (1.65% to 64.0%). Empirical normalized regret remains below the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in horizon T.

Conclusion: OCO-PAoI-Hard offers hard per-slot AoI guarantees in adversarial environments by recasting scheduling as time-varying constrained OCO over a polyhedral safe set, with solid regret analysis, tight lower bounds, and compelling empirical validation. This framework supports scalable, deadline-respecting scheduling in safety-critical IoT, subject to modeling assumptions and computational feasibility per slot.

Abstract: Safety-critical IoT systems such as industrial closed-loop control, V2X coordination, and remote teleoperation require every sensor's peak Age of Information (peak AoI, also abbreviated PAoI) to stay below a hard per-slot deadline, not merely an average bound. Existing approaches meet this requirement only under restrictive assumptions: stochastic channels for Whittle-index AoI, simulator rollouts for deep reinforcement learning, or sublinear cumulative violation for long-term constrained online convex optimization. Under adversarial coefficients, OCO-PAoI-Hard guarantees zero per-slot violation of the modeled AoI state under one-step viability and O(sqrt(T)) regret against any static safe comparator; packet-level safety requires stronger service assumptions. Our key observation is that the fractional peak-AoI deadline collapses exactly to an affine half-space constraint on the resource-allocation vector, turning hard real-time scheduling into time-varying constrained online convex optimization over a polyhedral safe set. A strictly causal proposal-shield-update loop enforces feasibility through one Euclidean projection per slot, the gradient step preserves no-regret behavior, and the classical virtual queue is reduced to an a-posteriori certificate. We establish closed-form static and dynamic regret bounds, a matching Omega(sqrt(T)) minimax lower bound, a margin-safe variant against execution noise, and a deadline-induced competitive ratio. On a four-sensor adversarial fluid-model trap channel, OCO-PAoI-Hard attains zero modeled-state deadline violations across all ten seeds, while four representative baselines miss between 1.65 percent and 64.0 percent of slots, and the empirical normalized regret stays below the theoretical envelope across two orders of magnitude in T.

</details>


### [303] [First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization Over Distributed Networks for Robust Coreset Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27632)
*Yang Jiao,Kaixuan Jiao,Kai Yang,Nadjib Aitsaadi,Ilhem Fajjari,Renwei,Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes F^2CTO, a Federated First-order Constrained Trilevel Optimization framework for distributed robust coreset selection, achieving non-asymptotic convergence to an ε-stationary point (O(ε^{-3/2})), with empirical validation in reliable continual learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The explosion of IoT edge data makes full-data training costly; robust coreset selection in a privacy-preserving distributed setting is essential but underexplored. The work aims to jointly address data efficiency, robustness, and privacy in distributed learning by formulating and solving a trilevel optimization problem.

Method: Formulates distributed robust coreset selection as a trilevel optimization with level-wise constraints. Introduces F^2CTO, combining a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation with a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm to solve the problem in a federated setting.

Result: Establishes a non-asymptotic convergence rate of O(ε^{-3/2}) to an ε-stationary point for the proposed method. Empirically demonstrates effectiveness and efficiency on reliable continual learning tasks.

Conclusion: F^2CTO is the first distributed method for robust coreset selection and the first to address trilevel optimization with level-wise constraints in a distributed setting, showing theoretical convergence guarantees and practical performance benefits.

Abstract: With the rapid advancement of the Internet of Things (IoT), massive amounts of data are generated across distributed edge networks. Training models on full data incurs significant computational overhead and storage bottlenecks, rendering coreset selection a critical paradigm. Furthermore, given the privacy-sensitive nature of local data and the escalating demand for model robustness in real-world deployments, developing an effective distributed optimization framework for robust coreset selection is vital, yet remains largely unexplored. To this end, this work first characterizes the hierarchical dependencies among coreset selection, robust optimization, and distributed learning, and formulates the distributed robust coreset selection as a trilevel optimization problem with level-wise constraints. Furthermore, to effectively solve the trilevel problem in a distributed manner, the \underline{F}ederated \underline{F}irst-order \underline{C}onstrained \underline{T}rilevel \underline{O}ptimization (F$^2$CTO) is proposed, which synergistically integrates a hierarchical composite value-function reformulation and a distributed alternating projected gradient algorithm. To the best of our knowledge, F$^2$CTO is the first method developed for distributed robust coreset selection, as well as the first distributed optimization approach for trilevel optimization problems with level-wise constraints. Additionally, we prove that the proposed method achieves a non-asymptotic convergence rate of $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-3/2})$ for finding an $ε$-stationary point. Extensive empirical evaluations on reliable continual learning demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed F$^2$CTO.

</details>


### [304] [Certifying when decision-time information justifies adaptive experimentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27651)
*Jia Bi,Samuel Pinilla,Chenyang Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OPAL introduces an authorization layer governing when adaptation is allowed in adaptive experiments; derives impossibility bounds under outcome shift and offers a target-calibrated recovery; demonstrates safe, non-trivial adaptation with positive value and bounded false activation on a 11,265-compound Cell Painting task, outperforming alternatives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Regulate adaptation to prevent unsafe or wasteful experimentation under distribution shifts, ensuring non-trivial adaptation yields value. Provide a distinct safety layer for adaptive lab workflows.

Method: Propose a precommitted contract that requires non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk, and positive executed value. Prove an impossibility boundary under unrestricted conditional outcome shift and derive a target-calibrated recovery. Apply to an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition; compare six methods; report activation, opportunities, executed value, and false-activation bounds.

Result: In a frozen-gate setup, OPAL selected 595 compounds, identified 384 positive opportunities, and achieved strictly positive executed value under the least-favourable completion; the false-activation upper bound was 5.18%, below a 7.5% limit. Among six methods, only OPAL coupled non-zero activation with risk control.

Conclusion: Authorization operates as a distinct safety layer for safe adaptive science, differentiating policy misalignment from non-certifiability and enabling safe, non-trivial adaptation in practice.

Abstract: Adaptive laboratories choose measurements during experiments, yet most methods begin after adaptation is permitted. We introduce Opportunity-aware Policy Authorization for Laboratories (\OPAL{}), a framework that decides whether adaptation should be enabled at all. \OPAL{} uses a precommitted contract to require non-trivial adaptation, controlled target risk and positive executed value after cost. We establish an impossibility boundary: source outcomes and unlabelled target covariates cannot uniformly support non-trivial authorization under unrestricted conditional outcome shift, and derive a target-calibrated recovery. Applied to an unseen 11,265-compound Cell Painting partition, the frozen gate selected 595 compounds, captured 384 positive opportunities and achieved strictly positive executed value under least-favourable completion; its 5.18\% false-activation upper bound remained below a 7.5\% limit. Among six methods, only \OPAL{} combined non-zero activation with this risk control. Locked pharmacogenomic and finite-campaign studies distinguish policy misalignment from non-certifiability, establishing authorization as a distinct layer for safe adaptive science.

</details>


### [305] [Evaluation Protocols and Cross-Subject Generalization in EEG Emotion Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27655)
*Hanting Suo,Yuwen Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper argues that reported EEG emotion recognition accuracy is highly dependent on evaluation protocol and reporting rules, not just the classifier, and demonstrates substantial variability across protocols (subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session) and data splits, questioning comparability and generalization claims.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To disentangle target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rules in EEG emotion recognition to enable fairer, more reproducible comparisons of classifiers.

Method: Re-examine an archived dynamical graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) pathway on SEED and SEED-IV across multiple evaluation setups: protocol-matched subject-dependent checks, five-fold subject-disjoint validation, and hold-out subject tests; analyze checkpoint selection, training/test splits, and time-scale/representation effects.

Result: Protocol-matched SEED results were within 1.47 percentage points of a public reference; SEED-IV differed by 3.40 points (unresolved). Checkpoint selection on repeated test-set evaluation raised mean window accuracy from 0.7855 (epoch 80) to 0.8892. In five-fold subject-disjoint tests, validation-selected checkpoints yielded training-participant trial accuracies of 0.9990 (SEED) and 0.9920 (SEED-IV). Held-out subject accuracies were 0.5348 (SEED; 95% BCa [0.4667, 0.5985]) and 0.3954 (SEED-IV; [0.3343, 0.4648]). Train-to-held-out gaps suggest factors beyond simple underfitting, including representation, preprocessing, and distributional effects; rankings depended on representation/time scale; tail-risk ensembles did not provide robust gains. Conclude that subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results answer different questions and should be reported separately.

Conclusion: Accurate comparison and interpretation of EEG emotion-recognition performance require explicit reporting of multiple evaluation protocols and data splits; current single-score reporting can be misleading due to protocol leakage and varied generalization conditions.

Abstract: Reported accuracy in electroencephalography (EEG) emotion recognition depends on the complete evaluation procedure, not only the classifier. We separate the target quantity, development procedure, and reporting rule, then use one archived dynamical graph convolutional neural network (DGCNN) pathway on SEED and SEED-IV as an illustrative case. In a protocol-matched subject-dependent check, the SEED result was within 1.47 percentage points of the public reference value; the 3.40-point SEED-IV difference remained unresolved. Across 30 matched SEED subject-session trajectories, checkpoint selection based on repeated test-set evaluation increased mean window accuracy from 0.7855 at epoch 80 to 0.8892. Under five-fold subject-disjoint evaluation, validation-selected checkpoints achieved training-participant trial accuracies of 0.9990 on SEED and 0.9920 on SEED-IV. Accuracy for entirely held-out participants was 0.5348 (95% conditional subject-level bias-corrected and accelerated [BCa] interval [0.4667, 0.5985]) on SEED. The SEED-IV estimate was 0.3954 ([0.3343, 0.4648]) and is reported only as secondary sensitivity evidence because its protocol-matched compatibility check remained unresolved. The observed train-to-held-out-subject gaps are inconsistent with simple optimization underfitting, but they do not isolate subject identity from implementation, preprocessing, representation, or distributional factors. Supporting analyses further showed that participant rankings depended on representation and time scale, while a development-selected tail-risk ensemble did not establish a positive gain in a separate final evaluation. Subject-dependent, subject-disjoint, and cross-session results should therefore be reported as answers to different questions.

</details>


### [306] [Looped Transformers with Source-Centered State Evolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27656)
*Bum Jun Kim,Kohei Hayashi,Shunsuke Kamiya,Masanori Koyama,Yusuke Iwasawa,Yutaka Matsuo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SCSE introduces Source-Centered State Evolution to reconcile input conditioning with shared recurrence in looped transformers, achieving anchor invariance and improved recurrent quality across language modeling benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address how additive input conditioning interacts with a shared recurrent block in looped transformers, which can undermine stable state evolution and anchor invariance across depths.

Method: Define anchor and initial deviation; allow nonzero deviations to drive recurrence while mapping zero deviation to zero; enforce exact anchor invariance with a zero-deviation mask; set zero-deviation forcing bias to zero; treat anchor as a one-step fixed point; analyze via ablations and case studies.

Result: SCSE improves recurrent quality frontier across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA; ablations show anchor and anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence as primary contributors; case study links anchor-response to recurrent motion.

Conclusion: The zero-deviation forcing bias is a design degree of freedom, which SCSE neutralizes by enforcing zero bias, yielding exact anchor invariance and improved state evolution in looped transformers.

Abstract: Looped Transformers create a useful train- and test-time compute axis by reusing the same Transformer block over recurrent depth, increasing effective depth at a fixed parameter count. However, that shared block must then govern an entire trajectory of varying hidden states over trained and extrapolated depths. Furthermore, in additive-injection looped Transformers, an input-conditioned signal is reintroduced at every recurrent step, so applying the shared transition at an input-conditioned reference can still move the hidden state. In this paper, we propose Source-Centered State Evolution (SCSE), which is designed to reconcile input conditioning with reference-preserving shared recurrence. Specifically, SCSE retains input dependence through its learned anchor and initial deviation, allows nonzero deviations to drive recurrent computation while mapping zero deviation to zero, and guarantees exact anchor invariance through its zero-deviation mask. The designated anchor is thereby a one-step fixed point by construction. The zero-deviation forcing bias is the next deviation produced from the anchor itself and vanishes in SCSE, while nonzero deviations remain active and support state-dependent recurrent computation. Our theory shows that the zero-deviation forcing bias is a design degree of freedom whose task effect can be harmful, neutral, or beneficial; SCSE resolves this choice in favor of exact anchor invariance by setting the bias to zero. Across WikiText-2, WikiText-103, direct web-corpus pretraining, held-out web-text transfer, and LAMBADA completion, SCSE improves the controlled recurrent quality frontier. Ablation studies identify the learned anchor and the anchor-coordinate deviation recurrence as the primary contributors to the gain, and a trained-model case study grounds the anchor-response diagnostic in observed recurrent motion.

</details>


### [307] [Understanding Submodular Information Measure Based Objectives for Representation Learning: A Variance and Separation Perspective](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27660)
*Rishabh Iyer,Truong Pham,Anay Majee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Unified theory for submodular information measures (SIMs) linking TI/MI objectives to intra-/inter-class structure across TI/MI variants (Graph Cut, LogDet, Facility Location); validated with synthetic experiments; guides design of SIM-based representation learning objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Clarify how different SIM-based objectives shape geometric and statistical properties of representations (variance, covariance, imbalance, separation, overlap), to inform objective design in SIM-based learning.

Method: Develop theoretical mappings from Total Information (TI) and Mutual Information (MI) variants (Graph Cut TI, LogDet TI, Facility Location TI; Graph Cut MI, LogDet MI, Facility Location MI) to intra- and inter-class notions (variance, generalized variance, covariance volume, Fisher-style discrimination, Mahalanobis distance, nearest-mode overlap). Propose a unified framework and validate with controlled synthetic experiments varying variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap.

Result: A unified geometric-statistical understanding of SIMs: TI objectives characterize intra-class structure (within-class variance, generalized variance, imbalance-aware separation) and MI objectives capture inter-class structure (centroid separation, covariance-aware separation, nearest-mode overlap). Theoretical mappings align with empirical behavior in controlled simulations, enabling principled objective selection.

Conclusion: This work provides the first unified framework for SIMs, enabling principled design and selection of SIM-based objectives in representation learning, with potential extensions to handling imbalance and multimodal overlap in practical tasks.

Abstract: Submodular Information Measures (SIMs) have recently emerged as a powerful framework for representation learning and multimodal learning. In particular, the SCORE framework~\cite{majee2024score} demonstrated that SIMs can serve as effective objectives for supervised contrastive learning. Despite their empirical success, however, the geometric and statistical properties induced by different submodular information measures remain poorly understood.
  In this work, we develop a unified theoretical framework connecting SIMs to classical concepts in representation learning and statistical pattern recognition. We show that Total Information (TI) objectives characterize intra-class structure: Graph Cut TI recovers within-class variance, LogDet TI recovers generalized variance and covariance volume, and Facility Location TI induces imbalance-aware separation that emphasizes rare and confusable classes. We further show that Mutual Information (MI) objectives capture complementary notions of inter-class structure: Graph Cut MI is closely related to centroid separation and Fisher-style discrimination, LogDet MI captures covariance-aware separation through Mahalanobis distance, and Facility Location MI measures nearest-mode representational overlap.
  We validate these theoretical characterizations using controlled synthetic experiments that independently vary variance, covariance, class imbalance, class separation, and multimodal overlap. Across all settings, the empirical behavior closely matches the proposed theory. Our results provide the first unified geometric and statistical understanding of submodular information measures and offer principled guidance for selecting and designing SIM-based objectives for representation learning.

</details>


### [308] [FedOGL: Combating Catastrophic Forgetting in Federated Open-World Multimodal Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27665)
*Zekai Chen,Haodong Lu,Shihao Li,Weiwei Ji,Xunkai Li,Xun Wu,Yinlin Zhu,Rong-Hua Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FedOGL is a semantic-structural memory preservation framework for federated graph learning that mitigates catastrophic forgetting in multimodal graphs by combining client-side replay and task-start distillation with projection onto a global structure basis, and server-side compact category prototypes for privacy-preserving cross-client knowledge sharing; it reports a 42.67% reduction in forgetting compared to strong baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In federated multimodal graphs, new classes can emerge while historical categories must be retained, and samples outside the known class space must be rejected. Catastrophic forgetting is compounded by modality-semantic overwriting, topology-driven erosion, and federated memory fragmentation, necessitating mechanisms to preserve semantic and structural memory across clients.

Method: Client side: preserve historical decision behavior through replay and task-start distillation; protect graph-propagation memory by projecting onto a globally shared structure basis. Server side: maintain and transfer compact category prototypes to facilitate cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data.

Result: Experiments show FedOGL reduces performance degradation due to catastrophic forgetting by 42.67% relative to the best-performing baselines, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.

Conclusion: FedOGL effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting in federated multimodal graph learning by jointly preserving semantic and structural memory, achieving improved robustness and generalization across clients.

Abstract: Federated graph learning enables collaborative training over decentralized graph data without sharing raw graph information. As such risks evolve, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams, retain historical categories, and reject samples outside the known class space. In this setting, clients must learn emerging classes from private multimodal graph streams while preserving historical categories and rejecting samples outside the current known class space. The core challenge is catastrophic forgetting, which in federated multimodal graphs is not merely a classifier-level failure: old knowledge can be erased through modality-semantic overwriting, topology-induced structural erosion, and federated memory fragmentation. To address this challenge, we propose \textbf{FedOGL}, a semantic-structural memory preservation framework. On the client side, FedOGL preserves historical decision behavior through replay and task-start distillation, while protecting graph-propagation memory via projection onto a globally shared structure basis. On the server side, FedOGL maintains and transfers compact category prototypes to facilitate cross-client knowledge sharing without exposing raw graph data. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared with the best-performing baselines, FedOGL reduces performance degradation caused by catastrophic forgetting by \textbf{42.67\%}, while maintaining or improving performance on downstream tasks.

</details>


### [309] [Tight Sample Complexity for Low-Rank Adaptation: Matching Bounds and Rank Selection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27680)
*Arunan J*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A study closes the gap between upper and lower bounds for LoRA fine-tuning under rank constraint: excess risk scales as rd/n (up to log factors) and is tight via a matching Omega(rd/n) minimax lower bound. It reveals a rank-selection dichotomy between constrained ERM (optimal rank equals intrinsic rank r*) and adaptive nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators (over-ranking is harmless and achieves Theta~(r* d / n)). Empirical validation shows the predicted U-shaped validation loss and loss inflation at large ranks on DistilBERT/RoBERTa tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning, address missing lower bounds and provide formal guidance on how to choose the LoRA rank r under well-specified, locally quadratic models.

Method: (1) Upper bound via local Rademacher complexity giving excess risk O~(rd/n) for rank-r LoRA when target rank ≤ r. (2) Minimax lower bound Omega(rd/n) via Fano-type packing over rank-r subspaces. (3) Analysis of estimators: constrained ERM yields optimal r*=intrinsic rank; adaptive nuclear-norm-then-truncate estimators tolerate over-ranking with rate Theta~(r* d / n). (4) Empirical validation on synthetic trace-regression and real LoRA fine-tuning across DistilBERT/SST-2 and RoBERTa/MRPC, observing U-shaped loss and rank-induced inflation.

Result: The excess risk for rank-r LoRA is fundamentally limited by rd/n; a matching lower bound confirms tightness. For constrained ERM, choosing r equal to the intrinsic rank r* is optimal; over-ranking hurts beyond r*. For adaptive estimators, over-ranking does not hurt asymptotically and yields rate Theta~(r* d / n). Empirical results corroborate the theory, showing U-shaped validation loss and statistically significant loss inflation at high ranks in some settings.

Conclusion: The work fully characterizes LoRA fine-tuning’s statistical complexity in the well-specified locally quadratic regime, highlighting that the empirically observed over-parameterization penalty arises from unregularized ERM rather than the LoRA class itself. It provides practical guidance: use intrinsic rank for constrained ERM; if using nuclear-norm-then-truncate, over-ranking is acceptable. The predictions hold across synthetic and real NLP tasks.

Abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard mechanism for fine-tuning large pretrained models, yet its statistical properties remain only partially understood. Existing generalization results provide upper bounds of the form O~(sqrt(rd/n)) or O~(rd/n), but a matching lower bound is missing, and the question of how to choose the LoRA rank r has no formal answer. Both gaps are closed here. A local Rademacher argument establishes an upper bound of O~(rd/n) on the excess risk of the empirical risk minimizer over rank-r LoRA, whenever the target adaptation has rank at most r. A matching minimax lower bound of Omega(rd/n) is then proved via a Fano-type packing of the rank-r subspace of R^{d x d}; the bound applies to any estimator whose output lies in the rank-r LoRA class. Combining the two yields a rank-selection dichotomy. For the constrained empirical risk minimizer, the optimal rank equals the intrinsic rank r*, and over-ranking strictly hurts. For adaptive estimators of the nuclear-norm-then-truncate type, over-ranking is harmless and the rate saturates at Theta~(r* d / n) regardless of r. Taken together, the three results characterize the statistical complexity of LoRA fine-tuning within the well-specified locally quadratic regime, and identify the empirically observed over-parameterization penalty as a property of unregularized empirical risk minimization rather than of the LoRA class itself. Predictions of the theory are verified on a synthetic trace-regression benchmark and on real LoRA fine-tuning across three (model, task) configurations covering DistilBERT and RoBERTa on SST-2 and MRPC. All configurations exhibit the predicted U-shape in validation loss, with two showing statistically significant loss inflation at large ranks (paired permutation p = 0.016).

</details>


### [310] [Event-Structured Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Differentiable Critical Clearing Boundaries](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27681)
*Baoli Hao,Chenxi Hu,Ming Zhong,Ren Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: An event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) for transient stability and critical clearing time (CCT) estimation, enabling differentiable CCT boundaries, local sensitivity analysis, and direct CCT readouts, with improved accuracy and efficiency on standard IEEE bus systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CCT estimation is computationally intensive and sensitive to fault severities and clearing times; existing surrogates struggle with boundary extraction and state-interface consistency across fault events.

Method: Introduce ES-PINN that aligns with pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics and enforces exact state chaining at event interfaces. Build a smooth trajectory-induced stability margin as a differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary, enable boundary extraction and local sensitivity analysis, and optionally provide a distillation-based readout for direct CCT. Prove a local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error bound leveraging exact event chaining, and validate with extended DAE checks, multi-fault tests, and runtime analyses.

Result: Empirical results on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show ES-PINN improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across various contingencies and clearing configurations, with additional validation indicating computational efficiency and scalability.

Conclusion: ES-PINN offers accurate, differentiable CCT boundary estimation and sensitivity analysis for transient stability, with strong generalization across fault scenarios and improved computational efficiency, making it a robust framework for real-time stability assessment.

Abstract: Transient-stability assessment determines whether a power system can recover after a disturbance and is therefore essential to preventing generator trips and cascading outages. A key metric is the critical clearing time (CCT), which specifies the maximum time available to clear a fault before synchronism is lost. Reliable CCT estimation is challenging because complicated fault-clearing dynamics require repeated simulations over many fault severities and clearing times. We propose an event-structured physics-informed neural network (ES-PINN) that aligns its representation with the pre-fault, fault-on, and post-clearing swing dynamics and enforces exact state chaining across event interfaces. A smooth trajectory-induced stability margin defines a differentiable approximation of the CCT boundary, enabling accurate boundary extraction, local sensitivity analysis, and optional direct CCT prediction through a distilled readout. We further prove a local residual-to-trajectory-to-CCT error estimate, in which exact event chaining eliminates separate state-interface defect terms. Experiments on IEEE 9-, 14-, and 30-bus systems show that ES-PINN consistently improves held-out trajectory and stability-boundary accuracy over matched neural-surrogate baselines across mechanical and electrical contingencies with multiple clearing configurations. Additional full-network DAE validation, multi-fault experiments, and runtime analyses further demonstrate the effectiveness and computational efficiency of the proposed framework.

</details>


### [311] [NMINE: Normalized Mutual Information Neural Estimation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27710)
*Petra Eerikinharju,Marko Tuononen,Ville Hautamäki*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Neural estimator for normalized mutual information (NMI) of continuous, multidimensional variables using DV-based MI and neural marginal entropy; outperforms KSG-based NMI on Gaussian data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mutual information is unbounded and not directly comparable across datasets; normalized mutual information addresses comparability but existing estimators suffer from sensitivity to dimensionality and numerical stability.

Method: A fully neural NMI estimator that combines a MINE-based neural MI estimator (via the Donsker–Varadhan representation) with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators (divergence from a uniform reference to recover entropy).

Result: On Gaussian data from 1 to 8 dimensions, the proposed estimator achieves higher accuracy than a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline.

Conclusion: Neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings and can outperform traditional k-NN-based approaches.

Abstract: Mutual information is a general measure of statistical dependence that captures both linear and nonlinear relationships between random variables. For continuous and multidimensional variables For continuous multidimensional variables, mutual information must be estimated from samples. Because mutual information is unbounded, its values are not directly comparable across datasets, dimensions, or applications. Normalized mutual information addresses this limitation by converting mutual information into a normalized dependency score. Recent work has demonstrated the practical value of normalized mutual information in applications such as molecular dynamics {arXiv:2405.04980} and interpretable machine learning {arXiv:2409.16768}, but existing estimators remain sensitive to dimensionality and numerical stability {arXiv:2410.07642}.
  In this paper, we propose a fully neural normalized mutual information estimator for continuous variables. The proposed approach combines a MINE-based neural mutual information estimator {arXiv:1801.04062} with MI-NEE-inspired neural marginal entropy estimators {arXiv:1905.12957}. Mutual information is estimated using the Donsker--Varadhan representation, while marginal entropies are estimated by learning the divergence between each marginal distribution and a uniform reference distribution, from which entropy is recovered. The resulting estimator provides a neural alternative to k-nearest-neighbor-based normalized mutual information estimation {arXiv:2405.04980}.
  Experiments on Gaussian data from one to eight dimensions show that the proposed estimator improves accuracy over a KSG-based normalized mutual information baseline. These results indicate that neural estimation is a promising direction for normalized dependency measurement in continuous multidimensional settings.

</details>


### [312] [VESTIGE: A Knowledge-Guided Masking Strategy for Corruption-Aware Fine-Tuning of Genomic Transformers, Validated on Ancient DNA Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27712)
*Angshuman Chakravertty,Rahul Maheshwari*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VESTIGE is a parameter-free MLM collator that aligns masking with per-position degradation profiles, improving reconstruction on degraded sequences (e.g., ancient DNA cytosine deamination) and generalizing to domain-agnostic corruption profiles.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard MLM masking assumes position-agnostic difficulty; targeted degradation at predictable positions causes peak damage where models underperform compared with random predictors; a knowledge-guided masking strategy may yield better learning under degradation.

Method: Introduce VESTIGE as a drop-in, parameter-free collator that reshapes the MLM masking distribution to match an empirical per-position corruption profile (e.g., mapDamage2 PMD in ancient DNA). Rescale so mean masking rate equals 15% to match standard MLM. Evaluate on two DNABERT-2 runs over a mammoth CDS corpus (two specimens, seven genes), across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows. Assess with validation cross-entropy, and validate reconstructions via ESMFold TM-scores; additionally test a 1D CNN biosecurity classifier on reconstructed windows.

Result: VESTIGE outperforms standard MLM at every width (Delta of 4.18–10.35 pp, all p<1e-8). Reduces validation cross-entropy by ~13% (3.274 vs 3.757). Yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score >0.95 across six reconstructions (three genes), even when damage is amplified 10–30x beyond authentic PMD rates. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier achieves AUC 0.935 and correctly rejects 98.2% of reconstructed windows; the remaining 1.76% attribution is to reference-genome features, not artefacts.

Conclusion: The approach is domain-agnostic: any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile can replace PMD arrays, enabling knowledge-guided MLM training for degraded or noisy inputs. VESTIGE thus generalizes beyond ancient DNA to FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, or nanopore contexts where degradation follows a predictable pattern.

Abstract: Standard masked-language-model fine-tuning applies a uniform masking probability across every token position, assuming reconstruction difficulty is position-agnostic. When the degradation process is characterised and concentrated at predictable positions, this assumption fails: at peak damage sites the model can underperform a frequency-matched random predictor. We introduce VESTIGE, a parameter-free, drop-in replacement for the standard MLM collator that aligns the masking distribution with an empirically measured per-position corruption profile. We apply it to ancient DNA (aDNA) reconstruction, where cytosine deamination produces a position-dependent C-to-T / G-to-A gradient quantified per-position by mapDamage2. Rescaling so the mean C/G masking rate equals 15% - identical to standard MLM - isolates spatial redistribution as the sole variable, with model, data, seed, and hyperparameters held fixed across both DNABERT-2 runs on a mammoth CDS corpus (two specimens, seven genes). Across six terminal-zone widths and 626 paired windows, VESTIGE leads standard MLM at every width (Delta = +4.18 to +10.35 pp, all p < 10^-8), cuts validation cross-entropy by 13% (3.274 vs. 3.757), and yields ESMFold reconstructions with TM-score > 0.95 across all six reconstructions (three genes) even under damage amplified 10-30x beyond authentic PMD rates. A 1D CNN biosecurity classifier returns AUC = 0.935 and clears 98.2% of reconstructed windows, the 1.76% remainder attributable to reference-genome features, not reconstruction artefacts. The principle is domain-agnostic: any measurable position- or context-specific corruption profile - FFPE, bisulfite, metagenomic, or nanopore - substitutes directly for the PMD array, making VESTIGE a knowledge-guided training routine for intelligent systems operating on degraded or noisy sequence inputs.

</details>


### [313] [Towards joint scaling laws with optimal batch size schedules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27731)
*Jiaxiang Li,Zhiqi Bu,Shiyun Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A convex-optimization analysis links learning-rate and batch-size schedules, yielding a closed-form optimal batch-size schedule for any given learning-rate trajectory and joint scaling laws that surpass static batch baselines, with implications for large language model training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To understand training dynamics by treating batch size and learning rate as interdependent schedules, addressing the common practice of using a fixed batch size.

Method: Develop a convex-optimization framework that yields a joint characterization of the loss as a function of both schedules across optimizers and architectures; derive a closed-form optimal batch-size schedule for any prescribed learning-rate schedule; establish joint scaling laws.

Result: Derivation of a closed-form optimal batch-size schedule corresponding to any learning-rate schedule; joint scaling laws showing improved performance over static batch baselines; evidence of significant effects for large language model training.

Conclusion: Dynamic batch-size scheduling materially enhances training efficiency and performance, especially in large-scale models, by optimally coordinating batch size with the learning-rate schedule.

Abstract: Modern deep learning typically keeps the batch size static throughout training, thus overlooking the joint effect of learning rate and batch size on the training dynamics. In this paper, we study the deep learning dynamics through the lens of convex optimization and derive a joint characterization of loss in terms of both schedules, applicable to general optimizers and model architectures. This characterization yields a closed-form optimal batch size schedule for any prescribed learning rate schedule, and further leads to joint scaling laws that consistently outperform static batch size baselines, highlighting the significance of dynamic batch size schedule in large language model training.

</details>


### [314] [Improving the Robustness/Accuracy Tradeoff Against Adversarial Attacks Using Information Bottleneck Distillation Through Dual Teachers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27737)
*Vincent Ryusuke Takahashi,Yoshinari Takeishi,Jun'ichi Takeuchi,Kave Salamatian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Extends IBD by adding a clean teacher and cross-layer attention to fuse clean and robust features in distillation, improving clean accuracy while preserving robustness; competitive with state-of-the-art in harmonic mean.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: IBD improves robustness at the cost of clean accuracy; the goal is to maintain or improve clean accuracy without sacrificing adversarial robustness.

Method: Introduce a second teacher trained on clean data (clean teacher) alongside the robust teacher from adversarial training; transfer features to the student via a cross-layer attention matrix that integrates both teachers' representations; analyze how attention settings affect performance; validate on CIFAR-10/100.

Result: Achieves higher clean accuracy than the original IBD while maintaining similar robust accuracy; competitive with B-MTARD in terms of harmonic mean of clean and robust accuracy; attention module settings influence outcomes.

Conclusion: Dual-teacher distillation with cross-layer attention is effective for preserving clean accuracy without sacrificing robustness, and attention design plays a significant role; the approach is competitive with current state-of-the-art methods.

Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved remarkable success in classical machine learning problems. However, they are known to be vulnerable to adversarial attacks. Countermeasures proposed in the literature, notably Information Bottleneck Distillation (IBD) introduced by Kuang et al., degrade the classification accuracy on clean inputs while improving the robustness to adversarial inputs. In this work, we extend the IBD framework by introducing an extra teacher model (clean teacher) trained with only clean inputs, into the distillation process from a robust teacher model trained by adversarial training. The features of both clean and robust teachers are transferred to the student through a cross-layer attention matrix. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets show that the proposed method improves classification accuracy on clean samples compared to the original IBD, while maintaining similar accuracy on adversarial samples. Furthermore, our methods are competitive with state-of-the-art approaches, including the recent dual-teacher distillation framework B-MTARD, particularly in terms of the harmonic mean between clean and robust accuracy. We also analyze the impact of different training settings that have different influences on the attention module.

</details>


### [315] [ROCS: Request-Oriented Compute Sharing for Efficient Large-Scale Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27744)
*Yuxin Chen,Liang Luo,Buyun Zhang,Jian Jiao,Boda Li,Haoyu Wang,Tongyi Tang,Ao Cai,Zijian Shen,Zhengkai Zhang,Wenyi Xie,Ryan Dick,Han Liu,Neng Shi,Bin Yu,Jianbo Xiao,Shuyao Bi,Hongtao Yu,Yuanwei Fang,Zhuoran Zhao,Sijia Chen,Yang Chen,Shuqi Yang,Qianru Li,Zikun Liu,Wei Ling,Sihan Zeng,Longhao Jin,Jiaxin Lu,Yinbin Ma,Jiawei Li,Yichen Ruan,Yong Ler Lee,Birmingham Guan,Zijian Li,Jianbo Sun,Zhengyu Zhang,Zeliang Chen,Xiaohan Wei,Yuchen Hao,GP Musumeci,Venkatesh Ranganathan,Yantao Yao,Chunqiang Tang,Wenlin Chen,Santanu Kolay,Ellie Dingqiao Wen*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ROCS introduces Request-Oriented Compute Sharing to shift compute from per-candidate to per-request in recommender inference, using GLM, DCA, and IKBO to maintain or improve accuracy while boosting efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Production cost constraints cap scaling of feature-interaction and sequence modules; leverage shared request features across candidates to improve throughput.

Method: ROCS paradigm defers request-candidate interactions, isolates candidate-dependent representations, and reuses computations per request. It adds Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) for candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend sharing to sequence architectures, and In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) for efficient GPU deployment.

Result: Empirical results show ROCS improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across backbones. On production workloads, ROCS yields up to 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality loss and a 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. ROCS has been deployed across large-scale systems, spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking, handling orders-of-magnitude more inference complexity while delivering online gains at reduced cost.

Conclusion: ROCS demonstrates a practical, generalizable approach to per-request shared inference in recommendation systems, enabling substantial efficiency gains with maintained or improved predictive quality.

Abstract: Modern recommendation models gain prediction quality by scaling feature-interaction and sequence modules, but production cost constraints cap how far systems can scale.
  In this work, we propose Request-Oriented Compute Sharing (ROCS), a modeling and inference paradigm that exploits a unique property of recommendation inference: each user request is evaluated against many candidates, while request-side features are shared across candidates. ROCS defers request-candidate interactions as late as possible, isolates candidate-dependent representations, and evaluates substantial portions of the model once per request rather than once per candidate, significantly improving inference efficiency while maintaining or improving prediction quality. To realize this paradigm, we develop Generalized Layer Masking (GLM) to enforce candidate isolation in feature-interaction architectures, and Deep Cross Attention (DCA) to extend request-oriented sharing to sequence architectures. To support efficient GPU deployment, we co-design In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) that significantly accelerates ROCS model execution.
  Experiments on public benchmarks show that ROCS consistently improves the quality-efficiency tradeoff across recommendation backbones. On production-scale workloads, ROCS achieves up to a 3x QPS improvement on retrieval models without quality degradation and a 0.5% relative LogLoss improvement with a 50% QPS gain on a short-form video ranking model. ROCS has been deployed across large-scale recommendation systems spanning ads and organic surfaces, retrieval and ranking stages, and more than two orders of magnitude in inference complexity, delivering significant online gains at reduced infrastructure cost.

</details>


### [316] [DAS-PMVC: A Framework for Partial Multi-View Clustering via Dual Alignment and Structure Enhancement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27761)
*Shubin Ma,Liang Zhao,Chuanye He,Zhenjiao Liu,Liang Zou,Lin Yuanbo Wu,Yu Shao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DAS-PMVC addresses partial multi-view clustering with misalignment by a three-part framework: (1) anchor graph-based initial view alignment, (2) structure-enhanced feature learning via multi-view GCNs and pretraining, and (3) a dual alignment mechanism using contrastive loss and Hungarian algorithm to refine latent-feature alignment. It reportedly outperforms state-of-the-art methods on multiple datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The PVAP (partial view alignment problem) arises from data misalignment across views due to device limitations and view asymmetry. Effective multi-view clustering requires aligning samples across views while exploiting latent structure and semantic relevance.

Method: 1) Anchor graph structure alignment to derive joint embeddings in a consistent latent space from anchor point relations. 2) Structure-enhanced feature learning by pretraining to capture view structure and applying multi-view graph convolutional networks to extract deep latent features from the aligned graph. 3) Dual alignment: pretraining-based anchor graph alignment followed by training-phase refinement using contrastive learning loss and Hungarian matching to optimize latent feature alignment.

Result: Empirical results on various datasets show that DAS-PMVC outperforms existing state-of-the-art clustering methods in PVAC scenarios, demonstrating improved clustering performance.

Conclusion: Integrating anchor-based prealignment, structure-aware representation learning, and dual (contrastive + matching) optimization yields robust partial multi-view clustering under misalignment and view asymmetry, with enhanced discriminative latent features.

Abstract: In recent years, multi-view clustering has attracted widespread research interest. However, due to limitations in data collection devices, data across different views often suffer from misalignment, leading to the partial view alignment problem (PVAP). To mitigate the impact of view asymmetry and irrelevant samples, this paper proposes a framework for partial multi-view clustering via dual alignment and structure enhancement (DAS-PMVC), which leverages view structure consistency and semantic relevance. Specifically, DAS-PMVC includes three parts: \textbf{anchor graph structure alignment}, where sample joint embedding representations with consistent latent space are derived from anchor point relationships for initial view alignment; \textbf{structure-enhanced feature learning}, where the model learns view structure information through pretraining and combines multi-view graph convolutional networks to further extract deep latent features from the aligned graph structure to improve the discriminative power of representations; and \textbf{a dual alignment strategy}, where initial alignment is performed through the anchor graph in the pretraining phase, and contrastive learning loss and the Hungarian algorithm are introduced in the training phase to further optimize the alignment of latent features. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that the DAS-PMVC framework outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in clustering performance, showcasing its effectiveness and superiority.

</details>


### [317] [Train Small, Deploy Large: Zero-Shot GNN Transfer Through Geometric Renormalization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27767)
*Robert Jankowski,Pedro Almagro-Blanco,Marián Boguñá,Melanie Weber,M. Ángeles Serrano*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Zero-shot transfer of GNNs trained on GR-coarsened graphs to full-resolution graphs; preserves much of original performance while reducing training cost, with representations and trajectories aligned across scales, suggesting structure can trump size in transferability and enabling scale-equivariant GNNs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GNNs on massive graphs face infrastructure challenges and high training costs. It is unclear whether a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down graph can be deployed on the full graph without retraining. Investigating cross-scale transfer informs efficient deployment and potential scale-equivariant designs.

Method: Apply geometric renormalization (GR) to produce coarse-grained graph replicas. Train GNNs on these GR graphs, then transfer the resulting weights directly to the original, full-resolution network without retraining. Evaluate on synthetic and real-world networks, examining predictive performance, learned representations, and trajectories across scales.

Result: Training on GR-scaled-down replicas preserves a substantial portion of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. Learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales.

Conclusion: Structural similarity across scales may be more critical than graph size for GNN transferability, suggesting a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) can operate on large graphs but become infrastructure-sensitive at the scale of millions of nodes and typically require scalable training techniques for even larger graphs. This raises a central question: when can a model trained on a smaller, scaled-down replica of a graph be deployed on the full-resolution graph without retraining? We introduce a zero-shot transfer protocol in which a GNN is trained on a graph coarse-grained by geometric renormalization (GR), and the resulting weights are transferred directly to the original network. Across synthetic and real-world networks, training on GR scaled-down replicas preserves much of the original-scale predictive performance while significantly reducing training cost. We further find that learned representations and predictive trajectories remain aligned across scales. These findings suggest that structural similarity may be more important than network size in determining GNN transferability, opening a path toward scale-equivariant graph architectures.

</details>


### [318] [Beyond the Best Teacher: Expanding and Compressing the Reasoning Solution Manifold](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27770)
*Songshuo Lu,Zhi Chen,Yaohua Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes an expand-then-compress multi-teacher distillation framework that builds a complementary union of teachers to train a stronger student (Qwen3-1.7B), outperforming the best single teacher in math reasoning, code generation, and instruction following.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL-trained policies trained from a single run often reflect only a subset of valid solution modes; to obtain robust, generalizable performance, views policies as local probes of a multi-basin solution manifold and fuse diverse experts instead of relying on a single supervisor.

Method: Expansion stage: Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from a common initialization, redirecting each later round towards examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. Compression stage: reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) lets the student learn from its own response prefixes; only reliable teachers contribute, and their sampled-token OPD losses are weighted by per-example quality. Consensus-Residual Decomposition preserves a winner teacher’s excess token preferences over reliable peers to avoid suppressing specialists during aggregation.

Result: Empirical evaluation on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following shows the Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms the strongest individual teacher across all three domains, with relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%, while retaining a single-model inference capability.

Conclusion: Stronger students arise from constructing and compressing a complementary union of teachers rather than selecting a single best teacher; the expand-then-compress framework offers a simple, effective path to improve performance across diverse tasks.

Abstract: A single reinforcement-learning run can produce a strong reasoner yet an incomplete teacher: it often amplifies only a subset of the valid solution modes. We argue that reinforcement learning (RL)-trained policies should therefore be viewed as local probes of a multi-basin reasoning solution manifold, rather than as globally reliable supervisors. Based on this view, we propose an expand-then-compress framework that couples teacher construction with multi-teacher policy distillation. In the expansion stage, Residual Group Relative Policy Optimization (RGRPO) trains a sequence of teachers from a common initialization and redirects each later round toward examples not yet covered by the accumulated teacher union. In the compression stage, reliability-gated Teacher-Union On-policy Distillation (TU-OPD) lets the student learn from its own response prefixes. For each example, only reliable teachers contribute, and their sampled-token OPD losses are weighted by their per-example quality. We further introduce Consensus-Residual Decomposition, which preserves a winner teacher's excess token preferences over its reliable peers, preventing specialist behavior from being suppressed during teacher aggregation. Experiments on mathematical reasoning, code generation, and instruction following show that the resulting Qwen3-1.7B student consistently outperforms the strongest individual teacher across all three domains, yielding relative improvements of 2.0%, 8.3%, and 6.9%, respectively, while retaining single-model inference. These results establish a simple but powerful principle: stronger students can be obtained not by selecting a single better teacher, but by deliberately constructing and compressing a complementary teacher union.

</details>


### [319] [RIPPLE: Generating Multi-Channel Phase, Not Recovering It](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27775)
*Jaehyuk Lee,Yeajin Lee,Dayeon Shin,Donghun Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RIPPLE reframes Griffin–Lim as a phase prior for multi-channel synthesis, learning to preserve inter-channel phase relations to improve coherence, outperforming channel-wise recovery in both audio and seismic tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Inter-channel phase relations encode spatial/seismic content; magnitude-only generation with independent phase recovery discards essential physics and degrades downstream analyses.

Method: RIPPLE initializes phase from Griffin–Lim as a prior and uses a rectified flow with an explicit inter-channel phase loss to refine toward the target; evaluated on first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation.

Result: Outperforms recovery-based pipelines in coherence metrics; in seismic experiments, S-wave polarization error decreases from 57.3° (random baseline) to 33.8°, robust across architecturally distinct generators.
