Conclusion: Generating phase as a learned inter-channel prior improves physical fidelity and downstream coherence in multi-channel synthesis, with demonstrated cross-domain applicability.

Abstract: Generative models synthesize magnitude spectra with high fidelity, while phase is delegated to a recovery module---Griffin--Lim, a vocoder, or a latent decoder---applied independently to each channel. For multi-channel waveforms this delegation is costly: the physical content of spatial audio and three-component seismograms lives in the phase relationships between channels, precisely what channel-independent recovery cannot produce. The cost is also invisible, since the magnitude-based metrics common to both fields barely move when inter-channel phase coherence collapses---so a pipeline can discard the physical information in its output while still scoring well. We argue that phase should be generated, not recovered, and present RIPPLE (Rectified Inter-channel Phase with Prior-based LEarning), which reinterprets Griffin--Lim as a phase **prior** rather than a final estimator: initialized from the source phase, this prior carries the inter-channel structure to be preserved, and a rectified flow refines it toward the target under an explicit inter-channel phase loss. Tested on first-order ambisonics environment transfer and seismic cross-station translation---two physically unrelated domains---RIPPLE outperforms recovery-based pipelines on the coherence metrics that downstream analyses consume. The seismic case is decisive: across architecturally distinct generators, per-channel recovery leaves S-wave polarization error near the $57.3^\circ$ random expectation, whereas learned phase reduces it to $33.8^\circ$.

</details>


### [320] [LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO): A Sampling-Time Low-Rank Scaffold for Recovering Reinforcement-Learning Gradient on Zero-Reward Cliff Prompts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27787)
*Ken Ding*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LSPO recovers gradient lost at cliff prompts in RLVR for mathematical reasoning by using a LoRA adapter during sampling: identify cliffs, supervise-fit a small adapter on cliff solutions, re-roll cliffs with base+adapter and apply importance sampling, then update the base via GRPO and discard the adapter. Yields base-only model with improved performance on math benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In RLVR for mathematical reasoning, group-normalized advantages become zero on cliff prompts (where all rollouts fail), yielding no gradient and hindering learning at the frontier of model capability.

Method: During each RL step, detect cliff prompts; train a small LoRA adapter briefly in supervision on ground-truth solutions for these cliffs; re-roll cliffs with base+adapter; apply importance sampling to incorporate these outcomes; perform a GRPO update on the base only; discard the adapter at checkpoint so the final model is base-only.

Result: Empirical evaluation on DeepMath-103K using DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with n=5 seeds per arm over a 1000-step horizon shows LSPO’s 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins, 1 tie). Gains include up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1; average improvement across 16 cells is +3.8 points.

Conclusion: LSPO successfully recovers the missing gradient at cliff prompts, enabling the base model to improve in mathematics reasoning tasks while keeping a base-only model after checkpoint. The approach demonstrates the efficacy of a sampling-time LoRA adapter as a supervised boost integrated via importance sampling in RL with structured reasoning tasks.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) for mathematical reasoning suffers from a structural blind spot: on "cliff" prompts-those on which every sampled rollout in a group fails-the group-normalized advantage is identically zero, so GRPO produces no gradient on precisely the prompts at the frontier of the model's capability. We introduce LoRA Scaffolded Policy Optimization (LSPO), a sampling-time mechanism that recovers this lost gradient. Each RL step, LSPO detects cliff prompts, fits a small low-rank (LoRA) adapter by a brief supervised step on their ground-truth solutions, re-rolls the cliffs with the base-plus-adapter model, splices the now-successful completions back into the RL batch with an importance-sampling correction, and takes a GRPO step on the base alone; the adapter receives only the supervised gradient and is discarded at checkpoint, yielding a base-only model. On DeepMath-103K with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, evaluated over n=5 paired seeds per arm at a matched 1000-step reporting horizon, LSPO's 5-seed mean matches or beats a DAPO baseline on all 16 (benchmark, pass@k) cells (15 strict wins and one exact tie), with gains of up to +10.7 points on AIME24/pass@4, +6.7 points on AIME24 and AIME26 at pass@16, and +2.4 points on MATH500/pass@1; averaged over the 16 cells the improvement is +3.8 points.

</details>


### [321] [Revisiting Predictive Process Monitoring in the Age of Foundation Models: A Comparative Study of Sequence, Tabular, and LLM Approaches](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27797)
*Lennart Fertig,Lukas Kirchdorfer,Tobias Sesterhenn*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Benchmarking three paradigms for predictive process monitoring (sequence models, LLMs, and tabular foundation models). Finds sequence models excel at next activity prediction; tabular foundations competitive for temporal predictions; LLMs costly and generally underperforming.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: PPM tasks forecast future process behavior from event logs. With rising use of foundation models, it is unclear which paradigm yields best performance across tasks and datasets. A systematic benchmark is needed to guide model choice and research directions.

Method: Controlled benchmark across multiple PPM datasets and prediction tasks comparing (i) classical sequence models trained from scratch (e.g., LSTM/GRU), (ii) large language models and other foundation models, and (iii) tabular foundation models with in-context learning. Evaluates next activity and remaining time (temporal) predictions, plus cost considerations.

Result: Sequence models consistently outperform for next activity prediction. Tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal remaining time tasks. LLMs generally lag behind and incur higher compute cost.

Conclusion: Classical sequence models remain strong baselines for discrete event forecasting in PPM. Tabular foundation models offer competitive performance for temporal tasks, and LLMs are not yet the best choice across tasks, especially given cost. The findings inform model selection and highlight the need for further benchmark efforts and efficiency considerations.

Abstract: Predictive process monitoring (PPM) leverages event logs to forecast the future of running process instances, for instance, predicting the next activity, the remaining time until case completion, or the time to the next event. While PPM research in recent years has been dominated by deep sequence models trained from scratch, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) models, foundation-model approaches---particularly large language models (LLMs)---are increasingly explored for PPM. At the same time, tabular foundation models with in-context learning capabilities offer a promising alternative but have not yet been systematically benchmarked for PPM. Thus, it remains unclear whether classical sequence-based models remain competitive in this evolving landscape. This paper compares the three modeling paradigms both conceptually and empirically through a controlled benchmark across multiple datasets and prediction tasks. The results show that sequence models consistently perform best for next activity prediction, whereas tabular foundation models are competitive on temporal tasks, with LLMs usually lagging behind despite higher cost.

</details>


### [322] [Learning-Augmented and Randomized Algorithms for Line Aggregation with Delays](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27807)
*Tianhang Lu,Runtian Ren,Shengcai Liu,Ke Tang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A study of learning-augmented and randomized online aggregation with delays on a line metric, presenting a parameterized deterministic Balance algorithm with robustness and consistency guarantees, a randomized algorithm with near-optimal competitive ratio, a stronger lower bound for randomized online algorithms, and a combined learning-augmented approach, complemented by numerical experiments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address robustness-consistency trade-offs in online aggregation with advice (learning-augmented) and delays; to improve competitive guarantees in adversarial settings, and to understand the limits for randomized online algorithms on line metrics.

Method: - For λ in (0,1], design a deterministic Balance algorithm with robustness 4/λ + 1/λ^2 and consistency 4 + λ. - Develop a randomized algorithm in the classical adversarial model achieving (e+1)-competitive against an oblivious adversary. - Prove a lower bound of e for randomized online algorithms, improving previous e/(e-1). - Combine the two ideas into a randomized learning-augmented algorithm achieving (e/λ + 1/λ^2)-robust and (e + λ)-consistent. - Conduct numerical experiments to evaluate empirical performance.

Result: - Deterministic Balance is (4/λ + 1/λ^2)-robust and (4 + λ)-consistent for each λ∈(0,1]. - Randomized algorithm is (e+1)-competitive against an oblivious adversary, beating the prior deterministic 5-competitive Balance and approaching the lower bound (and lower than the deterministic 4-bound). - A lower bound of e on the competitive ratio of randomized online algorithms is established, improving the previous bound e/(e-1). - The combined randomized learning-augmented algorithm achieves (e/λ + 1/λ^2)-robust and (e + λ)-consistent. - Numerical experiments corroborate theoretical bounds and illustrate empirical performance.

Conclusion: The work advances the theory of learning-augmented and randomized online aggregation with delays on a line metric, providing near-tight guarantees and favorable trade-offs between robustness and consistency. It also tightens lower bounds for randomized online algorithms and demonstrates practical viability through experiments.

Abstract: This paper studies learning-augmented and randomized online aggregation with delays on a line metric. We consider advice given as online suggested service lengths, and evaluate the algorithms in terms of robustness and consistency. For each $λ\in (0,1]$, we first propose a deterministic learning-augmented \textsc{Balance} algorithm that is $(4/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(4+λ)$-consistent. We also propose a randomized algorithm for the problem in the classical adversarial model, which is $(e+1)$-competitive against an oblivious adversary, improving over the deterministic $5$-competitive \textsc{Balance} benchmark~\cite{bienkowski2013chain}. Notably, this competitive ratio is even lower than the lower bound of $4$ for deterministic online algorithms. Moreover, we establish a lower bound of $e$ on the competitive ratio of randomized online algorithms, improving the previous lower bound of $e/(e-1)$. Besides, we combine the two ideas and obtain a randomized learning-augmented algorithm that is $(e/λ+1/λ^2)$-robust and $(e+λ)$-consistent. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments to complement our theoretical analysis and evaluate the empirical performance of our algorithms.

</details>


### [323] [Contrastive Concept Importance: Explaining Pairwise Class Decisions Through Automatically Extracted Concept Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27904)
*Roel Visser,Isaac Roberts,Barbara Hammer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces Contrastive Concept Importance (CCI) to attribute the logit margin between a target class and a foil class to semantic concepts, providing signed, decomposable scores that reveal which concepts support distinctions between class pairs and how they relate to hierarchical semantics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional concept attribution is non-contrastive (explain why P). In misclassification or confusion scenarios, the natural question is why P rather than Q, requiring contrastive explanations.

Method: Define CCI using an automatically extracted concept basis (e.g., CAPCRAFT-style concepts). Attribute the logit margin to concepts, producing signed scores that decompose into target-logit and foil-logit effects; enable analysis of global vs class-pair-specific importance and one-sided vs directly contrastive effects.

Result: On ImageNet class pairs, CCI uncovers class-pair-specific model behavior not captured by standard concept importance, identifies highly contrastive concepts, and allows evaluation against semantic superclass structure to assess whether distinctions are fine-grained or broad.

Conclusion: CCI enables explicit contrastive reasoning in concept-based explanations, helping interpret which concepts drive distinctions between specific class pairs and how they align with semantic hierarchies.

Abstract: Concept-based explanations are a prevalent way to explain the decisions of complex black-box methods through semantically meaningful, human-interpretable concepts. To attribute the contribution of such concepts to a model's decisions, feature attribution methods are used to quantify how strongly each concept contributes to a model output. These attributions are typically computed for a single output class and therefore answer a non-contrastive "why P?" question. In many situations, however, such as cases of misclassification, class confusion, and low-margin predictions, the more natural question to ask is "why P rather than Q?".
  We introduce contrastive concept importance (CCI), which attributes the logit margin between a target class and a contrast, or foil, class to concepts in an automatically extracted visual concept basis. The resulting scores are signed, indicating whether a concept supports the target over the foil or the foil over the target, and can be decomposed into target-logit and foil-logit effects. This makes it possible to distinguish globally important concepts from concepts that specifically influence a class-pair distinction, including whether their effect is shared, one-sided, or directly contrastive.
  We evaluate the method on ImageNet class pairs using CRAFT-style concept bases, insertion and deletion curves, logit-wise decomposition analysis, and semantic class hierarchy. The results show that contrastive concept importance reveals class-pair-specific model behavior that is not captured by ordinary concept importance alone, and that highly contrastive concepts can be evaluated against semantic superclass structure to assess whether they affect fine-grained distinctions rather than broad category evidence.

</details>


### [324] [Class-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Counterfactual Explanation Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27905)
*Muhammad Adil Saleem,Syed Ali Raza,Mary-Anne Williams*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Class-aware RL for counterfactual explanations improves training efficiency and validity versus class-blind RL, across seven datasets, with class-based features ranking highly via SHAP/LIME.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Investigate whether including the instance's predicted class in the RL state improves exploration and policy optimality for generating CFEs.

Method: Compare class-aware RL (state includes predictors' features plus the predicted class) against class-blind RL (state excludes class) across seven diverse datasets; evaluate convergence speed, reward optimization, episode length, and validity of CFEs; analyze feature importance with SHAP and LIME.

Result: Class-aware RL converges faster, achieves higher rewards, shorter episodes, and generates more valid CFEs; instance's class feature is among top predictors in action selection per SHAP/LIME.

Conclusion: Incorporating class information into the RL state enhances CFE generation performance and interpretability across varied datasets, highlighting the role of class-awareness in RL-based CFEs.

Abstract: Counterfactual explanations (CFEs) enhance the interpretability of black-box models by generating alternative instances with adjusted feature values that achieve a contrastive outcome. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach for CFE generation, enabling efficient exploration of counterfactual instances while ensuring control over key metrics like validity, sparsity, and proximity. Previous studies have formulated RL states exclusively using features derived from the predictors in the supervised dataset. This study explores the impact of including an instance's predicted class, alongside features derived from the predictors, in the RL state representation for generating CFEs. The hypothesis is that class-awareness enhances exploration efficiency and improves policy optimality. We compare the proposed class-aware RL method with the class-blind RL method, which is similar but excludes the instance's class information from the state representation. The comparison was conducted using seven datasets from diverse domains, varying in size. The results show that during training, class-aware RL offers benefits in terms of convergence speed, reward optimization, and episode length reduction. Moreover, it generates significantly more valid CFEs compared to class-blind RL. Finally, the instance's class-based feature consistently ranks among the most influential predictors in RL's action-selection, as shown by the SHAP and LIME values, underscoring the significance of class-awareness in RL for CFE generation. The impact is heightened clarity, faster learning, improved validity, and more effective counterfactual generation across diverse datasets.

</details>


### [325] [S-CEReBrO: Breaking the Memory Barrier in Continuous EEG Monitoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27913)
*Glenn Anta Bucagu,Thorir Mar Ingolfsson,Yawei Li,Luca Benini*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: S-CEReBrO introduces Windowed Alternating Attention for streaming EEG with fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, enabling constant memory KV cache and 100× longer contexts than full/self-attention (and 3× longer than low-rank linear attention). It achieves memory savings (55%), higher throughput (2.1×), and state-of-the-art on 7 of 11 tasks after pretraining on 25k+ hours from 12k+ subjects, with up to 60% fewer parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Overcome the memory bottleneck of global attention in Transformer-based EEG models for continuous monitoring, while maintaining generalization from large unlabeled data.

Method: Windowed Alternating Attention that factorizes attention into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, ensuring constant KV cache by only maintaining attention maps for the active window; evolution of the CEReBrO architecture and streaming design.

Result: Scaling analysis shows the approach supports 100× longer contexts than full self-attention and 3× longer than low-rank linear attention; memory reduced by ~55% versus low-rank linear attention, with a 2.1× throughput gain; pretraining on >25,000 hours across >12,000 subjects; achieves state-of-the-art on 7 of 11 downstream EEG tasks with up to 60% fewer parameters.

Conclusion: Windowed Alternating Attention enables efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring at scale, addressing the memory limitations of attention while preserving performance; code is released.

Abstract: Foundation models offer a promising paradigm for Electroencephalography (EEG) analysis, leveraging generalizable representations from vast unlabeled datasets. Yet, Transformer-based architectures face a critical bottleneck: global attention mechanisms couple the attention memory state to the signal duration, causing memory overflow during continuous monitoring. To address this, we introduce S-CEReBrO (Streaming CEReBrO), an evolution of the CEReBrO architecture designed for continuous monitoring. Our novel Windowed Alternating Attention mechanism factorizes attention computation into fixed-size spatiotemporal windows, guaranteeing constant KV cache memory as only the active window requires resident attention maps. Empirical scaling analysis confirms that windowed alternating attention can process signals 100X longer than full self-attention and 3X longer than low-rank linear attention. Compared to low-rank linear attention on long contexts, windowed alternating attention requires 55% of the memory while increasing inference throughput by 2.1X. Pre-trained on >25,000 hours of recordings from >12,000 subjects, S-CEReBrO achieves state-of-the-art performance on 7 of 11 downstream tasks, with up to 60% fewer parameters. This work represents a significant step toward the realization of efficient, generalizable, and continuous EEG monitoring. An accompanying code repository is available.

</details>


### [326] [Exact Action Values Are Not Enough: Rollout-Verified Reinforcement Fine-Tuning of a Reasoning Model for Multi-Zone VAV Control](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27914)
*Takumi Shioda,Kohei Terashima,Tatsuo Nagai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Frontier reasoning LLMs can drive VAV control from text without building-specific training; TD3-guided RFT on open-weight models fails to improve performance; GPT-5 yields the best energy savings but lowers ventilation margin; transition-focused supervised fine-tuning appears necessary before value-based RFT.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To overcome deployment scalability barriers in multi-zone VAV control by evaluating whether inference-time LLM reasoning and reinforcement learning transfer can generalize across buildings without bespoke modeling/training.

Method: Evaluate five controllers on a four-zone physics-based emulator over three hot days. Compare against Guideline 36 baseline. Assess a frontier-reasoning LLM (text-based inputs with extra inference compute) and a TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) of an open-weight model. Use deterministic rollouts and a rollout verifier for RFT. Analyze energy use, temperature/CO2 compliance, and prediction/transition dynamics. Include GPT-5 as a high-ability text-based controller and compare with GPT-5’s transition predictions.

Result: TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% with improved temperature and CO2 compliance versus the baseline. GPT-5 achieved the largest energy reduction at 6.2% but reduced the ventilation margin. RFT with an open-weight model produced no sustained improvement; it used more electricity and had worse five-minute predictions than persistence. Deterministic rollouts helped rank actions but revealed unreliable within-state ranking by the learned critic (only 5 of 10 states chose the rollout-best). 200 RFT steps did not yield sustained gains. GPT-5 predicted transitions better. Exact rollout scores rank sampled actions but do not reveal next-state effects or an improvement direction. The unchanged transition errors motivate transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based RFT.

Conclusion: The results indicate that a transition-focused supervised fine-tuning stage is needed before applying value-based RFT, as the critic’s within-state ranking can be misleading and rollout-based improvements are not guaranteed. Frontier LLMs (GPT-5) show promise for energy savings but may compromise ventilation margins; overall, scalable deployment remains challenging without better modeling of transition dynamics and robust evaluation methods.

Abstract: Multi-zone variable-air-volume control must balance thermal comfort, indoor air quality, and electricity use across several continuous actuators. Model predictive control and reinforcement learning are widely studied, but deployment typically requires building-specific modeling or training, limiting scalability. We first test whether a frontier reasoning model (an LLM trained to use additional inference-time computation) can achieve competitive VAV control from text without building-specific training. With that capability established, we then test whether TD3-guided reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) can transfer control knowledge into a locally deployable open-weight model. Five controllers are evaluated over three summer days in a physics-based four-zone emulator. Relative to a Guideline 36-based baseline, TD3 reduced HVAC electricity by 4.5% while improving temperature and CO$_2$ compliance. Without building-specific training, GPT-5 achieved the largest reduction (6.2%) but reduced the ventilation margin. For RFT, deterministic rollouts restore a saved state, apply one candidate, and follow TD3 to score each action. Auditing a learned critic against these rollouts exposed a failure hidden by its near-perfect across-time correlation ($r=0.9998$): within-state ranking was unreliable; the critic selected the rollout-best candidate in only 5 of 10 states. Even with the rollout verifier, 200 RFT steps produced no sustained improvement in sampled-action return; the open-weight controller used more electricity than the baseline before and after training, and its five-minute predictions remained worse than persistence. GPT-5 predicted transitions far better. Exact rollout scores rank sampled actions but reveal neither next-state effects nor an improvement direction. The unchanged transition errors motivate transition-focused supervised fine-tuning before value-based RFT.

</details>


### [327] [Harnessing the Potential of Optimizing Data Mixtures via Bayesian Domain Reweighting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27928)
*Xiang Yuan,Kaiqing Lei,Zhenyu Jin,Jun Shu,Deyu Meng,Zongben Xu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Bayesian domain weighting for multi-domain pre-training using Dirichlet distribution with Gamma priors improves stability and data efficiency over proxy-function and search-based methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robust, data-efficient domain weighting without relying on strong structural assumptions (e.g., rank invariance, scaling laws) and without expensive search.

Method: Infer domain weights with a Dirichlet distribution, incorporating Gamma priors learned from observations to regularize the weighting scheme in a Bayesian framework.

Result: Demonstrates stable and efficient learning of domain weights and identifies optimal mixtures while requiring substantially less data than search-based function-fitting methods.

Conclusion: Bayesian weighting revitalizes optimization-based domain weighting for large-scale pre-training by delivering stable, data-efficient weight learning.

Abstract: The performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) is fundamentally influenced by the distributional composition of multi-domain pre-training data. While manual heuristics were prevalent in early models, they increasingly fail to capture the intricate synergies between domains as data complexity grows. To overcome the issue, a dominant approach seeks to fit a proxy function mapping between domain weights and their corresponding validation losses, and then find the optimal domain weights to minimize validation losses. These methods rely on strong structural assumptions, such as rank invariance or scaling laws, which are often violated, resulting in non-negligible estimation bias. A promising approach is to directly optimize the weighting scheme from data. However, it suffers from unstable optimization trajectory and prohibitive computational overhead, limiting its potential to search better domain weights configurations. This paper presents a Bayesian domain weighting method to infer the weights from a Dirichlet distribution via introducing Gamma prior information learned from observations. Experimental results demonstrate that proposed method could achieve stable and efficient domain weights learning, and identifies optimal mixtures while consuming substantially less data than search-based function-fitting methods, revitalizing optimization-based domain weighting for large-scale applications.

</details>


### [328] [TriShield: Zero-Utility-Loss Defense Against Privacy Backdoors in Federated Language Model Fine-Tuning via Orthogonal Gradient Projection and Optimizer State Entanglement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27940)
*Cheng Wei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TriShield—an in-parameter-layered defense against NeuroImprint-like privacy backdoors in federated LLM fine-tuning—achieves zero reconstruction risk with no utility loss and no extra communication, via a Parameter Artifact Detector, Stateful Virtual Iteration, and Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the NeuroImprint attack that enables a malicious server to reconstruct client data from trained PEFT adapters in federated fine-tuning of LLMs. Existing defenses (LDP, gradient clipping) either fail or degrade utility; a zero-utility, communication-free defense is needed.

Method: A three-layer deterministic defense: (1) Parameter Artifact Detector detects memorization-neuron signatures in model parameters before local training; (2) Stateful Virtual Iteration entangles Adam/AdamW momentum across virtual steps to invalidate NeuroImprint's inversion; (3) Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection projects local gradient updates onto the main-task semantic subspace via SVD, removing memorization components. The authors prove that mutual information between uploaded gradients and any single sample is zero after layers 2 and 3, and validate on GPT-2 (117M) and Llama-Guard-3-1B.

Result: TriShield reduces NeuroImprint reconstruction to 0% across tested variants, while preserving or improving training accuracy, with less than 5% additional GPU computation overhead.

Conclusion: TriShield provides a complete, zero-utility defense against NeuroImprint-style privacy backdoors in federated LLM fine-tuning, without extra communication rounds.

Abstract: Federated fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) enables collaborative training without exposing raw data. However, a recent attack, NeuroImprint [1] (arXiv:2606.20553), demonstrates that a malicious parameter server can corrupt a PEFT adapter into a privacy backdoor: by assigning a dedicated memorization neuron to each training sample and ensuring each neuron updates at most once, the server can analytically reconstruct 59\%--79\% of client training data with high semantic fidelity. Existing defenses---including local differential privacy (LDP) [8] and gradient clipping---either fail against this attack or impose unacceptable utility degradation. We present \textbf{TriShield}, a three-layer deterministic defense that completely prevents NeuroImprint-style reconstruction with \textbf{zero model utility loss} and \textbf{no additional communication rounds}. TriShield consists of: (1) a \textbf{Parameter Artifact Detector} that identifies memory-neuron signatures in distributed model parameters before local training begins; (2) a \textbf{Stateful Virtual Iteration} mechanism that forces Adam/AdamW's momentum state to irreversibly entangle gradients across virtual steps, invalidating NeuroImprint's closed-form inversion; and (3) a \textbf{Zero-Utility Orthogonal Projection} operator that projects all local gradient updates onto the main-task semantic subspace computed via SVD, physically eliminating any gradient components that carry private memorization. We prove theoretically that after Layers 2 and 3, the mutual information between the uploaded gradient and any individual training sample is zero. Experiments on GPT-2 (117M) and Llama-Guard-3-1B verify that TriShield reduces NeuroImprint reconstruction rate to \textbf{0\%} across all tested attack variants, while maintaining or improving training accuracy, with less than 5\% additional GPU computation overhead.

</details>


### [329] [AutoPref: Automatic Discovery of Task-Specific Preference Objectives for Neural Combinatorial Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27953)
*Shengda Gu,Kai Li,Xinyi Ke,Haobo Fu,Yifan Zhang,Jian Cheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AutoPref is an LLM-guided framework that automates discovery of preference-based objective functions for neural combinatorial optimization by factorizing into pairwise learning signals and set-aware weights; uses staged search with behavioral gates; demonstrates superior performance over hand-designed baselines on TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Combinatorial optimization problems have exponentially large search spaces; neural combinatorial optimization with reinforcement learning and relative preferences improves sample efficiency, but current preference objectives rely on hand-crafted, inflexible formulations that may not generalize across problems or scales.

Method: AutoPref factorizes the objective into a pairwise loss program (learning signal) and a set-aware weighting program (pair contributions). The composed objective space contains existing preferences as special cases. It employs a staged conditional search with behavioral gates to prune inadmissible programs before short-horizon training/evaluation, guided by LLMs.

Result: AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP, demonstrating scalability and the benefits of automated objective discovery for NCO.

Conclusion: Automated objective discovery via AutoPref is effective for neural combinatorial optimization, offering a modular framework that subsumes existing preferences and yields superior performance across multiple COPs.

Abstract: Combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) underpin many real-world decisions, but their exponentially large search spaces make high-quality solutions costly to obtain. Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) learns fast construction policies, typically with reinforcement learning (RL), while preference-based NCO improves sample efficiency by learning from relative solution quality. However, existing preference objectives combine two distinct design choices in manually specified, one-size-fits-all formulations: what learning signal to extract from each solution pair and how to weight each pair relative to the sampled set. We present AutoPref, the first LLM-guided framework for automated preference-objective discovery in NCO. AutoPref factorizes the objective into a pairwise loss program, which defines the learning signal, and a set-aware weighting program, which determines each pair's relative contribution. Their composition forms a unified programmatic objective space containing existing preference objectives as special cases. To make its search tractable, we introduce a staged conditional search strategy with behavioral gates that filter inadmissible programs before short-horizon training and evaluation. Across TSP, CVRP, FFSP, and JSSP, AutoPref consistently outperforms strong hand-designed baselines across problem scales, demonstrating the benefits and scalability of automated objective discovery for NCO.

</details>


### [330] [What Makes Graph Unified? Principles and Generative Sliding-Window Transformer for Graph Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27966)
*Dongxiao He,Siqi Liu,Jitao Zhao,Yawen Li,Yi Wang,Di Jin*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SliGFM proposes topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding to unify heterogeneous node features for graph foundation models, enabling cross-domain transfer via a smoothness-aware transformer and a generative reconstruction objective.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Heterogeneous node features across graph domains hinder cross-domain transfer; dimension alignment alone does not preserve semantics or transferable patterns. Four desiderata guide cross-domain feature unification.

Method: Order feature dimensions by topological smoothness, apply a shared sliding-window feature encoder to obtain fixed-dimensional feature tokens, use a smoothness-aware transformer to capture relational patterns among tokens, and employ a generative reconstruction objective to preserve original feature information; designed for backbone compatibility in GFMs.

Result: Conceptual architecture and objective; abstract outlines the approach and its aims, but provides no empirical results within the abstract.

Conclusion: The framework offers a principled path toward cross-domain feature unification for GFMs, contingent on effective preservation of semantics and transferability; warrants empirical validation and analysis of design choices (window size, ordering, reconstruction loss).

Abstract: Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose graph learning, aiming to learn reusable knowledge that generalizes across diverse graph domains and downstream tasks, reducing the need for specific model development. Achieving this goal requires reconciling the substantial heterogeneity in node features, graph structures, and semantic information across domains. Among them, heterogeneous node features constitute a fundamental input-level barrier, as their dimensionality and semantics vary substantially across datasets. Existing studies typically project or map heterogeneous node features into a fixed-dimensional space, often implicitly equating dimensional uniformity with effective feature unification. Yet dimensional consistency alone does not ensure that the unified features preserve informative semantics and capture transferable patterns that can support cross-domain knowledge transfer. To bridge this conceptual gap, we distill four desiderata for cross-domain graph feature unification: formal uniformity, cross-domain transferability, information preservation, and backbone compatibility. Guided by these principles, we propose SliGFM, a graph foundation model built upon topology-aware sliding-window feature encoding and generative reconstruction. SliGFM orders feature dimensions by topological smoothness and scans the reordered features with a shared sliding-window feature encoder, transforming heterogeneous features into a common space of ordered fixed-dimensional feature tokens. This formulation enables a smoothness-aware transformer to capture transferable relational patterns among feature tokens within each node, while the generative reconstruction objective encourages preservation of the original feature information.

</details>


### [331] [Beyond Binary Rewards: A Comparative Study of Reward Design for Reinforcement Unlearning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27968)
*Efstratios Zaradoukas,Davide Gabrielli,Bardh Prenkaj,Gjergji Kasneci*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Reward design in Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) improves efficiency: two new rewards (exponential, PageRank-inspired) outperform sparse binary rewards on RWKU, achieving up to 3× faster forgetting with preserved utility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Unlearning under privacy regimes requires efficient removal of knowledge. Sparse binary rewards in RLVR provide weak learning signal and slow convergence; decoupling verifiability from sparsity may enhance efficiency.

Method: Introduce Reward Decomposition Framework; propose exponential reward based on count of forbidden-concept occurrences; propose PageRank-inspired reward weighting penalties by semantic importance; evaluate on RWKU benchmark.

Result: Both rewards outperform binary rewards in forgetting performance while achieving up to 3× faster convergence and preserving model utility.

Conclusion: Reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency; the proposed framework offers scalable, efficient machine unlearning and practical guidance for RL-based unlearning.

Abstract: Machine unlearning seeks to selectively remove specific knowledge from trained language models without full retraining, a growing necessity under privacy regulations such as GDPR and the EU AI Act. Recent work has reformulated unlearning as a Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) problem, where models are optimized against verifiable rewards computed directly from their outputs. However, existing methods rely on sparse binary rewards that provide minimal learning signal, indicating only whether forbidden content was avoided, and limiting convergence speed. In this paper, we study how reward design affects unlearning efficiency within the Reinforcement Unlearning (RUL) framework. We introduce a principled reward decomposition framework that decouples verifiability from sparsity, and propose two new reward functions: an exponential reward that provides graded penalties based on the count of forbidden-concept occurrences, and a PageRank inspired reward that weights penalties by semantic importance. We conduct experiments on the Real World Knowledge Unlearning (RWKU) benchmark, demonstrating that both rewards consistently outperform the binary setting, while reaching similar forgetting performance up to $3\times$ faster and preserving general model utility. Our results show that reward design is a key driver of unlearning efficiency offering a practical path toward scalable and efficient machine unlearning.

</details>


### [332] [TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27973)
*Cong Li,Peixi Peng,Yisen Zhao,Xinyu Hu,Shudong Liu,Zhan Su,Zhuojian Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TAPO introduces Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM agents by alternating policy updates with action-conditioned next-observation prediction using rollout data. This transition supervision is lightweight, plug-and-play, and improves performance without extra data or sampling costs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Generalization in multi-step, goal-oriented tasks benefits from predictive knowledge of environmental consequences. Existing RL for LLM agents mostly relies on sparse rewards and underutilizes dense environmental feedback available during online interaction.

Method: TAPO alternates policy optimization with transition supervision. It repurposes rollout data to train an action-conditioned next-observation predictor on a shared backbone, leveraging environmental transitions to improve sensitivity to action consequences. It is designed as a plug-and-play module compatible with various RL algorithms, without requiring extra expert data or sampling or inference-time overhead.

Result: Empirical evaluations on WebShop and ALFWorld show TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines across foundation model scales and different policy optimization algorithms.

Conclusion: Incorporating transition-aware supervision into RL for LLM agents enhances generalization and decision quality by leveraging environmental dynamics, providing a lightweight, reusable enhancement to existing agent RL pipelines.

Abstract: Recently, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as a crucial paradigm for the post-training of Large Language Model (LLM) agents. However, existing methods predominantly rely on sparse task rewards for policy optimization, failing to fully exploit another class of inherently dense supervisory signals naturally present during online interaction: environmental feedback following action execution. Recent theoretical studies suggest that generalization in multi-step, goal-oriented tasks hinges on predictive knowledge of environmental consequences. Inspired by this, we propose TAPO: Transition-Aware Policy Optimization for LLM Agents, a unified training framework that alternates between policy optimization and transition supervision. Beyond standard RL updates, TAPO repurposes rollout data to apply action-conditioned next-observation prediction supervision on a shared backbone model. This approach enhances the model's sensitivity to environmental transition dynamics and action consequences while concurrently optimizing the policy. It serves as a computationally lightweight, plug-and-play enhancement module for existing agent RL algorithms, requiring no additional expert data, extra sampling costs, or inference-time overhead. We conduct systematic experiments on WebShop and ALFWorld, integrating foundation models of various scales with different policy optimization algorithms. Empirical results demonstrate that TAPO consistently improves task performance over pure policy optimization baselines.

</details>


### [333] [Generalization Bounds on Optimal Control for Transformer Training and Wasserstein Distributional Robustness](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27975)
*Kağan Akman,Naci Saldi,Serdar Yüksel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformer training framed as a measure-valued dynamic-programming problem, using quantization and concentration to derive bounds, and a Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization interpretation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Understand and quantify Transformer generalization under a dynamic-programming/optimal-control view; connect generalization to distributionally robust optimization with Wasserstein distance.

Method: 1) Reformulate Transformer dynamics via a doubly lifted, measure-valued framework. 2) Treat datasets as probability laws over pairs of empirical input-output measures, turning training into a finite-horizon Markov decision process. 3) Analyze a quantized model by discretizing state, action, and measure-state spaces. 4) Derive explicit finite-sample generalization bounds using concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces and a Lipschitz stability bound for the value function. 5) Transfer bounds to the base model with an explicit approximation error. 6) Show that the same machinery yields a distributionally robust control formulation, linking Transformer generalization to Wasserstein DRO.

Result: Explicit finite-sample generalization bounds for the quantized Transformer model are derived; these bounds transfer to the base model with a quantified approximation error. The approach also yields a distributionally robust training formulation in the Wasserstein sense, providing a unifying control-theoretic interpretation of Transformer generalization.

Conclusion: A unified finite-sample analysis framework for Transformer generalization is established, integrating measure-valued dynamic programming, quantization-based bounds, and Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization, with explicit error Trade-offs between discretization and generalization.

Abstract: We derive finite-sample generalization bounds for Transformers trained with dynamic programming recursions. Building on the doubly lifted, measure-valued formulation of Transformer dynamics, we view data sets as probability laws on pairs of empirical input-output measures, allowing us to interpret the training problem as a finite-horizon Markovian control problem. We then analyze a quantized model, derived by quantizing the state, action, and measure-state spaces, and derive explicit finite-sample generalization bounds using concentration inequalities for empirical laws on finite metric spaces together with a Lipschitz stability estimate for the value function. These bounds are transferred to the base model at the cost of an explicit approximation error. Finally, we show that the same machinery yields a distributionally robust control formulation of the training problem, connecting Transformer generalization to Wasserstein distributionally robust optimization.

</details>


### [334] [It's All Just Vectorization: einx, a Universal Notation for Tensor Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.27987)
*Florian Fervers,Sebastian Bullinger,Christoph Bodensteiner,Michael Arens*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper proposes einx, a universal tensor-operation notation grounded in vectorization, aiming to unify and simplify tensor programming beyond einsum/einops, with a Python-embedded implementation (GitHub).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To address readability/shape-errors in NumPy-like syntax and the limited generality of existing notations; seek a universal, extensible model for tensor operations.

Method: Reinterpret vectorization as a function that transforms tensor operations; show lifting of lower-order ops and decomposition of higher-order ops via vectorization; define declarative, pointful syntax analogous to loop notation; develop einx; implement in Python and integrate with current frameworks.

Result: Conceptual framework and a working Python implementation; reduces large tensor-APIs to a small set of elementary operations under consistent rules; enables readable/writable representations; codebase at GitHub.

Conclusion: einx offers a unified, readable, and extensible paradigm for tensor programming; promising foundation but requires empirical evaluation, formal semantics, and performance assessment; accessible via provided implementation.

Abstract: Tensor operations represent a cornerstone of modern scientific computing. However, the Numpy-like notation adopted by predominant tensor frameworks is often difficult to read and write and prone to so-called shape errors, i.a., due to following inconsistent rules across a large, complex collection of operations. Alternatives like einsum and einops have gained popularity, but are inherently restricted to few operations and lack the generality required for a universal model of tensor programming.
  To derive a better paradigm, we revisit vectorization as a function for transforming tensor operations, and use it to both lift lower-order operations to higher-order operations, and conceptually decompose higher-order operations to lower-order operations and their vectorization.
  Building on the universal nature of vectorization, we introduce einx, a universal notation for tensor operations. It uses declarative, pointful expressions that are defined by analogy with loop notation and represent the vectorization of tensor operations. The notation reduces the large APIs of existing frameworks to a small set of elementary operations, applies consistent rules across all operations, and enables a clean, readable and writable representation in code. We provide an implementation of einx that is embedded in Python and integrates seamlessly with existing tensor frameworks: https://github.com/fferflo/einx

</details>


### [335] [Building a User Foundation Model for the Open Web](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28019)
*Solal Vernier,Ivan Can Arisoy,Merwan Barlier,Blaž Škrlj*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A Transformer-based user representation for open-web RTB learned via self-supervised pre-training (MLM + sequence contrastive) and fine-tuned on click prediction; augmented with an LLM-in-the-loop optimizer for pre-training edits; yields measurable gains in production metrics in live tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Open-web RTB presents fragmented, non-persistent user identities and limited history; historical signals are aggregated; need to exploit sequential structure to improve downstream tasks.

Method: Pre-train Transformer encoder on user browsing histories using masked language modeling and a sequence-level contrastive objective; fine-tune on click prediction; use LLM-in-the-loop search over a catalog of edits (lifters) to optimize the pre-training pipeline; evaluate on production bid win-rate and CTR ranker; live A/B test.

Result: +1.197% relative improvement (RIG) on the production bid win-rate model; +1.354% RIG on production CTR ranker; 7-day live A/B shows +2.13% CTR and -1.13% eCPC with 80% CI excluding zero on both metrics.

Conclusion: Demonstrates viability of user foundation models for open-web, showing that sequential, self-supervised user representations can improve core monetization tasks under privacy- and session-fragmented data.

Abstract: User foundation models have demonstrated strong results in e-commerce and social recommendation, but most industrial deployments assume environments where user identity is stable and persistent. Open-web real-time bidding (RTB) operates on a structurally different data distribution: user identity is fragmented and non-persistent across browsing sessions, and the availability of browsing history depends on user privacy choices. Consequently, a significant portion of traffic carries no historical data, and available records often consist of relatively short, disjointed sessions. As a result, historical signals in this domain are typically represented as aggregated counters and recency buckets, leaving the sequential structure unexploited. To address this limitation, we present a user foundation model that applies self-supervised learning on user browsing histories and show that the learned representation improves multiple downstream production tasks, demonstrating the viability of this approach on the open web. We pre-train a Transformer encoder with masked language modeling and a sequence-level contrastive objective, then fine-tune it on the click prediction task. We optimize the encoder's pre-training pipeline with an LLM-in-the-loop search over a curated catalog of reviewable, code-level edits (lifters), instantiating the LLM-as-optimizer paradigm in an industrial setting. The same encoder representation yields +1.197% RIG on the production bid win-rate model and +1.354% RIG on the production CTR ranker; a 7-day live A/B test confirms +2.13% CTR, -1.13% eCPC (80% CI excluding zero on both metrics).

</details>


### [336] [Flux-OPD: On-Policy Distillation with Evolving Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28022)
*Yuran Wang,Zekun Wang,Bohan Zeng,Ruixu Zhang,Wenxuan Liu,Liu Yang,Yifan Dai,Yang Shi,Bozhou Li,Chengzhuo Tong,Daili Hua,Yuanxing Zhang,Wentao Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Flux-OPD introduces evolving contexts into open-ended policy distillation, using contextual difference signals and conflict-aware weighting to integrate context-conditioned teachers with a context-free anchor, yielding superior results over prior OPD approaches.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In open-ended domains, there are no verifiable task rewards, making supervision via preferences difficult. Contexts can encode these preferences but naive use leads to unstable targets and conflicting distributions as the student evolves; thus, a mechanism to stabilize supervision and handle inter-teacher conflicts is needed.

Method: Decompose the reverse KL objective to show that the student tends to the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers and that a conflict term captures disagreements among them. Introduce Flux-OPD, which treats differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual correction signals, injects them into a context-free teacher anchor, and weights their corrections by the conflict term to manage conflicts.

Result: Empirical results on open-ended tasks show Flux-OPD outperforming existing OPD paradigms, indicating that evolving contexts can be effectively harnessed for supervision when guided by the proposed contextual difference signals and conflict-aware weighting.

Conclusion: Evolving contexts, when combined with a conflict-aware, difference-signal correction mechanism, can enhance supervision in open-ended LLM training, making Flux-OPD a promising direction for integrating teacher guidance with dynamic contextual cues.

Abstract: Large language model training in open-ended domains lacks verifiable rewards, making task preferences difficult to formalize as effective supervision. Contexts can convey such preferences, yet provide little additional supervision once distilled into the student, motivating contexts that evolve with student performance. However, directly using evolving contexts as in-training supervision results in an unstable distillation target and conflicting distributions, requiring mechanisms to stabilize target and downweight conflicts. In this paper, we analyze the effect of contexts through a decomposition of the reverse KL objective, revealing two findings: the student is distilled toward the geometric mean of context-conditioned teachers, and the objective contains a conflict term that measures conflicts among these teachers. Based on this decomposition, we propose Flux-OPD, an OPD paradigm that uses evolving contexts as in-training supervision to capture task preferences in open-ended domains. Flux-OPD treats the differences between context-conditioned and context-free teachers as contextual difference signals, injects them as contextual corrections into the context-free teacher anchor, and weights their correction strength using the conflict term as an indicator. Experiments on open-ended tasks show that Flux-OPD outperforms existing OPD paradigms, highlighting the potential to combine teacher supervision with evolving contexts.

</details>


### [337] [Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization via Privileged Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28026)
*Xingjian Wu,Junlin Liu,Xingchen Liu,Xuhang Zhu,Jianing Wang,Linsen Guo,Xiaoyu Li,Xuezhi Cao,Xunliang Cai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CRPO reframes agentic OPSD as contrastive learning with predictive entropy, separating positive (reflective exploration) from negative (exposure bias) positions via group-wise contrast to maintain fine-grained optimization in long-horizon reasoning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OPSD suffers from exposure bias due to privileged self-teacher information, causing reasoning route convergence and unclear optimization directions in multi-turn agentic settings; there is a need for stable, generalizable optimization signals in long-horizon interactions.

Method: CRPO formulates agentic OPSD as a contrastive learning objective, using predictive entropy to label positive and negative positions and performing group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals.

Result: CRPO consistently outperforms RL and self-distillation baselines across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks, improving training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.

Conclusion: CRPO provides a robust contrastive framework for agentic OPSD that mitigates exposure bias and route convergence, yielding stronger optimization signals and better generalization in long-horizon decision-making.

Abstract: Recent advances in post-training Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) or On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD). While OPSD provides dense, logit-level supervision, it inherently suffers from exposure bias due to the privileged information of the self-teacher. In multi-turn agentic settings, this leads to reasoning route convergence and the loss of clear optimization directions. To tackle these challenges, we introduce Contrastive Reinforced Policy Optimization (CRPO), which reformulates agentic OPSD from a contrastive learning perspective. By leveraging predictive entropy to distinguish between positive positions (reflective exploration) and negative positions (exposure bias), CRPO conducts group-wise contrast to preserve reliable, fine-grained optimization signals. Extensive evaluations across 13 challenging reasoning and deep-search benchmarks demonstrate that CRPO consistently outperforms existing reinforcement learning and self-distillation baselines, significantly enhancing training stability and generalization in long-horizon interactions.

</details>


### [338] [Enhancing Irregular Time Series Forecasting with Continuous-Time Modeling Framework](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28035)
*Tianen Shen,Zhengyu Li,Yutong Li,Xiangfei Qiu,Xingjian Wu,Bin Yang,Jilin Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WrapFlow: a continuous-time framework for irregular multivariate time series forecasting using Continuous-Time Tokenization and a simulation-free Residual Flow Matching training paradigm, enabling high-quality forecasting with a Transformer backbone and few rollout steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Irregular sampling, non-uniform intervals, and the need to preserve continuous-time semantics while avoiding discretization artefacts and costly ODE solvers.

Method: On input, Continuous-Time Tokenization encodes raw observation events and gap-aware tokens to represent long unobserved intervals; a standard Transformer backbone processes the resulting continuous-time tokens. On output, a simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions without numerical solver simulation or backpropagation during training, enabling accurate continuous forecasting with few fixed rollout steps at inference.

Result: Empirical experiments on real-world datasets show state-of-the-art performance of WrapFlow.

Conclusion: WrapFlow achieves accurate continuous-time forecasting for irregular multivariate time series with efficient training and inference by combining continuous-time tokenization and a solver-free residual flow matching framework.

Abstract: Irregular multivariate time series are widely encountered in applications such as healthcare monitoring, human activity recognition, and environmental sensing. Their core challenges stem from asynchronous observations, non-uniform sampling intervals, and the fact that temporal patterns themselves carry critical dynamic information. Existing approaches either rely on discretization-based preprocessing (e.g., interpolation, imputation, or aggregation), which disrupts the underlying continuous-time semantics, or adopt continuous-time modeling via ODE-based frameworks, which typically require specialized architectures and incur substantial computational overhead due to numerical solvers. To address these limitations, we propose WrapFlow, a continuous-time modeling framework for irregular time series forecasting. On the input side, WrapFlow introduces Continuous-Time Tokenization, which directly encodes raw observation events and explicitly models long unobserved intervals via gap-aware tokens. The resulting continuous-time tokens are then processed by a standard Transformer backbone to capture long-range temporal dependencies. On the output side, we develop a simulation-free training paradigm for Residual Flow Matching, which learns conditional residual vector fields around base predictions while avoiding numerical-solver simulation and backpropagation during training. This design enables high-quality continuous forecasting using only a small number of fixed rollout steps at inference. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that WrapFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance.

</details>


### [339] [Learning features from Newton's algorithm: a way to accelerate nonlinear parametrized PDE solvers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28036)
*Rémy Vallot,Florian de Vuyst,Thibault Dairay,Mathilde Mougeot*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A two-stage Newton strategy uses learning-based initialization plus GMRES correction to speed up convergence for large-scale nonlinear PDEs; it builds reduced spaces from Newton trajectories, predicts a surrogate solution for unseen parameters, then applies a quick residual-based correction before high-fidelity Newton iteration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce Newton iterations and CPU time for solving parameterized nonlinear systems arising from PDEs, leveraging offline data-driven features and a lightweight online correction.

Method: Construct two reduced spaces from discrete Newton trajectories: a solution feature space from converged states and a corrective search direction space from Newton increments. Train a regression model to predict a surrogate solution for new parameters. Apply a GMRES-based residual-minimizing correction (small least-squares solve) to refine the surrogate. Use resulting state as initial guess for a high-fidelity Newton method.

Result: Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show substantial speedups over using a standalone surrogate initialization. The method reduces the number of Newton iterations and CPU time.

Conclusion: A generic, weakly intrusive approach that can be applied to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems, with offline data driving online acceleration via a lightweight corrective step.

Abstract: It is well known that Newton's method converges faster when the initial guess is closer to a root of a system of nonlinear equations. In this paper, a two-stage Newton initial guess strategy is proposed by learning features from a parameter-space sampling and a database of precomputed solutions. The method uses discrete Newton trajectories to construct two complementary reduced spaces: a solution feature space, built from converged states, and a corrective search direction feature space, built from intermediate Newton increments. For an unseen parameter, a regression model is used to predict a surrogate solution approximation. Then, in a second step, a residual-minimizing correction is computed using a dedicated GMRES-based approach. The resulting state is then used as an initial guess for the high-fidelity Newton method, which completes convergence. The corrective step is computationally inexpensive since it only requires residual evaluations and the solution of a small least-squares problem. The methodology is weakly intrusive once the high-fidelity residual fields and a script-based programming interface are available. This strategy reduces the number of Newton iterations and decreases the overall CPU time. Numerical experiments on representative PDE problems show quantifiable speedups compared with standalone surrogate initialization. Significant speedups are observed. This generic approach can be applied to a broad class of large-scale nonlinear problems.

</details>


### [340] [ClawTrack: Towards Trace-Level Evaluation and Improvement of Real-World Autonomous Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28037)
*Xingjian Wu,Xuhang Zhu,Xingchen Liu,Junlin Liu,Jianing Wang,Linsen Guo,Xiaoyu Li,Xuezhi Cao,Xunliang Cai*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ClawTrack introduces a dual-task/process benchmark for LLM agents, evaluating both Task Score and Process Score across 320 tasks in 8 domains using 25+ deterministic mock services, with a Process Grader assessing reasoning on four dimensions via 12,541 rubric items; 21 models over 16k+ trials show process scores attribute outcomes, dimensions are complementary with verification bottleneck, evaluator-robustness, and trajectory filtering improves performance across scales.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks predominantly report final outcomes, obscuring whether success arises from sound reasoning or luck, and fail to diagnose deficiencies in long-horizon workflows. A process-aware evaluation can diagnose specific reasoning issues and guide training.

Method: A dual-assessment framework (Task Score and Process Score) using 8-domain, 320-task suite with deterministic mock services. A Process Grader scores each reasoning turn along four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, result verification) anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items. Evaluations span 21 models and 16k+ trials, enabling analysis of attribution, complementarity of dimensions, evaluator robustness, and trajectory-based improvements.

Result: Process scores successfully attribute success/failure to specific reasoning dimensions, filtering lucky passes unseen by outcome-only metrics; the four dimensions are complementary with result verification as a systematic bottleneck; the framework shows robustness to evaluator LLMs; process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.

Conclusion: A process-aware benchmark like ClawTrack provides richer diagnostics for long-horizon LLM tasks, enabling attribution of outcomes to reasoning steps, highlighting the critical role of result verification, and offering a scalable signal for supervision that persists across model sizes.

Abstract: As LLM-based agents are deployed in complex, multi-step workflows, a critical evaluation gap has emerged: most existing benchmarks judge only final outcomes, unable to distinguish reliable reasoning from lucky success or attribute failures to specific process deficiencies, hindering attribution in long-horizon tasks.
  In this work, we present ClawTrack, a dual-assessment benchmark that simultaneously measures what an agent achieves (Task Score) and how it achieves it (Process Score). ClawTrack comprises 320 tasks across 8 domains with 25+ deterministic mock services. A Process Grader scores each reasoning turn along four dimensions (goal alignment, efficiency, information utilization, and result verification), anchored by 12,541 task-specific rubric items. Evaluating 21 models over 16,000+ trials, we find that: (1) process scores effectively attribute success and failure to specific reasoning dimensions, filtering lucky passes invisible to outcome-only evaluation; (2) the four dimensions are complementary, with result verification as the systematic bottleneck; (3) the framework is robust to evaluator choice across different judge LLMs; and (4) process-based trajectory filtering yields consistent post-training improvements across model scales.

</details>


### [341] [GVR-Coder: A Visual-Feedback Framework for Structured SVG Generation in Complex Document and Meeting Scenarios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28073)
*Yiming Xu,Jihua Kang,Chunsai Du,Qifan Zhang,Wangqiu Zhou,Yiting Wu,Tianqi Li,Qi Song*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: GVR-Coder generates high-quality logical diagrams (SVG) from lengthy professional texts, addressing data scarcity, layout priors, and feedback; introduces DocMeetSVG-100K dataset and a curriculum-driven, feedback-guided training loop including generate-verify-repair.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In professional settings, transforming verbose text into clear diagrams reduces cognitive load. SVG is suitable due to editability and resolution independence. Current 텍츠-to-SVG efforts struggle with limited complex-logic diagrams, missing explicit layout priors, and lack of fine-grained visual feedback.

Method: Data: DocMeetSVG-100K; Model: GVR-Coder. Curriculum-driven rejection sampling to progressively model complex structures; explicit incorporation of layout constraint knowledge during training; reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback to optimize structural complexity and visual aesthetics; generate-verify-repair loop for explicit, targeted refinement.

Result: GVR-Coder outperforms competitive baselines and reliably produces logically coherent and visually appealing diagrams across experiments.

Conclusion: The approach effectively tackles data scarcity, layout priors, and feedback challenges in text-to-SVG generation, demonstrating strong practical performance; code and data are released.

Abstract: In demanding professional environments and meeting review scenarios, lengthy text often imposes a high cognitive load. To facilitate efficient information communication, transforming verbose text into logically clear diagrams is essential. Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) provide an effective representation for this purpose due to their editability and resolution independence. However, current research on Text-to-SVG generation remains hindered by three major challenges: (1) the scarcity of datasets for complex, logic-rich diagrams; (2) the absence of explicit layout priors, which leads to chaotic spatial arrangements; and (3) the lack of fine-grained visual feedback to validate rendered outputs and correct aesthetic defects. To address these challenges, at the data level, we introduce DocMeetSVG-100K, a large-scale SVG dataset tailored for document authoring and meeting review scenarios. At the model level, we propose GVR-Coder, a novel framework designed to generate high-quality logical diagrams from lengthy professional texts. Specifically, we adopt a curriculum-driven rejection sampling fine-tuning to progressively enhance the model's capability in modeling complex structures, while explicitly incorporating layout constraint knowledge during training. In addition, we introduce reinforcement learning from dual rendering feedback, a mechanism that provides implicit feedback through reward signals to jointly optimize structural complexity and visual aesthetics. Furthermore, we design a generate-verify-repair agent loop, which improves generation quality through explicit, fine-grained feedback and targeted refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GVR-Coder outperforms competitive baselines and reliably produces logically coherent and visually appealing diagrams. Code and data are available at https://github.com/CurryaNa/GVR-Coder.

</details>


### [342] [Chem World: A Large-Scale Benchmark and Physics-Informed Framework for Trustworthy Chemical Property Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28079)
*Tianyou Bai,Huan Wang,Mingchen Gao,Fangyue Lin,Pinze Ren,Zhenlin Zhao,Siming Dong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Chem World unifies 17 chemical datasets (800k samples) into a single benchmark for chemical property prediction; introduces Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed framework leveraging chemical priors to improve accuracy and robustness; demonstrates improved performance over baselines on the benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address fragmentation and inconsistent evaluation in existing chemical property benchmarks; enable trustworthy AI in computational chemistry by standardizing diversity and evaluation protocol; integrate physics-informed learning to leverage domain knowledge.

Method: Assemble a large-scale benchmark (Chem World) consolidating 17 datasets with 800k samples; use Mixture-PINN that incorporates chemical priors into a neural network for property prediction; evaluate across multiple properties; compare with existing methods.

Result: Experimental results show Mixture-PINN improves accuracy, robustness, and reliability relative to baselines on Chem World; benchmark provides unified evaluation platform.

Conclusion: Chem World with physics-informed learning provides a foundation for trustworthy AI in computational chemistry and accelerates AI-driven discovery.

Abstract: Chemical property prediction plays a critical role in accelerating scientific discovery in chemistry, materials science, and drug development. However, existing benchmarks often suffer from limited task diversity, fragmented datasets, and inconsistent evaluation protocols, making it challenging to systematically assess the reliability and generalization of AI models. In this work, we introduce Chem World, a comprehensive benchmark for chemical property prediction that integrates 17 diverse chemical datasets with over 800,000 molecular samples, covering various properties including density, electrical conductivity, solubility, and other molecular characteristics. Chem World provides a unified platform for evaluating AI models across multiple property prediction tasks. Furthermore, we propose Mixture-PINN, a physics-informed neural network based prediction framework that incorporates chemical prior knowledge into data-driven learning, improving the accuracy, robustness, and reliability of chemical property prediction. Extensive experiments on Chem World demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared with existing methods. By combining large-scale standardized evaluation with physics-informed learning, Chem World establishes a foundation for developing trustworthy AI systems for computational chemistry and advancing AI-driven scientific discovery.

</details>


### [343] [From Expert Reduction to Behavioral Divergence: Tracing Numerical State through Sparse MoE Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28097)
*Tianyang Zhu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Mathematically equivalent expert-reduction orders in sparse MoE can yield observable execution differences. By freezing MoE state and varying aggregation semantics across multiple schemes and prompts, the study shows distinct continuation basins and state trajectories, with post-mHC delineating intra-token and persistent state delineating cross-token boundaries. This implies operand conversion, precision, and reduction order form a numerical compatibility contract for runtimes/hardware, not guaranteed invariance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Quantify sensitivity of sparse MoE runtimes to aggregation semantics and reduction order; determine whether mathematical equivalence translates into identical autogressive behavior; understand how state boundaries affect cross-token continuations and what hardware/software guarantees are needed.

Method: Use native DeepSeek-V4-Flash with four schemes separating operand representation from accumulator precision. Analyze a layer-5 fork with 720 A-mode orders and 720 B-mode orders, yielding multiple classes and basins. Test under a Chinese prompt; track 192 persistent trajectories per scheme; compare P, A, B vs C variants; perform exact post-mHC endpoint reconstruction for controlled B branch; perform FP64 reconstruction of full persistent state across seven steps; identify intra-token vs cross-token boundaries and assess token-based divergence.

Result: Observed 10 continuation basins from 720 A-mode orders; 360 exact structural classes and 11 basins from 720 B-mode orders. Under a Chinese prompt, B classes split into 202 layoffs, 113 hiring, 45 other continuations. Maximum-L-infinity B-branch selection separates multiple prompts by token counts. Across 192 trajectories per scheme, some schemes (P, A, B) vary with routes, while C preserves routes and texts. A separate 192-trajectory C check matches native MoE states bitwise. For a controlled B branch, exact post-mHC endpoint reconstruction reproduces the downstream trajectory; FP64 reconstruction across a boundary yields agreement for 301 downstream post-mHC states, 301 checkpoints, 301 routes, predictions, and text over seven steps. Identifies post-mHC as intra-token boundary and full persistent state as cross-token continuation boundary. Divergence can persist across token boundaries. Conclude that operand conversion, accumulator precision, and reduction order are part of a numerical compatibility contract; C invariance is limited to evaluated six-term states/schedules.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates controlled causal possibilities rather than deployment incidence. It establishes that operand/reduction choices affect observable trajectories and must be considered in the design of sparse MoE runtimes and hardware backends; invariance is bounded and context-dependent, requiring explicit numerical compatibility guarantees.

Abstract: Mathematically equivalent expert-reduction orders can produce observably different sparse-MoE executions. We isolate this effect in native DeepSeek-V4-Flash by freezing local MoE state and varying only aggregation semantics. Four schemes separate operand representation from accumulator precision. At one layer-5 fork, 720 A-mode orders yield 10 continuation basins; 720 B-mode orders form 360 exact structural classes and 11 basins. Under one Chinese prompt, the B classes split into 202 layoffs, 113 hiring, and 45 other continuations. Maximum-L-infinity B-branch selection separates 12, 24, and 36 of 50 prompts by 8, 16, and 32 tokens.
