Across 192 persistent trajectories per scheme, P32, A, and B change every native-reference route trajectory, while C preserves routes, token sequences, and texts. A separate 192-trajectory C check matches native MoE, post-mHC, next-router, and LM states bitwise. For one controlled B branch, exact post-mHC endpoint reconstruction reproduces the measured downstream trajectory. At the next decode boundary, exact FP64 reconstruction of the branch's full persistent state yields agreement for 301 downstream post-mHC states, 301 persistent-state checkpoints, 301 routes, predictions, and text over seven steps, given the same naturally generated next input. These controls identify post-mHC as an intra-token boundary and full persistent state as a cross-token continuation boundary. Identical tokens need not imply identical autoregressive state: divergence can survive a token boundary and become visible later. These results make expert operand conversion, accumulator precision, and reduction order part of a numerical compatibility contract for sparse-MoE runtimes and hardware backends. They establish controlled causal possibility, not deployment incidence; C's order invariance is limited to evaluated six-term states and schedules.

</details>


### [344] [Information Bottleneck Learning for Faithful Time Series Forecasting Explanations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28124)
*Xu Zheng,Wei Cheng,Zhuomin Chen,Mo Sha,Jingchao Ni,Dongsheng Luo*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: IB-Forecast is an inherently interpretable multivariate time-series forecasting framework that achieves faithful explanations via a learned periodic component plus a residual explained by masks; it uses an information bottleneck to control explanation sparsity and matches state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy with explanations at no extra cost, outperforming baselines under the same sparsity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: There is a gap: interpretable-by-design forecasters may not faithfully reflect evidence; faithfulness-oriented methods are usually for post-hoc classification. Forecasting demands faithful explanations to support decision-making in energy, transportation, and healthcare.

Method: Decompose forecast into periodic component and residual; compute residual with explainable masks over input tokens; apply budget-constrained information bottleneck to enable end-to-end optimization of sparse, faithful explanations; evaluate faithfulness with a rigorous protocol; end-to-end training with no extra inference cost for explanations.

Result: Matches forecasting error of leading black-box models; provides faithful explanations with low cost; under matched sparsity, outperforms gradient-based, occlusion-based, optimization-based baselines across datasets; native explanations require only 14-20% of observations to deliver low-error predictions.

Conclusion: IB-Forecast delivers high explanation fidelity while maintaining competitive forecasting accuracy and enabling sparse, faithful explanations without additional inference cost; it bridges interpretability and faithfulness in forecasting.

Abstract: As forecasts increasingly drive decisions in fields such as energy, transportation, and healthcare, understanding the historical data behind these predictions has become as crucial as the predictions themselves. Although existing interpretable-by-design forecasters reveal their internal structures, they offer no guarantee that these structures faithfully reflect the underlying evidence driving the predictions. In contrast, while faithfulness-oriented methods explicitly verify model behavior, they are almost exclusively designed for post-hoc classification tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose IB-Forecast, an inherently interpretable multivariate time-series forecasting framework. It decomposes forecasting into a learned periodic component and a residual component computed with explainable masks over input tokens. With a budget-constrained information bottleneck, end-to-end optimization enables users to directly control explanation sparsity. With a rigorous faithfulness evaluation protocol, extensive experiments demonstrate that IB-Forecast matches the forecasting error of leading black-box models while providing faithful explanations at no additional inference cost. Furthermore, under a matched sparsity budget, these native explanations consistently surpass gradient-based, occlusion-based, and optimization-based baselines across all evaluated datasets. Ultimately, whereas the native explanations of existing interpretable forecasters exhibit poor faithfulness, IB-Forecast guarantees high explanation fidelity, requiring only 14-20% of the observations to deliver low-error predictions.

</details>


### [345] [LM-GRASP: Instance-Specific Language Models for Combinatorial Construction via Online Imitation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28135)
*Mohand Mezmaz,Grégoire Danoy*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Online imitation-learning for GRASP construction: LM-GRASP uses a decoder-only Transformer trained online via behavioral cloning against a local-search expert, removing offline pretraining and data dependencies; achieves significant gains on Taillard PFSP vs GPU-GRASP.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce pretraining costs and poor generalization of offline neural constructors by replacing static heuristics with a per-instance, data-driven policy learned on the fly from elite trajectories.

Method: Reformulate GRASP's randomized constructive phase as an online imitation-learning task. Use a local search procedure as the expert oracle and a decoder-only Transformer as the constructive policy. Train online via behavioral cloning on a dynamic archive of elite trajectories, no external data or offline pretraining. Iterate through learn-infer-improve with an objective evaluator interface.

Result: LM-GRASP outperforms GPU-GRASP on Taillard PFSP (ta51-ta60) by 28.4 makespan units on average; performance comparable to the gain from GPU acceleration over sequential (27.2 units); overlapping standard deviations.

Conclusion: Instance-specific, online-trained language models are a practical alternative to hand-engineered constructors for combinatorial optimization, particularly for landscapes resistant to classical greedy construction.

Abstract: Machine learning for combinatorial optimization typically relies on neural constructors trained via reinforcement learning on large offline datasets for a fixed problem class-incurring high pretraining costs and generalizing poorly outside the training distribution. We propose an alternative: a metaheuristic framework that reformulates the randomized constructive phase of GRASP as an online imitation learning task, trained from scratch on each problem instance. A local search procedure acts as an expert oracle, while a decoder-only Transformer serves as the constructive policy. Unlike classical GRASP, which relies on static, myopic heuristic rules based on localized scalar costs, our approach is fully data-driven: the construction policy emerges from high-quality solutions discovered during the search itself, with no problem-specific feature engineering required.
  We instantiate this as LM-GRASP, a hybrid metaheuristic following an iterative learn-infer-improve cycle, training the policy online via behavioral cloning on a dynamic archive of elite trajectories-no external data or offline pretraining needed. The pipeline interfaces with the domain solely through the objective evaluator used by local search.
  Evaluated on the Taillard PFSP benchmark (ta51-ta60), the most discriminating block due to half its optima being unknown, LM-GRASP outperforms GPU-GRASP by 28.4 makespan units on average-comparable to the gain from GPU acceleration over sequential execution (27.2 units), though with overlapping standard deviations. This suggests instance-specific, online-trained language models are a promising, practical alternative to hand-engineered constructors, especially for landscapes resistant to classical greedy construction.

</details>


### [346] [Search Strategies for Optimal Classification and Regression Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28170)
*Jacobus G. M. van der Linden,Mim van den Bos,Emir Demirović*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A general framework for optimal decision trees (ODTs) to compare search strategies; evaluates 18 strategies; best strategy improves classification anytime performance and regression runtime by >10x.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: ODTs are interpretable models with globally optimized objectives, but scalability hinges on search strategies. A unified framework is needed to disentangle each strategy's contribution and to enable fair comparisons.

Method: Introduce a general algorithmic framework that instantiates previously used search strategies and supports new ones; perform a comprehensive empirical study of 18 strategies across classification and regression tasks.

Result: The best strategy achieves significantly better anytime performance for classification and reduces regression runtime by more than an order of magnitude.

Conclusion: A common framework clarifies the impact of search strategies on ODT scalability and performance, enabling principled comparisons and identification of highly effective strategies.

Abstract: Optimal decision trees (ODTs) are compact, interpretable machine learning models that globally optimize a given objective, but their scalability remains challenging. While recent work has proposed a variety of search strategies to improve scalability, the precise contribution of each strategy remains unclear. To address this gap, we introduce a general algorithmic framework for ODTs that instantiates previously used search strategies and enables the definition of new ones. This provides a common lens through which to understand and compare different strategies, which we use to empirically investigate the effect of 18 search strategies. Compared to the state of the art, the best strategy in our evaluation achieves significantly better anytime performance for classification, and improves runtime by more than an order of magnitude for regression.

</details>


### [347] [Multi-channel Uplift Policy Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28182)
*Changjian Liu,Tianyu Wang,Xiaoxuan Deng,WenTao Zhu,Yuwei Xu,Jungqi Jin,Yong Gao,Chuan Yu,Jian Xu,Bo Zheng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: ReAlloc is a fast-slow causal framework for simplex-constrained multi-channel budget allocation in e-commerce, combining an Orthogonal Teacher for unbiased local gradients with an Explanation-Guided Student to form a long-horizon marginal field, enabling conservative, support-aware decisions that account for cross-channel substitutions; validated by simulations and Taobao A/B tests.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard predict-then-optimize approaches fail under observational confounding and extreme extrapolation in compositional budget problems. There is a need for causal, budget-aware methods that respect simplex constraints and model channel substitutions to maximize business utility.

Method: A two-component architecture: (1) Orthogonal Teacher (fast) extracts unbiased local gradients from short-term observational logs; (2) Explanation-Guided Student (slow) distills these gradients into a structured marginal field representing long-term effects over channels and time horizons, operating under simplex constraints to capture cross-channel substitutions and ensure conservative, support-aware decisions.

Result: Extensive simulations and large-scale online A/B tests on the Taobao platform show that ReAlloc achieves simultaneous lifts in pay order and income, indicating effective causal budget reallocation across channels.

Conclusion: ReAlloc demonstrates that a fast-slow, causal, and constraint-aware framework can overcome observational confounding and extrapolation in multi-channel budget optimization, delivering robust, long-horizon gains in utility while respecting budget constraints.

Abstract: E-commerce platforms must allocate fixed marketing budgets across multiple channels to maximize business utility. However, standard predict-then-optimize (PTO) paradigms fail in this compositional space due to observational confounding and severe extrapolation. We formulate this challenge as a simplex-constrained uplift decision problem and propose ReAlloc, a fast-slow causal framework. Specifically, an agile Orthogonal Teacher extracts unbiased local gradients from short-term logs, while an Explanation-Guided Student distills them into a structured marginal field over long-term horizons. This design enables support-aware, conservative decisions that capture cross-channel substitutions. Extensive simulations and large-scale online A/B tests on Taobao platform demonstrate that ReAlloc achieves simultaneous lifts in both pay order and income.

</details>


### [348] [Persistent Gaussian Perturbations Prevent Oversmoothing in Recurrent Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28185)
*Mostafa Haghir Chehreghani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Injecting Gaussian noise after each propagation in recurrent GNNs yields a geometrically ergodic Markov chain with a unique invariant measure; the stationary Dirichlet energy has a positive lower bound proportional to noise and graph spectral gap, preventing oversmoothing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Oversmoothing causes node representations to collapse across layers in deep GNNs, limiting expressiveness. Introducing stochastic perturbations may maintain representation diversity and provide rigorous guarantees against vanishing variation.

Method: Model a recurrent GNN with independent Gaussian noise added after every propagation step, analyze as a stochastic dynamical system under a global contraction assumption for the deterministic update. Prove geometric ergodicity and existence of a unique invariant measure; derive a positive lower bound on the stationary Dirichlet energy, proportional to noise variance and spectral gap; support with numerical experiments on linear and nonlinear recurrent GNNs.

Result: Hidden representations form a geometrically ergodic Markov chain with a unique invariant distribution. The expected stationary Dirichlet energy has a positive lower bound that scales with noise variance and the graph spectral gap, ensuring non-vanishing diversity at stationarity and preventing asymptotic oversmoothing. Numerical experiments corroborate the theory, showing convergence to a stationary distribution and Dirichlet energy behavior as predicted.

Conclusion: Persistent stochastic perturbations provide a fundamental mechanism to counter oversmoothing, complementing existing deterministic approaches (residual connections, normalization, graph rewiring). The results offer theoretical and empirical support for noise-based strategies to preserve representation diversity in deep GNNs.

Abstract: Oversmoothing is a fundamental limitation of deep graph neural networks (GNNs), where repeated message passing causes node representations to become increasingly similar, eventually collapsing toward a low-dimensional subspace. This phenomenon limits the effective depth of message-passing architectures and motivates the search for mechanisms that preserve representation diversity. In this paper, we study a recurrent graph neural network in which independent Gaussian noise is injected after every propagation step and analyze the resulting architecture as a stochastic dynamical system. Under a standard global contraction assumption on the deterministic update, we prove that the hidden representations form a geometrically ergodic Markov chain admitting a unique invariant probability measure. Our main theoretical result establishes an explicit positive lower bound on the expected stationary Dirichlet energy, proportional to both the noise variance and the spectral gap of the underlying graph. Consequently, the stationary representations cannot collapse onto the constant manifold, providing a rigorous guarantee that asymptotic oversmoothing is prevented in the sense of non-vanishing Dirichlet energy. Our analysis reveals persistent stochastic perturbations as a fundamentally different mechanism for combating oversmoothing, complementing existing deterministic approaches based on residual connections, normalization, and graph rewiring. Finally, numerical experiments on both linear and nonlinear recurrent graph neural networks closely match the theoretical predictions, illustrating the emergence of a stationary distribution and the predicted dependence of the limiting Dirichlet energy on the noise intensity.

</details>


### [349] [TopoFormer: Topology Meets Attention for Graph Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28259)
*Md Joshem Uddin,Astrit Tola,Cuneyt Gurcan Akcora,Baris Coskunuzer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Topoformer uses Topo-Scan to parse graphs into multi-scale topological sequences processed by Transformer, delivering scalable, stable graph representations with state-of-the-art results; avoids heavy persistent homology computations.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of traditional persistent homology pipelines (costly diagram computations, limited integration with DL) by providing a parallelizable, end-to-end learnable topological encoding that can be fed into standard attention-based models.

Method: Decompose graphs into an ordered sequence of topological tokens via node- or edge-filtrations (Topo-Scan) capturing local to global structure; feed the sequence to a Transformer to produce graph embeddings; prove stability of encodings.

Result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks; matches or surpasses strong GNN and topology-based baselines; demonstrates predictable and efficient compute.

Conclusion: Presents a parallelizable, unified approach that integrates topological inductive biases into attention frameworks for scalable graph representation learning.

Abstract: We introduce Topoformer, a lightweight and scalable framework for graph representation learning that encodes topological structure into attention-friendly sequences. At the core of our method is Topo-Scan, a novel module that decomposes a graph into a short, ordered sequence of topological tokens by slicing over node or edge filtrations. These sequences capture multi-scale structural patterns, from local motifs to global organization, and are processed by a Transformer to produce expressive graph-level embeddings. Unlike traditional persistent homology pipelines, Topo-Scan is parallelizable, avoids costly diagram computations, and integrates seamlessly with standard deep learning architectures. We provide theoretical guarantees on the stability of our topological encodings and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across graph classification and molecular property prediction benchmarks. Our results show that Topoformer matches or exceeds strong GNN and topology-based baselines while offering predictable and efficient compute. This work opens a new path for parallelizable and unifying approaches to graph representation learning that integrate topological inductive biases into attention frameworks.

</details>


### [350] [HARGO: Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization for RL Post-Training of LLMs on HPC Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28301)
*Tiangang Li,Xiangbo Tian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: HARGO introduces heterogeneity-aware reward-guided optimization for reinforcement learning post-training in HPC tasks, using per-response importance weighting via confidence-modulated advantage to handle diverse task types without task-type labels, achieving state-of-the-art alignment and metrics across multiple tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: SFT yields domain knowledge but may produce task-incorrect outputs; HPC tasks are highly heterogeneous (classification, QA, generation) with widely varying reward structures and output lengths. Uniform RL methods struggle to optimize across such heterogeneity without task-type signals.

Method: Compute a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast and a confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities. Modulate the policy advantage with these signals to obtain per-response weights, enabling heterogeneity-aware, reward-guided optimization without requiring task-type labels.

Result: Across four HPC tasks and nine methods, HARGO achieves the best scores on three primary metrics: WinRate 54.62%, Data Race F1 91.30%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablations show both signals contribute, and HARGO yields superior alignment quality for heterogeneous HPC tasks.

Conclusion: HARGO effectively addresses task heterogeneity in RL post-training for HPC by combining discrimination-based rewards and confidence-based weighting, achieving robust alignment across diverse task types without explicit task-type labeling.

Abstract: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can equip large language models (LLMs) with domain knowledge for high-performance computing (HPC) tasks such as data race detection and benchmark question answering. However, knowledge alone does not guarantee task-appropriate behavior: the same SFT model that correctly classifies 88.65\% of C/C++ data race samples produces verbose, imprecise answers to factual queries, with 65.9\% of MLPerf responses exceeding 40 characters. Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training addresses this gap by optimizing for task-specific rewards rather than token-level imitation. Yet HPC tasks exhibit extreme heterogeneity, with binary classification, factual QA, and semantic generation differing by 58x in answer length, spanning three distinct reward distributions, and showing widely varying SFT accuracy. This makes uniform-weight RL methods such as GRPO suboptimal. We propose HARGO, Heterogeneity-Aware Reward-Guided Optimization, which introduces per-response importance weighting via confidence-modulated advantage: computing a discrimination signal from group-level reward contrast and a confidence signal from reference model log-probabilities, then modulating the advantage before computing per-response weights, without requiring task-type labels. Across four HPC tasks and nine methods, HARGO achieves the best performance on all three primary metrics: WinRate 54.62\%, Data Race F1 91.30\%, and PLP Similarity 0.8558. Ablation confirms complementary contributions from both signals. HARGO establishes the best overall alignment quality among compared methods for heterogeneous HPC tasks.

</details>


### [351] [Semi-Supervised Learning for Molecular Graphs via Ensemble Consensus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28304)
*Rasmus Tirsgaard,Laurits Fredsgaard,Marisa Wodrich,Mikkel Jordahn,Mikkel N. Schmidt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Ensemble-consensus semi-supervised learning improves molecular property prediction across datasets and GNN architectures, providing robustness, a distillation-like effect, and reduced calibration error.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Labeling molecular data is expensive; abundant unlabeled data calls for semi-supervised approaches that do not rely on fragile label-preserving augmentations.

Method: Train models with an ensemble-consensus objective over unlabeled data, leveraging consensus among ensemble members to supervise each other; demonstrate across diverse molecular datasets, tasks, and graph neural networks.

Result: Ensemble-consensus training yields higher predictive accuracy across datasets and architectures; an individual ensemble member can outperform a full traditional supervised ensemble; reduces calibration error.

Conclusion: Ensemble-consensus semi-supervised learning provides robust, distillation-like gains for molecular ML that generalize across tasks and architectures and mitigates calibration issues.

Abstract: Machine learning is transforming molecular sciences by accelerating property prediction, simulation, and the discovery of new molecules and materials. Acquiring labeled data in these domains is often costly and time-consuming, whereas large collections of unlabeled molecular data are readily available. Standard semi-supervised learning methods often rely on label-preserving augmentations, which are challenging to design in the molecular domain, where minor changes can drastically alter properties. In this work, we show that semi-supervised methods that rely on an ensemble consensus can boost predictive accuracy across a diverse range of molecular datasets, task types, and graph neural network architectures. We find that training with an ensemble consensus objective increases robustness in models and exhibits an effect similar to knowledge distillation; an individual member of an ensemble trained this way outperforms a full ensemble trained in a traditional supervised fashion in almost all cases. In addition, this type of semi-supervised training reduces calibration error.

</details>


### [352] [Beyond Geometric Complementarity: Coherent Overlap in Sparse Mixture-of-Experts Routing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28308)
*Huiyuan Tian,Bonan Xu,Shijian Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Sparse MoE routing leverages a shared geometric neighborhood of expert subspaces; whether an expert is selected matters more for representation than raw subspace dissimilarity, and adding more experts can improve accuracy even when subspaces overlap significantly. A unified notion of coherent overlap explains why geometry alone cannot predict redundancy or pruning value.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Disentangle the intertwined factors in sparse MoE effectiveness: route coherence, candidate quality, and context interaction, and establish metrics (ESSI, matched-route residuals) and controlled experiments to separate them.

Method: Introduce Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI), matched-route residuals, and a prefix-controlled 2x2 factorial design; perform frozen-route interventions and controlled Top-k studies. Conduct three paired contrasts across six MoE architectures and across 39 factorial cells in OLMoE, Mixtral, and DeepSeek to compare routed vs matched representations, selectivity vs unselected rivals, and the effect of adding later experts; complement with training studies.

Result: Finding 1: Expert subspaces overlap substantially across architectures, yet actual routed representations explain token representations better than matched alternatives. Finding 2: In all 39 factorial cells, the selected candidate explains more of the residual than the strongest unselected rival, but the prefix narrows this advantage; all interactions are negative with CIs below zero. Finding 3: Coherent overlap persists as adding later experts improves next-token prediction in 24/39 frozen-route cases; 15 inconclusive; training favors Top-2 over Top-1 across seeds. This supports a view where routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood without implying disjoint linear coverage. 

Conclusion: Coherent overlap articulates why geometric similarity cannot alone determine redundancy or pruning value in sparse MoE: routing leverages shared subspaces to exploit token-relevant directions while benefiting from multi-expert computation; separating route quality, geometry, and interaction clarifies pruning decisions.

Abstract: Sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models route each token to multiple experts, suggesting a geometric account of their benefit: co-selected experts should contribute distinct representation directions. Existing evidence often conflates route coherence, candidate quality, and candidate-by-context interaction. We distinguish these quantities using an Expert Subspace Separation Index (ESSI), matched-route residuals, and a prefix-controlled $2\times2$ factorial; frozen-route interventions and a controlled Top-$k$ study assess functional value. Three paired contrasts organize the findings. First, across six MoE architectures, expert subspaces overlap substantially, yet actual routes explain token representations better than matched alternatives. Second, across the 39 factorial cells in OLMoE, Mixtral, and DeepSeek, the selected candidate explains more of the residual representation than the strongest unselected rival in every cell, yet the actual prefix narrows this advantage throughout: all interactions are negative, and every 95% confidence interval lies below zero. Third, this geometric narrowing does not imply functional redundancy: adding later experts improves next-token prediction in 24 of 39 frozen-route comparisons, while the other 15 estimates are inconclusive; a controlled training study also favors Top-2 over Top-1 in all three seeds. We call this joint pattern coherent overlap: routing selects token-relevant experts from a shared geometric neighborhood, while useful multi-expert computation persists without disjoint linear coverage. Separating these quantities clarifies why geometric similarity alone cannot determine redundancy or pruning value.

</details>


### [353] [Measuring Distortion in the Empty Regions of Dimensionality Reduction Scatterplots with the Gap Index](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28324)
*Jaume Ros,Alessio Arleo,Fernando Paulovich*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Gap Index (GI) is a new 2D projection quality metric that captures visual distortion in empty areas by decomposing the layout into empty triangles and comparing them to their high-dimensional analogs; GI detects small deformations, is fast to compute, and can be visualized as regional distortion maps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing projection quality metrics emphasize pairwise relationships (distances, neighborhoods) and often ignore distortions in empty regions of the layout, which can be visually salient. A metric that accounts for empty-space distortion could provide a more perceptually faithful assessment and support better interpretation of 2D projections.

Method: Partition the 2D projection space into empty triangles (triangulation of empty areas). For each empty triangle, map or compare with the corresponding high-dimensional structure to compute a per-triangle deformation. Aggregate per-triangle deformations into a single scalar GI or overlay a distortion heatmap on the projection to visualize regional distortion patterns.

Result: GI is highly sensitive to small structural deformations that have high visual impact, addressing a blind spot of traditional metrics. It is fast to compute and yields an interpretable measure, and its per-triangle decomposition enables visualization of localized distortion patterns.

Conclusion: GI complements existing projection quality metrics by capturing distortions in empty areas, offering a perceptually aligned, efficient tool for evaluating and visualizing 2D projections, and aiding interpretation of visual analysis results.

Abstract: Quality metrics play a crucial role in the proper use of dimensionality reduction projections for visual analysis of high-dimensional data. They quantify the degree of distortion of a projection compared to the high-dimensional data and provide a reliable indication of how confident users can be in the structures they see in the resulting layouts. However, most popular metrics focus on capturing direct relationships between points (e.g., distances or neighborhoods) while neglecting distortions in empty areas of the layout, even though these often compose visually relevant features of a 2D layout. In this paper, we introduce the Gap Index (GI), a quality metric for 2D projections that captures visual distortion by measuring spatial distortion in empty areas of a projection. It does so by decomposing the space into empty triangles, which are then compared to their high-dimensional counterparts to compute the deformation. This per-triangle deformation can be aggregated into a single scalar value or overlaid on a projection to visualize regional distortion patterns. Results show that, contrary to popular quality metrics, the GI is sensitive to small structural deformations that have high visual impact. It is also fast to compute and interpretable.

</details>


### [354] [Encryption-Compatible Clustered Federated Learning via Distributed Expectation-Maximization over Metadata](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28338)
*Michael Ben Ali,Imen Megdiche,André Péninou,Olivier Teste*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Proposes FLAMECHE, a privacy-compatible, metadata-based CFL method implemented as a distributed EM algorithm with additive server updates, achieving stronger clustering and model performance under the CFL trilemma.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: CFL faces a trilemma among privacy, communication, and computation; existing metadata-based clustering conflicts with FL privacy; there is a need for a method that preserves privacy while remaining efficient.

Method: Reformulate metadata-based CFL as a distributed EM procedure; constrain server updates to additive operations to preserve privacy and compatibility with secure FL; enable encryption-friendly metadata handling within the EM framework.

Result: Empirical evaluation across multiple datasets and heterogeneous scenarios shows that FLAMECHE improves client model effectiveness and enables encryption-compatible clustering, advancing performance within the CFL trilemma.

Conclusion: FLAMECHE advances clustered federated learning by delivering a privacy-preserving, communication- and computation-efficient clustering method compatible with secure FL, thus improving practical deployment under data heterogeneity.

Abstract: Clustered Federated Learning (CFL) addresses data heterogeneity in federated settings by grouping clients with similar data distributions to enable effective training. Existing methods face a trade-off between privacy preservation, communication cost, and computational efficiency. We formalize this as the CFL trilemma, according to which improving two of these dimensions comes at the expense of the third. A prominent paradigm relies on metadata (i.e., low-dimensional representations of client datasets shared with the server) to enable communication- and computation-efficient clustering. However, such approaches are not compatible with standard FL privacy-preserving mechanisms. To address this limitation, we propose FLAMECHE, which reformulates metadata-based CFL as a distributed Expectation-Maximization (EM) procedure, restricting server updates to additive operations while preserving efficiency. This design enables compatibility with practical secure FL schemes. We conducted extensive experiments on multiple datasets under various heterogeneous scenarios. Results show that FLAMECHE improves the effectiveness of client models. It enables encryption-compatible metadata-based clustering, enhancing its positioning within the CFL trilemma.

</details>


### [355] [LEDGERMIND: Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28374)
*Enjun Du,Hange Zhou,Chenxu Du,Siyi Liu,Zirong Chen,Ziyu Zheng,Yongqi Zhang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LedgerMind enforces a provenance-constrained, evidence-led reasoning trace to boost accuracy and faithfulness in multimodal VQA.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Final-answer accuracy alone masks whether the answer rests on grounded evidence, priors, or accidental error cancellation; there is a need for trajectory-level provenance, grounded verification, and repair mechanisms.

Method: Treat agent reasoning as a provenance-constrained state machine. Normalize tool outputs into a Structured Evidence Ledger as the trajectory state; downstream reasoning/claims may cite only active ledger entries; grounding is checked at the entity and numeric level; repair occurs via typed state transitions that cannot introduce content without tool-produced provenance. Key components include LedgerMind architecture with a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher, and Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine with a provenance non-amplification guarantee.

Result: Demonstrated across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs that LedgerMind improves both final-answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness, targeting four recurring failure patterns: unsupported intermediate reasoning, phantom grounding, over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification.

Conclusion: Provenance-constrained, ledger-based reasoning enhances trustworthiness in multimodal reasoning by preventing ungrounded claims, reducing hallucinations, and improving alignment between evidence and conclusions.

Abstract: Multimodal agents for visual question answering increasingly operate as multi-step trajectories that interleave perception, retrieval, and reasoning, yet evaluation still largely reduces to final-answer accuracy. This aggregate signal cannot tell whether a correct answer was reached through grounded evidence, language priors, or accidental error cancellation. We propose to treat a multimodal agent trajectory as a provenance-constrained state machine: tool outputs are normalized into a Structured Evidence Ledger that serves as the trajectory state, downstream reasoning and decision claims may cite only active ledger entries, grounding is checked at the entity and numeric level, and repair is realized as typed state transitions that cannot introduce content without tool-produced provenance. We instantiate this design as LedgerMind (Provenance-Constrained Multimodal Agentic Reasoning with a Structured Evidence Ledger), augmented by a Three-Layer Grounding Protocol, an Adaptive Dual-Path Dispatcher that matches reasoning depth to question complexity, and an Event-Triggered Verification-and-Repair engine with a formal provenance non-amplification guarantee. We use LedgerMind to target four recurring failure patterns that final-answer accuracy tends to obscure: unsupported intermediate reasoning, citation-backed entity hallucination (Phantom Grounding), over-reasoning on simple queries, and repair-time amplification. Experiments across multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks and backbone MLLMs show that LedgerMind improves both answer accuracy and trajectory-level faithfulness.

</details>


### [356] [Hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo for Order-Optimal Neural Actor-Critic in Average-Reward CMDPs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28390)
*Ankur Naskar,Vaneet Aggarwal*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Introduces a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic for average-reward CMDPs that enables first-order-optimal convergence of primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic with neural critics, without requiring knowledge of the mixing time.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Safety-critical RL with CMDPs requires long-horizon reward maximization under constraints. While primal-dual actor-critic methods with linear critics have established guarantees, extending order-optimal convergence to neural critics in the average-reward setting is hindered by a bias-cost trade-off under Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) analysis; reducing bias inflates critic optimization cost, preventing optimality.

Method: Propose a hierarchical MLMC neural critic that debiases across both trajectory sampling and critic optimization, achieving the bias of a long critic optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost. Build a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm that leverages this estimator.

Result: The estimator attains an optimality gap and a constraint violation of order tilde{O}(T^{-1/2}); establishes the first-order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics, without requiring prior knowledge of the mixing time; novel even in the unconstrained setting.

Conclusion: Demonstrates feasibility of order-optimal convergence for average-reward CMDPs with neural critics and eliminates the need to know the mixing time, expanding practicality of neural-critic methods in constrained RL.

Abstract: Constrained Markov Decision Processes (CMDPs) provide a natural framework for reinforcement learning in safety-critical applications, where agents maximize long-term reward while satisfying long-term constraints. Although primal-dual actor-critic methods with linear critics are well understood, extending order-optimal convergence guarantees to neural critics in average-reward CMDPs has remained open. The main challenge is a fundamental bias-cost trade-off in neural critic estimation: under Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) analysis, reducing critic bias substantially increases critic optimization cost, preventing order-optimal convergence in the primal-dual framework. We resolve this bottleneck by introducing a hierarchical Multilevel Monte Carlo (MLMC) neural critic that performs debiasing simultaneously across trajectory sampling and critic optimization. The resulting estimator attains the bias of a long critic optimization run with only logarithmic expected sample cost. Building on this estimator, we develop a primal-dual Natural Actor-Critic algorithm that achieves both an optimality gap and a constraint violation of order $\tilde{O}(T^{-1/2})$. This establishes the first order-optimal convergence guarantees for infinite-horizon average-reward CMDPs with general policy parameterization and neural critics, while eliminating the need to know the underlying mixing time. Our results are novel even in the unconstrained setting.

</details>


### [357] [Why Are GUI Agents Correct but Late? Decode on the Decision-Time Critical Path, Tested with Pre-Compiled Policy Trees](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28399)
*Zihan Dong,Rui Qian,Qishi Zhan,Dongshen Peng,Kaixin Li,Yu Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: AAPT reduces decision-time latency in GUI agents by precomputing a bounded policy tree during idle times and routing to pre-authorized actions at runtime, significantly boosting success without generating text during execution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Combat the latency-induced failures in autoregressive, decision-time critical GUI actions where the relevant window closes before inference completes.

Method: Freeze a multimodal model; in idle periods construct a bounded conditional policy tree with observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines. At runtime, a lightweight observer maps frames to a prepared branch, executing the action without text decoding. Evaluate via paired trials with pre-registered endpoints and exact McNemar tests; perform ablations, an oracle probe, and reproduce on another model; extend to external benchmark.

Result: Success rate improves from 0.50 to 0.79 within the decision window (p=1.8e-3); no incorrect actions. Open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines fail (decode during execution). Replication on an independent model yields a similar effect (p=4.9e-13). External benchmark shows comparable overall performance to a reactive baseline; AAPT excels when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance. Ablations identify fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing as key components; branch routing identified as the causal bottleneck by a pre-registered oracle probe.

Conclusion: AAPT can mitigate latency by preplanning and fast routing rather than altering the base model, performing best when action spaces are enumerated in advance and complementing reactive strategies when they are not.

Abstract: Computer-use agents often fail on transient GUI events because they produce the correct action only after the relevant window has already closed. We identify the main cause as expensive autoregressive decoding on the decision-time critical path. We propose Adaptive Anticipatory Policy Trees (AAPT), which eliminates this delay without modifying the underlying model. During idle screen periods, the same frozen multimodal model constructs a bounded conditional policy tree with observable guards, pre-authorized actions, and branch-specific deadlines. The tree is sized to cover the model's own decoding latency. When an event occurs, a lightweight observer matches change-gated frames to a prepared branch and immediately executes the corresponding action without generating new text. In paired trials with pre-registered endpoints and exact McNemar tests, AAPT improves the success rate from 0.50 to 0.79 within a contested decision window ($p=1.8\times10^{-3}$), while producing no incorrect actions. Both open-loop and predict-and-replan baselines achieve zero success because they still decode during execution. A preparation-time sweep shows that the gain emerges where the latency-based tree-sizing rule predicts, and ablations reveal three key requirements: fast observer decoding, valid tree planning, and accurate branch routing. A pre-registered oracle probe rejects our initial hypothesis and instead points to branch routing as the causal bottleneck. We further reproduce the effect on an independent general-purpose multimodal model over 126 paired trials ($p=4.9\times10^{-13}$). On an external benchmark, AAPT matches the overall performance of a reactive baseline, although the two methods exhibit complementary strengths. Together, these results suggest that AAPT performs best when candidate actions can be enumerated in advance, whereas reactive execution remains stronger when they cannot.

</details>


### [358] [On-Policy and Off-Policy Learning for Large Action Spaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28408)
*Imad Aouali*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Structured Bayesian on-policy and off-policy learning for large-action contextual bandits; introduces meTS, dTS, sDM, and differentiable pessimistic objectives with PAC-Bayes guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Contextual bandits in large action spaces suffer from exploration inefficiency, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance weights, extrapolation bias, and difficult optimization. The work seeks scalable, provably sound methods across on- and off-policy settings.

Method: On-policy: meTS (mixed-effect Thompson sampling) and dTS (diffusion-inspired priors) to share information across actions and enable regret guarantees tied to an effective action count. Off-policy: sDM (structured direct method) using latent-variable modeling; analysis showing optimization error can dominate estimation error; concave, efficiently optimizable policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives. Differentiable pessimistic methods: exponential smoothing and PAC-Bayesian bounds to control bias-variance of regularized importance-sampling estimators.

Result: Regret guarantees that depend on an effective number of actions for on-policy methods; practical optimization considerations in large action spaces for off-policy learning; introduction of concave, scalable objectives; theoretical framing for bias-variance trade-offs via PAC-Bayes in differentiable pessimism.

Conclusion: The thesis advances large-action contextual bandit learning by integrating structured Bayesian on-policy and off-policy methods with provable guarantees and practical optimization objectives, offering scalable, robust approaches for real-world interactive systems.

Abstract: This thesis studies policy learning in interactive systems where an agent observes a context, selects an action from a very large set, and receives partial feedback. The main framework is contextual bandits, with two paradigms: on-policy learning, where the agent interacts sequentially with the environment and minimizes regret, and off-policy learning, where it learns from logged data collected by a logging policy. In large action spaces, both settings face major challenges: inefficient exploration, sparse data coverage, high-variance importance weights, extrapolation bias, and difficult optimization landscapes. The first part develops structured Bayesian methods for on-policy learning. We introduce meTS, a mixed-effect extension of Thompson sampling, and dTS, which leverages diffusion-inspired priors to model dependencies between actions. These methods share information across actions and yield regret guarantees depending on an effective number of actions. The second part addresses off-policy learning. We propose sDM, a structured direct method based on latent variables, show that optimization error can dominate estimation error in large action spaces, and introduce concave, efficiently optimizable policy-weighted log-likelihood objectives. Finally, we develop differentiable pessimistic methods based on exponential smoothing and PAC-Bayesian bounds to control the bias-variance trade-off of regularized importance-sampling estimators.

</details>


### [359] [QAdapt: A Noise-Adaptive Neural Pre-Decoding Framework for Quantum Error Correction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28422)
*Ran Miao,Rui Luo,Xiaohan Shan,Xiaoming Sun*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Noise-adaptive neural pre-decoder for surface-code QEC (QAdapt) that uses local spatiotemporal syndrome correlations to adapt to evolving hardware noise, improving logical error rate and backend decoding latency by forwarding residual syndrome to a conventional decoder.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FTQC performance is limited not only by physical noise but also by decoder latency and nonstationary hardware noise; simulation-to-hardware distribution shifts can degrade fixed neural decoders; a robust, decoder-compatible solution is required.

Method: A neural pre-decoder that captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, sequentially adapts to evolving noise conditions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and passes the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder for final correction.

Result: Across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations for rotated surface-code memory circuits, QAdapt reduces the logical error rate relative to a neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google's Willow benchmark data, without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves up to 5.79% reduction in logical error rate and 9.32% reduction in backend decoding latency on the residual syndrome.

Conclusion: QAdapt presents a practical, decoder-compatible approach to enhancing the robustness and backend decoding efficiency of quantum error correction under evolving hardware noise.

Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) relies on quantum error correction to suppress physical errors and preserve logical information at scale. In practice, however, performance is constrained not only by physical noise but also by the latency of classical decoders processing rapidly generated syndrome data. This challenge is exacerbated by hardware noise that is strong, heterogeneous, and nonstationary, as well as by the simulation-to-hardware distribution shift that can substantially degrade fixed neural decoders. We present QAdapt, a noise-adaptive neural pre-decoding framework for surface-code quantum error correction. QAdapt captures local spatiotemporal correlations in syndrome data, sequentially adapts to evolving noise conditions while mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and forwards the residual syndrome to a conventional global decoder. Across 110 synthetic out-of-distribution noise configurations for rotated surface-code memory circuits, QAdapt consistently reduces the logical error rate relative to the neural pre-decoding baseline. On Google's Willow benchmark data, without target-domain fine-tuning, it achieves reductions of up to 5.79 percent in logical error rate and 9.32 percent in backend decoding latency on the residual syndrome. These results demonstrate that QAdapt provides a practical and decoder-compatible approach to improving the robustness and backend decoding efficiency of quantum error correction under evolving hardware noise.

</details>


### [360] [Kohn-Sham Spectral Embedding on Sparse Graphs at the Nishimori Temperature for Image Classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28428)
*V. S. Usatyuk,D. A. Sapozhnikov,S. I. Egorov*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KSSE is a physics-inspired sparse spectral embedding that replaces dense CNN classifiers with a sparse graph spectral method. It uses Nishimori temperature from a Random-Bond Ising Model, maps features to quasi-cyclic LDPC graphs, and solves D spectral problems via FFT on circulant blocks with Rayleigh refinement. The approach introduces six theoretical results and achieves competitive ImageNet-1000 performance with far fewer parameters (88.93% Top-1 with ~21.24M) in a transductive setting, outperforming Swin-L and matching ViT-H/14 while greatly reducing model footprint.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Provide a physics-informed, energy-based, sparse spectral framework for vision that preserves accuracy with drastically fewer parameters. Leverage connections between belief propagation, Laplacian spectra, and coding theory to yield scalable, well-behaved optimization landscapes and provable properties.

Method:  KSSE maps pre-trained features onto quasi-cyclic LDPC-like graphs, constructs a regularized Laplacian acting as a Kohn–Sham Hamiltonian, and solves D independent spectral problems in O(N log N + k^2_mode N) time using FFT on circulant blocks. Uses star-domain surgery to optimize graph topology by creating local convexity around codewords, with residual frustration bounded. Incorporates multi-scale fractal analysis (D2 spectrum) to certify landscape transitions (D2>3 rough to D2<1 star-domain basins) enabling Rayleigh refinement with k_mode=5. Proves six results: generalized Ihara–Bass identity linking belief propagation to the Laplacian; trapping-set eigenvalue correspondence; additive channel separability with an exchange-correlation bound; a surgery theorem bounding frustration with attractor width Ω(1/√d_min); quasi-stationarity perturbation bound; and a fixed-point convergence theorem. Experimental setup: transductive protocol on ImageNet-1000 with frozen EfficientNet-B4 features (D=1792).

Result: Attains 88.93% Top-1 accuracy with ~21.24M parameters, outperforming Swin-L (86.4–87.3% with 197M) and matching ViT-H/14 (88.0–89.5% with 632M) in standard inductive ranges, while reducing model footprint by about 10× and 30× respectively.

Conclusion: KSSE demonstrates that a physics-inspired, sparse spectral embedding can achieve competitive or superior accuracy with far fewer parameters compared to dense CNNs and large transformers, supported by six theoretical results and a scalable algorithm via FFT-based spectral solves and topology surgery.

Abstract: We introduce Kohn--Sham Spectral Embedding (KSSE), a physics-inspired energy-based model replacing dense CNN classifiers with a sparse-graph spectral embedding evaluated at the Nishimori temperature of an associated Random-Bond Ising Model. By mapping pre-trained features onto quasi-cyclic low-density parity-check graphs and constructing a regularized Laplacian acting as a Kohn--Sham Hamiltonian, we solve $D$ independent channel spectral problems in $\mathcal{O}(N\log N + k^2_{\text{mode}} N)$ time via FFT on circulant blocks (leveraging Pontryagin self-duality of $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$) and low-order Rayleigh refinement. Graph topology is optimized using \emph{star-domain surgery}: rather than destroying information-carrying codewords by removing frustrated cycles, we construct edge shifts creating local convexity around codewords while bounding residual frustration to $ρ(B_γ)\leq 1+δ$. Multi-scale fractal analysis ($D_2$ spectrum) and fractal learning-rate landscape certifies a landscape transition from rough regimes ($D_2>3$) to star-domain basins ($D_2<1$), enabling Rayleigh refinement with $k_{\text{mode}}=5$ modes. We prove six theoretical results: a generalized Ihara--Bass identity linking belief propagation to the Laplacian; trapping-set eigenvalue correspondence; additive channel separability with an explicit exchange-correlation bound; a surgery theorem bounding frustration with attractor width $Ω(1/\sqrt{d_{\min}})$; a quasi-stationarity perturbation bound; and a fixed-point convergence theorem. In a transductive protocol on ImageNet-1000 with frozen EfficientNet-B4 features ($D=1792$), KSSE achieves \textbf{88.93\%} Top-1 accuracy using $\approx 21.24$M parameters, outperforming Swin-L (197M, 86.4--87.3\%) and matching ViT-H/14 (632M, 88.0--89.5\%) under standard inductive setups, while reducing model footprint by $10\times$ and $30\times$, respectively.

</details>


### [361] [Oracle-Budgeted Molecular Optimization with Short-Term Graph Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28437)
*Jiannan Yang,Veronika Thost,Xiang Ling,Tengfei Ma*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A plug-in short-term graph memory surrogate guides oracle queries in molecular optimization under limited budget, improving top-10 performance without extra oracle calls across multiple generators.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Under a restricted oracle budget, decide what to evaluate by learning from past evaluations; improve efficiency by prioritizing high-utility candidates.

Method: Introduce short-term graph memory (STGM) as a plug-in; maintain an online graph neural surrogate; pre-screen candidate pools each round; allocate oracle budget to higher predicted utility; preserves generator architecture and update rule.

Result: On a fragment-based generator for standard benchmarks, improves mean top-10 score without extra oracle cost; never worse than base; gains extend to four generators at 1000 oracle calls.

Conclusion: Surrogate-guided selection interacts with exploration/exploitation; benefits depend on backbone search breadth and its exploitation of oracle feedback; provides a simple approach to spend fixed budget more selectively and identifies which generators benefit.

Abstract: Molecular optimization is commonly performed under a limited oracle budget, which makes deciding what to evaluate as important as deciding what to generate. We introduce short-term graph memory, a plug-in module that preserves the generator architecture and native update rule while learning from previously evaluated molecules to prioritize subsequent oracle queries. The module maintains an online graph neural surrogate that pre-screens each round's candidate pool, so the fixed oracle budget is spent on molecules with higher predicted utility. Applied to a fragment-based generator on a standard molecular optimization benchmark, it improves the mean top-10 score at no extra oracle cost and never falls behind the base on any oracle; the gain extends to all four generators we tested at a tight budget of one thousand calls. We then analyze how surrogate-guided selection interacts with the exploration and exploitation behavior of different generators. Its benefit at larger budgets is consistent with two properties of the backbone: how broadly it searches, and how effectively its native search already exploits oracle feedback. We provide a simple way to spend a fixed oracle budget more selectively, and evidence on which generators benefit from it.

</details>


### [362] [Cybersecurity Detection Classification with Reasoning-enabled Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28460)
*Amol Khanna,Manu Nandan,Cristian Viorel Popa,Joan Pujol-Roig,Diana Bolocan,Laura Vasilie,Alexandru Apostu,Chase Helwig,Mihaela Gaman,Michael Brautbar,Edward Raff,Chase Midler,Sven Krasser*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CoT-enabled triage classifier with a calibrator improves automated triage in SOCs, outperforming direct-label LLMs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reduce alert fatigue in Security Operations Centers by enabling accurate, high-confidence triage judgments from detections while filtering out benign alerts.

Method: Train a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier using automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. CoT reasoning reduces label-token probabilities, so a separate calibrator reads the full reasoning trace to estimate verdict correctness. Evaluation on real Windows endpoint detections yields 82.6% test accuracy; high-confidence operation improves benign recall and malicious recall versus direct-label LLM; finetuned 30B model outperforms frontier models.

Result: 82.6% test accuracy. At high-confidence threshold for automated triage: benign recall increases by 43.0%; malicious recall increases by 18.3% compared with a direct-label LLM. Calibrator is necessary; untrained confidence judge collapses high-confidence recall. A finetuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models.

Conclusion: Targeted training with CoT reasoning and a calibrated verdict estimator yields superior automated triage performance for SOC detections, highlighting the importance of task-specific training over mere model scale.

Abstract: A major issue in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) is alert fatigue, as the number of detections reported is more than staff can triage in a given day. Prior work prompts or fine-tunes large language models (LLMs) to emit a triage label directly, but does not train them to reason about whether a detection is a genuine threat. We train a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning-enabled triage classifier on real, human-labeled Windows endpoint detections by combining automated prompt optimization, self-training, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. We find that CoT reasoning also degrades the label-token probabilities that automated triage relies on, so we separately train a calibrator that reads the full reasoning trace and estimates the probability that the verdict is correct. Our system reaches 82.6% test accuracy and, at the high-confidence operating point that governs automated triage, improves benign recall by 43.0% and malicious recall by 18.3% over a direct-label LLM classifier. We further show that the trained calibrator is necessary - an untrained confidence judge collapses high-confidence recall to zero - and that a finetuned 30B model significantly outperforms frontier general-purpose models, motivating targeted training over scale.

</details>


### [363] [Stage-Replay Divergence Follows the KV Cache: Fixed-Prefix Precision Controls and Bidirectional Cache Transplantation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28495)
*Alexander Boesgaard Lorup*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Stage-replay cache diagnostics show that exact-token replay is largely repeatable and causally governed by boundary key/value caches, with numerical precision moderating outcomes: FP32 is essentially bit-exact; BF16 exhibits limited divergence across suffixes and correctness labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Evaluate whether stage-replay semantics (treating fresh-prefill as continuation from the original decoder state) hold at a reasoning-stage boundary, and whether cache states and numeric precision affect repeatability of divergent trajectories in a Qwen2.5-derived system.

Method: 200-item experiment comparing retained live cache versus one-shot prefill of identical integer tokens, with exact replicas on both sides. Tests include BF16 vs FP32 precision, fixed-prefix 2x2 tests, prospective token-by-token incremental caching, saved-ledger audits, and bidirectional transplantation of 48 key/value layers across primary and later checkpoints. Metrics include decoded disagreements, Wilson intervals, and trajectory footprints.

Result: BF16 shows replicas remaining exact for many tokens but diverging on 166 suffixes and 20 correctness labels; accuracy difference ~1 point (95% CI [-3.5, +5.5]). FP32 yields no decoded disagreements (95% Wilson upper bound 1.88%). Boundary K/V cache can carry divergent trajectories; all-200 saved-ledger audits reproduce retained trajectories; token-by-token caches produced bit-exact results on 12/12 rows; cross-checks across checks reproduce trajectories and fingerprints. Exact-token replay is repeatable without preserving live-state fidelity. Precision modulates behavioral expression, while the boundary cache acts as a causally sufficient carrier for divergence.

Conclusion: Stage-replay diagnostics demonstrate that exact-token replay can be repeatable without live-state fidelity when the boundary K/V cache is the driving carrier of the trajectory, with precision playing a key role in the magnitude of discrepancies. FP32 enables near bit-exact reproducibility; BF16 permits limited divergence. The method validates cache-transferability of divergent continuations and supports reproducible auditing of token-level trajectories across checkpoints.

Abstract: Stage-replay diagnostics reconstruct intermediate token prefixes and treat fresh-prefill continuation as continuation from the decoder state that originally reached the prefix. We audit that assumption at a whole reasoning-stage boundary in a Qwen2.5-derived system. A matched 200-item experiment compares retained live cache with one-shot prefill of identical integer tokens and places an exact replica on both sides. In BF16, replicas remain exact while the constructions differ on 166 suffixes and 20 correctness labels; the accuracy difference is only one point (paired 95% CI [-3.5, +5.5]). A fixed-prefix 2x2 holds all 200 token states constant while crossing construction and precision. The BF16 disagreements recur, whereas FP32 produces no decoded disagreement (95% Wilson upper bound 1.88%). A prospective bridge makes token-by-token incremental and retained live caches bit-exact on 12/12 rows; an all-200 saved-ledger audit reproduces every retained trajectory and comparison fingerprint. Bidirectional transplantation of all 48 key/value layers makes every tested divergent continuation follow its cache donor, both on a selected set at the primary checkpoint (24/24) and an outcome-blind replication at a later checkpoint (43/43). Exact-token replay can therefore be repeatable without preserving live-state fidelity. On the tested states, boundary K/V cache is a causally sufficient carrier of the divergent trajectory, while numerical precision moderates its behavioral expression.

</details>


### [364] [The Role of Causality in Algorithmic Recourse](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28497)
*Srikanth Avasarala,Varun Gupta,Shahin Jabbari,Saber Salehkaleybar,Juba Ziani*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Formalizes algorithmic recourse within a causal performative framework to account for how recourse actions affect true qualifications, addressing gaming and distribution shifts; shows conditions for performatively stable solutions that can be computed iteratively; empirical results indicate improved robustness and reduced retraining needs compared to standard ERM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address the gap where recourse policies optimize for flipping predictions without considering whether actions improve the true label, leading to gaming and degraded performance after model updates.

Method: Embed recourse actions in a structural causal model of the domain, analyze how actions propagate to features and the true label, and study the resulting non-convex optimization. Propose iterative dynamics to reach performatively stable equilibria. Provide theoretical conditions for existence and computeability, supported by semi-synthetic and real credit-data experiments.

Result: Characterizes conditions under which performatively stable solutions exist and are efficiently computable. Demonstrates that causal recourse reduces misaligned behavioral responses and gaming, and yields stable equilibria. Empirical results show superior performance over standard ERM and less need for retraining under distribution shifts caused by strategic behavior.

Conclusion: Incorporating causal structure into recourse yields stability against strategic responses, mitigating gaming and retraining costs, and improving robustness of predictive performance in high-stakes domains.

Abstract: Algorithmic recourse aims to provide individuals with actionable changes to improve their predicted outcomes in high-stakes classification settings, such as loan and mortgage applications. However, most existing approaches focus only on flipping a model's prediction, without accounting for whether the recommended changes lead to genuine improvement in an individual's true qualifications or merely enable strategic gaming of the classifier. Consequently, deployed recourse policies can induce behavioral responses that degrade predictive accuracy and become ineffective after model retraining.
  In this work, we formalize this failure mode through a causal performative framework for recourse. We model how recourse actions propagate through a structural causal model, capturing interactions among features as well as their effect on the true label. These causal responses induce a non-convex optimization problem, even under standard convex losses. We characterize conditions under which performatively stable solutions exist and can be efficiently computed via simple iterative dynamics. Our analysis reveals that recourse policies that ignore causal structure can induce large, misaligned behavioral responses, whereas causal recourse leads to stable equilibria that reduce incentives for gaming. Experiments on both semi-synthetic and real credit datasets demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms standard empirical risk minimization while reducing the need for repeated model retraining to accommodate distribution shifts caused by strategic agent behavior.

</details>


### [365] [Same Graph Cross-Task Transfer in GNNs: Protocols and Predictors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28525)
*Neelam Akula,Surbhi Kumar,Murat Kantarcioglu,Baris Coskunuzer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Same-graph NC-LP transfer is strongly directional and explainable by graph homophily; NC improves LP on homophilic graphs, while LP helps NC mainly in structure-dominant regimes; introduces CoTask Score and leakage-free evaluation; homophily guides mechanism choice to avoid negative transfer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world graphs support multiple predictive tasks (node classification and link prediction) on the same structure. Existing evaluations use incompatible splits and leakage assumptions, making cross-task transfer conclusions unreliable. A formal framework and leakage-free protocol are needed to study transfer between NC and LP on the same graph.

Method: Formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and propose a leakage-free evaluation protocol: fixed node and edge splits, a shared message-passing graph that excludes evaluated edges, and fixed negatives for LP. Evaluate across three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS) and introduce a CoTask Score (CTS) to quantify joint NC+LP utility when a single encoder serves both tasks.

Result: Transfer is strongly directional and predictable: NC → LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs; LP → NC is fragile and can degrade accuracy with naive representation reuse. LP → NC becomes reliably positive mainly in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is not yet saturated, suggesting LP acts as structural pretraining. CTS summarizes joint utility for shared encoders. Simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, can guide mechanism choice and help avoid negative transfer.

Conclusion: Cross-task transfer between NC and LP on the same graph is predictable and depends on data properties like homophily. A leakage-free protocol is essential for reliable evaluation, and the CoTask Score provides a practical metric for designing shared encoders that serve both tasks.

Abstract: Many real-world graphs support multiple predictive tasks over the same underlying structure, creating an opportunity to reuse supervision across node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP). However, existing evaluations often rely on incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and negative sampling rules, making conclusions about same-graph cross-task transfer unreliable. We formalize same-graph NC-LP transfer and propose a leakage-free protocol that fixes node and edge splits, uses a shared message-passing graph that excludes evaluated edges, and employs fixed negatives for LP. Across three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS), we find that transfer is strongly directional and predictable: NC $\to$ LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP $\to$ NC is fragile and can even degrade accuracy under naive representation reuse. LP $\to$ NC becomes reliably positive mainly in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated, suggesting that LP acts as structural pretraining. Finally, we introduce the CoTask Score (CTS) to summarize joint NC+LP utility when a shared encoder must serve both tasks, and show that simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, can guide mechanism choice and help avoid negative transfer.

</details>


### [366] [APO: Unsupervised Atomic Policy Optimization for 3D Structure Prediction of Atomic Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28553)
*Shentong Mo,Yatao Bian*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Unsupervised alignment for 3D atomic structure prediction via Atomic Policy Optimization (APO) that uses group-relative policy optimization with dual rewards—latent structural mode reinforcement via eigen-decomposition of sample similarities, and thermodynamic stability enforcement—achieving state-of-the-art match rates and efficiency on crystal and antibody benchmarks, surpassing supervised baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Ground-truth structural labels are expensive or unavailable for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins, making supervised alignment impractical in data-scarce regimes. A physics-informed, unsupervised alignment framework is needed.

Method: APO extends group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments, employing two reward signals: (i) an eigen-decomposition-based reward that reinforces dominant latent structural modes derived from sample similarities; (ii) a thermodynamic stability reward to ensure physically plausible configurations. The method enables self-correction by exploring sampled groups and selecting configurations that satisfy physical constraints, with improved inference efficiency via straightened probability paths.

Result: Benchmark results on crystal and antibody structure prediction show APO outperforms fully supervised baselines, achieving new state-of-the-art match rates and structural fidelity. Inference paths are more efficient, and the approach demonstrates that intrinsic physical consistency can guide alignment more effectively than supervised coordinate matching.

Conclusion: Unsupervised, physics-informed alignment can surpass supervised coordinate matching for 3D structural predictions, particularly in data-scarce settings; APO provides a general framework that leverages latent structure and thermodynamic principles to improve both accuracy and efficiency.

Abstract: Predicting the 3D structures of atomic systems is fundamental to advancing material science and drug discovery. While flow-matching models (, FlowDPO) have recently shown promise in this domain, their performance relies heavily on alignment with ground-truth coordinates via supervised preference learning. However, obtaining experimental labels for novel crystal phases or de novo proteins is prohibitively expensive, creating a bottleneck for structural modeling in data-scarce regimes. In this work, we propose (Atomic Policy Optimization), a fully unsupervised alignment framework that eliminates the need for ground-truth reference structures. APO adapts group-relative policy optimization to 3D atomic environments, utilizing a novel dual-reward mechanism: (i) a that reinforces the policy's dominant latent structural modes through eigen-decomposition of sample similarities, and (ii) a that enforces thermodynamic stability. Our framework enables the model to ``self-correct'' by identifying physically plausible configurations within sampled groups. Extensive benchmarks on crystal and antibody structure prediction demonstrate that APO consistently outperforms fully supervised baselines, achieving a new state-of-the-art in match rates and structural fidelity. Furthermore, we show that APO effectively straightens probability paths, significantly improving inference efficiency. Our results suggest that intrinsic physical consistency can serve as a superior guide for alignment compared to noisy, supervised coordinate matching.

</details>


### [367] [$β$-OPSD: Deriving with Policy Optimization, Training with Self-Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28582)
*Jiawei Xu,Minghui Liu,Juzheng Zhang,Tom Goldstein,Furong Huang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Beta-OPSD introduces a β-parameterized on-policy self-distillation that interpolates between a reference policy and a privileged teacher, turning the KL anchor into a tunable regularizer. It converts the RL optimum into distillation targets via logit mixing, improving stability and reasoning with inexpensive training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: OPSD improves reasoning but is brittle; making KL regularization explicit via a tunable β can stabilize optimization and leverage teacher guidance more flexibly.

Method: Derive the optimal policy of β-OPSD as a geometric interpolation between a reference policy and a privileged teacher. Avoid costly RL by turning the RL solution into a distillation target through token-level logit mixing; employ return-to-go for sequence-level credit assignment.

Result: β-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, improving optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance.

Conclusion: Provides a principled link between self-distillation and policy optimization, preserving OPSD efficiency while enabling a controllable trade-off between staying close to a reference policy and following privileged teacher guidance.

Abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a promising approach to improve reasoning language models, but it remains brittle in practice: making it work reliably often requires substantial engineering effort. We identify a structural source of this difficulty: vanilla OPSD is precisely the $β=1$ member of a broader policy-optimization family, where $β$ weights the KL penalty anchoring the student to a reference policy. This equivalence turns $β$ from an implicit value fixed at one into a controllable regularization parameter, yielding a more general formulation that trades off proximity to a reference policy against privileged teacher guidance. We introduce $β$-OPSD and derive its optimal policy as a geometric interpolation between the reference policy and the privileged teacher. Directly optimizing this objective with reinforcement learning, however, would be costly and high-variance. Rather than optimize the RL objective directly, we turn its closed-form solution into a distillation target. Each value of $β$ selects a target along the reference-to-teacher path, which we implement efficiently by mixing their token-level logits. In this way, inexpensive distillation approximates the solution of expensive policy optimization. Return-to-go credit assignment further aligns token updates with the sequence-level objective while retaining the simplicity of OPSD. Experiments on mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that $β$-OPSD consistently outperforms vanilla OPSD, improving optimization stability and downstream reasoning performance.
