Our results provide a principled route from self-distillation to policy optimization and back without sacrificing the efficiency that makes OPSD practical.

</details>


### [368] [KAISEN: Reproducible Subgroup Fairness Auditing for Clinical Risk Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28608)
*Sparsh Roy,Samuel Girmachew,Nishita Chavan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: KAISEN is a five-phase audit framework for clinical risk-model fairness, validated on a synthetic benchmark. It reveals mixed reliability across components: significance tracking varies with floor effects, per-group threshold optimization reduces equalized odds difference (EOD) while group-wise Platt scaling shows high variance; mechanism diagnostics detect controlled cases but fail under proxy misspecification; CUSUM drift detects cohort-driven rather than disease-driven shifts and is seed-sensitive; results are synthetic with known ground truth, and code is released for reproducibility.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Audit pipelines for clinical risk models often produce similar aggregate performance but unequal error rates across subgroups. Existing components lack stress-testing, which undermines trust in their reliability. KAISEN aims to stress-test the audit pipeline itself to identify failure modes and conditions under which audits can be trusted.

Method: KAISEN comprises five phases: (1) subgroup stratification, (2) disparity measurement, (3) mechanism diagnostics, (4) post-hoc mitigation, and (5) drift monitoring. It is evaluated on a synthetic benchmark spanning 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections. Experiments include: significance tracking of axes via EOD gaps, per-group threshold optimization, group-wise Platt scaling for calibration, mechanism diagnostics across controlled vs model-driven cases with proxy misspecification, and CUSUM-based drift detection across seeds and thresholds.

Result: Four main findings: (i) Significance counts track each axis’s gap relative to its own minimum detectable effect; raw EOD correlations: rho=0.56, rising to rho=0.78 when EOD is standardized by the floor. (ii) Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in all 48 held-out runs (paired delta = -0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]); group-wise Platt scaling performs as a coin flip on EOD with 19/48 improvements and mean effect near zero; thus audits should report variance rather than mean effects. (iii) The mechanism diagnostic correctly classifies 144/144 controlled cases but fails to recover any of 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, with no signal of failure. (iv) CUSUM alarms/false alarms track cohort realization far more than disease; at the reference threshold, 27 false alarms and 7 of 8 missed shifts arise from different seeds (chi-squared p=0.002), indicating poor transfer across cohorts. All results are synthetic with known ground truth; clinical validity not established; authors release code, artifacts, and scripts to reproduce every number.

Conclusion: KAISEN reveals that even well-structured audit pipelines exhibit mode-specific failures and high sensitivity to design choices (e.g., calibration method, threshold settings, seed selection). It underscores the need for reporting variance and conducting cross-cohort transfer tests. While the study provides a rigorous synthetic evaluation and transparency for reproducibility, real-world validation is essential before clinical deployment.

Abstract: Clinical risk models routinely achieve strong aggregate performance while producing materially different error rates across patient subgroups. Audit pipelines have been proposed to catch this, but their components are rarely stress-tested, so it is unclear which parts of an audit can be trusted and under what conditions. We present KAISEN, a five-phase audit pipeline covering subgroup stratification, disparity measurement, mechanism diagnostics, post-hoc mitigation, and drift monitoring, evaluated to the point of failure on a synthetic benchmark of 16 disease tasks, 15 social-determinant axes from Healthy People 2030, and three prespecified intersections. Four findings follow. (i) Significance tracks each axis's gap against its own minimum detectable effect: rank correlation between significance count and raw equalized-odds difference (EOD) across the 15 axes is rho = 0.56, rising to rho = 0.78 once EOD is standardized by that floor. (ii) Per-group threshold optimization reduces EOD in 48 of 48 held-out runs (paired delta = -0.285, 95% CI [-0.313, -0.252]), while group-wise Platt scaling -- the better calibrator -- behaves as a coin flip on EOD (19 of 48 runs improved, 95% CI [0.26, 0.55]) with mean effect near zero, so what an audit should report is the variance, not the average. (iii) The mechanism diagnostic classifies 144 of 144 controlled cases correctly but recovers none of 48 model-driven cases under proxy misspecification, with no signal that it failed. (iv) CUSUM failures and false alarms track cohort realization far more than disease: at the reference threshold, all 27 false alarms and 7 of 8 missed shifts come from different seeds (chi-squared p = 0.002), so a threshold tuned on one cohort fails to transfer. All results are synthetic with known ground truth and do not establish clinical validity. Code, artifacts, and scripts reproducing every number are released.

</details>
